{"lessons": ["

In the store: asking and trying on

In Spain, the salesperson (el dependiente, la dependienta) often speaks to you with tú, especially in clothing stores. You can do the same, or use usted in a more traditional shop.

You want to…You sayTranslation
ask for an item¿Tienen esta camisa en la talla 40?Do you have this shirt in a size 40?
another color¿La tenéis en azul?Do you have it in blue?
another size¿Tienes una talla más? / ¿Una talla menos?Do you have one size up? / One size down?
shoesCalzo un 39. ¿Tienen este número?I'm a size 39. Do you have this size?
try something on¿Puedo probármelo?Can I try it on?
the fitting room¿Dónde están los probadores?Where are the fitting rooms?

Talla or número?

English says \"size\" for everything, but Spanish has two words. La talla is a clothing size (la 38, la M); el número is a shoe size. To give your shoe size, use calzar: calzo un 42 (I'm a size 42).

Probarse + pronoun

Probarse (to try on) is reflexive, and you know how to attach pronouns to the infinitive: ¿Puedo probármelo? (the sweater), ¿Puedo probármela? (the jacket), ¿Puedo probármelos? (the shoes). Two pronouns, so a written accent! You can also say ¿Me lo puedo probar?

Probar without a pronoun means \"to taste, to try (food)\": ¿Puedo probar el queso? And in the imperative, the salesperson will tell you: Pruébatelo (try it on).

", "

Me queda bien: the verb quedar

To say a piece of clothing \"fits well\" or \"is too big,\" Spanish uses quedar, which works like gustar: the person is an indirect pronoun, and the verb agrees with the item of clothing.

SpanishTranslation
Esta chaqueta me queda bien.This jacket looks good on me.
La falda me queda corta.The skirt is too short on me.
Estos zapatos me quedan pequeños.These shoes are too small for me.
Los pantalones te quedan largos.The pants are too long on you.
¿Qué tal me queda?How does it look on me?
Te queda genial.It looks great on you.

The adjective agrees with the item of clothing: la falda → corta, los zapatos → pequeños. Note: me queda grande already means \"it's too big for me\"; no need for \"demasiado.\"

Los pantalones is plural in Spanish, just like \"pants\" in English: Estos pantalones me quedan bien. And don't mix it up with quedar = to meet up (¿Quedamos?): the context makes it clear.

Comparing to choose

La azul me queda mejor que la negra.The blue one looks better on me than the black one.
Este jersey es más bonito, pero es carísimo.This sweater is nicer, but it's super expensive.
", "

Este, ese, aquel, then paying and exchanging

English has \"this\" and \"that.\" Spanish has three demonstratives, depending on distance:

Near me (aquí)Near you (ahí)Far from both of us (allí)
masculine singularesteeseaquel
feminine singularestaesaaquella
masculine pluralestosesosaquellos
feminine pluralestasesasaquellas
neuterestoesoaquello

The same forms work as pronouns, with no accent: Me llevo este (I'll take this one). The neuter esto, eso, aquello refers to something you don't name: ¿Qué es esto?

Careful: este ends in -e but estos ends in -os (not \"estes\"); and aquel has no -o in the masculine singular.

Paying, returning, exchanging

SpanishTranslation
¿Cómo va a pagar? / ¿Cómo vas a pagar?How would you like to pay? (usted / tú)
Con tarjeta. / En efectivo.By card. / In cash.
¿Está rebajado?Is it on sale?
Quería devolver esta camisa.I'd like to return this shirt.
¿Tiene el ticket?Do you have the receipt?
¿Me la puede cambiar por otra talla?Can you exchange it for another size?

The big sales (las rebajas) start in Spain in early January and early July: the stores go crazy!

es-u12-l3.title: A2 review: a whole trip
es-u12-l3.topic: big review of the A2 level
es-u12-l3.why: This big review covers the whole A2 level through a complete trip around Andalusia: the three past tenses for telling stories, travel phrases and complaints, pronouns, comparatives, the future, the conditional and the imperative. It closes A2 and takes stock of what the learner has mastered before moving on to B1.
es-u12-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Telling the story of the trip: three past tenses

To tell the story of a trip, you have three past tenses, and each one has its job:

TenseJobExample
perfectopast linked to today (hoy, esta semana, ya, todavía no), like English \"I have done\"Esta mañana he vuelto de Andalucía.
indefinidofinished action, at a finished time (ayer, el lunes, la semana pasada), like English \"I did\"El lunes fuimos a Córdoba.
imperfectobackground, description, habit (hacía, era, había), like \"it was…\" or \"I used to…\"Hacía calor y las calles estaban llenas de flores.
estar in the imperfect + gerundaction in progress, interrupted (\"I was doing\")Estábamos cenando cuando empezó el flamenco.

Here's a short story that mixes all three:

Esta semana he estado en Sevilla. El primer día fuimos a la catedral. Hacía muchísimo calor, pero en los patios había sombra y flores por todas partes. Por la noche, mientras cenábamos, un grupo empezó a tocar flamenco.This week I've been in Seville. On the first day, we went to the cathedral. It was incredibly hot, but in the patios there was shade and there were flowers everywhere. In the evening, while we were having dinner, a group started playing flamenco.

Reminder: in Spain, hoy and esta semana call for the perfecto, even where English might say \"I went this morning\"; ayer and el año pasado call for the indefinido. The imperfect sets the scene: \"it was hot,\" \"it was,\" \"there were.\"

To link the steps: primero, luego, después, de repente, al día siguiente, al final. And to react to a friend's story: ¡No me digas!, ¿Y qué pasó?, ¡Qué envidia!

SituationSentenceTranslation
at the stationUn billete de ida y vuelta para Sevilla, por favor.A round-trip ticket to Seville, please.

at the hotelTengo una reserva a nombre de Martín.I have a reservation under the name Martín.
a problemEl aire acondicionado no funciona. ¿Podría cambiarme la habitación?The air conditioning doesn't work. Could you give me a different room?
at the restaurant¿Qué me recomienda?What do you recommend?
directionsPerdone, ¿para ir a la catedral? —Siga todo recto y gire a la derecha.Excuse me, how do I get to the cathedral? — Go straight ahead and turn right.
in a store¿Puedo probármelo? Me queda un poco grande.Can I try it on? It's a little big on me.
comparingCórdoba es más tranquila que Sevilla.Córdoba is quieter than Seville.

Pronouns, everywhere

As soon as you've already named something, replace it: ¿Las entradas? Ya las he comprado. / ¿La llave? Se la he dado a la recepcionista. / ¿Me lo puede envolver? Es un regalo.

With usted (hotel, station, restaurant), the verb is in the 3rd person, the imperative takes its special form (siga, gire, perdone) and the indirect pronoun is le: ¿Le puedo hacer una pregunta?

", "

What's next? Plans, advice, invitations

To express…SentenceTranslation
a decided planEste verano voy a volver a Cádiz.This summer, I'm going to go back to Cádiz.
a distant plan, a promiseAlgún día viviré en Granada.Someday, I'll live in Granada.
a guessAhora habrá menos turistas.There must be fewer tourists right now.
a wishMe encantaría ver la Feria de Sevilla.I'd love to see the Seville Fair.
adviceYo que tú, iría en primavera.If I were you, I'd go in the spring.
an invitation¿Te apetece venir conmigo?Do you feel like coming with me?

Your A2 review

Congratulations: with this lesson, you've completed the A2 level. You can now:

  • tell stories in the past, choosing between perfecto, indefinido and imperfecto;
  • get by while traveling: tickets, hotel, restaurant, directions, complaints;
  • give instructions in the imperative, with tú and with usted;
  • replace nouns with pronouns, even double ones (se lo, dámelo);
  • talk about the future, be polite, give advice and invite people;
  • compare things and go shopping.

Next step, B1: the working world, relative pronouns, por and para, and a big newcomer, the subjunctive.

es-u13-l1.title: Introducing yourself at work
es-u13-l1.why: First lesson of the B1 level: the learner moves from everyday life to the working world and learns to present their job, their tasks and their career path. It sets up llevar + length of time and desde hace, and reuses the three past tenses from A2 in a work story.

{"lessons": ["

Saying what you do: me dedico a…

At work, the first question people ask you is ¿A qué te dedicas? (what do you do for a living?) or, formally, ¿A qué se dedica? There are several ways to answer, depending on what you want to highlight: your job, your field or your company.

SpanishEnglishNote
Soy enfermera.I'm a nurse.No article, unlike English \"a nurse.\"
Trabajo como profesor.I work as a teacher.como + job, no article.
Me dedico a la informática.I work in IT.dedicarse a + field.
Me dedico a vender pisos.I sell apartments for a living.dedicarse a + infinitive.
Trabajo en un banco.I work at a bank.en + place or company.
Soy responsable de ventas.I'm head of sales.responsable de, same form for a woman.

This is a classic mistake for English speakers: don't say \"soy un ingeniero\" for \"I'm an engineer.\" With ser and trabajar como, the job comes with no article: Soy ingeniera, Trabajo como camarero. In everyday speech in Spain, you'll also hear trabajo de camarero.

What you're in charge of

To describe your tasks, two very useful phrases: Me encargo de… (I'm in charge of…, I handle…) and Mis funciones son… (my duties are…). Encargarse de is reflexive, like levantarse: me encargo, te encargas, se encarga, nos encargamos, os encargáis, se encargan. It's followed by a noun or an infinitive.

Me encargo de los clientes nuevos y de los presupuestos.I handle new clients and quotes.
Carmen es la jefa del equipo: se encarga de organizar el trabajo.Carmen is the team leader: she's in charge of organizing the work.
", "

How long? Llevar + length of time

To say how long you've been somewhere, Spanish has a very common construction that doesn't exist in English: llevar + length of time + place. Word for word, \"I carry three years in the company.\"

Llevo tres años en la empresa.I've been at the company for three years.

Notice the tense: English uses \"I have been,\" but Spanish uses the present. Llevar is a regular -ar verb:

PersonllevarExample
yollevoLlevo dos meses en Madrid.
túllevas¿Cuánto tiempo llevas aquí?
él, ella, ustedllevaMarta lleva un año en el equipo.
nosotros, nosotrasllevamosLlevamos una semana en la oficina nueva.
vosotros, vosotraslleváis¿Lleváis mucho tiempo en Valencia?
ellos, ellas, ustedesllevanLlevan cinco años en el sector.

With desde and desde hace

You can also use the main verb in the present followed by desde or desde hace. Good news: it works exactly like English \"for\" and \"since.\"

  • desde hace + length of time = for + length of time: Trabajo aquí desde hace tres años. (I've been working here for three years.)
  • desde + date or moment = since + date: Trabajo aquí desde 2023, desde enero, desde el verano.

Don't mix them up: desde hace tres años (a length of time), but desde 2023 (a starting point); \"desde hace 2023\" doesn't exist. And remember: present tense, not \"he trabajado.\" To ask the question: ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas en la empresa? or ¿Desde cuándo trabajas aquí?

", "

Telling your career story

To present your career path, you reuse the three past tenses you already know. Each has its job, and the time marker helps you choose:

TenseUseExample
imperfectoa past situation, with no clear start or end (\"I used to…\")Antes trabajaba en un hotel. Vivía en Sevilla.
indefinidoa finished, dated stepEstudié Derecho en Salamanca. En 2019 entré en la empresa. Hace dos años cambié de puesto.
perfectosomething still connected to the present (hoy, este año, ya)Este año he empezado a teletrabajar.

Company vocabulary

La empresa (the company), el puesto (the position), el equipo (the team), el jefe / la jefa (the boss), el compañero / la compañera (the coworker), la oficina (the office). In Spain, un contrato indefinido is a permanent contract and un contrato temporal is a fixed-term contract. Teletrabajar (to work remotely) is a regular verb: teletrabajo dos días a la semana.

False friend: la carrera first of all means a university degree (terminé la carrera en 2018 = I finished my degree in 2018). For a \"career,\" be specific: la carrera profesional.

Me llamo Pablo. Soy ingeniero y trabajo como jefe de proyecto en una empresa de energía. Antes trabajaba en Bilbao, pero hace dos años me mudé a Madrid. Llevo un año en este puesto y me encargo de un equipo de seis personas.My name is Pablo. I'm an engineer and I work as a project manager at an energy company. I used to work in Bilbao, but two years ago I moved to Madrid. I've been in this position for a year and I'm in charge of a team of six people.

es-u13-l2.title: Writing an email
es-u13-l2.why: After learning to introduce themselves at work, the learner writes their first professional emails: opening, closing, attaching a file, following up and apologizing. The lesson also shows when to use tú or usted, a question on which Spain is far more relaxed than many learners expect.

{"lessons": ["

Opening and closing an email

Good news: Spanish business emails are short and direct, much like in English. No long, flowery formulas: two words are enough to sign off.

The greeting

RegisterTo startTo end
formal (first contact, government offices)Estimado señor Vidal: / Estimada señora Ruiz:Saludos cordiales / Atentamente
neutral (the most common)Hola, Lucía: / Buenos días:Un saludo / Saludos
close coworkerHola, Pablo: / ¡Hola, Pablo!Un abrazo

After the greeting, Spanish uses a colon, not the comma common in English emails: Estimada señora Ruiz:, then a new line starting with a capital letter. Estimado agrees: estimado for a man, estimada for a woman, estimados for a group.

Tú or usted?

English just has \"you,\" but in Spanish you have to choose. In the Spanish workplace, people switch to tú very quickly, a bit like going by first names: between coworkers it's almost always tú, and often with regular clients too. Keep usted for a formal first contact, government offices or an older person. If the other person writes back using tú, follow their lead.

With túWith usted
Te escribo para…Le escribo para…
Te envío el informe.Le envío el informe.
Quedo a la espera de tu respuesta.Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.
¿Podrías llamarme?¿Podría llamarme?
", "

The body of the email: useful phrases

A good Spanish email has three parts: why you're writing, what you're sending or asking for, and what you expect. Here are the phrases that come up again and again.

To…SpanishEnglish
say why you're writingLe escribo para confirmar la reunión.I'm writing to confirm the meeting.
refer to an earlier exchangeLe escribo en relación con su consulta.I'm writing regarding your inquiry.
attach a fileAdjunto le envío el presupuesto. / Te adjunto la factura.Please find the quote attached. / I'm attaching the invoice.
ask politely¿Podría enviarme el contrato?Could you send me the contract?
offer your helpPara cualquier duda, estoy a su disposición.Please don't hesitate to contact me with any questions.
thank in advanceGracias de antemano.Thanks in advance.
ask for a replyQuedo a la espera de su respuesta.I look forward to your reply.

In Adjunto le envío…, adjunto means \"attached.\" You can also use the verb adjuntar (to attach), which is regular: Te adjunto el archivo.

An email is el correo or el correo electrónico (you'll also hear el email). The subject line is el asunto, never \"el sujeto.\" And an attachment is el archivo adjunto.

Asunto: Presupuesto para la feria de MálagaSubject: Quote for the Málaga trade fair
", "

Following up, asking, apologizing

Following up without being curt

To follow up with someone, Spanish stays direct but friendly. The perfect tense (perfecto) is ideal for asking whether something has been done yet:

¿Has podido ver mi correo del lunes?Have you had a chance to look at my email from Monday?
Te recuerdo que el plazo termina el viernes.Just a reminder that the deadline is Friday.

Recordar has a stem change like poder: recuerdo, recuerdas, recuerda, recordamos, recordáis, recuerdan.

Apologizing for a late reply

You reuse the polite imperatives you already know: perdona (tú) and disculpe (usted).

  • Perdona el retraso en contestar. (Sorry for the late reply.)
  • Disculpe la demora. (Please excuse the delay.) La demora is more formal than el retraso.
  • Lo siento, esta semana he estado muy liado. (Sorry, I've been swamped this week.) Liado / liada is informal but very common between coworkers.

I'm attaching the March report. Could you send me the invoice before Friday? Thanks in advance. Best, Sergio

False friend: contestar means \"to answer, to reply,\" not \"to contest.\" Contestar un correo = to reply to an email; you can also say responder.

es-u13-l3.title: On the phone and on video calls
es-u13-l3.why: After writing comes speaking: the learner learns to answer the phone, ask to be put through, leave a message and handle the little problems of a video call. They discover oír and venir bien for setting up a meeting, which prepares the next lesson on meetings.

{"lessons": ["

Answering, introducing yourself, putting someone through

In Spain, people don't answer the phone with \"Hello?\" but with ¿Diga?, ¿Dígame? or just ¿Sí? At a company, you give the company name: Gráficas Norte, buenos días.

To introduce yourself on the phone, Spanish says \"I am Pablo,\" not \"this is Pablo\" or \"it's Pablo\": Hola, soy Pablo Ruiz, de Transportes Ibarra. In Latin America, people answer with ¿Aló?, and in Mexico with ¿Bueno?

You callThey answer
¿Podría hablar con Carmen Ruiz, por favor?
(Could I speak to Carmen Ruiz, please?)		¿De parte de quién?
(Who's calling?)
¿Está Javier?
(Is Javier there?)		Un momento, ahora le paso.
(One moment, I'll put you through.)
Quería hablar con el departamento de ventas.Le paso con ventas.
(I'll put you through to sales.)
¿Me pone con la extensión 214?Lo siento, está comunicando.
(Sorry, the line is busy.)
¿Puedo hablar con la directora?No está en este momento. / Está reunida.
(She's not here right now. / She's in a meeting.)

Pasar con + person = to put someone through on the phone: Te paso con mi jefa. And estar comunicando = to be busy (a phone line), a fixed expression to learn as is.

", "

On a video call: when it cuts out

For sound problems, you need the verb oír (to hear), which is irregular. Watch out for its written accent and the y that appears between two vowels.

PersonoírExample
yooigoNo te oigo bien.
túoyes¿Me oyes?
él, ella, ustedoye¿Me oye, señora Gil?
nosotros, nosotrasoímosAhora te oímos perfectamente.
vosotros, vosotrasoís¿Me oís todos?
ellos, ellas, ustedesoyenNo nos oyen.

Video call phrases

  • No se oye bien. (The sound isn't good.) Se ha cortado. (It cut out.): two set expressions with se; you'll understand how they're built in an upcoming lesson.
  • Tienes el micro apagado. (You're on mute.) Enciende la cámara. (Turn on your camera.)
  • Comparte la pantalla, por favor. (Share your screen, please.)
  • ¿Puedes repetir, por favor? ¿Puedes hablar un poco más alto? ¿Más despacio?
  • Te mando el enlace. (I'll send you the link.) Ahora sí te oigo. (Now I can hear you.)

Oír is \"to hear\" (the sound reaches you) and escuchar is \"to listen\" (paying attention), just like in English. To check the connection, the typical question in Spain is ¿Me oyes? (can you hear me?). You'll also hear ¿Me escuchas?, especially in Latin America.

", "

Setting up a meeting, leaving a message

Finding a time slot

To ask whether a date works, Spanish uses venir bien, which works like gustar: me viene bien, ¿te viene bien?, ¿le viene bien?

—¿Te viene bien el martes a las diez? —El martes me viene fatal. ¿Qué tal el jueves?— Does Tuesday at ten work for you? — Tuesday is really bad for me. How about Thursday?
Vale, quedamos el jueves a las diez. Te mando una invitación con el enlace.Okay, Thursday at ten, then. I'll send you an invite with the link.

Leaving a message

On voicemail or with a coworker, a message has four parts: who you are, why you're calling, your number, and what happens next.

Hola, soy Diego Martín, de Logística Norte. Le llamo en relación con el pedido de la semana pasada. Mi número es el 612 34 56 78. Le llamo otra vez mañana. Gracias.Hello, this is Diego Martín, from Logística Norte. I'm calling regarding last week's order. My number is 612 34 56 78. I'll call you again tomorrow. Thank you.

If you're taking the message: ¿Quiere dejarle un mensaje? (Would you like to leave a message?), ¿Le puede decir que he llamado? (Could you tell her I called?). To call someone back is devolver la llamada: Carmen le devuelve la llamada esta tarde.

Phone numbers are often read digit by digit or in groups: seis, uno, dos, treinta y cuatro, cincuenta y seis, setenta y ocho. To hang up is colgar (o → ue): Ahora cuelgo.

es-u13-l4.title: In a meeting
es-u13-l4.topic: taking the floor, making proposals, wrapping up
es-u13-l4.why: Last step of the work unit: the learner takes part in a meeting, takes the floor, makes proposals, agrees or disagrees, then wraps up. The lesson reuses the conditional and the connectors already seen, and locks in estar de acuerdo, tener razón and proponer + infinitive before the subjunctive arrives.
es-u13-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Opening the meeting and taking the floor

A meeting in Spanish follows the same pattern as in English: you open it, discuss the items on the agenda (el orden del día), make decisions and wrap up. To open:

  • Bueno, ¿empezamos? (Okay, shall we start?)
  • El objetivo de la reunión es… (The goal of the meeting is…)
  • Hoy vamos a hablar de tres puntos. (Today we're going to discuss three items.)

Taking the floor politely

SpanishEnglish
Si me permitís, …If I may, …
Perdona, ¿puedo decir una cosa?Sorry, can I say something?
Quería añadir que…I wanted to add that…
Me gustaría comentar algo.I'd like to comment on something.
Una pregunta: …A question: …

Quería (imperfect) and me gustaría (conditional) soften the request, exactly like \"I wanted to…\" and \"I'd like to…\" in English.

Vosotros around the table

English has just one \"you,\" but in Spain, when you speak to several coworkers, you use vosotros (a bit like \"you all\" or \"you guys\"), even in a meeting: ¿Qué os parece? (What do you all think?), ¿Estáis de acuerdo?, ¿Tenéis alguna pregunta?, Si me permitís… People keep ustedes for very formal settings, and in Latin America it's the only plural form.

Learn to spot the vosotros endings: tenéis, estáis, podéis, permitís, and the pronoun os: ¿Qué os parece?

", "

Proposing, agreeing, disagreeing

Proponer + noun or infinitive

Proponer (to propose, to suggest) is conjugated like poner:

Personproponer
yopropongo
túpropones
él, ella, ustedpropone
nosotros, nosotrasproponemos
vosotros, vosotrasproponéis
ellos, ellas, ustedesproponen

For now, follow it with a noun or an infinitive: Propongo una pausa. Propongo cambiar la fecha. The construction propongo que… + conjugated verb (\"I suggest that we…\") requires the subjunctive, a special verb form you'll learn soon.

Other ways to make a suggestion, which you already know: Podríamos… (We could…), Deberíamos… (We should…), ¿Y si…?, ¿Por qué no…?

Agreeing or not

To agreeTo disagree
Estoy de acuerdo (contigo, con Marta).No estoy de acuerdo.
Tienes razón.Yo no lo veo así.
Me parece bien. / Me parece buena idea.No sé, yo creo que es demasiado caro.
¡Exacto!Tienes razón en parte, pero…

The big trap: \"I agree\" is not a verb in Spanish but estar + de acuerdo, never with ser: Estoy de acuerdo. And \"to be right\" is tener razón (word for word \"to have reason\"), with no article: Tienes razón.

", "

Wrapping up and dividing the work

To close a discussion, you sum up, check there are no more questions and assign the tasks.

SpanishEnglish
En resumen, …To sum up, …
Entonces, quedamos en enviar el informe el lunes.So, we've agreed to send the report on Monday.
Laura se encarga de llamar al cliente.Laura will take care of calling the client.
¿Alguna pregunta? ¿Alguna duda?Any questions?
Si no hay más preguntas, terminamos aquí.If there are no more questions, let's wrap up here.
Para terminar, gracias a todos por venir.Finally, thank you all for coming.

Quedar en + infinitive means \"to agree to\": Hemos quedado en vernos el lunes. Don't confuse it with quedar on its own (to meet up) or with quedarse (to stay).

After the meeting, someone writes up el acta (the minutes). It's a feminine noun, but it takes el in the singular because it starts with a stressed a, like el agua: el acta, las actas.

En resumen: este año vamos a la feria con un espacio más pequeño y Lucía se encarga de la reserva. ¿Alguna pregunta?To sum up: this year we're going to the trade fair with a smaller space, and Lucía will take care of the booking. Any questions?

The connectors you already know give structure to what you say: primero, además, entonces, al final. With en resumen and para terminar, you'll instantly sound more professional.

es-u14-l1.title: Relative pronouns: que, quien, donde, lo que
es-u14-l1.why: To build richer sentences, the learner links two ideas with que, quien, donde, el que and lo que, compared with English who, which, that, whose and where. This lesson opens the unit on complex sentences and is useful everywhere afterward: describing, specifying, arguing.
es-u14-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Que: “who,” “which” and “that” all at once

In English, you choose between “who” (people), “which” (things) and “that.” In Spanish, it's simpler: one word, que, does it all. It works for people and things, as subject or object.

EnglishSpanish
The girl who works with me is from Toledo.La chica que trabaja conmigo es de Toledo.
The book (that) I'm reading is very good.El libro que leo es muy bueno.
The neighbors who live across the street are lovely.Los vecinos que viven enfrente son encantadores.
The apartment (that) we rent has two bedrooms.El piso que alquilamos tiene dos habitaciones.

Two traps for English speakers. First, translating “who” as quien: right after a noun, with no preposition, it's always que: la mujer que vive arriba, never “la mujer quien vive arriba.” Second, dropping the relative: English can say “the book I'm reading,” but Spanish can never leave the relative out.

The relative que has no accent: the accent is only for questions and exclamations (¿Qué haces?, ¡Qué bonito!).

El que, la que, los que: the one who, the one that

When the noun isn't repeated, you put the article before que. The article agrees with what it replaces:

Mi coche no es este, es el que está al lado.My car isn't this one, it's the one next to it.
Mi hermana es la que lleva gafas.My sister is the one wearing glasses.
Los que viven aquí conocen bien el barrio.Those who live here know the neighborhood well.
", "

After a preposition: con quien, en el que, donde

When the relative follows a preposition (with whom, in which, for which…), the preposition always comes first. English often puts it at the end (“the friend I traveled with”), but Spanish never does.

For…SpanishEnglish
a personla amiga con quien viajé / con la que viajéthe friend I traveled with
peoplelos vecinos con quienes hablo / con los que hablothe neighbors I talk to
a thingla empresa en la que trabajothe company I work for (in which I work)
a placeel barrio donde vivo / en el que vivothe neighborhood where I live

Quien (plural quienes) is only used for people, and here after a preposition. For things, use el que, la que, los que, las que, agreeing with the noun. For a place, donde means “where,” with no accent since it isn't a question.

“About which,” “that I told you about”

When English ends with “about” or “of,” Spanish usually uses de + el que / la que / quien, placed at the front:

Es el compañero del que te hablé.He's the coworker I told you about.
Es la película de la que todo el mundo habla.It's the movie everyone is talking about.

To recognize: cuyo, cuya, cuyos, cuyas means “whose.” Unlike English “whose,” it agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: una amiga cuyo padre es médico (a friend whose father is a doctor), un pueblo cuyas calles son estrechas. It's mostly written; in speech, people prefer other phrasings.

", "

Lo que: “what” (= the thing that)

When “what” or “the thing that” doesn't refer to a specific noun but to an idea, Spanish says lo que. Lo here is a neuter article.

EnglishSpanish
What I want is to rest.Lo que quiero es descansar.
What I like most about Madrid is the atmosphere.Lo que más me gusta de Madrid es el ambiente.
I don't like what you've done.No me gusta lo que has hecho.
Everything you need is in the drawer.Todo lo que necesitas está en el cajón.

Careful: in these sentences, English “what” is not the question word qué (with an accent) but “the thing that”: Lo que quiero es descansar. And todo lo que = everything that, all that.

Don't mix up lo que and el que: el que replaces a masculine noun (mi coche es el que está ahí), lo que an idea (lo que dices es verdad).

Summary

EnglishSpanish
who / which / that (after a noun)que
with whom, to whom, for whomcon quien, a quien, para quien (or con el que…)
which (after a preposition)el que, la que, los que, las que
wheredonde, en el que
about which / whosedel que, de la que, de quien ; cuyo (possession)
what (= the thing that)lo que
the one who, the one thatel que, la que

es-u14-l2.title: Impersonal and passive se
es-u14-l2.why: Where English uses a generic “you,” “people,” “they” or a passive (“Spanish is spoken here”), Spanish uses se + verb: this lesson shows how, with plural agreement in ads (se venden pisos), plus uno and la gente. It also explains expressions you've already met (no se oye, se ha cortado) and lets you describe customs and rules.

{"lessons": ["

Se + verb: Spanish's generic “you”

To talk about people in general, English says “you,” “people,” “they” or “one,” or uses a passive. Spanish's favorite tool is se + verb in the 3rd person.

EnglishSpanish
In Spain, people have dinner late.En España se cena tarde.
You eat well here.Aquí se come bien.
How do you say “window” in Spanish?¿Cómo se dice «window» en español?
They say this restaurant is very good.Se dice que este restaurante es muy bueno.
Life is good in this village.En este pueblo se vive bien.

You already know two expressions of this kind from phone calls: No se oye bien (I can't hear well) and Se ha cortado (it got cut off). The se works in every tense: Antes se trabajaba los sábados (people used to work on Saturdays).

Other ways to say it

  • La gente + singular verb: La gente cena tarde. Careful: la gente is singular in Spanish, unlike English “people”: la gente es, never “la gente son.”
  • The 3rd person plural, with no subject, when you don't know who: Dicen que va a llover. (They say it's going to rain.)
  • Uno (or una) + 3rd person, like English “one,” required when the verb is already reflexive, since “se se” is impossible: En verano uno se acuesta tarde.

Avoid using nosotros for people in general: Aquí se habla español (Spanish is spoken here), not “aquí hablamos español,” which means “we (specifically us) speak Spanish here.”

", "

Se venden pisos: plural agreement

When the verb has an object (what's being sold, what's wanted…), it agrees with that noun: singular if the noun is singular, plural if it's plural. It works like an English passive (“apartments are sold”). This is the rule for ads and signs.

SingularPlural
Se vende piso.
(Apartment for sale.)		Se venden pisos.
(Apartments for sale.)
Se alquila habitación.
(Room for rent.)		Se alquilan habitaciones.
(Rooms for rent.)
Se busca camarero.
(Waiter wanted.)		Se necesitan camareros.
(Waiters wanted.)
Se habla inglés.
(English spoken.)		Se hablan varios idiomas.
(Several languages spoken.)

The trap: writing “se vende pisos.” Look at the noun that follows: pisos is plural, so se venden. With a verb that has no object (se vive bien, se cena tarde), the verb stays singular.

Rules: se puede, no se puede

To say what's allowed or forbidden, use se puede + infinitive:

Aquí no se puede fumar.You can't smoke here.
¿Se puede pagar con tarjeta?Can I pay by card?
En esta calle no se puede aparcar.You can't park on this street.

On signs, you'll also see Prohibido fumar (no smoking) and the set phrase Se ruega silencio (silence, please).

Customs in Spain

Impersonal se is perfect for talking about a country's customs. Here are a few that everyone will describe to you this way:

SpanishEnglish
Se come entre las dos y las tres y se cena hacia las diez.People have lunch between two and three and dinner around ten.
Para saludar, se dan dos besos.To say hello, people give two kisses on the cheek.
En Navidad se come turrón.At Christmas, people eat turrón (nougat).
Después de comer, se hace la sobremesa.After a meal, people stay at the table to chat.
En los bares se deja poca propina.In bars, people leave a small tip.
En Granada, con cada bebida se pone una tapa.In Granada, they serve a tapa with every drink.

Notice the agreement: se dan dos besos (plural, because of besos), but se come turrón (singular).

In the past

To compare with the old days, the imperfect is ideal, like English “used to”: Antes se trabajaba los sábados por la mañana. En mi pueblo se vivía de la agricultura. Antes no se usaba tanto el móvil.

La sobremesa has no equivalent in English: it's the time, often long, when people stay at the table after a meal to chat. And on Sundays, se come en familia.

es-u14-l3.title: Por or para?
es-u14-l3.why: You've known para since the basics; this lesson introduces por and puts the two prepositions side by side, because English often has just one word, “for.” Purpose, destination, deadline and opinion on one side; cause, means, route, exchange and times of day on the other: the lesson wraps up the unit on richer sentences before the subjunctive.

{"lessons": ["

Para: toward a goal, toward a destination

English often uses one word, “for,” where Spanish has two. Good news: you already know para (purpose and recipient). Remember its core idea: para looks forward, toward a goal, a destination, a deadline.

UseSpanishEnglish
purpose (+ infinitive)Estudio español para trabajar en Madrid.I'm studying Spanish (in order) to work in Madrid.
recipientEste regalo es para ti.This present is for you.
destinationMañana salgo para Sevilla. / el tren para ValenciaTomorrow I'm leaving for Seville. / the train to Valencia
deadlineEl informe es para el viernes.The report is due Friday.
opinionPara mí, es demasiado caro.For me (in my opinion), it's too expensive.
usefulness¿Para qué sirve esto?What's this for?
employerTrabajo para una empresa alemana.I work for a German company.

A simple test: if you can replace “for” or “to” with “in order to,” “headed for,” “by (a certain date)” or “in my opinion,” it's para. So “to” + verb meaning “in order to” is always para, never a.

Necesito el coche para ir al trabajo.I need the car to get to work.
Hago una tarta para el cumpleaños de Lucía.I'm making a cake for Lucía's birthday.
", "

Por: cause, route, means

Por looks back or through the middle: what causes the action, the route you take, the means you use, what you give in exchange.

UseSpanishEnglish
cause, reasonGracias por tu ayuda. / Cerrado por vacaciones.Thanks for your help. / Closed for vacation.
because ofLlegamos tarde por la lluvia.We arrived late because of the rain.
meansTe llamo por teléfono. / Te lo mando por correo.I'll call you on the phone. / I'll send it to you by email.
route, place you go throughEl autobús pasa por Córdoba. / Damos un paseo por el centro.The bus goes through Córdoba. / We take a walk around downtown.
exchange, priceCompré la bici por cien euros. / Cambio mi turno por el tuyo.I bought the bike for a hundred euros. / I'll swap my shift for yours.
time of daypor la mañana, por la tarde, por la nochein the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening / at night
frequencydos veces por semanatwice a week
instead of, for (someone's sake)Hoy trabajo yo por ti.Today I'll work for you (in your place).

Set expressions with por

por favor (please), por eso (that's why), por fin (finally), por ejemplo (for example), por supuesto (of course), por aquí (this way, around here), por qué / porque (why / because).

“Thanks for” is always gracias por: gracias por todo, gracias por venir. And “in the morning” is por la mañana (not “en”): mañana por la mañana = tomorrow morning.

", "

Traps for English speakers

Some sentences completely change meaning depending on the preposition, even when English says “for” in both. Compare:

With paraWith por
Lo hago para ti.
(I'm doing it for you: it's a gift for you.)		Lo hago por ti.
(I'm doing it for you: in your place, or because I care about you.)
Trabajo para una empresa.
(It's my employer.)		Trabajo por la mañana.
(That's when I work.)
Salgo para Madrid.
(Madrid is my destination.)		Paso por Madrid.
(I'm going through Madrid.)
El informe es para mañana.
(It's due tomorrow.)		Te llamo mañana por la mañana.
(Tomorrow morning.)
¿Para qué estudias español?
(What for? For what purpose?)		¿Por qué estudias español?
(Why? For what reason?)

When in doubt, ask yourself: am I looking toward the goal or destination (para)? Or toward the cause, the means, the route, the exchange (por)?

Price: no preposition, or por

To say what something costs, you don't need a preposition: La bici cuesta cien euros. To say how much you paid for it, use por: La compré por cien euros. “For a hundred euros” is never para.

Por fin he terminado el informe para el cliente. Se lo mando por correo esta tarde.I've finally finished the report for the client. I'll email it to him this afternoon.

es-u15-l1.title: The present subjunctive
es-u15-l1.topic: forming the subjunctive and its triggers
es-u15-l1.why: Here comes the subjunctive, the big project of level B1: the learner learns to form it (swapped vowel, stem from the yo form, six irregulars) and to use it after querer que, esperar que, ojalá, es importante que and para que. The lesson leads straight into choosing between subjunctive and indicative and expressing opinions.
es-u15-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Forming the subjunctive: swap the vowel

English barely has a subjunctive anymore (you'll find traces in “if I were you” or “I suggest that he be on time”), but Spanish uses it all the time. Think of it as a special verb form for things that are wished, needed or not yet real. Luckily, it's very regular: start from the yo form of the present, drop the -o, and use the vowel “of the other group”:

  • -ar verbs → endings in -e: habl-o → hable
  • -er and -ir verbs → endings in -a: com-o → coma, viv-o → viva
Personhablarcomervivir
(que) yohablecomaviva
(que) túhablescomasvivas
(que) él, ella, ustedhablecomaviva
(que) nosotros, nosotrashablemoscomamosvivamos
(que) vosotros, vosotrashabléiscomáisviváis
(que) ellos, ellas, ustedeshablencomanvivan

You've already seen these forms! The usted commands (hable, coma, siga) and the phrases perdone, disculpe are subjunctives. Note that the 1st and 3rd person singular are identical: que yo hable, que ella hable.

A few spelling changes

To keep the same sound, some verbs change a letter: llegar → llegue, buscar → busque, empezar → empiece, coger → coja.

", "

Irregular verbs

The stem of the yo form

Since you start from the yo form of the present, every verb that's irregular in the 1st person keeps that irregularity in all persons of the subjunctive:

Infinitiveyo (present)Subjunctive
tenertengotenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan
hacerhagohaga, hagas, haga…
decirdigodiga, digas, diga…
salirsalgosalga, salgas, salga…
ponerpongoponga, pongas, ponga…
venirvengovenga, vengas, venga…
conocerconozcoconozca, conozcas, conozca…
oíroigooiga, oigas, oiga…

Stem-changing verbs keep their “boot” pattern, as in the present: pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos, podáis, puedan; quiera… queramos; entienda… entendamos (but dormir gives durmamos, durmáis). Verbs with e → i change everywhere: pida, pidas, pida, pidamos, pidáis, pidan.

The six truly irregular verbs

Personserirestarhabersaberdar
yoseavayaestéhayasepadé
túseasvayasestéshayassepasdes
él, ella, ustedseavayaestéhayasepadé
nosotrosseamosvayamosestemoshayamossepamosdemos
vosotrosseáisvayáisestéishayáissepáisdeis
ellos, ellas, ustedesseanvayanesténhayansepanden

Accents matter: esté, estés, estén; and dé (from dar) takes an accent so it isn't confused with the preposition de. Haya is the subjunctive of hay: Ojalá haya sitio. (I hope there's room.)

", "

When to use it: wishes and advice

The subjunctive appears after certain “triggers” followed by que. In this lesson: wanting, hoping, necessity and purpose.

TriggerExampleEnglish
querer queQuiero que vengas a la cena.I want you to come to the dinner.
esperar queEspero que estés bien.I hope you're well.
ojalá (que)¡Ojalá haga sol mañana!I really hope it's sunny tomorrow!
es importante queEs importante que descanses.It's important that you rest.
es mejor que, es necesario queEs mejor que vayamos en tren.It's better if we go by train.
para queTe lo explico para que lo entiendas.I'm explaining it so (that) you understand.

The big trap: English says “I want you to come” with an infinitive, but Spanish can't: it needs que + subjunctive. And “I hope you're well” uses a normal verb in English, but esperar que always takes the subjunctive in Spanish: Espero que estés bien, never “espero que estás bien.”

Only one subject? Use the infinitive

If the subject is the same in both parts of the sentence, keep the infinitive: Quiero ir (I want to go) but Quiero que vayas (I want you to go). Likewise, para + infinitive (same subject) / para que + subjunctive (different subjects).

Everyday wishes

Que + subjunctive on its own expresses a wish, a bit like English “May you…”. You'll hear these phrases everywhere in Spain: ¡Que aproveche! (Enjoy your meal!), ¡Que te mejores! (Get well soon!), ¡Que tengas buen día!, ¡Que lo paséis bien! (Have fun, all of you!), ¡Que tengas suerte!

es-u15-l2.title: Subjunctive or indicative?
es-u15-l2.why: Once the subjunctive is formed, the learner learns to choose between the two moods: an opinion stated or denied, feelings, and cuando for habits or for the future. English uses the same verb form in all these cases, so this is where English speakers slip most (especially cuando + future), hence a lesson packed with choice exercises before the debate in the next lesson.
es-u15-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

To believe or not to believe

When you state something you consider true, you use the indicative (the normal verb forms). When you deny it or doubt it, Spanish switches to the subjunctive. English doesn't change the verb at all (“I think he's right” / “I don't think he's right”), so you have to train yourself to spot the switch.

Stating → indicativeDenying, doubting → subjunctive
Creo que tiene razón.No creo que tenga razón.
Pienso que es una buena idea.No pienso que sea una buena idea.
Me parece que va a llover.No me parece que vaya a llover.
Es verdad que Madrid es cara.No es verdad que Madrid sea tan cara.
Estoy seguro de que viene.No estoy seguro de que venga.

Other expressions followed by the indicative: está claro que, es evidente que, es cierto que, sé que. In the negative, they switch to the subjunctive: no está claro que, no es cierto que.

The reflex to build: look for the no before the opinion verb. Creo que → indicative; no creo que → subjunctive. With the indicative, you can use any tense: Creo que vendrá, Creo que vino ayer.

", "

Feelings: always the subjunctive

When you express a feeling or reaction (joy, annoyance, regret) to what someone else does, Spanish uses the subjunctive, even if the fact is completely real. English just says “I'm glad you're here” with a normal verb, so watch out.

ExpressionExampleEnglish
me alegro de queMe alegro de que estés aquí.I'm glad you're here.
me molesta queMe molesta que los vecinos hagan ruido.It bothers me that the neighbors make noise.
me preocupa queMe preocupa que Pablo trabaje tanto.It worries me that Pablo works so much.
me encanta queMe encanta que vengáis a vernos.I love it when you all come to see us.
es una pena queEs una pena que no puedas venir.It's a shame you can't come.
¡qué pena que…!¡Qué pena que te vayas!What a shame you're leaving!

Don't forget the de: me alegro de que (alegrarse de). And if the subject doesn't change, keep the infinitive: Me alegro de verte (I'm glad to see you), Es una pena no poder ir.

Molestar, preocupar and encantar work like gustar: me molesta, te preocupa, nos encanta.

", "

Cuando: habit or future?

After cuando, the mood depends on the time you're talking about:

You're talking about…MoodExample
a habitpresent indicativeCuando llego a casa, me ducho.
(When I get home, I take a shower.)
the pastpast indicativeCuando era pequeña, iba a la playa.
Cuando llegué, ya no había nadie.
the futurepresent subjunctiveCuando llegues, llámame.
(When you arrive, call me.)

The English speaker's trap: in “when you arrive,” English uses the plain present, so you'll be tempted to use the present indicative after cuando (“cuando llegas”). But that means a habit (“whenever you arrive”). For a future event, Spanish needs the present subjunctive: cuando llegues. And never the future (“cuando llegarás”). The future is fine in the other half of the sentence: Cuando tenga tiempo, te llamaré.

Don't confuse it with the question ¿cuándo? (with an accent), which takes the indicative or the future normally: ¿Cuándo vienes?, ¿Cuándo terminarás?

Cuando sea mayor, viviré en el campo.When I grow up, I'll live in the country.
¿Me avisas cuando termines la reunión?Will you let me know when you finish the meeting?

Summary

  • Opinion stated (creo que, es verdad que) → indicative.
  • Opinion denied (no creo que, no es verdad que) → subjunctive.
  • Feeling (me alegro de que, es una pena que) → subjunctive.
  • Cuando + habit or past → indicative; cuando + future → subjunctive.

es-u15-l3.title: Debating
es-u15-l3.why: This lesson wraps up the unit on opinions: the learner puts the subjunctive of denied opinion to work in a real debate, with phrases for giving an opinion, adding nuance, and agreeing or disagreeing. The topics (city or country, Spanish schedules, remote work) prepare the long conversations at the end of level B1.
es-u15-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Giving your opinion

To debate, you first need phrases to announce your opinion. They go at the start of the sentence, followed by a comma, just like in English.

SpanishEnglishRegister
En mi opinión, …In my opinion, …neutral
Para mí, …For me, …neutral, spoken
A mi modo de ver, …The way I see it, …more formal
Desde mi punto de vista, …From my point of view, …more formal
Yo creo que… / Pienso que…I believe that… / I think that…neutral

“According to me” doesn't work in Spanish either: “según yo” isn't said in Spain. Say en mi opinión or para mí. Según is mostly used with a noun (según Marta, según los expertos) or with tú, él, ella (según tú).

Asking for other people's opinions

  • ¿Tú qué opinas? / ¿Tú qué piensas? (What do you think?)
  • ¿Qué piensas del teletrabajo? (What do you think of remote work?): pensar de to ask for an opinion.
  • ¿Qué os parece? (What do you all think?)

Reminder: denied opinions

Remember the previous lesson: creo que + indicative, but no creo que + subjunctive. It's the go-to structure in a debate for disagreeing gently:

No creo que el teletrabajo sea la solución para todos.I don't think remote work is the solution for everyone.
No es verdad que en el campo no haya nada que hacer.It's not true that there's nothing to do in the country.
", "

Adding nuance: on the one hand, on the other

A good debate isn't black and white. These connectors help you weigh the pros and cons:

SpanishEnglish
Por un lado…, por otro (lado)…On the one hand…, on the other (hand)…
Sin embargo, …However, …
En cambio, …On the other hand, by contrast, …
Es cierto que…, pero / sin embargo…It's true that…, but / however…
Además, …Besides, what's more, …
Depende (de)…It depends (on)…
No es tan sencillo.It's not that simple.
Por un lado, en el campo se vive con más tranquilidad; por otro, hay menos trabajo.On the one hand, life in the country is more peaceful; on the other, there's less work.
Es cierto que el teletrabajo es cómodo; sin embargo, a veces aísla.It's true that remote work is convenient; however, it can be isolating.

Es cierto que and es verdad que state facts: they're followed by the indicative. You use them to concede a point before answering: Es cierto que Madrid es cara, pero… And depende takes de (English says “depends on”): depende del trabajo, depende de la persona.

Sin embargo is written as two words, and en cambio contrasts two people or two situations: Mi hermano vive en el campo; yo, en cambio, prefiero la ciudad.

", "

Agreeing… or not quite

Between “totally agree” and “not at all,” Spanish has a whole range of shades:

SpanishEnglish
Estoy totalmente de acuerdo. / Tienes toda la razón.I totally agree. / You're absolutely right.
Estoy de acuerdo contigo.I agree with you.
Tienes razón, pero…You're right, but…
Estoy de acuerdo en parte.I partly agree.
No estoy del todo de acuerdo.I don't completely agree.
No estoy de acuerdo en absoluto.I don't agree at all.
¡Qué va!No way! Not at all! (informal)

Note that “to agree” is not a single verb in Spanish but estar de acuerdo, and “to be right” is tener razón (literally “to have reason”), never “ser.” Watch del todo (= completely), with the contracted article: no estoy del todo de acuerdo. And tienes toda la razón takes the article, while tienes razón doesn't.

Holding the floor tactfully

If someone interrupts you: Perdona, déjame terminar. (Sorry, let me finish.) To pick up again: Como decía, … (As I was saying, …). To wrap up: En resumen, … or Al final, todo depende de la persona.

Three very Spanish debate topics

  • ¿Vivir en la ciudad o en el campo? El tráfico, la contaminación, la tranquilidad, los servicios.
  • Los horarios españoles: se cena tarde, la jornada es larga; ¿es fácil conciliar la vida laboral y familiar?
  • El teletrabajo: las ventajas (no pierdes tiempo en el transporte) y los inconvenientes (te sientes solo).

es-u16-l1.title: If I had…: hypotheses
es-u16-l1.why: With the conditional (unit 11) and the present subjunctive (unit 15), the learner has everything needed to imagine: this lesson introduces the -ra imperfect subjunctive, built from the indefinido, and the sentence “si tuviera…, viajaría.” It opens the unit “Imagining and regretting,” before the past conditional and the pluperfect.

{"lessons": ["

The imperfect subjunctive: a form born from the indefinido

To imagine a situation that isn't real, English shifts the verb into the past: “if I had time,” “if I were rich.” Spanish does something similar, but with a special tense: the imperfect subjunctive. Si tuviera tiempo… = “If I had time…”. Good news: it's built from a form you already know very well, the indefinido.

The recipe in three steps

  • Take the 3rd person plural of the indefinido: hablaron, comieron, tuvieron.
  • Drop -ron: habla-, comie-, tuvie-.
  • Add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran.

Two details to remember: the yo form and the él form are identical (si yo tuviera, si él tuviera), and nosotros always has a written accent: habláramos, tuviéramos, fuéramos.

Irregular verbs: no extra effort

Verbs that are irregular in the indefinido keep exactly the same irregularity. If you know tuvieron, you already know tuviera.

InfinitiveIndefinido (ellos)Imperfect subjunctive (yo)
ser / irfueronfuera
tenertuvierontuviera

For hay, just learn the form hubiera: si hubiera = “if there were.” As in the indefinido, ser and ir share the same form: si fuera más joven (if I were younger), si fuera a Sevilla (if I went to Seville). Context tells them apart.

You'll also come across a second form in -se: hablase, tuviese, fuese. It means exactly the same thing and is mostly seen in writing. You just need to recognize it: in your own sentences, use the -ra form.

Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más

The hypothetical sentence works just like English: after si, the imperfect subjunctive (where English uses the past: “if I had”), and in the other half, the conditional (English “would”), which you saw in unit 11.

EnglishSpanish
If I had time, I'd travel more.Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más.
If I were rich, I'd buy a house.Si fuera rico, compraría una casa.
If the weather were nice, we'd eat outside.Si hiciera buen tiempo, comeríamos fuera.
What would you do if you won the lottery?¿Qué harías si ganaras la lotería?

As in English, the order can be reversed: Viajaría más si tuviera tiempo. And the negative doesn't change anything: Si no lloviera, saldríamos.

Trap #1: never the conditional after si

In English, “if I would have time” is wrong. Same in Spanish: never say “si tendría.” And no present subjunctive either: “si tenga” doesn't exist. After hypothetical si, there's only one option: the imperfect subjunctive.

Si tuviera dinero, me compraría un coche nuevo.If I had money, I'd buy myself a new car.

Real or imaginary?

It all depends on how likely the situation is. If it's possible, keep the structure you know: si + present, then future or command. If it's unlikely or impossible, switch to the imperfect subjunctive. English works the same way (“if I have time, I'll go” / “if I had time, I'd go”).

SituationStructureExample
possiblesi + present → futureSi tengo tiempo, iré al gimnasio.
possible, advicesi + present → commandSi tienes tiempo, llámame.
imaginary, unlikelysi + imperfect subjunctive → conditionalSi tuviera tiempo, iría al gimnasio.

To give advice, you know yo que tú (unit 11). Here's its long version, very common, and just like English: Si yo fuera tú, aceptaría el trabajo. (If I were you, I'd take the job.)

Ojalá…: dreaming out loud

You know ojalá + present subjunctive for a possible wish: Ojalá haga sol mañana (I hope it's sunny tomorrow). With the imperfect subjunctive, ojalá expresses an unlikely or even impossible wish, like English “I wish…” or “if only…”, which also shift to the past.

WishSpanishEnglish
possibleOjalá apruebe el examen.I hope I pass the exam.
unlikelyOjalá tuviera más vacaciones.I wish I had more vacation!
impossibleOjalá estuvieras aquí.I wish you were here!

The choice depends on what you think: Ojalá venga Pablo (he might come), Ojalá viniera Pablo (I'd love that, but I don't really believe it).

  • The nosotros accent: si fuéramos, si pudiéramos, si habláramos.

  • Hay becomes hubiera: Si hubiera menos tráfico, iría en bici.
Si viviera en Madrid, iría al Retiro todos los domingos.If I lived in Madrid, I'd go to the Retiro every Sunday.
¡Ojalá pudiéramos quedarnos una semana más!I wish we could stay one more week!

es-u16-l2.title: The past conditional
es-u16-l2.why: After hypotheses about the present (si tuviera…), the learner learns to talk about what could have happened: habría + participle for regrets, reproaches and the future in the past (dijo que vendría). The lesson stops short of “if I had known” (level B2) and prepares the pluperfect in the next lesson.

{"lessons": ["

Habría + participle: I would have done

The past conditional is built just like English “would have done”: the auxiliary in the conditional, then the past participle. The auxiliary is always haber, with the conditional endings you know: habría, like tendría or podría.

haberexample: ir
yohabríahabría ido
túhabríashabrías ido
él, ella, ustedhabríahabría ido
nosotros, nosotrashabríamoshabríamos ido
vosotros, vosotrashabríaishabríais ido
ellos, ellas, ustedeshabríanhabrían ido

The participle never changes: Ella habría ido, Nosotras habríamos ido. The irregular participles are those of the pretérito perfecto: hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, vuelto, puesto, abierto, roto.

Always haber

Good news for English speakers: just as English always says “would have,” Spanish always uses haber, even with verbs of movement and reflexive verbs. “I would have gone” = habría ido; “she would have stayed” = se habría quedado; “we would have gotten up” = nos habríamos levantado.

Pronouns go before habría, and nothing comes between habría and the participle: Lo habría comprado. (I would have bought it.) Me habría quedado. (I would have stayed.)

Don't confuse habría (conditional: “would have”) with había (imperfect: “had”), which you'll practice in the next lesson. One letter changes everything: habría comido = he would have eaten; había comido = he had eaten.

", "

Regrets and reproaches

Expressing a regret

The past conditional says what could have happened but didn't. You don't know the sentence “if I had known…” yet (level B2): replace the condition with a short phrase like con más tiempo, sin ti, en tu lugar or yo que tú.

Habría preferido quedarme en casa.I would have preferred to stay home.
Me habría gustado conocer a tus padres.I would have liked to meet your parents.
Con más tiempo, lo habría hecho mejor.With more time, I would have done it better.
Sin ti, no lo habría conseguido.Without you, I wouldn't have made it.
Yo que tú, habría aceptado la oferta.If I were you, I would have accepted the offer.

Making a reproach

EnglishSpanish
You could have told me!¡Me lo habrías podido decir! / ¡Podrías habérmelo dicho!
You should have called me.Deberías haberme llamado.
You (all) could have let us know.Habríais podido avisar. / Podríais haber avisado.

Haber + participle is the perfect infinitive, like “to have done”: deberías haber llamado = “you should have called.” Pronouns attach to it: haberme llamado, habérmelo dicho (with a written accent, like dímelo).

“You should have” is almost always deberías haber + participle, and “you could have” is podrías haber + participle: the same order as in English. The form “habrías debido” exists, but it sounds clunky.

Regret, miss, be sorry

MeaningSpanishExample
to regret an actionarrepentirse deMe arrepiento de no haber estudiado más.
to miss someone or somethingechar de menosEcho de menos a mis amigos de Lyon.
to be sorrysentirSiento llegar tarde.
", "

He said he would come: the future in the past

As in English, the conditional is also used for the future seen from the past. When the main verb moves into the past, “will” becomes “would”: the future becomes the conditional.

In the presentIn the past
Dice que vendrá. (He says he'll come.)Dijo que vendría. (He said he would come.)
Creo que lloverá. (I think it will rain.)Creía que llovería. (I thought it would rain.)
Sé que te gustará. (I know you'll like it.)Sabía que te gustaría. (I knew you would like it.)

It's very useful for talking about a broken promise or a forecast that turned out wrong:

Me prometió que me llamaría, pero no me llamó.He promised me he would call me, but he didn't.
Pensaba que el viaje sería más barato.I thought the trip would be cheaper.

Simple or past conditional?

  • Simple conditional (“would do”): a wish, advice, a hypothesis about the present or the future. Me gustaría ir. (I'd like to go.)
  • Past conditional (“would have done”): what didn't happen in the past. Me habría gustado ir. (I would have liked to go.)
  • Same logic for advice: Yo que tú, iría (the decision is still ahead) / Yo que tú, habría ido (it's too late).

In Spain, you'll often hear hubiera instead of habría: Hubiera preferido quedarme. Here, both mean the same thing. For now, you just need to recognize it; you'll study this form at level B2.

es-u16-l3.title: The pluperfect
es-u16-l3.topic: pluscuamperfecto; what had happened earlier in the past
es-u16-l3.why: After the imperfect and the indefinido (units 7 and 8), the pluperfect completes the storytelling toolkit: había + participle to say what had happened before another moment in the past. The lesson wraps up the unit “Imagining and regretting” and prepares reported speech in unit 18, where it's used to report what people said.

{"lessons": ["

Había + participle: I had done

Good news: the Spanish pluperfect (pluscuamperfecto) works almost exactly like the English past perfect, “I had done.” Take haber in the imperfect and add the past participle.

haberexample: empezar
yohabíahabía empezado
túhabíashabías empezado
él, ella, ustedhabíahabía empezado
nosotros, nosotrashabíamoshabíamos empezado
vosotros, vosotrashabíaishabíais empezado
ellos, ellas, ustedeshabíanhabían empezado

As with the pretérito perfecto and the past conditional, the auxiliary is always haber, just as English always uses “had”: “he had left” = había salido, “we had gotten up” = nos habíamos levantado. The participle never agrees: Ellas habían llegado.

Where do ya, todavía no, nunca and pronouns go?

Nothing goes between había and the participle (unlike English “I had already left”). Ya, todavía no and nunca usually go before; pronouns go before había.

Cuando llegué, Lucía ya se había ido.When I arrived, Lucía had already left.
Nunca lo había visto tan contento.I had never seen him so happy.

Three forms not to confuse

SpanishEnglishTense
he comidoI have eatenpretérito perfecto
había comidoI had eatenpluperfect
habría comidoI would have eatenpast conditional

You already know había with another meaning: “there was / there were” (Había mucha gente). Followed by a participle, it's the pluperfect: Había llovido (it had rained).

", "

The past of the past

The pluperfect shows that an action happened before another moment in the past. Compare:

SentenceWhat happened
Cuando llegué, la película empezó.I arrive, then the movie starts.
Cuando llegué, la película ya había empezado.The movie starts, then I arrive: I missed the beginning.

Nunca he… / Nunca había…

English makes the same distinction between “I've never seen” and “I had never seen”:

Nunca he visto la nieve.I've never seen snow. (up to today)
Hasta aquel viaje, nunca había visto la nieve.Before that trip, I had never seen snow. (up to that moment in the past)

Phrases that call for it

  • ya / todavía no in a story: Cuando llamé, todavía no habían cenado. (When I called, they hadn't had dinner yet.)
  • darse cuenta de que: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado el pasaporte. (I realized I had forgotten my passport.)
  • porque, for an earlier cause: Estaba cansada porque había trabajado diez horas. (She was tired because she had worked ten hours.)
  • hasta entonces, hasta aquel día: Hasta entonces, nunca había hablado en público. (Until then, I had never spoken in public.)

In speech, with antes or después, the order of events is already clear and Spaniards often just use the indefinido, as English often uses the simple past: Comimos después de visitar el museo. The pluperfect becomes essential when nothing else shows what happened first.

", "

Telling a story with three past tenses

To tell a story, you now have three past tenses, each with its own role, much like English “was doing / used to do,” the simple past and the past perfect:

TenseRoleExample
imperfectothe background, states, habitsEra viernes y hacía calor.
indefinidothe events that move the story forwardLlegamos al restaurante a las diez.
pluscuamperfectowhat had happened beforeHabíamos reservado una mesa.

A ruined evening in Granada

Era viernes y hacía muchísimo calor en Granada.It was Friday and it was incredibly hot in Granada.
Habíamos reservado una mesa en un restaurante con vistas a la Alhambra.We had booked a table at a restaurant with a view of the Alhambra.
Pero cuando llegamos, vimos que estaba cerrado: el dueño se había ido de vacaciones.But when we got there, we saw it was closed: the owner had gone on vacation.
Entonces buscamos otro sitio, y en ese momento me di cuenta de que había dejado la cartera en el hotel.So we looked for another place, and at that moment I realized I had left my wallet at the hotel.
Al final cenamos un bocadillo en un banco. ¡Nunca me había reído tanto!In the end, we had a sandwich on a bench for dinner. I had never laughed so much!

Before each verb, ask yourself: is it the background (imperfect), an event (indefinido) or something that had happened earlier (pluperfect)?

es-u17-l1.why: With all the past tenses and the conditional under their belt, the learner can talk about culture: this lesson gives the phrases for introducing a movie (trata de, está ambientada en), summarizing it in the narrative present and giving a nuanced opinion. It opens the unit “Culture and leisure,” before reading a newspaper article and idiomatic expressions.

{"lessons": ["

¿De qué trata? Introducing a movie

To introduce a movie, Spanish has a few ready-made phrases that are easy to reuse:

SpanishEnglish
La película trata de una familia que…The movie is about a family that…
Cuenta la historia de un hombre que…It tells the story of a man who…
Está ambientada en Sevilla, en los años cincuenta.It's set in Seville, in the fifties.
El protagonista es un profesor jubilado.The main character is a retired teacher.
Es la primera película de una directora gallega.It's the first movie by a Galician director.

Careful: película is feminine, so everything agrees in the feminine: está ambientada, la recomiendo, me ha parecido preciosa. Among friends, people also ask: ¿De qué va la película? (What's it about?)

Genres

una comedia, un drama, una película de terror, una película de ciencia ficción, una película de dibujos animados, una película de aventuras, un documental, un thriller.

Tricky movie words

  • el argumento: the plot, the story (not an “argument,” which is una discusión).
  • el guion: the script; el guionista, la guionista: the screenwriter.
  • la banda sonora: the soundtrack, the movie's music.
  • rodar: to shoot a movie; el rodaje: the shoot, the filming.
  • estrenarse: to come out, to be released; el estreno: the release, the premiere.
  • el actor, la actriz, plural las actrices (z becomes c).

Spanish cinema has its own awards, the Goyas, handed out every winter. Argentine and Mexican cinema are also very lively: when you watch them, you'll hear ustedes instead of vosotros.

", "

Summarizing a story in the present

As in English, you summarize a movie in the present: it's the narrative present. To link the stages, reuse the storytelling connectors: al principio, un día, entonces, mientras tanto, poco a poco, al final.

An example: “El verano de las cartas”

Here's the summary of an imaginary movie, written for this lesson:

«El verano de las cartas» está ambientada en un pueblo de Asturias en los años sesenta.“The Summer of the Letters” is set in a village in Asturias in the sixties.
La protagonista es Inés, una chica de dieciséis años que sueña con ser fotógrafa.The main character is Inés, a sixteen-year-old girl who dreams of being a photographer.
Un día, encuentra en casa una caja con cartas de su abuela, que nunca había hablado de su juventud.One day, she finds a box of letters at home from her grandmother, who had never talked about her youth.
Poco a poco, Inés descubre que su abuela vivió en Buenos Aires y que tuvo una vida muy diferente.Little by little, Inés discovers that her grandmother lived in Buenos Aires and had a very different life.
Mientras tanto, tiene que decidir si se queda en el pueblo o si se va a estudiar a Madrid.Meanwhile, she has to decide whether to stay in the village or go to Madrid to study.

The present is used for the main story, but what happened earlier stays in the past (vivió, había hablado), just as in English.

To avoid spoiling the surprise: No te cuento el final. (I won't tell you the ending.) In Spain, people also say hacer spoiler or, more colorfully, destripar el final (literally “to gut the ending”).

", "

Giving your opinion

For a movie you've just seen, the pretérito perfecto is natural in Spain: ¿Qué te ha parecido? For a movie you saw a long time ago, switch to the indefinido: La vi el año pasado y me encantó.

To say…Spanish
your overall impressionMe ha parecido muy original. / Me ha encantado. / No me ha gustado nada.
the best and the worstLo mejor es la banda sonora. / Lo peor es el final.
that it hooks youEngancha desde el principio.
that it's boring (informal)Es un rollo. / Se me ha hecho larguísima.
that you recommend itTe la recomiendo. / No te la recomiendo.

Parecer works like gustar: me ha parecido + adjective, and the adjective agrees with what you're judging: La película me ha parecido lenta, Los actores me han parecido geniales. Se me ha hecho larguísima (“it felt endless to me”) is a set expression.

Adjectives for judging

emocionante (exciting, moving), divertida (funny, fun), aburrida (boring), lenta (slow), sorprendente (surprising), previsible (predictable), preciosa (beautiful), original.

In Spain, most foreign movies are dubbed (doblados). If you prefer the actors' real voices, look for showings in versión original, often with subtítulos: they're marked VOSE, original version with Spanish subtitles.

es-u17-l2.title: Reading a simple article
es-u17-l2.why: After movies, the learner tackles another authentic everyday text: a short news article written for the lesson, with its structure (titular, entradilla, cuerpo) and the journalist's voice (según, se espera que, figures). It reuses impersonal se, the subjunctive and the past tenses, and prepares reported speech in unit 18.

{"lessons": ["

How an article is built

A Spanish news article has the same structure as an English one. Knowing the name of each part helps you know where to look for information.

PartRoleIn English
el titulara short, catchy sentencethe headline
el subtítuloadds detail to the headlinethe subheading
la entradillathe first paragraph: who, what, where, whenthe lead (lede)
el cuerpodetails, figures, quotesthe body of the article
el pie de fotothe sentence under the photothe caption

Headline style

Headlines get straight to the point: often in the present, even for something that's already happened, sometimes with no article or verb, just like English headlines.

El ayuntamiento abre una nueva biblioteca en el barrio del CarmenCity Hall opens new library in the Carmen neighborhood
Récord de visitantes en los museos de MálagaRecord number of visitors at Málaga's museums
Los jóvenes leen más que hace diez añosYoung people read more than ten years ago

In the body of the article, the journalist uses the pretérito perfecto for recent news (El número de turistas ha aumentado) and the indefinido with a date (El estudio se publicó en marzo).

To ask what a text, a sign or a newspaper says, Spaniards say ¿Qué pone?: ¿Qué pone en el periódico? (What does the paper say?); Aquí pone que… (It says here that…).

", "

Read the article

Here's a short article written for this lesson. First read each part in Spanish without looking at the translation, then check. Find the headline, the lead, the figures and the sources.

El titular

Los huertos urbanos conquistan ValenciaUrban gardens take over Valencia

La entradilla

El número de huertos vecinales ha aumentado un 40 % en cinco años, según un estudio del Ayuntamiento publicado este lunes.The number of community gardens has risen by 40% in five years, according to a City Hall study published this Monday.

El cuerpo

Tomates, lechugas y vecinos que se saludan por la calle. Los huertos urbanos ya no son una rareza en Valencia: la ciudad cuenta hoy con 56 espacios de cultivo, frente a los 40 de 2021. Según la encuesta que acompaña al estudio, la mitad de los participantes son jubilados, aunque cada vez hay más jóvenes y familias con niños.Tomatoes, lettuce and neighbors who say hello in the street. Urban gardens are no longer a rarity in Valencia: the city now has 56 growing spaces, compared with 40 in 2021. According to the survey that accompanies the study, half of the participants are retirees, although there are more and more young people and families with children.
«Vivo en el barrio desde hace treinta años y aquí, por fin, he conocido a mis vecinos», explica Carmen López, de 68 años, que cultiva su parcela en Benimaclet desde 2023. Para muchos, el huerto es también una manera de comer mejor y de pasar menos tiempo delante de una pantalla.“I've lived in the neighborhood for thirty years, and it's here that I've finally gotten to know my neighbors,” explains Carmen López, 68, who has been growing her plot in Benimaclet since 2023. For many, the garden is also a way to eat better and spend less time in front of a screen.
El Ayuntamiento abrirá diez huertos más el próximo año, uno de ellos junto al colegio público de Ruzafa. Se espera que la demanda siga creciendo: según fuentes municipales, más de 800 personas están ya en lista de espera.City Hall will open ten more gardens next year, one of them next to the public school in Ruzafa. Demand is expected to keep growing: according to municipal sources, more than 800 people are already on the waiting list.

El pie de foto

Vecinos de Benimaclet, en uno de los huertos del barrio.Benimaclet residents in one of the neighborhood's gardens.
", "

The journalist's voice

Citing sources

SpanishEnglish
según el estudioaccording to the study
de acuerdo con la encuestaaccording to the survey
según fuentes municipalesaccording to municipal sources
al parecerapparently

Trap: unlike “according to,” según takes no preposition at all (no de, no a): según el ayuntamiento, never “según del ayuntamiento” or “según al ayuntamiento.” With a pronoun, you say según él, según ella, según tú.

Letting people speak

To introduce a quote, the journalist varies the verbs: explica, afirma, asegura, añade, reconoce. Spanish quotation marks look different from English ones: angle quotes, with no space: «Estoy muy contenta», explica.

Forecasts and estimates

Se espera que + subjunctive (it's expected that): Se espera que la demanda siga creciendo. But se calcula que and se cree que + indicative: Se calcula que 800 personas esperan un huerto. You'll recognize the impersonal se from unit 14, very common in the press.

Figures

  • Percentages take the article, unlike English: el 40 % de los vecinos (40% of residents).
  • aumentar un 10 % = to increase by 10%: you say un: not por, and not de.
  • la mitad (half), un tercio (a third), uno de cada cuatro (one in four).
  • Going up: aumentar, crecer, subir; going down: disminuir, bajar. The nouns: el aumento, la bajada.

To read quickly, start with the headline and the lead: they give you the essentials. The body only adds details, from most to least important.

es-u17-l3.title: Idiomatic expressions
es-u17-l3.why: To understand Spaniards in everyday life and speak more naturally, the learner discovers about fifteen very common idioms (meter la pata, estar hecho polvo, costar un ojo de la cara…) and their English equivalents. It wraps up the unit “Culture and leisure” by reusing the past tenses, the subjunctive and pronouns.
es-u17-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Body and head

Like English, Spanish loves images taken from the body. Some expressions are very close to ours, others are completely different. In each one, only the verb is conjugated: the rest never changes.

ExpressionLiterallyIn English
costar un ojo de la carato cost an eye from the faceto cost an arm and a leg
tomar el pelo a alguiento take someone's hairto pull someone's leg
no tener pelos en la lenguato have no hairs on your tonguenot to mince words
meter la patato put your paw into put your foot in it, to blow it
echar una manoto throw a handto lend a hand
no pegar ojonot to stick an eye shutnot to sleep a wink
en un abrir y cerrar de ojosin an opening and closing of eyesin the blink of an eye
Este piso cuesta un ojo de la cara.This apartment costs an arm and a leg.
¿Me estás tomando el pelo?Are you pulling my leg?
¿Me echas una mano con las maletas?Can you give me a hand with the suitcases?
Mi abuela no tiene pelos en la lengua.My grandmother doesn't mince words.

Different body parts, same idea: Spain pays with an eye (un ojo de la cara, just one!), English with an arm and a leg; Spain takes your hair, English pulls your leg. And meter la pata is exactly “putting your foot in it”: saying or doing the wrong thing.

", "

Tiredness, ease, success

ExpressionLiterallyIn English
estar hecho polvoto be turned to dustto be wiped out, exhausted
estar en las nubesto be in the cloudsto have your head in the clouds
ser pan comidoto be eaten breadto be a piece of cake
dar en el clavoto hit on the nailto hit the nail on the head
ponerse las pilasto put your batteries into get your act together, to buckle down
tirar la toallato throw the towelto throw in the towel
ser uña y carneto be nail and fleshto be joined at the hip, inseparable
estar como una cabrato be like a goatto be nuts (informal)
llover a cántarosto rain by the pitcherfulto rain cats and dogs, to pour
Después de la mudanza, estoy hecha polvo.After the move, I'm wiped out.
Este ejercicio es pan comido.This exercise is a piece of cake.
¡Has dado en el clavo!You've hit the nail on the head!
Si quieres aprobar, tienes que ponerte las pilas.If you want to pass, you need to buckle down.
Lucía y Marta son uña y carne desde el colegio.Lucía and Marta have been inseparable since school.

Estar en las nubes works just like English “to have your head in the clouds” (distracted, daydreaming). Don't confuse it with “on cloud nine” (very happy): for that, Spanish says estar en el séptimo cielo.

", "

Using them well

The verb is conjugated, the adjective agrees

These expressions behave in a sentence like any other verb: Ayer metí la pata, Me he puesto las pilas, Siempre me tomas el pelo. In estar hecho polvo, hecho agrees with the person:

SpanishEnglish
Javier está hecho polvo.Javier is wiped out.
Lucía está hecha polvo.Lucía is wiped out.
Mis padres están hechos polvo.My parents are wiped out.
Mis hermanas están hechas polvo.My sisters are wiped out.

Ser or estar?

The verb is part of the expression: ser pan comido, ser uña y carne, but estar en las nubes, estar hecho polvo, estar como una cabra. Always learn them with their verb.

To whom? The indirect pronoun

With tomar el pelo and echar una mano, the person involved is an indirect object: Me tomas el pelo (you're pulling my leg), Le eché una mano a mi vecina (I gave my neighbor a hand).

These expressions are informal, but everyone uses them, at any age. Just avoid them in a formal work email. And never translate an English idiom word for word: “it's raining cats and dogs” is llueve a cántaros, not “llueve gatos y perros.”
