es-u18-l1.title: He says that…: reported speech
es-u18-l1.topic: reported speech in the present and the past
es-u18-l1.why: Now that the learner has mastered the imperfect, the pluperfect and the conditional, they can report what other people say: dice que + same tense, dijo que + tenses shifting back, questions with si and commands with que + subjunctive. It's the second-to-last lesson of level B1, right before the big review.
es-u18-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Dice que…: reporting in the present

To report what someone says, Spanish works like English: a verb like decir, then que. When the reporting verb is in the present, the tenses don't change; only the persons change (yo becomes él, mi becomes su…).

What's saidWhat's reported
«Estoy cansada.»Ana dice que está cansada.
«Mañana iré al médico.»Dice que mañana irá al médico.
«He comprado las entradas.»Dice que ha comprado las entradas.
«Mi hermano vive en Bilbao.»Dice que su hermano vive en Bilbao.

The que is required: English can drop “that” (“Ana says she's tired”), but Spanish never can: never “Dice está cansada.”

Questions

A yes/no question is reported with si (“if, whether”); an open question keeps its question word, with its written accent.

«¿Vienes al cine?» → Me pregunta si voy al cine.“Are you coming to the movies?” → He asks me if I'm going to the movies.
«¿Dónde vives?» → Me pregunta dónde vivo.“Where do you live?” → He asks me where I live.

Commands and requests

Watch out, trap: English says “he tells me to come,” with an infinitive, but Spanish says me dice que venga, with the present subjunctive you've known since unit 15.

«Ven a las ocho.» → Me dice que venga a las ocho.“Come at eight.” → He tells me to come at eight.

Preguntar is for asking a question (Me pregunta si…); pedir is for asking for something or a favor (Me pide que lo ayude). English uses “ask” for both.

", "

Dijo que…: tenses shift back

When the reporting verb is in the past (dijo, me contó, explicó, me preguntó), the tenses shift back one step, just like in English: “He said he was tired.”

Direct speechReported speech in the past
present: «Estoy cansado.»imperfect: Dijo que estaba cansado.
perfecto: «He perdido las llaves.»pluperfect: Dijo que había perdido las llaves.
indefinido: «Llegué tarde.»pluperfect: Dijo que había llegado tarde. (in speech also: que llegó tarde)
future: «Te llamaré.»conditional: Dijo que me llamaría.
imperfect: «Antes vivía en Cádiz.»no change: Dijo que antes vivía en Cádiz.
conditional: «Me gustaría ir.»no change: Dijo que le gustaría ir.

Questions follow the same rule: «¿Tienes hambre?» → Me preguntó si tenía hambre.

Commands reported in the past

The command becomes the imperfect subjunctive, the form you saw with si tuviera. For now, you just need to recognize it:

«Llámame.» → Me dijo que lo llamara.“Call me.” → He told me to call him.
«Compra pan.» → Mi madre me pidió que comprara pan.“Buy bread.” → My mother asked me to buy bread.

If what was said is still true as you speak, you can keep the present: Me dijo que vive en Toledo (he still lives there). When in doubt, shift the tenses back: Me dijo que vivía en Toledo is always correct.

", "

Reference words that change

When you report words later or somewhere else, words for time and place change too, as in English (“tomorrow” becomes “the next day”).

Direct speechReported speechEnglish
hoyaquel día, ese díathat day
mañanaal día siguientethe next day
ayerel día anteriorthe day before
la semana que vienela semana siguientethe following week
ahoraentonces, en ese momentothen, at that moment
aquíallíthere
este, estaese, esa / aquel, aquellathat

In the same way, venir and traer can become ir and llevar when the person reporting is no longer in the same place.

A complete example

Lunes: «Mañana iré a tu casa y llevaré la tarta.»Monday: “Tomorrow I'll come to your place and bring the cake.”
Viernes: Elena me dijo que al día siguiente iría a mi casa y llevaría la tarta.Friday: Elena told me that the next day she would come to my place and bring the cake.

Reporting verbs

decir (to say, to tell), contar (to tell, to recount), explicar (to explain), comentar (to remark), añadir (to add), contestar or responder (to answer), prometer (to promise), preguntar (to ask a question), pedir (to ask for something).

In speech, Spaniards often add a que before a reported question: Me preguntó que si quería venir. It's very common, but in writing, go with Me preguntó si quería venir.

es-u18-l2.title: B1 review: a real conversation
es-u18-l2.why: This big review brings together all of level B1 (opinion and the subjunctive, hypotheses, the past conditional, storytelling tenses, relative pronouns, por / para, reported speech) around a long conversation about work, life plans and a trip to Latin America. It closes level B1 and checks that the learner is ready for level B2.
es-u18-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Your B1 toolbox

You've reached the end of level B1. Here, at a glance, is everything that now lets you hold a real conversation. Each row matches a lesson in the level: if a structure feels fuzzy, go back and review it.

To…StructureExample
give your opinioncreo que + indicative / no creo que + subjunctiveCreo que tienes razón. / No creo que sea fácil.
express a wishquiero que, espero que, ojalá + subjunctiveEspero que te guste.
talk about the future after cuandocuando + subjunctiveCuando llegues, llámame.
imaginesi + imperfect subjunctive + conditionalSi pudiera, viviría en Granada.
express regrethabría + participleHabría preferido ir en tren.
link the past to the presentpretérito perfectoHoy he madrugado mucho.
tell a storyimperfecto, indefinido, pluscuamperfectoLlovía y me di cuenta de que había olvidado el paraguas.
be specificque, quien, donde, lo queEs el pueblo donde nació mi abuela.
generalizeimpersonal seEn España se cena tarde.
express purpose, causepara / porEs para ti. / Gracias por todo.
report speechdijo que + tenses shifting backMe dijo que vendría.

In a conversation, nobody expects perfection: people expect you to get your meaning across and keep the exchange going. But these structures make the difference between “survival” Spanish and a real B1.

", "

Traps for English speakers

Here are the most common mistakes English speakers make at level B1. Reread your messages with this list in mind.

AvoidSayWhy
Si tendría tiempo…Si tuviera tiempo…Never the conditional after si (just like “if I would”).
Cuando llegas mañana…Cuando llegues mañana…Cuando + a future event = present subjunctive, even though English uses the plain present.
Quiero tú venir.Quiero que vengas.“I want you to…” = querer que + subjunctive.
Me dijo venir.Me dijo que viniera.A reported command = que + subjunctive.
Espero que estás bien.Espero que estés bien.Esperar que always takes the subjunctive.
Estudio por aprobar.Estudio para aprobar.Purpose (“in order to”) = para + infinitive.
El libro leo es bueno.El libro que leo es bueno.The relative que can never be dropped.
Según a el estudio…Según el estudio…Según takes no preposition, unlike “according to.”
La gente son simpáticos.La gente es simpática.La gente is feminine singular, unlike “people are.”
Conozco Marta.Conozco a Marta.A person as direct object takes the personal a.

A reflex to keep

Before conjugating, ask yourself two questions: which time (present, past linked to the present, finished past, past of the past, future) and which mood (a fact = indicative; a wish, a doubt, a future after cuando = subjunctive; a hypothesis = conditional). These two questions settle most hesitations.

", "

Keeping a conversation going

Speaking isn't just making correct sentences: it's also keeping things going, reacting and buying time. These little words bring your Spanish to life.

To…Spanish
buy timePues… / A ver… / Bueno… / ¿Cómo te diría?
keep it going¿Y tú qué opinas? / ¿Y qué pasó después? / ¿En serio?
react¡Qué envidia! / ¡No me digas! / ¡Qué fuerte! / ¡Qué bien!
add nuanceDepende. / Por un lado…, por otro… / No estoy del todo de acuerdo.
rephraseO sea… / Es decir… / Lo que quiero decir es que…

In Spain, after a meal with family or friends, people stay at the table chatting for hours: it's the sobremesa. It's the perfect moment to practice everything you've learned.

Next stop: Latin America

If you travel to Peru, Colombia or Mexico, your Spanish from Spain will be understood everywhere. A few differences worth knowing so you can understand the people you talk to:

In SpainIn Latin AmericaEnglish
vosotros tenéisustedes tienenyou (all) have
el cocheel carro, el autothe car
el móvilel celularthe cell phone
el ordenadorla computadorathe computer
conducirmanejarto drive
coger el autobústomar el autobústo take the bus

In several Latin American countries, the verb coger has a vulgar meaning. There, say tomar instead: tomar un taxi, tomar el autobús.

fr-u01-l1.title: Être and avoir
fr-u01-l1.topic: être and avoir in the present; subject pronouns; definite and indefinite articles; gender and plural of nouns
fr-u01-l1.why: This first lesson lays the foundations: être and avoir, the subject pronouns, tu or vous, and the articles that carry the gender of every noun. With them you can already say who you are, where you are, how old you are and what you have.
fr-u01-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Être and avoir: the two key verbs

Like English, French builds a huge number of sentences on two verbs: être (to be) and avoir (to have). Both are irregular, so learn them by heart, as a little chant: they are the foundation of everything that follows.

être (to be)avoir (to have)
je / j'je suisj'ai
tutu estu as
il, elle, onil estil a
nousnous sommesnous avons
vousvous êtesvous avez
ils, ellesils sontils ont

The subject pronouns

  • je becomes j' before a vowel: always j'ai, never “je ai”. This is called elision.
  • il and elle mean “he” and “she”, but also “it”: a thing is il or elle depending on its gender.
  • on means “we” in everyday speech, with the verb of il: on est à Paris = nous sommes à Paris.
  • ils is for men or a mixed group; elles only for a group of women.

Tu or vous?

English has one “you”, French has two. Use tu with a friend, your family or a child. Use vous with a stranger, in a shop, with your boss… and whenever you speak to several people.

Tu es anglais ?Are you English? (to a friend)
Vous êtes anglais ?Are you English? (formal, or to several people)

Listen to the plural: ils‿ont (they have) has a buzzing “z” sound, ils sont (they are) a hissing “s”. Same for nous‿avons and vous‿êtes: the final s of the pronoun is linked to the vowel with a “z”.

", "

Le, la, les; un, une, des

In French, every noun has a gender: masculine or feminine. Not only people, but also objects and ideas: le livre (the book) is masculine, la clé (the key) is feminine. There is no real logic, so always learn a noun with its article, as one block: not “livre” but le livre, un livre.

thea / some
masculinele livreun livre
femininela voitureune voiture
before a vowel or silent hl'école, l'amiune école, un ami
plural (both genders)les livresdes livres

Before a vowel, le and la both become l', so the article no longer shows the gender: that's why dictionaries write l'école (f.) or l'ami (m.).

A silent plural

The plural usually adds an -s, but this -s is not pronounced: le livre and les livres sound exactly the same, except for the article (“luh” / “lay”). In French, you hear the plural on the little word in front, not on the noun.

J'ai des livres et des stylos.I have books and pens.
Les clés sont à l'école.The keys are at school.

des is the plural of un / une. English often uses no word at all (“I have books”), but French needs one: j'ai des livres, never “j'ai livres”.

", "

Nationality, age and a few jobs

Nationalities change with the person: add an -e for a woman. Two differences with English: they take no capital letter after être (je suis anglais), and the feminine changes the sound.

masculinefeminineEnglish
françaisfrançaiseFrench
anglaisanglaiseEnglish
américainaméricaineAmerican
canadiencanadienneCanadian
irlandaisirlandaiseIrish

In the masculine, the final consonant is silent: anglais ends on the vowel. With the -e of the feminine, the s is heard as a “z”: anglaise. In the plural, add -s: ils sont américains, elles sont canadiennes (no change for français, which already ends in -s).

Je suis anglaise et Paul est irlandais.I'm English (a woman speaking) and Paul is Irish.

For your studies or your job, French uses no article after être: je suis étudiant (I'm a student), elle est médecin. Lesson 5 comes back to this.

Age: with avoir, never être

In French, you have your years: j'ai trente ans, literally “I have thirty years”. English speakers often say “je suis trente”: it means nothing in French. And ans (years) is never left out. Take vingt (20), trente (30) and quarante (40) as they are for now: numbers come in unit 2.

Tu as vingt ans ? — Non, j'ai trente ans !Are you twenty? — No, I'm thirty!

A question can be just a statement with a rising voice: Tu as un stylo ? In writing, French puts a space before ? and !.

fr-u01-l2.title: Verbs in -er
fr-u01-l2.topic: present tense of regular -er verbs; negation ne… pas
fr-u01-l2.why: After être and avoir, this lesson opens the biggest family of French verbs, the regular -er verbs, and the negation ne… pas. You can now say your name, where you live, what you do and what you like, and spot the silent -ent that trips up English speakers.
fr-u01-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

One pattern for hundreds of verbs

Most French verbs end in -er in the infinitive: parler (to speak), habiter (to live), travailler (to work)… And good news: they are almost all regular. Take off -er and add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.

parler (to speak)habiter (to live)aimer (to like, to love)
je / j'je parlej'habitej'aime
tutu parlestu habitestu aimes
il, elle, onil parleelle habiteon aime
nousnous parlonsnous habitonsnous aimons
vousvous parlezvous habitezvous aimez
ils, ellesils parlentelles habitentils aiment

Four forms, one sound

Here is the surprise: parle, parles, parle and parlent are pronounced exactly the same, “parl”. Only parlons and parlez sound different. The -ent of ils parlent is completely silent: it never sounds like the “-ent” of “parent” or “went”. This is the classic mistake of English speakers reading aloud.

As with j'ai, je becomes j' before a vowel or a silent h: j'habite, j'aime, j'écoute, j'étudie. And the s of nous, vous, ils, elles is linked to a vowel with a “z” sound: nous‿habitons, vous‿aimez, ils‿arrivent.

Ils parlent anglais et elles habitent à Lyon.They speak English and they live in Lyon.

étudier keeps its i everywhere: j'étudie, nous étudions, ils étudient (the -ent is silent here too).

", "

Ne… pas: saying no

To make a sentence negative, French puts two words around the verb: ne before, pas after. Before a vowel or a silent h, ne becomes n'.

Je ne travaille pas le samedi.I don't work on Saturdays.
Elle n'habite pas à Lyon.She doesn't live in Lyon.
Nous ne sommes pas anglais.We aren't English.
Je n'aime pas le sport.I don't like sports.

No “do” in French

English needs “do” or “does” to make a negative or a question: “I don't work”, “Do you work?”. French has nothing of the kind: just the verb with ne… pas, or the verb with a rising voice.

EnglishFrench
I don't speak Spanish.Je ne parle pas espagnol.
Do you speak French?Tu parles français ?
Does she work here?Elle travaille ici ?

Never add a verb for “do” and never forget ne in writing. In relaxed speech, the French often drop it (je travaille pas): you'll hear it everywhere, but write the full form.

le samedi means “on Saturdays”, every Saturday. Take it as an expression for now: days of the week come in unit 2.

", "

One present, three Englishes

French has a single present tense. Je travaille can mean “I work”, “I'm working” or “I do work”: the context does the rest. Never try to translate “am working” word for word (“je suis travaille” does not exist).

Je travaille à la gare.I work at the station. / I'm working at the station.

Verbs without a preposition

Some verbs need a little word in English but not in French. These are false friends of structure:

  • écouter = to listen to: j'écoute la radio.
  • regarder = to look at, to watch: il regarde la télévision.
  • chercher = to look for: je cherche la gare.
  • rester = to stay, not “to rest”: je reste à Paris (I'm staying in Paris).

Likes and dislikes

With aimer and détester, French uses le, la, les for things in general, where English uses nothing: j'aime la musique (I like music), je déteste le sport. Same with languages you study: j'étudie le français, but je parle français, with no article after parler.

Your name

To give your name, say je m'appelle (literally “I call myself”): tu t'appelles, il s'appelle, elle s'appelle. Learn it as a fixed expression: verbs like this one are explained in unit 2.

Je m'appelle Julien, j'habite à Nantes et j'aime le cinéma.My name is Julien, I live in Nantes and I like movies.

dîner is both a verb (to have dinner) and a noun, le dîner: nous dînons à la maison.

fr-u01-l3.title: The sounds of French
fr-u01-l3.topic: nasal vowels; u vs ou; the French r; silent final letters; liaison and elision
fr-u01-l3.why: A pronunciation lesson built on the words of lessons 1 and 2: nasal vowels, u versus ou, the French r, silent letters, liaison and elision. It gives you the keys to read French aloud correctly and to understand why so many letters stay silent.
fr-u01-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Vowels English doesn't have

French spelling looks scary, but it is quite regular once you know a few rules. Let's start with the sounds that don't exist in English.

Nasal vowels

In a nasal vowel, the air goes through the nose and mouth at the same time, and the n or m is not pronounced as a consonant: it only colors the vowel. There are three main ones:

spellingsoundexamples
an, en, am, ema deep “ah” through the noseFrance, enfant, anglais
on, oma round “oh” through the nosebonjour, non, nous avons
in, ain, un, iena flat “a” (as in “bag”) through the nosevin, pain, un, canadien

As soon as a vowel or a second n or m follows, the nasal disappears and you hear a real n: bon / bonne, américain / américaine, canadien / canadienne, un / une. So the feminine of a nationality is not just a spelling change: it sounds different.

u and ou

ou is easy: it's the “oo” of “food”: tout (all), vous, bonjour. But u is a sound English doesn't have: say “ee” and, without moving your tongue, round your lips as for a kiss. That's tu, rue (street), dessus (on top). Practice the pairs: tu / tout, rue / roue (wheel), dessus / dessous (underneath).

é, è and e

é is a short, closed “ay” with no glide: été, étudiant. è and ê are open, as in “bed”: mère, vous êtes. A plain e at the end of a short word is a soft “uh”: le, je, ne.

The French r is made in the throat, a little like gargling softly, not with the tip of the tongue: Paris, rue, bonjour. Try saying “k” and letting air rub at the back of your mouth.

", "

Silent letters

French writes many letters it doesn't pronounce, especially at the end of words. Most final consonants are silent: petit, Paris, vous, les, beaucoup, il est. The plural -s is silent too, and so is the -ent of ils parlent, as you saw in lesson 2.

The CaReFuL rule

Four final consonants are usually pronounced: the letters of the word CaReFuL, c, r, f and l.

letterpronouncedcareful!
cavec, le sacle tabac (c silent)
rbonjour, le professeurthe -er of verbs and many nouns: parler, le dîner sound like “é”
fneuf, actifla clef (an old spelling of la clé)
lil, elle, Michelgentil (l silent)

A final -e with no accent is silent too: la clé ends in “ay”, but la musique ends on the k sound. That's precisely why anglaise makes the s heard: the -e “protects” the consonant before it.

The silent h

The h is never pronounced in French. In most words, it's as if the word began with a vowel: l'hôtel, j'habite, les‿hôtels.

Stress: at the end

English stresses one syllable per word (“HOtel”, “aMErican”). French gives every syllable the same weight and adds a slight stress on the last syllable of a group of words: hô-TEL, a-mé-ri-CAIN, je suis an-GLAIS. Keep your voice even, and lean on the end.

When in doubt, don't pronounce a final consonant: you'll be right far more often than wrong.

", "

Linking words: liaison and elision

French glues words together. A silent final consonant can come back to life when the next word starts with a vowel or a silent h: that's liaison. An s or x then sounds like “z”, a d like “t”, and n links as n.

liaisonexamples
requiredles‿amis, vous‿êtes, nous‿avons, un‿ami, ils‿habitent
forbidden after etun livre et / un stylo
forbidden before an h aspiréles / héros (heroes), le héros, never “l'héros”

An h aspiré is still silent, but it acts like a wall: no liaison and no elision. Dictionaries mark these words, often with an asterisk.

Les‿enfants‿arrivent à l'hôtel.The children arrive at the hotel.

Elision

Some short words lose their vowel before a vowel or a silent h and take an apostrophe. This one is written, so it is never optional:

  • le, la → l': l'ami, l'école, l'hôtel
  • je → j': j'ai, j'habite
  • ne → n': je n'aime pas
  • de → d': un livre d'anglais
Je n'habite pas à l'hôtel, j'ai un ami à Lille.I don't live at the hotel, I have a friend in Lille.

Liaison is why ils‿ont (they have, with a “z”) and ils sont (they are, with an “s”) never sound the same. Say them aloud ten times: it's the best pronunciation drill of the unit.

fr-u01-l4.title: Asking questions
fr-u01-l4.topic: three ways to ask: intonation, est-ce que, inversion (fixed phrases); question words
fr-u01-l4.why: This lesson teaches you to ask questions the way the French really do: with intonation, with est-ce que, and with a few fixed inverted phrases, plus all the question words and quel in its four forms. Now you can not only introduce yourself but also get to know someone.
fr-u01-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Yes or no? Three ways to ask

English builds questions with “do” and by swapping words: “Do you live in Paris?”, “Are you French?”. French has three ways, from the most relaxed to the most formal.

wayexampleregister
1. Rising intonationTu habites à Paris ?everyday speech, the most common
2. Est-ce que + statementEst-ce que tu habites à Paris ?neutral, spoken and written
3. Inversion (verb-subject)Habites-tu à Paris ?formal, written

Intonation is the simplest: take a normal sentence and raise your voice at the end. Est-ce que (literally “is it that”) is a question marker placed in front of an ordinary sentence; it becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel: Est-ce qu'elle parle anglais ?

Inversion is studied much later. For now, learn just a few fixed phrases that use it:

Comment allez-vous ?How are you? (formal)
Comment vous appelez-vous ?What's your name? (formal)
Quel âge as-tu ?How old are you? (to a friend)

Answering a negative question: si

To contradict a negative question, French doesn't say oui but si:

Tu ne parles pas français ? — Si, je parle français !Don't you speak French? — Yes, I do!

In writing, French puts a space before ? and ! (and before : and ;): Tu es anglais ? Never “anglais?” glued to the word.

", "

Question words

To ask for information, you need a question word. Here are the essential ones:

FrenchEnglishexample
quiwhoQui est le professeur ?
qu'est-ce que / quoiwhatQu'est-ce que tu regardes ? / Tu regardes quoi ?
oùwhereOù est la gare ?
d'oùwhere… fromVous êtes d'où ?
quandwhenTu arrives quand ?
commenthowTu t'appelles comment ?
pourquoi → parce quewhy → becausePourquoi ? — Parce que j'aime Paris.
combien (de)how much, how manyTu parles combien de langues ?

Where does the question word go?

In everyday speech, the French love to put it at the end, in the place of the missing information: Tu habites où ?, Tu t'appelles comment ?. In more careful French, it goes first, followed by est-ce que: Où est-ce que tu habites ?, Comment est-ce que tu t'appelles ?. Both are correct.

“What” has two forms: qu'est-ce que at the start, quoi at the end: Qu'est-ce que tu cherches ? = Tu cherches quoi ? Never put quoi first in this kind of question.

Watch the accent: où (where) vs ou (or). Tu habites où ? but Tu travailles ou tu étudies ?

", "

Quel, quelle, quels, quelles

Quel means “which” or “what” in front of a noun, and like everything in French, it agrees with the noun. The four forms sound exactly the same: only the spelling changes.

singularplural
masculineQuel âge as-tu ?Quels livres est-ce que tu aimes ?
feminineQuelle est ton adresse ?Quelles langues est-ce que tu parles ?

With être, quel agrees with the noun that follows: Quelle est ton adresse ? (l'adresse is feminine). Take ton (your) as part of the phrase for now: possessives come in unit 5.

Getting to know someone

Here are the questions you'll ask and hear all the time. Notice the tu and vous versions:

  • Tu t'appelles comment ? / Comment vous appelez-vous ?
  • Tu habites où ? / Où est-ce que vous habitez ?
  • Tu es d'où ? / Vous êtes d'où ?
  • Quel âge as-tu ? / Tu as quel âge ?
  • Pourquoi est-ce que tu étudies le français ? — Parce que j'aime la France.

And to return the question, just say Et toi ? (to a friend) or Et vous ? (formal): take them as fixed phrases.

Tu parles combien de langues ? — Trois. Et toi ?How many languages do you speak? — Three. And you?

Combien needs de (or d') before a noun: combien de langues, combien d'amis. No article after it: never “combien des langues”.

fr-u01-l5.title: C'est, il est, il y a
fr-u01-l5.topic: c'est vs il/elle est; jobs without article; il y a
fr-u01-l5.why: Here is one of the classic traps for English speakers: c'est or il est, and jobs without an article. The lesson also adds il y a, to describe what there is around you, with the names of places in town.
fr-u01-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

C'est or il est?

English says “he is”, “she is”, “it is” for everything. French has two structures, c'est (literally “this is”) and il est / elle est, and the choice depends on what comes after.

after the verbuseexamples
a namec'estC'est Julie. C'est Paris.
a noun with un, une, le, la…c'estC'est un ami. C'est la gare.
a stressed pronounc'estC'est moi ! C'est toi ? C'est lui. C'est elle.
an adjective about a person or thingil est / elle estIl est grand. Elle est canadienne.
a job or nationality, with no articleil est / elle estElle est médecin. Il est irlandais.

The big trap for English speakers: “she is a doctor” makes you want to say “elle est une médecin”. Wrong! After il est / elle est, a job takes no article: elle est médecin. But if you use an article, you must switch to c'est: c'est un médecin.

Voici Thomas. C'est un collègue. Il est ingénieur.This is Thomas. He's a colleague. He's an engineer.
C'est mon collègue.He's my colleague.

Take mon (my) as part of the phrase for now: possessives are studied in unit 5. In the negative, c'est becomes ce n'est pas: Ce n'est pas Julie, c'est Léa.

moi, toi, lui, elle are the stressed pronouns: Qui est-ce ? — C'est moi ! You also know them from Et toi ? The French love to start a sentence with them: Moi, je suis infirmière.

", "

Jobs, comments and the plural

Most job names have a masculine and a feminine form, built like nationalities:

masculinefeminineEnglish
il est étudiantelle est étudiantestudent
il est infirmierelle est infirmièrenurse
il est serveurelle est serveusewaiter / waitress
il est ingénieurelle est ingénieureengineer
il est professeurelle est professeureteacher
il est médecinelle est médecindoctor

Ingénieure and professeure sound exactly like the masculine: only the spelling shows the woman. Médecin does not change.

C'est + adjective: a general comment

To react to a situation, a place or an idea in general, use c'est + a masculine adjective: C'est beau ! (It's beautiful!), C'est difficile., C'est super ! To describe one specific noun you've already named, use il or elle: Le musée ? Il est grand.

Le français ? C'est difficile, mais c'est beau !French? It's difficult, but it's beautiful!

The plural: ce sont

In careful French, c'est becomes ce sont before a plural: Ce sont des étudiants. In everyday speech, most people simply say c'est des étudiants. Both are understood; in writing, prefer ce sont.

Pick up the reflex: name, article or moi after the verb → c'est; adjective, bare job or nationality → il est / elle est.

", "

Il y a: there is, there are

Il y a means both “there is” and “there are”. It never changes, singular or plural:

Il y a un café dans la rue.There's a café in the street.
Il y a des étudiants à la gare.There are students at the station.

In the negative, un, une and des become de (or d' before a vowel). Learn il n'y a pas de as a fixed block for now: the full rule comes in unit 4.

Il n'y a pas de banque ici.There's no bank here.
Il n'y a pas d'hôpital.There's no hospital.

To ask, use intonation or est-ce que: Il y a une pharmacie ici ? / Est-ce qu'il y a une pharmacie ici ?

Places in town

FrenchEnglish
la boulangeriethe bakery
la pharmaciethe pharmacy
la banquethe bank
la postethe post office
le marchéthe market
le muséethe museum
le parcthe park
l'hôpital (m.)the hospital

Don't confuse il y a (there is, it exists) and c'est (it is, identifying something): Il y a un musée. C'est le musée des Beaux-Arts.

fr-u01-l6.title: Review: getting acquainted
fr-u01-l6.topic: unit review: être, avoir, -er verbs, questions, c'est / il est
fr-u01-l6.why: This review closes unit 1 with no new point: you combine être, avoir, -er verbs, negation, questions, c'est / il est and il y a to introduce yourself in detail and get to know someone. It is the moment to check the classic traps before moving on to daily life in unit 2.
fr-u01-l6.json:
{"lessons": ["

Introducing yourself in detail

This unit gave you everything you need to talk about yourself for a good minute. Let's put it all together. Here is a complete self-introduction, with the tool behind each sentence:

what you sayFrenchtool
nameJe m'appelle Chloé.fixed expression
ageJ'ai vingt-cinq ans.avoir + ans
nationalityJe suis française.être + agreement
cityJ'habite à Lyon.-er verb + à
jobJe suis infirmière.être + job, no article
languagesJe parle français et anglais.parler + language, no article
likesJ'aime la musique, je déteste le sport.aimer + le / la / les
what you don't doJe ne travaille pas le samedi.ne… pas

Say this little text aloud with your own details. Then try it in the third person, to introduce a friend: Elle s'appelle Chloé, elle a vingt-cinq ans, elle est infirmière… Watch the agreements if your friend is a woman.

Voici Hugo. C'est un ami. Il est canadien, il habite à Lyon et il est ingénieur.This is Hugo. He's a friend. He's Canadian, he lives in Lyon and he's an engineer.

Remember: c'est + name or article + noun, il est / elle est + adjective, job or nationality with no article.

", "

Asking: tu or vous

Getting acquainted also means asking. Choose tu with someone your age in a relaxed setting, vous with a stranger who is older, in a shop or at work. At a language exchange evening, the French usually switch to tu very quickly. When in doubt, start with vous: the other person will often say On se tutoie ? (Shall we say tu?).

with tuwith vous
nameTu t'appelles comment ?Comment vous appelez-vous ?
originTu es d'où ?Vous êtes d'où ?
cityTu habites où ?Où est-ce que vous habitez ?
ageQuel âge as-tu ?Quel âge avez-vous ?
jobTu travailles ou tu étudies ?Est-ce que vous travaillez ?
languagesTu parles combien de langues ?Quelles langues est-ce que vous parlez ?
how they are—Comment allez-vous ?

Remember the three ways of asking: a rising voice (Tu parles anglais ?), est-ce que (Est-ce que tu parles anglais ?), and the few inverted phrases you learned as they are. And to contradict a negative question, answer si.

Tu n'habites pas à Lyon ? — Si, j'habite ici !Don't you live in Lyon? — Yes, I do, I live here!

On se tutoie ? uses a verb form you'll study in unit 2: just take it as a fixed phrase. It's the friendly way to suggest using tu.

", "

Traps to avoid

Here are the mistakes English speakers make most often in this unit. Check each one before you speak:

  • Age: j'ai trente ans, never “je suis trente”.
  • Jobs: elle est médecin, never “elle est une médecin”; but c'est un médecin.
  • No “do”: Tu travailles ici ?, Je ne travaille pas. No extra verb.
  • One present: j'étudie = I study, I'm studying.
  • Gender: learn every noun with its article, la gare, le musée, l'école (f.).
  • General articles: j'aime la musique, with la, where English says “I like music”.
  • Il y a never changes: il y a des cafés.

Pronunciation reminders

The -ent of the plural is silent: ils parlent sounds like il parle. Make the liaisons: vous‿êtes, nous‿habitons, les‿amis, ils‿ont (with “z”, unlike ils sont). And don't pronounce final consonants, except c, r, f, l.

Les amis de Léa habitent à Lyon. Ils ont trente ans et ils sont anglais.Léa's friends live in Lyon. They're thirty and they're English.

Spoken French often drops the ne: je parle pas espagnol. You'll hear it all evening in a café, but write je ne parle pas espagnol.

fr-u02-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Verbs with me, te, se

Many verbs of daily routine are pronominal in French: they come with an extra pronoun that refers back to the subject. Je me lave is literally “I wash myself”. English usually drops the “myself”: “I get up”, “I shower”, “I get dressed”. French never drops it.

se réveiller (to wake up)s'habiller (to get dressed)
jeje me réveilleje m'habille
tutu te réveillestu t'habilles
il, elle, onil se réveilleelle s'habille
nousnous nous réveillonsnous nous habillons
vousvous vous réveillezvous vous habillez
ils, ellesils se réveillentelles s'habillent

The endings are those of the -er verbs you know. Only the pronoun is new: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Before a vowel or a silent h, me, te, se become m', t', s'. Yes, nous nous and vous vous are normal!

S'appeler, explained at last

Je m'appelle is a pronominal verb: “I call myself”. Note the spelling: two l's when the ending is silent (je m'appelle, tu t'appelles, ils s'appellent), one l with nous and vous (nous nous appelons, vous vous appelez). Se lever works the same way with an accent: je me lève, ils se lèvent, but nous nous levons.

The negative

Ne goes before the pronoun, pas after the verb: the pronoun stays glued to its verb.

Je ne me lève pas tôt le dimanche.I don't get up early on Sundays.
Tu ne te reposes pas ?Aren't you resting?

Some verbs change meaning without the pronoun: je lave la voiture (I wash the car) / je me lave (I wash, myself). Je couche alone is not what you want: say je me couche (I go to bed).

", "

Quelle heure est-il ?

To ask the time, say Quelle heure est-il ? (a fixed inverted phrase) or, more casually, Il est quelle heure ? The answer always starts with il est and always includes the word heure(s), which English often leaves out (“it's eight” → il est huit heures).

timeFrenchnote
1:00Il est une heure.singular, feminine: une heure
8:00Il est huit heures.
8:10Il est huit heures dix.minutes after the hour
8:15Il est huit heures et quart.
8:30Il est huit heures et demie.demie with -e
8:45Il est neuf heures moins le quart.nine minus a quarter
8:50Il est neuf heures moins dix.nine minus ten
12:00Il est midi. / Il est minuit.noon / midnight: no heures

“At” a time is à: à huit heures, à midi. To avoid confusion, you can add du matin (in the morning), de l'après-midi (in the afternoon) or du soir (in the evening): à sept heures du soir.

The 24-hour clock

Timetables, shops, trains and appointments use the 24-hour clock, and the French say it aloud too: 20 h 30 = vingt heures trente. In this system, you never use et quart, et demie or moins: 18 h 45 is dix-huit heures quarante-cinq.

Le train arrive à 18 h 15.The train arrives at 6:15 p.m. (dix-huit heures quinze)

In writing, the French use h, not a colon: 8 h 30, 20 h. And there's no “a.m.” or “p.m.”.

", "

Meals and a French day

French meals have fixed names and fairly fixed times. Careful: the words don't match English one to one.

mealEnglishusual time
le petit-déjeunerbreakfast7 h – 8 h
le déjeunerlunch12 h – 13 h 30
le goûterafternoon snack (for children)16 h 30
le dînerdinner19 h 30 – 20 h 30

Déjeuner and dîner are also regular -er verbs: je déjeune à midi, nous dînons à vingt heures. In Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, le déjeuner is breakfast and le dîner is lunch (dinner is le souper): useful to know, but in France, stick to the table above.

A typical day

Je me réveille à sept heures. Je me lève, je me douche et je m'habille.I wake up at seven. I get up, I shower and I get dressed.
Je déjeune à midi et demi avec des collègues.I have lunch at twelve thirty with colleagues.
Le soir, je dîne à vingt heures, je me repose et je me couche à minuit.In the evening, I have dinner at eight, I relax and I go to bed at midnight.

Notice midi et demi, without an -e: midi is masculine, unlike heure. And when you're late: Je me dépêche ! (I'm hurrying!)

le matin, le soir with le mean “in the morning”, “in the evening” in general, like le samedi for “on Saturdays”.

fr-u02-l2.title: Numbers, days and dates
fr-u02-l2.topic: numbers from 0 to 100; days, months, dates; prices and age
fr-u02-l2.why: After telling the time, this lesson covers all the numbers up to 100, including the famous soixante-dix and quatre-vingts, then days, months, dates and prices. You can now give your age, a date, a phone number and understand what you pay at the market.
fr-u02-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

From 0 to 69

Up to 69, French numbers are fairly logical. Learn the first sixteen by heart; after that, it's tens plus units.

0 zéro1 un2 deux3 trois
4 quatre5 cinq6 six7 sept
8 huit9 neuf10 dix11 onze
12 douze13 treize14 quatorze15 quinze
16 seize17 dix-sept18 dix-huit19 dix-neuf
20 vingt30 trente40 quarante50 cinquante

60 is soixante. Between the tens, use a hyphen: vingt-deux, trente-cinq, quarante-huit. But with 1, it's et un, with no hyphen: vingt et un, trente et un, soixante et un. Before a feminine noun, un becomes une: vingt et une heures.

Six, dix, huit: three sounds

These numbers change their ending depending on what follows:

  • alone, the final consonant is heard: six (“sees”), dix (“dees”), huit (“weet”);
  • before a consonant, it's silent: six livres (“see”), dix stylos, huit jours;
  • before a vowel, liaison: six‿euros and dix‿euros with a “z”, huit‿euros with a “t”.

Also watch cinq (the q is heard: “sank”), sept (the p is silent: “set”) and vingt (the g and t are silent, but the t comes back in vingt-deux…vingt-neuf).

Age still takes avoir: Elle a dix-sept ans. And now you can say any age up to 100!

", "

70 to 100: French arithmetic

Here France does something surprising. There is no single word for 70, 80 or 90: you count with sixty and twenty.

numberFrenchliterally
70soixante-dixsixty-ten
71soixante et onzesixty and eleven
72soixante-douzesixty-twelve
79soixante-dix-neufsixty-ten-nine
80quatre-vingtsfour twenties
81quatre-vingt-unfour-twenty-one (no et)
90quatre-vingt-dixfour-twenty-ten
99quatre-vingt-dix-neuffour-twenty-ten-nine
100centa hundred (no un)

Three spelling details: soixante et onze keeps the et, but quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-onze don't; quatre-vingts takes an -s only when no other number follows it (quatre-vingts ans, but quatre-vingt-deux); and 100 is simply cent, never “un cent”.

Mamie Jeanne a quatre-vingt-deux ans.Grandma Jeanne is eighty-two.

In Belgium and Switzerland, people say septante (70) and nonante (90), and in parts of Switzerland huitante (80). Good to recognize, but in France, and in your answers, always use the French system.

Phone numbers

A French phone number has ten digits, written and read in pairs: 06 12 34 56 78 = zéro six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit. Mobile numbers start with 06 or 07.

To think fast: for 70 to 79, say soixante + 10 to 19; for 90 to 99, quatre-vingt + 10 to 19.

", "

Days, months, dates and prices

Days and months are masculine and, unlike English, written in lowercase: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche; janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre.

With a day, the article changes the meaning: lundi alone = this Monday; le lundi = on Mondays, every Monday.

Lundi, je travaille. Le samedi, je ne travaille pas.This Monday, I'm working. On Saturdays, I don't work.

The date

French uses le + number + month, with no “of” and no “-th”: le 14 juillet, le 3 mai. Only the 1st is different: le premier mai (written le 1er mai). To give today's date: Nous sommes le 3 mai. or On est le 3 mai. In writing, the day comes first: 03/05 is May 3rd.

Prices

To ask: Ça coûte combien ? or simply C'est combien ? To give the total: Ça fait… French uses a comma as the decimal point, and the € sign after the number, with a space: 12,50 €, read douze euros cinquante. One euro has a hundred centimes.

C'est combien, le livre ? — Ça fait quinze euros quatre-vingt-dix.How much is the book? — That's fifteen euros ninety.

coûter (to cost) is a regular -er verb: le livre coûte dix euros, les livres coûtent vingt euros.

fr-u02-l3.title: Describing with adjectives
fr-u02-l3.topic: agreement and position of adjectives; très and beaucoup
fr-u02-l3.why: This lesson teaches you to describe: adjectives that agree in gender and number, that mostly come after the noun, and the short group (beau, petit, vieux…) that comes before it. With très and beaucoup, you can now describe your city, your apartment and the things around you.
fr-u02-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Adjectives agree

In English, an adjective never changes: “a big house”, “big houses”. In French, it agrees in gender and number with the noun, exactly like the nationalities you already know. The basic rule: add -e for the feminine, -s for the plural.

masculinefeminine
singularil est grandelle est grande
pluralils sont grandselles sont grandes

Listen to the feminine: the -e makes the final consonant heard. petit ends on “ee”, petite on a clear t; gris / grise, grand / grande. The plural -s, as always, is silent.

Other patterns

patternmasculine → feminineexample
already ends in -eno changerouge, facile, moderne, jeune
-eux → -euseheureux → heureusehappy
-if → -ivesportif → sportiveathletic, sporty
-ien → -ienneancien → ancienneold, former
-er → -èrecher → chèreexpensive

In the plural, a few endings are special: an adjective in -s or -x doesn't change (gris, heureux: ils sont heureux), and -al becomes -aux in the masculine plural (normal → normaux).

La voiture est petite, mais elle est chère.The car is small, but it's expensive.

For a mixed group, use the masculine plural: Léa et Hugo sont sportifs.

", "

Where does the adjective go?

Here French reverses English: most adjectives come after the noun. “A red car” is une voiture rouge, “a modern apartment” is un appartement moderne. Colors, shapes, nationalities and most long adjectives always go after.

J'habite dans un appartement moderne, dans une rue calme.I live in a modern apartment, on a quiet street.

But a small group of very common, short adjectives come before the noun. A trick to remember them: beauty, age, goodness, size.

meaningadjectives (masculine / feminine)example
beautybeau / belle, joli / jolieune jolie ville
agejeune, vieux / vieille, nouveau / nouvelleun nouveau professeur
goodnessbon / bonne, mauvais / mauvaiseun bon café
sizegrand / grande, petit / petite, gros / grosseune grande maison

Bel, nouvel, vieil

Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, three of them have a special form, to link the sounds: un bel appartement, un nouvel ami, un vieil hôtel. They sound like the feminine belle, nouvelle, vieille.

masculinebefore a vowelfeminine
un beau parcun bel appartementune belle ville
un nouveau muséeun nouvel hôpitalune nouvelle école
un vieux quartierun vieil amiune vieille rue

In the plural, des before an adjective often becomes de in careful French: de belles rues. You'll hear des belles rues too; just recognize it for now.

", "

Très and beaucoup

English uses “very” and “a lot” in different places, and French does too, but learners mix them up constantly.

wordwithexample
très (very)an adjectiveLa ville est très belle.
beaucoup (a lot, very much)a verb, right after itJ'aime beaucoup Bordeaux.
beaucoup de (a lot of, many)a noun, with no articleIl y a beaucoup de cafés.

Never say “très beaucoup”: beaucoup already means “very much”. And after beaucoup de, no le, la, les or des: beaucoup de touristes, beaucoup d'amis.

Describing your city or your apartment

With être, c'est and il y a, you can now paint a full picture:

J'habite à Bordeaux. C'est une très belle ville. Il y a beaucoup de vieilles rues et de jolis cafés.I live in Bordeaux. It's a very beautiful city. There are lots of old streets and pretty cafés.
L'appartement est petit, mais il est moderne et très calme. J'aime beaucoup le quartier.The apartment is small, but it's modern and very quiet. I really like the neighborhood.

Notice: after c'est + a noun, the adjective agrees with the noun (c'est une belle ville); but alone after c'est, it stays masculine (Bordeaux ? C'est beau !).

Cher before or after? After: un appartement cher = an expensive apartment. Before, in a letter, Chère Léa means “Dear Léa”.

fr-u02-l4.title: Verbs in -ir and -re
fr-u02-l4.topic: present tense of regular -ir (finir) and -re (attendre) verbs
fr-u02-l4.why: After the -er verbs, here are the two other regular groups: finir and its -iss- plural, and attendre with its silent d. With them, you can describe errands and habits, and avoid the classic traps of attendre (no “for”) and entendre (to hear, not to intend).
fr-u02-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Verbs like finir: the -iss- group

After the -er verbs, French has a second regular group: verbs in -ir like finir (to finish). Their secret is a little -iss- that appears in the plural.

finir (to finish)choisir (to choose)réfléchir (to think)
jeje finisje choisisje réfléchis
tutu finistu choisistu réfléchis
il, elle, onil finitelle choisiton réfléchit
nousnous finissonsnous choisissonsnous réfléchissons
vousvous finissezvous choisissezvous réfléchissez
ils, ellesils finissentelles choisissentils réfléchissent

The singular endings are -is, -is, -it, and all three sound the same: “fee-nee”. The plural adds -iss- before the endings you know (-ons, -ez, -ent). So the plural is where you hear the difference: il finit (“fee-nee”) / ils finissent (“fee-neess”). The -ent is silent, as always, but the double s is heard.

Other common verbs on this pattern: réussir (to succeed, to pass), grandir (to grow up), remplir (to fill, to fill in).

Je finis le travail à dix-huit heures, mais Paul et Léa finissent à vingt heures.I finish work at six p.m., but Paul and Léa finish at eight.

Not every verb in -ir follows this pattern. Partir, sortir and dormir have no -iss- and come in unit 3: for now, the verbs of this lesson are your models.

", "

Verbs like attendre: the -re group

The third regular group ends in -re: attendre (to wait for), vendre (to sell), répondre (to answer). Take off -re: the stem ends in a d, and that d is silent in the singular.

attendre (to wait for)répondre (to answer)perdre (to lose)
je / j'j'attendsje répondsje perds
tutu attendstu répondstu perds
il, elle, onil attendelle répondon perd
nousnous attendonsnous répondonsnous perdons
vousvous attendezvous répondezvous perdez
ils, ellesils attendentelles répondentils perdent

Two things to notice. With il / elle, there is no ending at all: il attend, elle répond, and the d is silent. And again, the plural reveals the consonant: il attend (“a-tan”) / ils attendent (“a-tand”). Listen for that final d to tell singular from plural.

Other verbs on this pattern: vendre (to sell), entendre (to hear), descendre (to go down, to get off).

Le boulanger vend des croissants. Les clients attendent devant la boulangerie.The baker sells croissants. The customers are waiting outside the bakery.

The singular of -re verbs and -ir verbs ends in -s, -s, -t / -d: je finis, tu finis, il finit; j'attends, tu attends, il attend. When you write il, check the last letter.

", "

English traps and daily errands

These verbs hide a few traps for English speakers, all about little words:

FrenchEnglishwatch out
attendre le busto wait for the busno preposition: never “attendre pour”
répondre à Paul, répondre à la questionto answer Paul, to answer the questionFrench needs à
entendreto hearfalse friend: not “to intend”
réussir un examento pass an examnot “to succeed an exam”
choisirto choose, to pickje choisis un gâteau

Note that à + le becomes au: je réponds au professeur. Take it as it is for now: these contractions are explained in unit 3.

At the shops

With these verbs, you can describe your errands and habits:

Je descends à la boulangerie. J'attends un peu, puis je choisis un pain.I go down to the bakery. I wait a little, then I choose a loaf.
Vous vendez des livres ? — Non, désolé, ici, c'est une boulangerie ! La librairie est dans la rue.Do you sell books? — No, sorry, this is a bakery! The bookstore is down the street.
Les enfants grandissent vite et ils remplissent le panier !The children are growing up fast and they're filling the basket!

And another false friend in passing: la librairie is a bookstore, not a library (la bibliothèque).

Réfléchir means “to think it over”, before deciding: Je réfléchis = Let me think. It's not about mirrors!

fr-u02-l5.title: Review: telling your week
fr-u02-l5.why: This review brings together everything from unit 2: telling the time, days and dates, pronominal verbs, adjectives and the three regular verb groups. You put it all to work describing a real week, with a schedule and a grocery bill, before moving on to the big irregular verbs of unit 3.
fr-u02-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

A week in French

This lesson adds nothing new: it brings together everything from unit 2 so you can tell someone about your week, hour by hour and day by day. Let's start with the frame: days, times and the moments of the day.

Lundi or le lundi?

Days of the week are lowercase in French, like months: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. Without an article, a day means the next one coming, this week: Lundi, je travaille tard (this Monday, I'm working late). With le, it means every week: Le lundi, je travaille tard (on Mondays, I work late). English adds an -s to the day; French adds le and keeps the day singular.

Le samedi, je me lève tard. Mais samedi, je travaille.On Saturdays I get up late. But this Saturday I'm working.

Moments of the day

No preposition is needed for “in the morning” or “in the evening”: French simply uses the article. For a precise time, “at” is always à.

FrenchEnglish
le matinin the morning
l'après-midiin the afternoon
le soirin the evening
à sept heures et demieat half past seven
à midi / à minuitat noon / at midnight
à 18 h 15 (dix-huit heures quinze)at 6:15 p.m.

Midi and minuit never take heures: à midi, not “à midi heures”.

For schedules (trains, shops, classes, appointments) French uses the 24-hour clock: Le cours finit à 20 h 30, read vingt heures trente. In conversation, people also say huit heures et demie du soir.

", "

Your day: the three verb groups

A typical day in French is full of pronominal verbs. The little pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) always matches the subject, and it becomes m', t', s' before a vowel.

Je me réveille à six heures et demie, je me lève, je me douche et je m'habille.I wake up at half past six, I get up, I shower and I get dressed.

In the negative, ne… pas wraps the pronoun and the verb together: the pronoun stays glued to its verb.

Le dimanche, je ne me lève pas tôt.On Sundays, I don't get up early.

parlerfinirattendre
je (j')parlefinisattends
tuparlesfinisattends
il, elle, onparlefinitattend
nousparlonsfinissonsattendons
vousparlezfinissezattendez
ils, ellesparlentfinissentattendent
  • The -ent of ils parlent is silent: il parle and ils parlent sound the same.
  • Finir adds -iss- in the plural, and you can hear it: il finit / ils finissent.
  • Il attend has no ending and its d is silent; in ils attendent the d becomes audible.

“To wait for” is just attendre, with no preposition: J'attends le bus, Nous attendons Léa. But “to answer someone” needs à: Elle répond à Hugo.

", "

Numbers, prices and descriptions

A week also means shopping. Here's a receipt from a Saturday morning in Toulouse. Read each price aloud before you look at the right-hand column.

ItemPriceRead aloud
une baguette1,10 €un euro dix
un poulet11,90 €onze euros quatre-vingt-dix
des pommes4,35 €quatre euros trente-cinq
un fromage7,80 €sept euros quatre-vingts
des yaourts3,25 €trois euros vingt-cinq
un gâteau14,50 €quatorze euros cinquante
Total42,90 €quarante-deux euros quatre-vingt-dix

Remember the comma: 4,35 € is a French price, and you say the euros first: quatre euros trente-cinq. To ask for the total: Ça fait combien ? or C'est combien ? Watch out for 70 to 99: soixante-dix (60 + 10), quatre-vingts (4 × 20, with an -s), quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10), and no -s as soon as another number follows: quatre-vingt-cinq.

Describing your flat and your week

Adjectives agree with the noun and usually come after it, but a short group (beau, joli, bon, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, nouveau…) comes before.

L'appartement est petit, mais la cuisine est grande et très lumineuse.The apartment is small, but the kitchen is big and very bright.
C'est une semaine chargée : j'ai un nouveau travail !It's a busy week: I have a new job!

Très goes with adjectives (très chargée), beaucoup with verbs (Je travaille beaucoup) and beaucoup de with nouns (beaucoup de cours). Never “très beaucoup”.

fr-u03-l1.title: Aller, venir, partir, sortir
fr-u03-l1.topic: present of aller, venir, partir, sortir; à and de with places; au, aux, du, des
fr-u03-l1.why: Unit 3 opens with the verbs of movement: aller, venir, partir and sortir, the most frequent irregular verbs of everyday French. Along the way you learn the compulsory contractions au, aux, du, des and how to talk about cities, countries and transport.
fr-u03-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Aller and venir

Two of the most useful verbs in French are also two of the most irregular. Aller (to go) ends in -er, but it doesn't follow parler at all; venir (to come) has a stem that changes.

allervenir
jevaisviens
tuvasviens
il, elle, onvavient
nousallonsvenons
vousallezvenez
ils, ellesvontviennent
  • Aller mixes two stems: vais, vas, va, vont and allons, allez. Never “ils allent”.
  • Venir has the stem vien- when the ending is silent, but ven- for nous and vous. Ils viennent doubles the n, and you hear it.
  • Liaison with a z sound: nous‿allons, vous‿allez.

Aller also gives you the most common greeting: Comment ça va ? (How are you? How's it going?), answered with Ça va bien or simply Ça va.

— Salut Hugo ! Comment ça va ? — Ça va bien, merci !— Hi Hugo! How's it going? — I'm fine, thanks!
Je viens de Lyon, mais je vais à Paris ce soir.I come from Lyon, but I'm going to Paris tonight.

English often says “I'm going” with nothing after it. In French, aller needs a destination: Je vais au cinéma, Tu vas où ? And when someone calls you, “I'm coming!” is usually J'arrive !, not a form of venir.

", "

Partir, sortir, dormir

These three verbs share one pattern: in the singular they drop the consonant before the ending (partir → je pars), and in the plural they keep it (nous partons).

partirsortirdormir
jeparssorsdors
tuparssorsdors
il, elle, onpartsortdort
nouspartonssortonsdormons
vouspartezsortezdormez
ils, ellespartentsortentdorment

As with finir and attendre, your ear can tell the singular from the plural: in il part the t is silent, in ils partent you hear it.

Leave, go out, sleep

  • Partir = to leave, to set off: Le train part à huit heures. Je pars en vacances.
  • Sortir = to go out, to come out: Ce soir, on sort ! Careful: Il sort avec Léa means he's dating Léa!
  • Dormir = to sleep: Les enfants dorment.
Le samedi soir, nous sortons, et le dimanche, nous dormons tard !On Saturday nights we go out, and on Sundays we sleep late!

English “to leave” covers several French verbs. Partir means to set off, with no object: Je pars ! To say which place you're leaving, add de: Je pars de Lyon à midi. Never “je pars Lyon”.

", "

À, de and places

Aller goes with à (to, at), venir with de (from). When à and de meet le or les, they merge into a single word. These contractions are compulsory.

àde
+ leau cinémadu cinéma
+ laà la garede la gare
+ l'à l'aéroportde l'aéroport
+ lesaux États-Unisdes États-Unis

Cities and countries

Cities take à and de with no article: Je vais à Paris, Je viens de Lyon. For countries, it depends on the gender. Most countries ending in -e are feminine: they take en (to, in) and de (from). Masculine countries take au and du, plural ones aux and des.

Countryto / infrom
la Franceen Francede France
l'Italieen Italied'Italie
le Japonau Japondu Japon
le Canadaau Canadadu Canada
les États-Unisaux États-Unisdes États-Unis

One exception to remember: le Mexique ends in -e but is masculine, so au Mexique.

Getting there

Transport you get into takes en: en train, en voiture, en bus, en avion, en métro. When you're on it, or on your own feet, it's à: à pied, à vélo.

Inès vient d'Italie. Elle va au travail à pied.Inès comes from Italy. She walks to work.

Think of au and aux as single words: never “à le” or “à les”. English speakers often write “à le cinéma” or “de les États-Unis”: French doesn't allow it.

fr-u03-l2.title: Faire, prendre, mettre, dire
fr-u03-l2.topic: present of faire, prendre, mettre, dire and their expressions
fr-u03-l2.why: Faire, prendre, mettre and dire are four irregular verbs you'll use in almost every conversation. This lesson ties them to their everyday expressions, from household chores to the weather, and flags the forms English speakers get wrong, like vous faites and vous dites.
fr-u03-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Faire: to do and to make

English needs two verbs, “to do” and “to make”. French has only one: faire. Je fais un gâteau (I'm making a cake), Je fais la vaisselle (I'm doing the dishes). It's irregular and extremely frequent, so learn it by heart.

faire
jefais
tufais
il, elle, onfait
nousfaisons
vousfaites
ils, ellesfont
  • Nous faisons is pronounced as if it were written “fe-zon”: the ai sounds like the e of le.
  • Vous faites and ils font are irregular: never “vous faisez” or “ils faisent”.

Household chores

FrenchEnglish
faire les coursesto do the grocery shopping
faire la cuisineto cook
faire la vaisselleto do the dishes
faire du sportto exercise, to play sports

In faire du sport, take du as part of the expression for now: you'll study it in unit 4.

The weather

The weather also uses faire, with an impersonal il that means “it”. Quel temps fait-il ? (What's the weather like? A fixed question with inversion.) Il fait beau (it's nice), il fait chaud (it's hot), il fait froid (it's cold), il fait gris (it's gray, overcast). Rain and snow have their own verbs: il pleut (it's raining), il neige (it's snowing).

Don't translate “it is cold” word for word: for the weather, always il fait froid, never “il est froid”. And when a person feels cold, French uses avoir: J'ai froid (I'm cold), like J'ai trente ans.

", "

Prendre and its family

Prendre means “to take”, but it's also the verb for food, drinks and transport, where English says “have”, “get” or “catch”. Apprendre (to learn) and comprendre (to understand) are conjugated exactly the same way.

prendreapprendrecomprendre
je (j')prendsapprendscomprends
tuprendsapprendscomprends
il, elle, onprendapprendcomprend
nousprenonsapprenonscomprenons
vousprenezapprenezcomprenez
ils, ellesprennentapprennentcomprennent

The singular forms all sound the same, with a nasal vowel (the d of prend is silent). In the plural the nasal disappears: prenons, prenez, and prennent with a double n.

FrenchEnglish
prendre le train / le busto take (catch) the train / the bus
prendre un caféto have a coffee
prendre le petit-déjeunerto have breakfast
prendre une doucheto take a shower
apprendre le françaisto learn French
Le matin, je prends une douche, puis je prends le bus à huit heures.In the morning I take a shower, then I catch the bus at eight.

Probably the most useful sentence for a beginner: Je ne comprends pas. (I don't understand.) In speech you'll often hear Je comprends pas, without ne, but always write the full form.

", "

Mettre and dire

mettredire
jemetsdis
tumetsdis
il, elle, onmetdit
nousmettonsdisons
vousmettezdites
ils, ellesmettentdisent

Mettre keeps one t in the singular and two in the plural. Dire has the same trap as faire: vous dites, never “vous disez”.

  • Mettre = to put, to put on (clothes): mettre la table (to set the table), mettre un pull (to put on a sweater).
  • Dire = to say, to tell: dire bonjour (to say hello), dire que… (to say that…). English often drops “that”, French never drops que: Il dit qu'il pleut. (He says it's raining.)
Il fait froid : je mets un pull et je prends un parapluie.It's cold: I'm putting on a sweater and taking an umbrella.
Léa dit que vous faites la cuisine ce soir.Léa says you're cooking tonight.

To ask how to say something, use dire with on: Comment on dit « umbrella » en français ? — On dit « parapluie ». It's a sentence you'll use every day while learning.

fr-u03-l3.title: Wanting, being able, having to
fr-u03-l3.topic: vouloir, pouvoir, devoir + infinitive; il faut; polite requests
fr-u03-l3.why: With vouloir, pouvoir, devoir and il faut, you can finally say what you want, what you can do and what you have to do. The lesson also gives you the polite formulas for asking a favor (Tu peux… ?, Je voudrais…) and flags the traps of English must and can.
fr-u03-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Vouloir, pouvoir, devoir

These three verbs are the engine of everyday conversation: what you want, what you can do, what you have to do. Like English “want to”, “can” and “must”, they're followed directly by an infinitive.

vouloirpouvoirdevoir
jeveuxpeuxdois
tuveuxpeuxdois
il, elle, onveutpeutdoit
nousvoulonspouvonsdevons
vousvoulezpouvezdevez
ils, ellesveulentpeuventdoivent

Look at the shape: the vowel changes in the singular and with ils (veu-, peu-, doi-), but nous and vous keep the vowel of the infinitive (voulons, pouvons, devons). The singular forms of vouloir and pouvoir end in -x with je and tu (je veux, tu peux), and all three singular forms sound the same.

Je veux sortir, mais je dois travailler.I want to go out, but I have to work.
Tu peux venir samedi ?Can you come on Saturday?

The negative

Ne… pas goes around the conjugated verb, and the infinitive comes after it: Je ne peux pas venir. (I can't come.) Elle ne veut pas sortir. (She doesn't want to go out.) Don't put pas after the infinitive.

The English “to” disappears: “I want to leave” is Je veux partir, with nothing between the two verbs. Never “je veux à partir”.

", "

Must, have to, can: the traps

Devoir and il faut

Devoir covers both “must” and “have to”: Je dois partir (I must leave, I have to leave). With a noun, it means “to owe”: Je dois dix euros à Paul (I owe Paul ten euros).

Il faut + infinitive expresses a general, impersonal obligation: “you have to”, “we need to”, “it's necessary to”. It never changes: there is only il faut, no other person.

Il faut réserver : le restaurant est petit.You have to book: the restaurant is small.
Il faut partir tôt demain.We need to leave early tomorrow.

Careful with the negative. Il ne faut pas and tu ne dois pas mean “you must not”, not “you don't have to”: Il ne faut pas fumer ici = You must not smoke here.

Pouvoir: can, may

Pouvoir is “can” in the sense of possibility and permission: Je peux venir à huit heures (I can come at eight), Je peux ouvrir la fenêtre ? (Can I open the window?). But for a skill you've learned (swimming, driving, cooking), French uses another verb, savoir, which you'll see in the next lesson.

Je ne peux pas venir : je suis malade.I can't come: I'm sick.
", "

Asking politely

To ask for a favor, use pouvoir as a question, exactly like English “Can you…?” With a friend, Tu peux… ?; with a stranger, a shopkeeper or several people, Vous pouvez… ?

FrenchEnglish
Tu peux porter le carton ?Can you carry the box?
Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?Could you repeat that, please?
Tu peux m'aider ?Can you help me?
On peut réserver une table ?Can we book a table?
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.I'd like a coffee, please.

In Tu peux m'aider ?, m' means “me”: take the sentence as a fixed phrase for now. Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite formula for asking for something in a shop, a café or a hotel. Learn it as it is: it's a form of vouloir (the conditional) that you'll study in A2. Je veux (I want) is fine among friends but sounds blunt, even childish, with a waiter.

Answering

  • Yes: Oui, bien sûr ! (Yes, of course!), Pas de problème ! (No problem!)
  • No: Désolé, je ne peux pas. (a woman writes désolée), followed by a reason with devoir: Je dois travailler.
— Tu veux un café ? — Oui, je veux bien !— Do you want a coffee? — Yes, please!

Je veux bien is a soft, friendly yes: “I'd be glad to”, “yes, please”. It sounds much less demanding than a bare je veux.

fr-u03-l4.title: Savoir and connaître
fr-u03-l4.why: English has one verb “to know”; French has two. This lesson teaches savoir for facts and skills and connaître for people and places, with a simple test to choose between them, and finishes the work on can started in the previous lesson.
fr-u03-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Two verbs for “to know”

English has one verb, “to know”. French has two, and they're not interchangeable: savoir is for what you know in your head (facts, information, skills); connaître is for what you've met or experienced (people, places, works).

savoirconnaître
jesaisconnais
tusaisconnais
il, elle, onsaitconnaît
noussavonsconnaissons
voussavezconnaissez
ils, ellessaventconnaissent
  • The singular forms of savoir all sound the same and rhyme with mais; the plural uses another stem, sav-.
  • Connaître has a circumflex on the î before a t: connaître, il connaît. Since a 1990 spelling reform, il connait without the accent is also accepted, but you'll mostly see the traditional spelling. In the plural, -ss- appears: nous connaissons.
Je connais Julie, mais je ne sais pas où elle habite.I know Julie, but I don't know where she lives.

Je ne sais pas (I don't know) is one of the phrases you'll hear most. In casual speech it shrinks to je sais pas, or even “chais pas”. Understand them, but write je ne sais pas.

", "

Savoir: facts and skills

Use savoir for information. It's often followed by que (that), si (if, whether), or a question word: où, quand, comment, pourquoi, à quelle heure.

FrenchEnglish
Je sais que tu es fatigué.I know (that) you're tired.
Tu sais si le musée est ouvert ?Do you know if the museum is open?
Vous savez où est la gare ?Do you know where the station is?
Elle sait quand le train part.She knows when the train leaves.
Je sais la réponse !I know the answer!

As with dire, English can drop “that”, but French always keeps que.

Savoir + infinitive: a skill

Savoir + infinitive means “to know how to”, and it's how French says “can” for a skill you've learned:

Je sais nager, mais je ne sais pas conduire.I can swim, but I can't drive.
Tu sais cuisiner ?Can you cook?

Compare Je sais nager (I know how to swim) and Je peux nager (I'm able or allowed to swim right now: the pool is open, my arm is better). English says “can” for both; French separates them. And never “je sais comment nager”: the infinitive follows directly.

", "

Connaître: people, places, works

Connaître is always followed by a noun: a person, a place, a book, a movie, a restaurant. It means “to know” in the sense of “to be familiar with”, “to have been there”.

Tu connais Bordeaux ? — Non, mais je connais bien la Bretagne.Do you know Bordeaux? — No, but I know Brittany well.
Nous connaissons un très bon restaurant à Lyon.We know a very good restaurant in Lyon.

The quick test

  • A person or a place after the verb → connaître: Je connais Marie, Je connais Marseille.
  • que, si, où, quand or an infinitive after the verb → savoir: Je sais où elle habite, Je sais nager.

Regions of France

Regions take la or l' and, like feminine countries, en: la Bretagne (Brittany, en Bretagne), la Provence (en Provence), l'Alsace (en Alsace), la Normandie (Normandy, en Normandie).

Tu connais ? on its own is a very common way to ask “Have you heard of it? Have you been there?” Answer Oui, je connais ! or Non, je ne connais pas. And “Do you know Paul?” is always Tu connais Paul ?, never “tu sais Paul”.

fr-u03-l5.title: Spelling-change verbs
fr-u03-l5.topic: -er verbs with stem changes: acheter, préférer, appeler, manger, commencer, payer
fr-u03-l5.why: These -er verbs have regular endings but a stem that changes its spelling: j'achète, je préfère, j'appelle, nous mangeons, nous commençons, je paie. Once you understand the sound behind the boot pattern, you'll spell them right, and talk about preferences, shopping and food.

The boot: è and double consonants

Some -er verbs have perfectly regular endings but a stem whose spelling changes. The reason is pronunciation. When the ending is silent (-e, -es, -e, -ent), the last vowel of the stem is stressed and becomes an open “è” sound, which French writes with a grave accent or a double consonant. With nous and vous, the ending is pronounced, so the stem stays as in the infinitive. Draw a line around the forms that change and you get the shape of a boot.

acheterpréférerappeler
je (j')achètepréfèreappelle
tuachètespréfèresappelles
il, elle, onachètepréfèreappelle
nousachetonspréféronsappelons
vousachetezpréférezappelez
ils, ellesachètentpréfèrentappellent
  • e → è: acheter (to buy), se lever (je me lève: you already know it), se promener (to go for a walk).
  • é → è: préférer (to prefer), espérer (to hope), répéter (to repeat). Only the second accent changes: je préfère.
  • double consonant: appeler (to call), jeter (to throw away): je jette, nous jetons.
Je préfère la mer, mais nous préférons la montagne.I prefer the sea, but we prefer the mountains.

Now you can understand je m'appelle: it's appeler, “to call oneself”. That's why it has two l's, while nous nous appelons has only one.

", "

-ger, -cer and -yer

Here the change only affects nous, and it's purely a matter of spelling. Before -ons, a g would sound hard (as in “go”) and a c would sound like a k. So French adds an e after the g and puts a cedilla under the c, to keep the soft sound of the infinitive.

mangercommencerpayer
jemangecommencepaie
tumangescommencespaies
il, elle, onmangecommencepaie
nousmangeonscommençonspayons
vousmangezcommencezpayez
ils, ellesmangentcommencentpaient
  • Like manger: voyager (to travel), nager (to swim), partager (to share): nous voyageons, nous nageons, nous partageons.
  • Like commencer: avancer (to move forward), prononcer (to pronounce): nous prononçons.
  • -yer verbs change y to i before a silent ending: payer (je paie), envoyer (j'envoie, to send), essayer (j'essaie, to try). With payer and essayer, je paye and j'essaye are also correct.
Nous commençons à huit heures et nous mangeons à midi.We start at eight and we eat at noon.

“To pay for something” has no preposition in French: Je paie le café (I'm paying for the coffee). English speakers often add pour, which changes the meaning: payer pour Léa means paying instead of Léa, on her behalf.

", "

Preferences, shopping, food

These verbs are everywhere when you talk about what you like and what you buy. Here are some sentences to learn as they are:

FrenchEnglish
Tu préfères le thé ou le café ?Do you prefer tea or coffee?
J'achète une baguette le matin.I buy a baguette in the morning.
On mange à quelle heure ?What time are we eating?
Vous payez par carte ?Are you paying by card?
J'essaie la robe.I'm trying on the dress.
J'appelle Léa ce soir.I'm calling Léa tonight.
J'espère que tu vas bien.I hope you're well.
Vous pouvez répéter ?Can you repeat that?

Like aimer, préférer takes le, la, les when you talk about something in general: Je préfère le poisson (I prefer fish). It can also be followed by an infinitive: Je préfère rester ici (I'd rather stay here). To pay, you'll hear par carte (by card) or en espèces (in cash).

The best way to remember all these changes is to say the forms aloud. If you hear an open “è” at the end of the stem, there's an accent or a double consonant: j'achète, j'appelle. If you don't, there isn't: nous achetons, nous appelons.

fr-u03-l6.title: Review: planning an outing
fr-u03-l6.why: This review closes unit 3 by putting all its irregular verbs to work in one situation: proposing, accepting and turning down an outing. You'll combine vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, savoir, connaître and the verbs of movement to plan a Saturday in Marseille.
fr-u03-l6.json:
{"lessons": ["

Proposing an outing

This review lesson adds no new grammar: it brings together the verbs of unit 3 for a very real situation, planning an outing with friends. First, the verbs you need, at a glance:

jenousils, elles
allervaisallonsvont
venirviensvenonsviennent
sortirsorssortonssortent
fairefaisfaisonsfont
vouloirveuxvoulonsveulent
pouvoirpeuxpouvonspeuvent
devoirdoisdevonsdoivent
savoirsaissavonssavent
connaîtreconnaisconnaissonsconnaissent
préférerpréfèrepréféronspréfèrent

How to propose

  • Tu veux sortir ce soir ? / Vous voulez venir samedi ?: with vouloir.
  • On va au cinéma ?: with on and rising intonation, the most common way among friends.
  • Tu es libre samedi ?: to check first.
  • Ça te dit ?: “How about it? Do you feel like it?” Take it as a fixed phrase (te is a pronoun you'll study later).
Il fait beau samedi : on va à la plage ? Ça te dit ?The weather's nice on Saturday: shall we go to the beach? How about it?

French uses the present for plans: Samedi, on va à la plage = On Saturday, we're going to the beach. No future tense needed.

", "

Saying yes, saying no

FrenchEnglish
Avec plaisir !With pleasure! I'd love to!
Bonne idée !Good idea!
D'accord !OK! All right!
Pourquoi pas ?Why not?
Désolé, je ne peux pas.Sorry, I can't.
Je dois travailler.I have to work.
Je préfère rester à la maison.I'd rather stay at home.

A good refusal gives a reason, usually with devoir, and if possible a counter-proposal, with préférer or pouvoir:

Désolée, samedi, je ne peux pas : je dois travailler. Mais dimanche, je peux !Sorry, I can't on Saturday: I have to work. But on Sunday I can!
La plage ? Je préfère la randonnée : je ne sais pas nager !The beach? I'd rather go hiking: I can't swim!

Checking the details

Before you go, use savoir for information and connaître for places:

Tu connais la calanque de Sugiton ? Tu sais à quelle heure part le bus ?Do you know the Sugiton cove? Do you know what time the bus leaves?

Keep the two “can'ts” apart: je ne sais pas nager (I can't swim: a skill) vs je ne peux pas venir (I can't come: I'm not available).

", "

Getting organized

Once everyone agrees, you settle the time, the meeting point and the transport. All of this works in the present.

FrenchEnglish
On part à quelle heure ?What time are we leaving?
Rendez-vous à neuf heures au Vieux-Port.Let's meet at nine at the Old Port.
On va à la calanque en bus ?Shall we go to the cove by bus?
Il faut marcher une heure.You have to walk for an hour.
Je prends le maillot de bain et la crème solaire.I'm bringing my swimsuit and the sunscreen.
Il fait chaud : tu mets un chapeau !It's hot: put on a hat!
On se retrouve au restaurant.We'll meet up at the restaurant.

Marseille is the perfect setting: les calanques are rocky coves between Marseille and Cassis that you reach on foot or by boat, and le Vieux-Port (the Old Port) is the heart of the city.

Rendez-vous with a time and a place means “Let's meet…”: Rendez-vous à huit heures à la gare ! In English the word sounds romantic or secretive; in French it's an everyday word for any meeting or appointment, even with the dentist.

fr-u04-l1.title: Small words: à, de, en, dans, chez, avec, pour
fr-u04-l1.topic: simple prepositions; stressed pronouns moi, toi, lui…
fr-u04-l1.why: Unit 4 takes you into town, and that starts with the small words: à, de, en, dans, chez, avec, pour. You'll see where they differ from English (no ’s, chez, sur la photo) and learn the stressed pronouns moi, toi, lui… that follow them.
fr-u04-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

À, de, en

Prepositions are small words, but they rarely match English one for one. Learn them in context, with their typical uses:

PrepositionUseExample
àa place (in, at, to)à Paris, à la gare, au cinéma
àa time (at)à huit heures, à midi
deorigin (from)Je viens de Lille.
depossession (’s)la voiture de Paul
de… àfrom… tode neuf heures à midi, de Paris à Lyon
enfeminine countriesen France, en Italie
enmonths, seasonsen juin, en été, en hiver
entransporten train, en voiture
enmaterials (made of)une table en bois

No ’s in French

French has no “Paul's car”: it says “the car of Paul”, la voiture de Paul. With le and les, remember the contractions: le bureau du directeur (the director's office), la chambre des enfants (the children's room).

Voici la maison de Julien et le chien des voisins.Here's Julien's house and the neighbors' dog.

Seasons take en: en été, en automne, en hiver… except spring, au printemps, because printemps starts with a consonant. Months always take en: en juin, or au mois de juin.

", "

Dans, chez, avec, pour, sans, entre

  • dans = inside: Les clés sont dans le sac. (The keys are in the bag.)
  • chez = at or to someone's place: chez Paul (at Paul's), chez le médecin (at the doctor's). English needs “’s” or “place”; French just says chez + the person.
  • avec = with, sans = without: un thé avec ou sans sucre (tea with or without sugar).
  • pour = for: un cadeau pour Léa; also “in order to” + infinitive: Je travaille pour payer l'appartement.
  • entre = between: entre midi et deux heures, entre la gare et le musée.
Ce soir, je dîne chez Camille avec Hugo.Tonight I'm having dinner at Camille's with Hugo.

Where English and French differ

EnglishFrench
in the streetdans la rue
at homeà la maison / chez moi
in the photosur la photo
at eight o'clockà huit heures
in Juneen juin
in springau printemps
at the doctor'schez le médecin

Chez goes with a person, à with a place: chez le boulanger (at the baker's) but à la boulangerie (at the bakery). And English “in the photo” is sur la photo: French sees a picture as a surface.

", "

Moi, toi, lui…: the stressed pronouns

After a preposition, French can't use je, tu, il. It uses another set of pronouns, called stressed pronouns.

SubjectStressedExample
jemoiavec moi
tutoichez toi
illuipour lui
elleellesans elle
nousnousavec nous
vousvouschez vous
ilseuxchez eux
ellesellespour elles

They're also used:

  • for emphasis, at the start of a sentence: Moi, je suis de Lille. Et toi ? (I'm from Lille. What about you?)
  • in short answers: Moi aussi ! (Me too!), Pas moi ! (Not me!)
  • after c'est: C'est moi. (It's me.) C'est lui ! (It's him!)
Tu viens avec moi chez eux ? — Non, je reste chez moi.Are you coming with me to their place? — No, I'm staying home.

Chez moi is the everyday way to say “at my place” or “at home”: Je suis chez moi (I'm at home), Je rentre chez moi (I'm going home). After a preposition, always use the stressed form: never “avec je” or “pour il”.
