fr-u04-l2.title: Shopping: du, de la, des
fr-u04-l2.topic: partitive articles; de after negation and quantities
fr-u04-l2.why: This is the key lesson on partitive articles: du, de la, de l', des for “some”, and plain de after a negation or a quantity. You'll use them in the little ritual of French shops, at the bakery and at the market.
fr-u04-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Some bread, some jam: du, de la, des

In English you can say “I'd like bread” or “I'd like some bread”. In French, a noun almost never stands alone: when you talk about an unspecified quantity of something (“some”, “any”, or nothing at all in English), you use a partitive article.

PartitiveExample
masculinedudu pain, du fromage
femininede lade la confiture, de la salade
before a vowel or a silent hde l'de l'eau, de l'huile
pluraldesdes tomates, des œufs
Je voudrais du pain, de la confiture et de l'eau.I'd like (some) bread, (some) jam and (some) water.

Compare with what you already know. Un croissant: one croissant, something you count. Du pain: some bread, a quantity you don't count. Le pain: bread in general, or a specific bread; the next lesson looks closely at this contrast.

You've met du and des as contractions (le prix du pain, the price of bread). The partitive looks the same but means “some”. And the du of faire du sport? It was a partitive all along. The typical English speaker's mistake is to drop it: “je voudrais pain” is impossible in French.

Des is also the plural of un / une: un œuf, des œufs. Either way, it translates as “some” or nothing at all: J'achète des tomates = I'm buying (some) tomatoes.

", "

Pas de, beaucoup de: when the article disappears

After a negation

After ne… pas, du, de la, de l', des and un, une all become de, or d' before a vowel. It's the English “not any” or “no”:

Je n'ai pas de lait. Il n'y a pas d'œufs.I don't have any milk. There are no eggs.
Tu veux de la salade ? — Non merci, je ne veux pas de salade.Do you want some lettuce? — No thanks, I don't want any lettuce.

One exception: after ce n'est pas, the article stays: Ce n'est pas du sucre, c'est du sel ! (That's not sugar, it's salt!)

After a quantity

After a word of quantity, French uses de alone, with no article, just like English “of” in “a kilo of tomatoes”.

FrenchEnglish
un kilo de tomatesa kilo of tomatoes
200 grammes de fromage200 grams of cheese
une bouteille de vina bottle of wine
un paquet de pâtesa packet of pasta
une douzaine d'œufsa dozen eggs
beaucoup de mondelots of people
un peu de sucrea little sugar
assez de painenough bread
trop de seltoo much salt

The classic trap is “beaucoup des”: it's always beaucoup de, even in the plural: beaucoup de tomates. And English “a dozen eggs” has no “of”, but French needs it: une douzaine d'œufs.

", "

At the market and the bakery

Shopping in France follows a little ritual, with set phrases on both sides of the counter. Shopkeepers say vous, and you always start with Bonjour !

WhoFrenchEnglish
ShopkeeperBonjour, vous désirez ?Hello, what would you like?
CustomerJe voudrais une baguette et deux croissants.I'd like a baguette and two croissants.
ShopkeeperEt avec ça ?Anything else?
CustomerVous avez des tartes aux fraises ?Do you have strawberry tarts?
ShopkeeperCe sera tout ?Will that be all?
CustomerC'est tout, merci. Ça fait combien ?That's all, thanks. How much is it?
ShopkeeperÇa fait six euros vingt.That comes to six euros twenty.

Ce sera tout ? uses a future form: take it as a fixed phrase for now.

Where to buy what

  • la boulangerie (the bakery): une baguette, un croissant, un pain au chocolat
  • la fromagerie (the cheese shop): du fromage, du beurre, des yaourts
  • le marché (the market): des tomates, des pommes, des fraises, de la salade, des pommes de terre (potatoes)

At the market, you can ask for a weight (un kilo de pommes, cinq cents grammes de fraises) or a number (trois tomates). And une salade is usually a head of lettuce, not a prepared salad.

fr-u04-l3.title: At the café and the restaurant
fr-u04-l3.topic: ordering and paying; boire; definite vs partitive article
fr-u04-l3.why: After shopping, it's time to sit down: this lesson gives you everything to order and pay at a café or a restaurant, from un café to l'addition, plus the verb boire. It also settles the key contrast of the unit: J'aime le fromage, but je prends du fromage.
fr-u04-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

At the café

The French café has its own vocabulary, and a few words don't mean what an English speaker expects.

FrenchEnglish
un caféan espresso (small, strong, black)
un crème (un café crème)a coffee with hot milk
un décaa decaf
un théa tea
un chocolat chauda hot chocolate
un jus d'orangean orange juice
une pressiona draft beer
une carafe d'eaua jug of tap water (free)

Ordering

You have three polite ways to order: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. / Pour moi, un thé. / Je vais prendre un crème. The last one uses aller + infinitive, a future form you'll study in unit 6: take it as a fixed phrase for now. Waiters and customers say vous to each other, and you call the waiter with Monsieur !, Madame ! or S'il vous plaît !

Boire

boire
jebois
tubois
il, elle, onboit
nousbuvons
vousbuvez
ils, ellesboivent

Three stems: boi- in the singular, buv- for nous and vous, boiv- for ils. The singular forms all sound the same, like “bwa”.

If you want a longer black coffee, ask for un café allongé; a big milky one is un grand crème. And never call the waiter “garçon”: it's old-fashioned and sounds rude today.

", "

At the restaurant

Two famous false friends are waiting for you on the table.

FrenchEnglishCareful!
la cartethe menu (the list of dishes)La carte, s'il vous plaît.
le menuthe set menu (fixed price)le menu à 22 euros: starter, main course and dessert
l'entréethe starter, the appetizerIn American English, the “entrée” is the main course!
le platthe main course; the dishle plat du jour = today's special
le dessertthe dessertune tarte, une crème brûlée…
l'additionthe checkL'addition, s'il vous plaît !

How do you like your steak?

The waiter asks Quelle cuisson ? French steaks are cooked less than in the US or the UK:

  • bleu: very rare, almost raw
  • saignant: rare (literally “bleeding”)
  • à point: medium
  • bien cuit: well done

A carafe of tap water is free: just ask for une carafe d'eau. Bottled water is de l'eau plate (still) or de l'eau gazeuse (sparkling).

In France the service charge is included in the prices: that's what service compris means on the menu. A tip (un pourboire) is a small extra, a few coins for good service, never a fixed percentage.

", "

J'aime le fromage, je prends du fromage

This is the key contrast of the unit. With verbs of taste (aimer, adorer, détester, préférer), you talk about a thing in general, so French uses le, la, les. With verbs of consumption (prendre, boire, manger, vouloir, acheter), you talk about some of it, so you use du, de la, des. English uses no article in either case.

In generalSome
J'aime le fromage. (I like cheese.)Je prends du fromage. (I'll have some cheese.)
Elle adore le vin rouge.Elle boit du vin rouge.
Je déteste la bière.Je ne bois pas de bière.
Tu préfères les frites ?Tu veux des frites ?

Look at the third line: in the negative, the partitive becomes de (pas de bière), but the general article stays: Je n'aime pas la bière.

Je n'aime pas le poisson, alors je prends du poulet.I don't like fish, so I'll have some chicken.
Les enfants boivent du lait, mais ils détestent le café !The children drink milk, but they hate coffee!

A quick test: if you could add “in general” in English, use le, la, les. If you could add “some”, use du, de la, des.

fr-u04-l4.why: After shopping and ordering, you now learn to find your way around a French town: asking where something is, understanding directions given in the present, and placing things with à côté de, en face de or au coin de. The lesson also looks closely at tu and vous, so you know whom to address how, and when to switch.
fr-u04-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Excuse me, where is…?

You're in a French town and you're looking for the station, a pharmacy or a cash machine. There are three simple ways to ask, and all of them use words you already know. Always start with Bonjour or Excusez-moi: in France, a question fired at a stranger without a greeting sounds rude.

To ask…FrenchEnglish
the way to a placeExcusez-moi, pour aller à la gare ?Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
where a specific place isOù est la poste ?Where is the post office?
the same, a little more formalOù se trouve la mairie ?Where is the town hall?
if there is one nearbyIl y a une pharmacie près d'ici ?Is there a pharmacy near here?

Take Excusez-moi as a set phrase for now: it's an imperative, a form you'll study later. Se trouver (to be located) is a pronominal verb like se lever: la gare se trouve, les toilettes se trouvent.

Où est or il y a?

It works just like English. Où est + le / la asks for a specific place that you know exists: Où est la gare ? Il y a + un / une asks if there is any such place around: Il y a un distributeur près d'ici ? (Is there a cash machine near here?). And remember your contractions: pour aller au musée, à la gare, à l'hôtel, aux toilettes.

Understanding the answer

C'est tout près, à cinq minutes à pied.It's very close, five minutes' walk.
C'est un peu loin. Vous pouvez prendre le bus.It's a bit far. You can take the bus.
Désolé, je ne sais pas. Je ne suis pas d'ici.Sorry, I don't know. I'm not from around here.

Add Monsieur or Madame to your question: Pardon, Madame, où est la gare ? It sounds warm and polite, and nobody uses Mademoiselle anymore.

", "

Where things are: prepositions of place

To understand directions, you need the little words that place things in the street. Some take de, others don't: learn each one as a block.

FrenchEnglishExample
à côté denext toLa poste est à côté du musée.
en face deopposite, across fromLa pharmacie est en face de la gare.
près de / loin denear / far fromL'hôtel est près de la place.
au coin deat the corner ofLe café est au coin de la rue.
au bout deat the end ofLa mairie est au bout de la rue.
devant / derrièrein front of / behindLe parking est derrière la poste.
sur / souson / underLe plan est sur la table.
entre… et…between… and…La banque est entre le café et la boulangerie.
à gauche (de) / à droite (de)on the left (of) / on the right (of)La gare est à droite.
tout droitstraight aheadVous allez tout droit.

The trap: de + le = du

English says “next to the museum”, with no “of”. French needs de, and de contracts with le and les exactly as you've seen: à côté du musée (never à côté de le musée), en face des magasins, but en face de la gare and près de l'hôtel. On the other hand, devant, derrière, sur, sous and entre never take de: devant la mairie.

Il y a une boulangerie au coin de la rue, à côté du cinéma.There's a bakery at the corner of the street, next to the movie theater.
Le distributeur est entre la banque et la pharmacie.The cash machine is between the bank and the pharmacy.

À droite (on the right) and tout droit (straight ahead) sound alike and confuse everybody, French people included. If you have a doubt, point and ask: À droite ou tout droit ?

", "

Giving directions, and tu or vous?

To give directions, French people very often use the plain present with vous, where English uses an imperative (“Go straight on, turn left”). It sounds natural and polite, and you already know all the verbs. The real imperative will come later.

With vousWith tuEnglish
Vous allez tout droit.Tu vas tout droit.You go straight ahead.
Vous tournez à gauche.Tu tournes à gauche.You turn left.
Vous prenez la deuxième rue à droite.Tu prends la deuxième rue à droite.You take the second street on the right.
Vous traversez la place.Tu traverses la place.You cross the square.
Vous continuez jusqu'au feu.Tu continues jusqu'au feu.You keep going as far as the traffic light.

First, second, third

Ordinals are easy: number + -ième: deuxième, troisième, quatrième, dixième. Watch three details: cinq → cinquième (with a u), neuf → neuvième (f becomes v), and “first” is irregular and agrees: le premier carrefour, la première rue. Written short: 1er, 1re, 2e, 3e.

Tu or vous?

Use vous with strangers, in shops, with older people and at work until someone suggests otherwise. Use tu with friends, family, children, and often among young people. When you ask the way, it's always vous. When a relationship becomes friendlier, someone (usually the older person or the boss) proposes the switch: On se tutoie ? (Shall we say tu?). Saying tu too early can sound overfamiliar; saying vous too long can sound cold, but it's never rude.

If in doubt, say vous. The other person will tell you if they prefer tu.

fr-u04-l5.title: Review of the basics: verbs and prepositions
fr-u04-l5.why: This review brings together everything from units 3 and 4: the irregular verbs of the present, the small prepositions, partitives and quantities, and asking the way. You follow a tourist through a day in Bordeaux, from the market to the quays, to make sure the basics are solid before moving on to family and people.
fr-u04-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

The verbs of a day in town

A day in town uses the same handful of irregular verbs again and again. Here are the ones you need most, side by side. Read each column aloud: the singular forms often sound the same, and the plural is where the surprises are.

allerprendrefairevouloirpouvoir
jevaisprendsfaisveuxpeux
tuvasprendsfaisveuxpeux
il / elle / onvaprendfaitveutpeut
nousallonsprenonsfaisonsvoulonspouvons
vousallezprenezfaitesvoulezpouvez
ils / ellesvontprennentfontveulentpeuvent

Five reminders

  • Never vous faisez or vous disez: it's vous faites, vous dites.
  • Je voudrais is the polite way to ask for something in a shop or a café: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
  • Savoir for a fact, connaître for a person or a place: Je sais où est la gare, but Je connais bien Bordeaux.
  • Stem changes: j'achète but nous achetons, je préfère but nous préférons.
  • Boire: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent.
Vous voulez prendre le tram ou vous préférez aller à pied ?Do you want to take the tram or do you prefer to walk?
Je ne connais pas la ville, mais je sais où est le marché.I don't know the town, but I know where the market is.

English uses “know” for everything. Ask yourself: can I replace it with “know how” or “know that”? Then it's savoir. Is it “be familiar with” a person or a place? Then it's connaître.

", "

Small words: à, de, en, chez

Prepositions are where English speakers lose the most points, because English uses “to”, “in” and “at” in a completely different way. Here is the whole system in one table.

aller à (to)venir de (from)
le (masculine)au marchédu marché
la (feminine)à la garede la gare
l' (vowel)à l'hôtelde l'hôtel
les (plural)aux quaisdes quais
cityà Bordeauxde Bordeaux
feminine countryen Francede France
masculine countryau Canadadu Canada

Transport: en train, en bus, en voiture, en tram, but à pied and à vélo. Chez is for a person, never for a shop: chez le boulanger (at the baker's), but à la boulangerie (at the bakery). After a preposition, use a stressed pronoun: avec moi, chez eux, pour elle.

Common mistakes

Not thisBut this
je vais à le marchéje vais au marché
à côté de le pontà côté du pont
je vais chez la boulangerieje vais à la boulangerie
en piedà pied
dans Franceen France

Prepositions of place are blocks: à côté de, en face de, près de, au bout de. The de at the end contracts like any other: en face du musée.

", "

Some, the, none: articles at the market and the café

At the market and the café, the article you choose changes the meaning. English often uses no article at all, which is why this is so tricky.

You mean…FrenchEnglish
some, an unspecified amountJe voudrais du pain, de la confiture et de l'eau.I'd like (some) bread, jam and water.
after a negativeJe n'ai pas de lait.I don't have any milk.
after a quantityun kilo de tomates, une bouteille de vina kilo of tomatoes, a bottle of wine
in general, a tasteJ'aime le fromage.I like cheese.
a specific oneLe pain est très bon ici.The bread is very good here.

So you say Je prends du fromage (I'm having some cheese) but J'aime le fromage (I like cheese in general). After ne… pas and after any quantity (beaucoup de, un peu de, un morceau de, une douzaine de), du / de la / des all become a simple de or d'.

Shopping and ordering

Bonjour ! Je voudrais un kilo de pommes et une douzaine d'œufs.Hello! I'd like a kilo of apples and a dozen eggs.
— Et avec ça ? — C'est tout, merci. Ça fait combien ?— Anything else? — That's all, thanks. How much is it?
Pour moi, un café et une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît. L'addition aussi !For me, an espresso and a pitcher of water, please. And the check!

A local specialty in Bordeaux: the canelé, a small cake with a dark caramelized crust and a soft center. You'll ask for des canelés (some) or six canelés, and you'll probably say J'adore les canelés !

fr-u05-l1.title: Mon, ma, mes: possessives
fr-u05-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on the people around you with the possessive adjectives and the vocabulary of the family. You'll learn the rule that trips up every English speaker: in French, the possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.
fr-u05-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

My, your, our: the possessives

In English, “my” never changes: my brother, my sister, my parents. In French, the possessive is an adjective, so it agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows. You need three forms for most persons.

masculine nounfeminine nounplural noun
mymon frèrema sœurmes parents
your (tu)ton frèreta sœurtes parents
his / her / itsson frèresa sœurses parents
ournotre frèrenotre sœurnos parents
your (vous)votre frèrevotre sœurvos parents
theirleur frèreleur sœurleurs parents

For notre, votre and leur, masculine and feminine are the same: only the plural changes. In the plural, the final s is silent… except before a vowel, where you hear a liaison with a z sound: mes‿enfants, nos‿amis, leurs‿enfants.

Ton or votre?

The possessive follows your choice of tu or vous. With a friend: Comment s'appelle ta sœur ? With a stranger, someone older, or several people: Comment s'appelle votre sœur ? Mixing them (vous with ton) is a classic beginner's slip.

— Tu habites avec tes parents ? — Non, j'habite avec mon frère.— Do you live with your parents? — No, I live with my brother.
Madame, votre fils est dans la classe de Lucas ?Ma'am, is your son in Lucas's class?

Remember there is no “'s” in French: la sœur de Thomas = Thomas's sister. Once you know who you're talking about, the possessive takes over: sa sœur.

", "

The big trap: son, sa, ses

In English, “his” and “her” depend on the owner: a man's car is “his car”, a woman's car is “her car”. In French, son / sa / ses depend only on the thing owned. The owner doesn't matter at all.

Frenchcan meanbecause…
sa voiturehis car OR her carvoiture is feminine
son frèrehis brother OR her brotherfrère is masculine
ses enfantshis children OR her childrenenfants is plural
Thomas habite avec sa sœur.Thomas lives with his sister.
Léa adore son frère.Léa adores her brother.

Your English instinct will push you to say Léa et sa frère because Léa is a woman. Resist it: look at the noun, not the person. Context almost always tells you who the owner is. If you really need to insist, add a stressed pronoun: C'est sa voiture à elle (It's HER car).

Mon amie, not ma amie

Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or a silent h, ma / ta / sa become mon / ton / son, simply to avoid two vowels clashing: mon amie, ton école, son adresse, mon histoire. The noun stays feminine: mon amie est canadienne. So mon ami and mon amie sound exactly the same: only the spelling shows the difference.

Leur or leurs?

Leur = their, with one thing; leurs = their, with several things: leur fille (their daughter, they have one), leurs enfants (their children). Don't use ses for several owners: Les enfants et leurs grands-parents, never ses grands-parents here.

", "

The family

Family words are learned in pairs. Note that several of them have two meanings, depending on the context.

MasculineFeminineEnglish
le pèrela mèrefather / mother
le frèrela sœurbrother / sister
le filsla filleson / daughter
le marila femmehusband / wife
le grand-pèrela grand-mèregrandfather / grandmother
l'onclela tanteuncle / aunt
le cousinla cousinecousin
le neveula niècenephew / niece
le conjointla conjointespouse, partner (official)
  • la femme = woman AND wife: une femme (a woman), ma femme (my wife).
  • la fille = girl AND daughter: une fille (a girl), sa fille (his or her daughter).
  • les parents = parents, but also relatives in general: J'ai des parents à Lyon can mean “I have relatives in Lyon”.
  • les beaux-parents = the in-laws (and also a stepfather and stepmother); les grands-parents = grandparents.
  • le fils is pronounced “feess”: the l is silent and the s is heard.

Talking about your family

— Tu as des frères et sœurs ? — Oui, j'ai un frère et deux sœurs.— Do you have any brothers and sisters? — Yes, I have one brother and two sisters.
Je suis fille unique. Mes parents habitent à Nice.I'm an only child (girl). My parents live in Nice.
Quel âge a ton fils ? Il a sept ans.How old is your son? He's seven.

“Brothers and sisters” is frères et sœurs, with no article repeated before the second noun, as in the question Tu as des frères et sœurs ?. English “siblings” has no everyday French equivalent.

fr-u05-l2.title: Describing someone
fr-u05-l2.topic: physical description and character; être, avoir, porter
fr-u05-l2.why: After the family, you learn to describe the people around you: their height, hair and eyes, what they wear, and their personality. The lesson reviews adjective agreement with new irregular feminines and shows why French says « il a les yeux bleus » where English says “he has blue eyes”.
fr-u05-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

What does he look like?

To ask what someone is like, French has one very common question: Il est comment ? / Elle est comment ? It covers both looks and personality, like English “What's he like?” and “What does he look like?” at the same time. The answer starts with être + adjective, and the adjective agrees with the person, as you know.

MasculineFeminineEnglish
grandgrandetall
petitpetiteshort, small
minceminceslim
jeunejeuneyoung
brunbrunedark-haired
blondblondeblond, fair-haired
rouxroussered-haired

Listen to the feminine: the final consonant, silent in the masculine, is heard when an e follows: grand / grande, petit / petite, blond / blonde. Mince and jeune already end in e, so they don't change. Roux has an irregular feminine: rousse.

Mon frère est grand et brun. Ma sœur est petite et blonde.My brother is tall and dark-haired. My sister is short and blond.

False friend: brun describes hair, not skin or eyes. Il est brun = he has dark (brown or black) hair. For brown eyes, you'll use another word, marron, on the next screen.

", "

Eyes, hair, glasses: avoir and porter

For eyes and hair, English says “he has blue eyes”. French also uses avoir, but with the definite article les, not des and not a possessive: Il a les yeux bleus. Learn this pattern as a block.

FrenchEnglish
Il a les yeux bleus / verts / noirs.He has blue / green / black eyes.
Elle a les yeux marron.She has brown eyes.
Elle a les cheveux longs / courts.She has long / short hair.
Il a les cheveux frisés.He has curly hair.
Elle a les cheveux blonds / bruns / roux / gris.She has blond / dark / red / gray hair.

Three details: les yeux is the plural of un œil (one eye); les cheveux is masculine plural, so its adjectives take -s (courts, longs, frisés); and marron never changes: les yeux marron. You can combine two adjectives with et: Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés.

Porter: glasses, a beard, clothes

Porter (a regular -er verb) means to wear: Il porte des lunettes (He wears glasses), Il porte une barbe, Elle porte une robe rouge. You can also say Il a une barbe.

Ressembler à: to look like

“I look like my mother” is Je ressemble à ma mère: no “look”, and a compulsory à, which contracts as usual: Tu ressembles au voisin, Ils ressemblent à leurs parents.

Léa ressemble à son père : elle a les yeux verts et les cheveux roux.Léa looks like her father: she has green eyes and red hair.
", "

Personality

Many character adjectives have a feminine that is more than just an added e. These endings come back in hundreds of adjectives, so they're worth learning now.

EndingMasculineFeminineEnglish
-eux → -eusesérieuxsérieuseserious
-il → -illegentilgentillekind, nice
-if → -ivesportifsportivesporty, athletic
-eur → -eusetravailleurtravailleusehardworking
-et → -ètediscretdiscrètediscreet, reserved
-e (no change)drôledrôlefunny
-e (no change)timidetimideshy

Gentil is pronounced with a silent l (“zhan-tee”), but gentille ends with a y sound (“zhan-tee-y”). Sérieux doesn't change in the masculine plural: mes frères sont sérieux.

In everyday speech, you'll hear sympa all the time: it's short for sympathique and has the same form for a man and a woman: Il est sympa, Elle est sympa. Careful: sympathique means nice, friendly, not “sympathetic”.

Putting it all together

Remember the position of adjectives: these all go after the noun (une fille sportive, un garçon timide), while the short group grand, petit, jeune, beau goes before: une jeune femme sérieuse, un grand garçon sportif.

Ma cousine est grande et mince. Elle a les cheveux courts et elle porte des lunettes. Elle est très gentille, mais un peu timide.My cousin is tall and slim. She has short hair and wears glasses. She's very kind, but a little shy.

To soften a description, French people love un peu (a little) and assez (quite): Il est un peu timide, Elle est assez grande.

fr-u05-l3.title: What I like
fr-u05-l3.topic: aimer, adorer, détester, préférer + definite article or infinitive; moi aussi / moi non plus
fr-u05-l3.why: Now that you can describe people, you learn to talk about tastes: what you love, like, prefer or can't stand, and how to react to someone else's tastes. The key point is the definite article after aimer, where English uses no article at all.
fr-u05-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

J'aime le chocolat: the article English leaves out

To talk about tastes, you have a whole scale of regular -er verbs, from love to hate. Préférer has the stem change you know: je préfère, nous préférons.

FrenchEnglish
J'adore…I love…
J'aime beaucoup…I really like…
J'aime bien…I like…, I quite like…
Je n'aime pas beaucoup…I don't really like…
Je n'aime pas…I don't like…
Je déteste…I hate…
Je préfère…I prefer…

Here is the key point. English says “I like chocolate”, “I love movies”, “I hate rain”, with no article. French always needs the definite article after these verbs, because you're talking about the thing in general: J'aime le chocolat, J'adore les films, Je déteste la pluie, Je préfère l'été. Never j'aime chocolat, and never du: du chocolat means some chocolate, a quantity.

A taste (in general)A quantity (some)
J'aime le fromage.Je prends du fromage.
J'adore la confiture.Je voudrais de la confiture.
Je préfère l'eau.Je bois de l'eau.

The negative keeps the article

You learned that du / de la / des become de after ne… pas. That rule does not apply to le / la / les: Je n'aime pas le café, Il ne déteste pas les chats. Saying je n'aime pas de café is one of the most frequent mistakes.

With things you can count, use the plural: J'adore les croissants, Je n'aime pas les chiens. With a singular noun, French means the thing as a substance or an idea: le fromage, la musique, le sport.

", "

Aimer + infinitive, and aimer with people

To say you like doing something, put the second verb in the infinitive, as after vouloir or pouvoir. English often uses an -ing form here (“I love traveling”); French never does.

J'aime lire le soir.I like reading in the evening.
Ma sœur adore voyager, mais elle déteste attendre à l'aéroport.My sister loves traveling, but she hates waiting at the airport.
Je n'aime pas cuisiner. Je préfère faire la vaisselle !I don't like cooking. I prefer doing the dishes!

Je t'aime or je t'aime bien?

With things, bien makes aimer a little softer: J'aime bien le jazz (I quite like jazz). With people, the difference is huge. Je t'aime means “I love you” (a partner, your children, your parents). Je t'aime bien means “I like you” (a friend, a colleague). Adding bien, which normally means “well”, makes it weaker, not stronger: a classic misunderstanding for English speakers!

Take t' in je t'aime as a fixed form for now: pronouns like this one are the topic of the next lesson. For a person in general, simply say J'aime bien Thomas, Il est sympa.

Ça me plaît

You'll also hear Ça me plaît (I like it; literally “it pleases me”) and the question Ça te plaît ? (Do you like it?). Learn them as fixed expressions: Lyon ? Ça me plaît beaucoup !

Never say j'aime bien to your partner if you mean love: it sounds like friendship. And don't say je t'aime to a new colleague!

", "

Me too, me neither: hobbies

Reacting to what someone likes is easy in French, as long as you watch whether the first sentence is positive or negative.

They say…You agreeYou disagree
J'aime le jazz.Moi aussi. (me too)Pas moi. (not me)
Je n'aime pas le jazz.Moi non plus. (me neither)Moi si. (I do)

The English trap: after a negative sentence, “me neither” is moi non plus, never moi aussi. And si is the yes that contradicts a negative, as you saw with questions: — Je n'aime pas le fromage. — Moi si ! J'adore ça.

Jouer à, jouer de, faire de

English “play” covers sports, games and instruments. French splits them:

PatternUsed forExamples
jouer à (au, à la, aux)sports and gamesjouer au foot, au tennis, aux cartes
jouer de (du, de la, des)musical instrumentsjouer du piano, de la guitare, du violon
faire de (du, de la, de l')activities, many sportsfaire du vélo, du yoga, de la natation, de la randonnée
Mon frère joue au foot le samedi et ma sœur joue de la guitare.My brother plays soccer on Saturdays and my sister plays the guitar.
— Tu fais du sport ? — Oui, je fais de la natation et du vélo.— Do you do any sport? — Yes, I swim and I cycle.

Remember the contractions: à + le = au, de + le = du. So jouer au tennis but jouer du piano.

fr-u05-l4.title: Le, la, les: object pronouns
fr-u05-l4.topic: direct object pronouns in the present; lire and écrire
fr-u05-l4.why: To avoid repeating the same noun, French uses short object pronouns that go before the verb, the opposite of English “I see him”. This lesson covers le, la, l', les, me, te, nous and vous in the present, and adds two useful verbs, lire and écrire.
fr-u05-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Him, her, it, them: le, la, les

To avoid repeating a noun, English uses “him”, “her”, “it” or “them” after the verb: “I know her”. French uses a short pronoun too, but it goes before the verb: Je la connais, literally “I her know”. This is the big change to get used to.

— Tu connais Marie ? — Oui, je la connais.— Do you know Marie? — Yes, I know her.
— Tu regardes le film ? — Oui, je le regarde.— Are you watching the movie? — Yes, I'm watching it.
— Tu attends les enfants ? — Oui, je les attends.— Are you waiting for the children? — Yes, I'm waiting for them.
PronounReplacesExample
lea masculine noun: him, itLe bus ? Je le prends.
laa feminine noun: her, itLa clé ? Je la cherche.
l'le or la before a vowel or silent hParis ? Je l'aime beaucoup.
lesa plural noun: themLes livres ? Je les lis.

English “it” has no gender, but French does: you choose le or la according to the noun you're replacing. Le livre → le, la voiture → la. With a vowel, both become l', and with les you hear a liaison: je les‿attends.

Me, you, us

The other persons work the same way, before the verb: me (m'), te (t'), nous, vous.

Tu me cherches ? Je suis là ! Je t'attends devant la gare.Are you looking for me? I'm here! I'm waiting for you in front of the station.
Nos voisins nous invitent samedi. Ils vous invitent aussi ?Our neighbors are inviting us on Saturday. Are they inviting you too?
", "

Where does it go?

The rule is always the same: the pronoun sits right in front of the verb it belongs to. In a negative sentence, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the verb, so the pronoun stays glued to the verb.

FrenchEnglish
affirmativeJe le connais.I know him.
negativeJe ne le connais pas.I don't know him.
questionTu la connais ?Do you know her?
negative + vowelJe ne l'aime pas.I don't like it.
with an infinitiveJe veux le voir.I want to see him / it.
infinitive + negativeJe ne peux pas les prendre.I can't take them.

With vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, aimer + infinitive, the pronoun goes in front of the infinitive, because that's the verb it belongs to: Tu peux m'attendre ? (Can you wait for me?), Je dois l'appeler (I have to call him / her).

The English trap: verbs without a preposition

Four very common verbs take a preposition in English but none in French. Their object is direct, so they take le / la / les:

FrenchEnglishWith a pronoun
regarder la téléto look at, to watchJe la regarde.
écouter la radioto listen toJe l'écoute.
chercher mes clésto look forJe les cherche.
attendre le busto wait forJe l'attends.

So Je l'attends means “I'm waiting for him” or “I'm waiting for her”, and j'attends pour le bus is wrong. Never add pour after attendre or chercher.

", "

Two new verbs: lire and écrire

Two irregular verbs that go perfectly with object pronouns: you read a book, a message, the newspaper, and you write a letter, a postcard, a text.

lire (to read)écrire (to write)
je / j'lisécris
tulisécris
il / elle / onlitécrit
nouslisonsécrivons
vouslisezécrivez
ils / elleslisentécrivent

The singular forms all sound the same (“lee”, “ay-kree”): the final s and t are silent. The plural reveals a hidden consonant: an s pronounced like z in lisons, lisent, and a v in écrivons, écrivent. Décrire (to describe) is conjugated like écrire.

— Tu lis le journal le matin ? — Oui, je le lis avec mon café.— Do you read the newspaper in the morning? — Yes, I read it with my coffee.
— Elle écrit la carte postale ? — Oui, elle l'écrit pour sa grand-mère.— Is she writing the postcard? — Yes, she's writing it for her grandmother.
Mes enfants ne lisent pas les romans de Zola : ils les trouvent difficiles.My children don't read Zola's novels: they find them difficult.

Note the elision: j'écris, and with a pronoun je l'écris, je ne l'écris pas.

For now, use pronouns for the thing you read or write: Le message ? Je l'écris. Writing to a person uses a different kind of pronoun, which you'll learn later.

fr-u05-l5.title: Review: talking about your people
fr-u05-l5.why: This review brings together the whole unit: possessives and family words, physical and character description, tastes with aimer and the definite article, and object pronouns. Looking at family photos with a friend in Nantes, you put it all to work in one natural conversation.
fr-u05-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

My people: possessives and description

This unit gave you everything you need to talk about the people in your life. Let's review it piece by piece, starting with the possessives and the way you describe someone.

masc.fem.plural
mymonmames
your (tu)tontates
his / hersonsases
ournotrenotrenos
your (vous)votrevotrevos
theirleurleurleurs
  • The possessive agrees with the thing owned: Pierre et sa femme, Julie et son mari.
  • Mon / ton / son before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: mon amie, son école.
  • No “'s”: la sœur de Paul, then sa sœur.

Describing someone

Three verbs do almost all the work: être + adjective (Elle est grande et rousse), avoir + les for eyes and hair (Il a les yeux marron et les cheveux courts), and porter (Elle porte des lunettes). Adjectives agree with the person:

MasculineFemininePattern
blondblonde+ e
curieuxcurieuse-eux → -euse
sportifsportive-if → -ive
travailleurtravailleuse-eur → -euse
discretdiscrète-et → -ète
gentilgentille-il → -ille
rouxrousseirregular
Mon beau-frère est grand et brun. Il ressemble à son père : il est très calme et un peu timide.My brother-in-law is tall and dark-haired. He looks like his father: he's very calm and a bit shy.
", "

Tastes and pronouns

To say what people like, remember the definite article after aimer, adorer, détester and préférer, even in the negative: Ma nièce adore le chocolat, Mon père n'aime pas la musique classique. After these verbs, a second verb stays in the infinitive: Mes parents aiment voyager.

They say…AgreeDisagree
J'adore les chats.Moi aussi.Pas moi.
Je n'aime pas les chats.Moi non plus.Moi si.

And for hobbies: jouer au foot (sports, games), jouer du piano (instruments), faire de la natation (activities).

Le, la, les: don't repeat, replace

Object pronouns are perfect for talking about people and their tastes without repeating names. They go before the verb, or before the infinitive when there is one:

Le chocolat ? Ma nièce l'adore.Chocolate? My niece loves it.
Mes cousins ? Je ne les connais pas bien.My cousins? I don't know them well.
Ta grand-mère ? Je veux la rencontrer !Your grandmother? I want to meet her!
Les photos de famille ? Je les regarde avec ma mère.The family photos? I look at them with my mother.

A pronoun replaces a noun with le / la / les or a possessive in front of it: mon frère → le, ses amies → les. With aimer and a person, je l'aime means love; for a friend, say je l'aime bien.

", "

Putting it together: talking about a photo

Looking at family photos is a classic moment in France, and it uses everything in this unit. Here are the phrases you need to show who is where.

FrenchEnglish
C'est qui, sur la photo ? / Qui est-ce ?Who's that in the picture?
Sur la photo, il y a…In the picture, there is / are…
À gauche, c'est ma tante.On the left, that's my aunt.
Au milieu, ce sont mes grands-parents.In the middle, those are my grandparents.
Devant, c'est mon neveu, et derrière, ma belle-sœur.In front, that's my nephew, and behind, my sister-in-law.
C'est au mariage de mon frère.It's at my brother's wedding.

Notice: a photo is something you're “on” in French, not “in”: sur la photo.

Common mistakes to avoid

Not thisBut this
Léa et sa frèreLéa et son frère
ma amiemon amie
j'aime chocolatj'aime le chocolat
je n'aime pas de caféje n'aime pas le café
je connais laje la connais
— Je n'aime pas ça. — Moi aussi.— Je n'aime pas ça. — Moi non plus.

When you show someone your photos, French people often react with Il est mignon ! / Elle est mignonne ! (He's / She's cute!) for children, or Vous vous ressemblez ! (You look alike!).

fr-u06-l1.title: My plans: aller + infinitive
fr-u06-l1.why: With aller + infinitive, you can finally talk about the future: what you're going to do tonight, this weekend or next summer. It's the most common way to talk about plans in everyday French, and you already know all the pieces.
fr-u06-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Je vais + infinitive: going to

Good news: the most common way to talk about the future in French works exactly like English “going to”. Take aller in the present, which you know well, and add an infinitive.

aller+ infinitiveEnglish
jevaispartirI'm going to leave
tuvaspartiryou're going to leave
il / elle / onvapartirhe / she is, we're going to leave
nousallonspartirwe're going to leave
vousallezpartiryou're going to leave
ils / ellesvontpartirthey're going to leave
Ce soir, je vais dîner avec Léa.Tonight, I'm going to have dinner with Léa.
Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?What are you going to do this weekend?
Mes parents vont visiter la Bretagne en juin.My parents are going to visit Brittany in June.

Now you understand Je vais prendre…, which you used at the café as a fixed phrase: it simply means “I'm going to have…”. You can even say Je vais aller à Lyon: aller + aller is perfectly normal.

Plans in the present

English often uses the -ing form for arrangements: “I'm having dinner with Léa tonight”. French can use the near future or the plain present with a time word: Ce soir, je dîne avec Léa. And for a timetable, French uses the present, like English: Le train part à 8 h (The train leaves at 8), Le film commence à 21 h.

Don't confuse movement and plans: Je vais au marché (I'm going to the market: a place) and Je vais acheter du pain (I'm going to buy bread: a plan). Both use aller, as in English.

", "

Negation, pronouns and pronominal verbs

Since aller is the conjugated verb, the negation goes around it, and the infinitive stays outside:

Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir.I'm not going to go out tonight.
Elle ne va pas venir : elle est malade.She isn't going to come: she's sick.
On ne va pas prendre la voiture.We're not going to take the car.

Object pronouns go before the infinitive

As with vouloir and pouvoir, the pronoun belongs to the infinitive and goes right in front of it: Le film ? Je vais le voir demain. Tu vas l'appeler ? Je ne vais pas les attendre.

Pronominal verbs: the pronoun matches the subject

With a pronominal verb, the reflexive pronoun stays in front of the infinitive and changes with the subject. English “I'm going to bed” is Je vais me coucher.

se reposerEnglish
jevais me reposerI'm going to rest
tuvas te reposeryou're going to rest
il / elle / onva se reposerhe / she is, we're going to rest
nousallons nous reposerwe're going to rest
vousallez vous reposeryou're going to rest
ils / ellesvont se reposerthey're going to rest

A very common mistake: je vais se coucher. The pronoun is not part of the infinitive, it follows the person: je vais me coucher, nous allons nous lever tôt.

", "

When? Time markers

To place your plans in time, you need a set of markers. Most of them can go at the start or at the end of the sentence: Demain, je vais travailler or Je vais travailler demain.

FrenchEnglish
ce soirtonight, this evening
ce week-endthis weekend
demain / demain matintomorrow / tomorrow morning
après-demainthe day after tomorrow
lundi prochainnext Monday
la semaine prochainenext week
le mois prochainnext month
l'année prochainenext year
dans deux jours / dans une heurein two days / in an hour (from now)

Take ce soir and ce week-end as fixed markers for now. Prochain is an adjective: it goes after the noun here and agrees with it, le mois prochain, la semaine prochaine.

Dans, not en

To say when something will happen, counting from now, use dans: Je pars dans trois jours (I'm leaving in three days). En + duration means how long something takes: Je fais le trajet en trois heures (I do the trip in three hours). English uses “in” for both, so this is a frequent slip.

On part en vacances dans deux semaines. On va louer une maison à la mer.We're going on vacation in two weeks. We're going to rent a house by the sea.

Planning a trip? Visiter is for places: visiter Lyon, visiter un musée. For people, say voir des amis or aller chez mes parents.

fr-u06-l2.title: The present English doesn't use
fr-u06-l2.topic: depuis + present; être en train de; venir de + infinitive
fr-u06-l2.why: French has no -ing form and often uses the present where English uses another tense. This lesson shows how to stress an action in progress with être en train de, how to say how long something has been going on with depuis and ça fait… que, and how to say what has just happened with venir de.
fr-u06-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

No -ing: être en train de

French has no -ing tense. Je mange means “I eat”, “I'm eating” and “I do eat”, all at once. Most of the time, the simple present is all you need: — Tu fais quoi ? — Je regarde un film. (— What are you doing? — I'm watching a movie.)

When you want to stress that an action is happening right now, that you're in the middle of it, use être en train de + infinitive. Only être changes:

être en train de + infinitiveEnglish
jesuis en train de travaillerI'm (busy) working
tues en train de travailleryou're working
il / elle / onest en train de travaillerhe / she is, we're working
noussommes en train de travaillerwe're working
vousêtes en train de travailleryou're working
ils / ellessont en train de travaillerthey're working
Je ne peux pas parler : je suis en train de cuisiner.I can't talk: I'm in the middle of cooking.
Les enfants sont en train de dormir.The children are sleeping (right now).

De becomes d' before a vowel: Elle est en train d'écrire un message. The negation goes around être: Je ne suis pas en train de dormir !

Don't translate every English -ing with en train de. “I'm living in Paris” or “I'm learning French” are just J'habite à Paris, J'apprends le français. Keep en train de for something happening at this very moment.

", "

Depuis + present: still going on

Here is one of the biggest differences with English. To say how long something has been going on, English uses the present perfect: “I have lived here for three years”. French uses the present, because the action is still true now:

J'habite ici depuis trois ans.I've lived here for three years.
Il travaille à Lille depuis 2020.He's been working in Lille since 2020.
Je t'attends depuis une heure !I've been waiting for you for an hour!

Depuis translates both “for” (a duration: depuis trois ans, depuis deux heures) and “since” (a starting point: depuis lundi, depuis septembre, depuis 2020). Translating word for word with j'ai habité is a classic mistake: that tense, which you'll learn soon, would mean it's over.

Asking the question

QuestionAsks forAnswer
Depuis quand tu habites ici ?a starting point (since when?)Depuis janvier.
Depuis combien de temps tu habites ici ?a duration (how long?)Depuis six mois.

Ça fait… que

In speech, you'll often hear the same idea with ça fait + duration + que + present, with the duration at the front: Ça fait trois ans que j'habite ici (It's been three years that I've lived here). Que becomes qu' before a vowel: Ça fait deux mois qu'il apprend le français.

Ask yourself: is it still going on? If yes, French uses the present with depuis, even if English uses “have been”.

", "

Venir de + infinitive: just

To say that something has just happened, French uses venir de + infinitive. It's the mirror image of aller + infinitive: you're “coming from” the action.

venir de + infinitiveEnglish
jeviens d'arriverI've just arrived
tuviens de mangeryou've just eaten
il / elle / onvient de partirhe / she has, we've just left
nousvenons de finirwe've just finished
vousvenez de rentreryou've just got home
ils / ellesviennent de téléphonerthey've just phoned

Pronouns go before the infinitive, as usual: Je viens de me lever (I've just got up), Le message ? Je viens de le lire. Careful: venir de + a place means to come from: Je viens de Lyon (I'm from Lyon). Only an infinitive after de gives the meaning “just”.

Just did, doing now, going to do

You now have three ways to place an action around the present moment:

Just beforeRight nowJust after
Je viens de manger.Je suis en train de faire la vaisselle.Je vais me coucher.
I've just eaten.I'm doing the dishes.I'm going to go to bed.
— Allô ? Tu es où ? — Je viens d'arriver à la gare. Je suis en train de chercher un taxi.— Hello? Where are you? — I've just arrived at the station. I'm looking for a taxi.

On the phone, Je viens de… is everywhere: Il vient de sortir (He's just gone out), Elle vient de partir. It's a great way to talk about the recent past before you learn the past tenses.

fr-u06-l3.title: Linking ideas, and more negatives
fr-u06-l3.topic: connectors et, ou, mais, parce que, alors, donc, d'abord, puis, ensuite, enfin, quand; ne… jamais / plus / rien / personne
fr-u06-l3.why: To speak fluently, you need to link your sentences and say what you never, no longer or don't yet do. This lesson gives you the everyday connectors (mais, parce que, alors, donc, d'abord, ensuite, enfin, quand…) and the negatives ne… jamais, ne… plus, ne… rien, ne… personne and ne… pas encore.
fr-u06-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Linking your ideas

Short sentences are fine for a start, but to sound fluent you need to link them. French connectors are small, frequent words, and most of them work like their English equivalents.

FrenchEnglishExample
et / ouand / orJe prends un thé ou un café.
maisbutJ'aime Paris, mais c'est cher.
parce que (parce qu')becauseJe reste ici parce qu'il pleut.
carbecause (written)Le magasin est fermé car c'est dimanche.
alorsso, thenIl est tard, alors je rentre.
doncso, thereforeJe suis malade, donc je ne travaille pas.
quandwhenQuand il fait beau, je vais au travail à vélo.
aussitoo, alsoJe parle anglais et je parle aussi espagnol.

Alors is more spoken, donc a little more logical; both translate English “so”. Car belongs to writing: in conversation, say parce que. With quand, French uses the present for habits, as in English: Quand je rentre, je fais la cuisine.

Telling things in order

To describe a routine step by step, use d'abord (first), puis and ensuite (then), après (after that) and enfin (finally).

D'abord, je me lève à sept heures. Ensuite, je prends une douche et je m'habille. Puis je bois un café. Après, je pars au travail. Enfin, le soir, je me repose.First, I get up at seven. Then I take a shower and get dressed. Then I drink a coffee. After that, I leave for work. Finally, in the evening, I relax.

Vary your connectors: ensuite, puis and après all mean “then”, and French speakers avoid repeating the same one three times in a row.

", "

Never, no longer, nothing, nobody

You know ne… pas. The other negatives work exactly the same way: ne before the conjugated verb, and a second word after it, in place of pas.

FrenchEnglishExample
ne… pasnotJe ne fume pas.
ne… jamaisneverJe ne fume jamais.
ne… plusno longer, not anymoreJe ne fume plus.
ne… riennothing, not anythingJe ne mange rien le matin.
ne… personnenobody, not anyoneJe ne connais personne ici.
ne… pas encorenot yetJe ne travaille pas encore.

The second word replaces pas: never ne… pas jamais. Like ne… pas, these negatives go around the conjugated verb, and ne becomes n' before a vowel: Elle n'habite plus à Lyon, Il n'y a personne. The opposite of ne… jamais is toujours (always): Je prends toujours le métro.

English traps

  • English says “I don't eat anything”, with “not” + “anything”. French has only one negative word after the verb: Je ne mange rien.
  • Plus here means “no more, not anymore”, not “more”. In this negative, its s is silent: Je ne fume plus (“plu”).
  • With an infinitive, rien goes before it but personne goes after it: Je ne veux rien manger, Je ne veux voir personne.

In speech, French people often drop the ne: Je fume plus, J'ai rien, Je connais personne. You'll hear it everywhere, but always write the ne.

", "

De after negatives; rien and personne as subjects

Just as with ne… pas, the partitive du / de la / des and un / une become de (d') after all these negatives:

Je ne bois jamais de café.I never drink coffee.
Il n'y a plus de pain.There's no more bread.
Je n'ai pas encore d'enfants.I don't have any children yet.

But the definite article le / la / les doesn't change, especially after aimer: Je n'aime plus le café (I don't like coffee anymore).

Rien ne…, personne ne…

Rien and personne can also be the subject of the sentence. They go first, followed by ne and the verb, and there is no pas:

Personne ne parle dans le train.Nobody talks on the train.
Rien ne change dans ma rue.Nothing changes in my street.
Personne n'habite ici.Nobody lives here.

Short answers

QuestionAnswer
Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?Rien. (Nothing.)
Qui est là ?Personne. (Nobody.)
Tu fumes ?Non, jamais. (No, never.)
Tu travailles ?Pas encore. (Not yet.)

Don't confuse the pronoun personne (nobody) with the noun une personne (a person), which is always feminine: C'est une personne très gentille, even for a man.

fr-u06-l4.topic: frequent false friends and everyday expressions
fr-u06-l4.why: Before the big review of the basics, this lesson clears up the false friends that trip up every English speaker (actuellement, librairie, assister, sensible…) and gives you the little expressions French people use all day long. No new grammar: just words that make you sound natural and keep you out of trouble.

{"lessons": ["

False friends: words that lie

French and English share thousands of words: la table, important, possible, la question… Most of the time, that's a gift. But a handful of very common words look English and mean something else. The French call them les faux amis, \"false friends\", and they cause the funniest misunderstandings.

French wordWhat it really meansFor the English word, say…
actuellementcurrently, at the momentactually → en fait
une librairiea bookshoplibrary → une bibliothèque
assister àto attendto assist → aider
resterto stayto rest → se reposer
une locationa rentala location → un endroit
la monnaiechange (coins)money → l'argent
une vestea jacketa vest → un gilet
un cara coach, an intercity busa car → une voiture

The worst one is probably actuellement. When an English speaker says \"actually\", a French person hears \"at the moment\". To say \"actually\", use en fait.

Actuellement, je travaille à Lyon.At the moment, I work in Lyon.
En fait, je n'aime pas le café.Actually, I don't like coffee.
Je veux acheter un livre : il y a une librairie près d'ici ?I want to buy a book: is there a bookshop near here?
Demain, j'assiste à une réunion à neuf heures.Tomorrow, I'm attending a meeting at nine.
Vous avez de la monnaie sur vingt euros ?Do you have change for twenty euros?

Rester never means \"to rest\": Je reste à la maison ce soir = I'm staying home tonight. To rest is se reposer, which you know from your daily routine: Le dimanche, je me repose.

", "

More traps: sensible, éventuellement, journée…

A second group of false friends is more subtle: the meaning isn't completely different, but it has shifted.

  • sensible = sensitive (easily hurt, or delicate). \"Sensible\" in the English sense is raisonnable.
  • éventuellement = possibly, if need be. It never means \"eventually\", which is closer to finalement (a word you'll meet again soon).
  • formidable = great, wonderful. It's purely positive, never scary or impressive in a threatening way.
  • dur = hard, in both senses: not soft, and difficult. Travailler dur = to work hard; C'est dur ! = It's tough!
Ma fille est très sensible : elle n'aime pas les films tristes.My daughter is very sensitive: she doesn't like sad movies.
Tu es raisonnable : tu ne sors pas ce soir.You're sensible: you're not going out tonight.
On peut éventuellement dîner plus tard.We can possibly have dinner later.
Le spectacle est formidable !The show is wonderful!

Un jour or une journée?

English has one word, \"day\". French has two. Le jour is the day as a unit or a date; la journée is the day as a stretch of time, with everything you do in it. The same pattern exists for le soir / la soirée (evening) and le matin / la matinée (morning).

le jour: a unit, a datela journée: the whole day, its content
trois jours, quel jour, le jour de mon anniversaireBonne journée !, toute la journée, une journée difficile

When a long English word ends in -tion, -ible or -able, it usually means the same in French: une réservation, possible, confortable. The false friends are a short list: learn them as exceptions, and trust the other look-alikes.

", "

Everyday expressions

These little phrases are everywhere in France. They make your French sound natural immediately, and they cost no grammar at all.

ExpressionMeaningWhen to use it
d'accordOK, all rightto agree, in any situation
ça marchesounds good, OKcasual; waiters say it too
pas de soucino problemcasual and very frequent
ça ne fait riennever mind, it doesn't matterwhen something small goes wrong
ce n'est pas graveit's no big deal, don't worryto answer an apology
bon appétitenjoy your mealbefore eating, to everyone at the table
à tout à l'heuresee you later (today)when you'll meet again the same day
à plus tard, à plussee you latercasual; in texts, A+
oh là làoh dear, wowsurprise, annoyance, admiration
bofmehnot impressed, not really
ça dépendit dependswhen you can't answer yes or no
— Pardon, je n'ai pas de monnaie. — Ce n'est pas grave.—Sorry, I don't have any change. —Don't worry about it.
— On dîne à huit heures ? — Ça marche !—Shall we have dinner at eight? —Sounds good!
— Tu aimes ce film ? — Bof…—Do you like this movie? —Meh…

In speech, ce n'est pas grave often becomes c'est pas grave, without ne. You'll hear it all the time, but write the full form. In à plus, the final s is pronounced. And oh là là has nothing to do with romance: it's what a French person says when the train is cancelled.

La bise

Friends and family greet each other with la bise, a light kiss on each cheek (faire la bise). Two kisses in Paris, sometimes three or four in other regions. With strangers and in professional settings, people shake hands.

In Quebec, c'est correct means \"it's fine, it's OK\". In France, correct means \"correct, acceptable\": say ça va or pas de souci instead.

fr-u06-l5.title: Review of the basics: ten minutes of conversation
fr-u06-l5.why: This big review closes the basics: the present and its irregular verbs, partitives, possessives, object pronouns, the near future, depuis, venir de and the negatives, all used together in a real conversation. After it, you're ready to tackle the past tenses of level A2.
fr-u06-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

Talking about your life in the present

You now have everything you need for a real conversation: who you are, what you do, what you like and what you're going to do. This review puts it all together, with the traps English speakers fall into most often.

One present for everything

French has a single present: je travaille = I work, I'm working, I do work. No \"do\" in questions or negatives: Tu travailles ?, Je ne travaille pas. Remember the three regular groups and the big irregulars:

parlerfinirattendreallerfaire
jeparlefinisattendsvaisfais
tuparlesfinisattendsvasfais
il / elle / onparlefinitattendvafait
nousparlonsfinissonsattendonsallonsfaisons
vousparlezfinissezattendezallezfaites
ils / ellesparlentfinissentattendentvontfont

Where English uses another tense

  • depuis + present for something still going on: J'habite à Lille depuis cinq ans = I've lived in Lille for five years. Same with ça fait… que: Ça fait cinq ans que j'habite ici.
  • venir de + infinitive for something that has just happened: Je viens d'arriver = I've just arrived.
  • être en train de + infinitive to stress an action in progress: Je suis en train de cuisiner.
Ça fait trois ans que je travaille à l'hôpital.I've been working at the hospital for three years.

Don't translate \"I have lived\" word for word. If the action is still going on, French keeps the present: J'habite ici depuis deux ans. And remember avoir for age: J'ai trente ans, never je suis trente.

", "

Tastes, things and people

The article: le or du?

To talk about what you like in general, French uses le, la, les where English uses nothing: J'adore le fromage (I love cheese). To talk about an unspecified amount, it uses du, de la, de l', des: Je prends du fromage (I'm having some cheese). After a negative, all of them become de: Je n'ai pas de voiture.

J'aime le vin rouge, mais ce soir, je bois de l'eau.I like red wine, but tonight I'm drinking water.
Je ne mange jamais de viande.I never eat meat.

Possessives agree with the thing

Son frère = his brother or her brother; sa voiture = his car or her car. The possessive agrees with the noun that follows, not with the owner. Before a vowel, use mon, ton, son even for a feminine noun: mon amie Sarah.

Object pronouns before the verb

Tu connais Léa ? — Oui, je la connais. The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, or before the infinitive when there is one: Je vais la voir demain.

The other negatives

NegativeMeaningExample
ne… jamaisneverJe ne bois jamais de café.
ne… plusno longer, not anymoreIl n'habite plus à Lyon.
ne… riennothingJe ne veux rien.
ne… personnenobodyJe ne connais personne ici.
ne… pas encorenot yetJe ne travaille pas encore.

One negative word per idea: Je ne veux rien = I don't want anything. Never add pas to jamais, plus, rien or personne.

", "

Plans, questions and keeping it going

The near future

Aller + infinitive: Je vais déménager, On va dîner chez Manon. The negative goes around aller: Je ne vais pas sortir. Markers: ce soir, demain, la semaine prochaine, dans deux jours.

Asking questions

Three registers: rising intonation (Tu viens ?), est-ce que (Est-ce que tu viens ?) and a few fixed inversions (Comment allez-vous ?). In casual speech, the question word often goes at the end: Tu habites où ?

To ask about…Question
workQu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
where someone livesTu habites où ? Depuis combien de temps ?
tastesTu aimes la cuisine indienne ?
plansQu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?
familyTu as des frères et sœurs ?

Tu or vous?

At a dinner with friends of friends, people of your age will quickly say tu. With an older person you're meeting for the first time, start with vous and wait for On se tutoie ?

Keeping the conversation going

Answer, then bounce the question back: Et toi ? / Et vous ? Agree with moi aussi or moi non plus, link your ideas with parce que, mais, alors, d'abord, ensuite, and use the little expressions: d'accord, ça dépend, pas de souci.

— Je n'aime pas le froid. — Moi non plus ! Alors, cet hiver, je vais partir à Nice.—I don't like the cold. —Me neither! So this winter, I'm going to Nice.

Ten minutes of conversation is mostly questions. Prepare five questions you can always ask: job, city, family, tastes, plans.

fr-u07-l1.topic: passé composé with avoir; regular and irregular participles; hier, déjà, pas encore, il y a
fr-u07-l1.why: This lesson opens level A2 with the passé composé, the past tense of everyday conversation, built with avoir and a past participle. You'll learn the regular participles, the irregular ones you need every day, and how to place the negative, so you can finally tell what you did yesterday.

{"lessons": ["

One past tense for three English ones

Welcome to level A2! Up to now, you've lived in the present. Now you're going to tell what happened. The passé composé (literally \"compound past\") is the tense of conversation: what you did yesterday, last weekend, last year.

It's built like the English present perfect: a helper verb + a past participle. For most verbs, the helper is avoir, in the present.

parlerfinirattendre
je / j'j'ai parléj'ai finij'ai attendu
tutu as parlétu as finitu as attendu
il / elle / onil a parléelle a finion a attendu
nousnous avons parlénous avons fininous avons attendu
vousvous avez parlévous avez finivous avez attendu
ils / ellesils ont parléelles ont finiils ont attendu

Making the participle

  • -er verbs → -é: parler → parlé, manger → mangé, acheter → acheté
  • -ir verbs like finir → -i: finir → fini, choisir → choisi; also dormir → dormi
  • -re verbs like attendre → -u: attendre → attendu, vendre → vendu, répondre → répondu

Here's the good news: where English has three forms, French has one. J'ai parlé = I spoke, I have spoken, I did speak. No \"did\" in questions or negatives, just like in the present.

Hier, j'ai mangé chez mes parents.Yesterday, I ate at my parents' place.
Tu as fini ton travail ?Have you finished your work? / Did you finish your work?

Parlé, parler and parlez all sound the same. Only the spelling shows the difference: after avoir, it's always the participle, j'ai parlé, never j'ai parler.

", "

Irregular participles

Many of the verbs you use all the time have an irregular participle. There's no shortcut: learn them like English \"seen, taken, written\". Several end in -u, -is or -it, which helps.

InfinitiveParticipleExample
fairefaitJ'ai fait les courses.
prendre (apprendre, comprendre)pris (appris, compris)Nous avons pris le train.
mettremisTu as mis la table ?
direditIl a dit bonjour.
écrireécritJ'ai écrit à Paul.
lireluElle a lu le journal.
voirvuOn a vu un bon film.
boirebuVous avez bu du champagne ?
avoireuJ'ai eu un problème.
êtreétéIl a été malade.
pouvoirpuJe n'ai pas pu venir.
vouloirvouluIls ont voulu partir.
devoirdûJ'ai dû travailler.
savoirsuTu as su répondre ?
connaîtreconnuElle a connu des moments difficiles.
ouvrirouvertJ'ai ouvert la fenêtre.

Two forms surprise English speakers. Eu (from avoir) is pronounced like the French u, a single sound: j'ai eu. And être takes avoir as its helper: j'ai été = I was, I have been. Never je suis été.

Dû keeps its circumflex to tell it apart from du (some): J'ai dû partir (I had to leave) but J'ai bu du café (I drank some coffee).

", "

Negatives, questions and time markers

The negative goes around the helper

Ne and pas surround avoir, not the participle: Je n'ai pas mangé. The same goes for jamais, rien, plus and pas encore. One exception: personne goes after the participle.

Je n'ai pas fini.I haven't finished. / I didn't finish.
Je n'ai jamais vu la mer.I've never seen the sea.
Il n'a rien dit.He didn't say anything.
Je n'ai vu personne.I didn't see anybody.

Questions

Exactly as in the present: Tu as bien dormi ? / Est-ce que vous avez fini ? / Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier ? Short adverbs like bien, déjà, beaucoup go between the helper and the participle: On a beaucoup mangé.

Time markers

FrenchEnglish
hier, hier soiryesterday, last night
avant-hierthe day before yesterday
ce matinthis morning
la semaine dernière, l'année dernièrelast week, last year
il y a deux jourstwo days ago
déjàalready, ever
pas encorenot yet
— Tu as déjà mangé ? — Non, pas encore.—Have you eaten yet? —No, not yet.

Don't mix up il y a and depuis. Il y a + time = \"ago\", with a finished action in the past: J'ai vu Paul il y a deux jours. Depuis + present = still going on: J'habite ici depuis deux ans.

fr-u07-l2.title: The passé composé with être
fr-u07-l2.topic: verbs conjugated with être; agreement with the subject
fr-u07-l2.why: After avoir, here is the other helper of the passé composé: être, used with a short list of verbs of movement and change of state. You'll learn the list, the agreement of the participle with the subject, and above all how to choose between être and avoir, a split English doesn't have.
fr-u07-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Some verbs use être

In English, the present perfect always uses \"have\". In French, a small group of verbs builds the passé composé with être instead of avoir. They are mostly verbs of movement from one place to another and of change of state (being born, dying, becoming). Many come in pairs of opposites, which makes them easier to learn:

VerbParticipleIts oppositeParticiple
aller (to go)allévenir (to come)venu
arriver (to arrive)arrivépartir (to leave)parti
entrer (to go in)entrésortir (to go out)sorti
monter (to go up)montédescendre (to go down)descendu
naître (to be born)némourir (to die)mort
rester (to stay)restétomber (to fall)tombé

Add retourner (to go back), rentrer (to come or go back home), revenir (to come back) and devenir (to become): retourné, rentré, revenu, devenu.

aller (passé composé)
jeje suis allé / je suis allée
tutu es allé / tu es allée
il / elle / onil est allé / elle est allée / on est allés
nousnous sommes allés / nous sommes allées
vousvous êtes allé(e)(s)
ils / ellesils sont allés / elles sont allées

Many English-speaking learners use the name \"Dr and Mrs Vandertramp\" to remember the list: each letter starts one of the verbs (devenir, revenir, monter, rester, sortir…). Whatever trick you use, the list is short: every other verb takes avoir.

", "

Agreement: the participle acts like an adjective

With être, the participle agrees with the subject, exactly like an adjective after être (elle est grande): add -e for a feminine subject, -s for a plural one, -es for a feminine plural one.

Paul est parti à huit heures.Paul left at eight.
Julie est partie à huit heures.Julie left at eight.
Mes frères sont arrivés hier.My brothers arrived yesterday.
Mes sœurs sont arrivées hier.My sisters arrived yesterday.
  • A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Paul et Julie sont venus.
  • Je and tu agree with the real person: a woman writes je suis allée, a man je suis allé.
  • Formal vous for one person agrees with that person: Madame, vous êtes arrivée quand ? / Monsieur, vous êtes arrivé quand ?
  • With on meaning \"we\", the participle usually agrees with the people in everyday writing: On est allés au cinéma (a group), On est allées à la plage (only women).

Most of the time you can't hear the agreement: allé, allée, allés sound the same. It's a spelling matter. One exception you can hear: il est mort / elle est morte.

Negatives and questions

The negative goes around être: Elle n'est pas venue. Je ne suis jamais allé à Rome. Questions work as usual: Tu es rentré à quelle heure ? / Est-ce que vous êtes sortis hier soir ?

When you read French, the agreement gives you information English doesn't: je suis arrivée tells you the writer is a woman.

", "

Être or avoir? Drilling the choice

English speakers tend to use avoir everywhere, because English uses \"have\" everywhere. The question to ask: is it one of the verbs on the list? If yes, être; if no, avoir. Be careful: not every verb of movement is on the list. Marcher (to walk), voyager (to travel), courir (to run) and nager (to swim) take avoir.

with avoirwith être
J'ai voyagé en Italie.Je suis allé en Italie.
Nous avons marché deux heures.Nous sommes rentrés à pied.
Elle a dormi chez sa sœur.Elle est restée chez sa sœur.
Ils ont pris le train.Ils sont partis en train.

A trip, step by step

Samedi, je suis partie de Rennes à neuf heures. Je suis arrivée à Saint-Malo à dix heures. J'ai visité la vieille ville et je suis montée sur les remparts.On Saturday, I left Rennes at nine. I arrived in Saint-Malo at ten. I visited the old town and went up on the ramparts.

For recognition: avoir with an object

Monter, descendre and sortir take avoir when they have a direct object. Then they mean \"to take up\", \"to take down\", \"to take out\":

Je suis sorti. / J'ai sorti la poubelle.I went out. / I took the trash out.
Elle est descendue. / Elle a descendu les valises.She went down. / She took the suitcases down.

Je suis né means \"I was born\": English uses a passive, French uses the passé composé of naître. Ma fille est née à Nantes.

fr-u07-l3.why: After avoir and être, this lesson puts your daily routine in the past: pronominal verbs always take être, keep their pronoun before the helper and agree with the subject. It completes the passé composé, so you can tell a whole day from waking up to going to bed.

{"lessons": ["

Pronominal verbs always take être

You know the pronominal verbs of your daily routine: je me lève, je me douche, je m'habille. In the passé composé, the rule is simple and has no exceptions: they always take être. The pronoun stays in front, before the helper.

se lever (passé composé)
jeje me suis levé / je me suis levée
tutu t'es levé / tu t'es levée
il / elle / onil s'est levé / elle s'est levée / on s'est levés
nousnous nous sommes levés / nous nous sommes levées
vousvous vous êtes levé(e)(s)
ils / ellesils se sont levés / elles se sont levées

Look at the elision: me stays whole before suis (a consonant), but te and se become t' and s' before es and est: tu t'es levé, il s'est levé. The pattern is the same for every pronominal verb:

Ce matin, je me suis réveillé à six heures.This morning, I woke up at six.
Elle s'est douchée et elle s'est habillée.She took a shower and got dressed.
Nous nous sommes couchés tard.We went to bed late.

English often has no pronoun at all: \"I got up\", \"she got dressed\", \"we had fun\". In French, the pronoun is part of the verb, in the present and in the past: je me suis levé, never j'ai levé or je suis levé.

", "

Negatives and questions

In the negative, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the helper. The pronoun and être stay glued together in the middle:

nepronoun + êtrepasparticiple
Je neme suispasréveillé à l'heure.
Tu net'espasreposée ?
Ils nese sontjamaisennuyés.
Je ne me suis pas réveillé à l'heure.I didn't wake up on time.
Elle ne s'est pas dépêchée.She didn't hurry.

Questions

Use intonation or est-ce que, as usual. The pronoun never moves.

Tu t'es bien reposée ?Did you get a good rest? (to a woman)
Est-ce que vous vous êtes amusés ?Did you have fun? (to a group)
Tu t'es couché à quelle heure ?What time did you go to bed?

With nous and vous, you get the pronoun twice: nous nous sommes promenés, vous vous êtes amusés. The first nous is the subject, the second one is the reflexive pronoun. In everyday speech, many people say on s'est promenés instead, which is lighter.

In casual speech you'll hear Je me suis pas réveillé, without ne. Understand it, but write the full form: Je ne me suis pas réveillé.

", "

Agreement, and a lazy Sunday

Since these verbs take être, the participle agrees with the subject in the common cases, as you saw in the last lesson: elle s'est réveillée, ils se sont amusés, elles se sont promenées.

Just a note for now: when a direct object follows the verb, the participle doesn't agree: Elle s'est lavé les mains (no -e), but Elle s'est lavée. You'll study this case later; for now, the common cases are enough.

se leverje me suis levé(e)I got up
se reposerje me suis reposé(e)I rested
se promenerje me suis promené(e)I went for a walk
s'amuserje me suis amusé(e)I had fun
s'ennuyerje me suis ennuyé(e)I was bored
se dépêcherje me suis dépêché(e)I hurried
se tromper deje me suis trompé(e) de busI took the wrong bus

A real story mixes pronominal verbs (with être), other être verbs and avoir verbs:

Dimanche, je me suis réveillée à dix heures. J'ai pris un café, je me suis douchée, puis je suis sortie. Je me suis promenée au bord de la Garonne et je me suis couchée tôt.On Sunday, I woke up at ten. I had a coffee, took a shower, then went out. I went for a walk along the Garonne and went to bed early.

And the French art of the lazy morning: faire la grasse matinée, to sleep in. Dimanche, j'ai fait la grasse matinée.

{"lessons": ["

Avoir or être: the decision in two seconds

You now know the whole passé composé. This review is about speed: choosing the right helper without thinking, and getting the agreement right. Ask yourself two questions, in this order:

  • Is the verb pronominal (se lever, s'amuser)? → être, and the participle agrees.
  • Is it on the short list of movement and change of state (aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, rentrer, revenir, devenir)? → être, and the participle agrees.
  • Anything else → avoir, and the participle doesn't change.
avoirêtrepronominal
jej'ai mangéje suis parti(e)je me suis levé(e)
tutu as mangétu es parti(e)tu t'es levé(e)
il / elle / onil a mangéelle est partieon s'est levés
nousnous avons mangénous sommes parti(e)snous nous sommes levé(e)s
vousvous avez mangévous êtes parti(e)(s)vous vous êtes levé(e)(s)
ils / ellesils ont mangéelles sont partiesils se sont levés
Samedi, Chloé a fait une randonnée, elle est rentrée tard et elle s'est couchée tout de suite.On Saturday, Chloé went hiking, got home late and went to bed right away.

The most common mistake for English speakers is j'ai allé or j'ai resté, copied from \"I have gone\", \"I have stayed\". Say it out loud until je suis allé and je suis resté sound natural.

", "

Telling it in order

A weekend is a story: first this, then that. These connectors, which you met with the present, work just as well in the past:

ConnectorEnglish
d'abordfirst
ensuitethen, next
puisthen
après, après le déjeunerafterwards, after lunch
enfinfinally, at last
D'abord, je suis allé au marché. Ensuite, j'ai préparé un pique-nique. Puis on s'est installés au parc. Enfin, on est rentrés à pied.First, I went to the market. Next, I made a picnic. Then we settled down in the park. Finally, we walked home.

The negative with each helper

The negative always surrounds the helper. With a pronominal verb, ne goes before the pronoun:

avoirêtrepronominal
Je n'ai pas travaillé.Je ne suis pas sorti.Je ne me suis pas levé.
Je n'ai rien fait.Je ne suis jamais allé à Lyon.Je ne me suis pas ennuyé.

When was it?

Samedi (last Saturday), dimanche soir, hier, le week-end dernier, il y a deux semaines. With a day of the week and no article, French means the last one: Samedi, je suis allé au cinéma. With le, it means every week: le samedi.

Il y a + time is \"ago\", for a finished event: Je suis allée à Nice il y a deux semaines. Don't use depuis here: depuis is for what is still going on.

Asking about someone's weekend

On Monday morning, the conversation at the coffee machine is always the same. Here are the questions you'll hear, and can ask:

QuestionEnglish
Tu as passé un bon week-end ?Did you have a good weekend?
Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ?What did you do?
Tu es parti(e) ? / Tu es allé(e) où ?Did you go away? Where did you go?
Tu es rentré(e) quand ?When did you get back?
Tu t'es bien reposé(e) ?Did you get a good rest?
Vous êtes sortis samedi soir ?Did you (all) go out on Saturday night?

React to keep the story going: Super !, Oh là là !, Pas mal ! (not bad), Moi aussi !, Moi non plus ! And answer briefly before bouncing the question back: Très bien, merci ! Je suis allé à la campagne. Et toi ?

Checklist before you speak

  • Helper: être for pronominal verbs and the list, avoir for the rest.
  • Agreement with être: elle est allée, ils sont partis, elles se sont amusées.
  • No agreement with avoir: elle a mangé, elles ont vu.
  • Irregular participles: fait, pris, mis, vu, lu, bu, eu, été, dû.

Passer means \"to spend\" with time: J'ai passé un bon week-end, J'ai passé deux jours à Lyon. Don't use dépenser, which is only for money.
