fr-u08-l1.title: When I was little: the imparfait
fr-u08-l1.topic: formation and uses of the imparfait
fr-u08-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on memories with the imparfait, the second past tense of French, used for habits, descriptions, age and weather in the past. It's the easiest tense to form, and it lets you talk about your childhood before learning, next time, how to combine it with the passé composé.
fr-u08-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

A second past tense: the imparfait

The passé composé tells what happened. But to talk about your childhood, describe a house or say what you used to do, French uses a second past tense: the imparfait. Good news: it's the most regular tense in French.

How to build it

Take the nous form of the present, remove -ons, and add the endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

Infinitivenous formStemje form
parlernous parlonsparl-je parlais
finirnous finissonsfiniss-je finissais
prendrenous prenonspren-je prenais
fairenous faisonsfais-je faisais
avoirnous avonsav-j'avais
allernous allonsall-j'allais
parlerfinirêtre
je / j'je parlaisje finissaisj'étais
tutu parlaistu finissaistu étais
il / elle / onil parlaitelle finissaiton était
nousnous parlionsnous finissionsnous étions
vousvous parliezvous finissiezvous étiez
ils / ellesils parlaientelles finissaientils étaient

Only être is irregular, with the stem ét-. The endings are the same for every verb. And -ais, -ait and -aient all sound the same, like the è of mère: je parlais, il parlait and ils parlaient are identical to the ear.

Spelling-change verbs keep the sound of the present: je mangeais (with an e, to keep the soft g), je commençais (with ç). But before -ions and -iez, no need: nous mangions, nous commencions.

", "

What the imparfait is for

1. Habits in the past

What you did regularly, over and over: English says \"used to\" or \"would\".

Quand j'étais petit, je jouais dans la rue.When I was little, I used to play in the street.
Le mercredi, j'allais chez ma grand-mère.On Wednesdays, I would go to my grandmother's.

2. Descriptions

What things and people were like, the setting of a scene.

La maison était grande et il y avait un jardin.The house was big and there was a garden.
Mon grand-père avait une barbe blanche.My grandfather had a white beard.

3. Age, time and weather in the past

J'avais dix ans. Il était huit heures. Il faisait beau.I was ten. It was eight o'clock. The weather was nice.

4. An action in progress

What was going on at a given moment: English \"was -ing\".

À midi, nous mangions sur la plage.At noon, we were eating on the beach.
EnglishFrench
I used to swimje nageais
I would swim (every summer)je nageais
I was swimmingje nageais

Careful with \"would\": only the \"would\" of habit becomes an imparfait (\"Every summer we would go to the sea\" = Tous les étés, on allait à la mer). The other \"would\", as in \"I would like\", is a different tense: je voudrais.

The passé composé and the imparfait work together: the first tells events, the second describes and sets the scene. Choosing between them is the subject of the next lesson.

Holidays at Grandma's in Brittany

Here's how a childhood memory sounds in French. Every verb is in the imparfait, because it's all habits and description:

Quand j'étais petite, je passais tous mes étés chez mes grands-parents, en Bretagne. Ils habitaient une vieille maison près de la mer. Le matin, mon grand-père allait au port et il achetait du poisson. L'après-midi, on allait à la plage avec mes cousins. Il faisait souvent gris, mais on adorait ça !When I was little, I spent every summer at my grandparents' in Brittany. They lived in an old house near the sea. In the morning, my grandfather would go to the harbor and buy fish. In the afternoon, we'd go to the beach with my cousins. It was often gray, but we loved it!

Then and now

The imparfait is perfect for comparing the past with the present:

Avant, j'habitais à Brest ; maintenant, j'habite à Paris.I used to live in Brest; now I live in Paris.
Avant, il n'y avait pas de téléphone portable.In the past, there were no cell phones.

Il y avait is the imparfait of il y a: there was, there were. It's one of the most useful forms for describing the past.

fr-u08-l2.title: Imparfait or passé composé?
fr-u08-l2.topic: choosing between imparfait and passé composé
fr-u08-l2.why: Now that you know both past tenses, this lesson teaches you to choose between them: the imparfait for the scene, habits and actions in progress, the passé composé for events and interruptions. It's the central difficulty of the French past for English speakers, practiced with many examples in context.
fr-u08-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

The scene and the action

This is the central difficulty of the French past for English speakers, because English often uses the same simple past for both (\"it rained\", \"I went out\"). Think of a film. The imparfait is the set: the weather, the place, what people were doing. The passé composé is the action: what happens, step by step, and moves the story forward.

imparfait: the scenepassé composé: the events
background, descriptionan action that happened, complete
an action in progress (\"was -ing\")an action that interrupts it
a habit (\"used to\", \"would\")one single occurrence
no clear beginning or enda precise moment or a defined period
Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti.It was raining when I went out.
Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.I was sleeping when the phone rang.
Il faisait beau, alors on a pique-niqué au parc.The weather was nice, so we had a picnic in the park.

The pattern \"action in progress + interruption\" is extremely common: the long action in the imparfait, the short one that cuts in, in the passé composé. You can also use être en train de in the imparfait to stress the action in progress:

J'étais en train de cuisiner quand Paul est arrivé.I was in the middle of cooking when Paul arrived.

A quick English test: if you can say \"was -ing\" or \"used to\", it's an imparfait. If it's a step in the story that answers \"and then what happened?\", it's a passé composé.

", "

Habit or one time?

The same verb can go either way, depending on whether it's a habit or a single event. Compare:

Le dimanche, on allait au marché.On Sundays, we used to go to the market. (every week)
Dimanche, on est allés au marché.On Sunday, we went to the market. (once, last Sunday)
D'habitude, je prenais le bus, mais ce jour-là, j'ai pris un taxi.Usually I took the bus, but that day I took a taxi.

Words that point the way

Often with the imparfaitOften with the passé composé
d'habitude, souvent, toujoursun jour, une fois
tous les jours, le lundihier, lundi dernier
autrefois, quand j'étais petittout à coup, soudain
pendant queà ce moment-là

Pendant que (while) introduces a background action, so it's followed by the imparfait: Pendant que je cuisinais, Paul a mis la table. Tout à coup and soudain (suddenly) announce an event: Tout à coup, j'ai entendu un bruit.

A defined period, even a long one, takes the passé composé when you see it as finished: J'ai habité trois ans à Lyon (and then I left). Without the limit, it's description: À cette époque, j'habitais à Lyon.

To ask what happened, learn this question as a fixed phrase: Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ? = What happened?

", "

Verbs that change meaning

Some verbs change meaning from one tense to the other. The imparfait describes a state; the passé composé marks the moment when something started or happened.

Verbimparfaitpassé composé
connaîtreje connaissais Marie: I knew Mariej'ai connu Marie: I met Marie (for the first time)
savoirje savais la vérité: I knew the truthj'ai su la vérité: I found out the truth
devoirje devais partir: I was supposed to leavej'ai dû partir: I had to leave (and I did)
avoirj'avais un chien: I had a dogj'ai eu un chien: I got a dog
Je devais venir, mais j'ai eu un problème.I was supposed to come, but I had a problem.
J'ai connu mon mari à Lyon. À cette époque, je ne connaissais personne.I met my husband in Lyon. At the time, I didn't know anybody.

Putting it together

Il était onze heures du soir. Il pleuvait et je rentrais chez moi en voiture. Tout à coup, la voiture est tombée en panne. Je n'avais plus de batterie sur mon téléphone, alors j'ai attendu.It was eleven at night. It was raining and I was driving home. Suddenly, the car broke down. My phone battery was dead, so I waited.

Look at the rhythm: the first sentences set the scene (était, pleuvait, rentrais), then tout à coup launches the events (est tombée, ai attendu). In the middle, je n'avais plus de batterie goes back to description.

When in doubt, ask: if I stop the film at this moment, is this something that is going on (imparfait) or something that happens (passé composé)?

fr-u08-l3.title: Telling a story
fr-u08-l3.topic: organizing a past narrative; time connectors; adverbs in -ment
fr-u08-l3.why: This lesson closes the unit on memories by turning the two past tenses into real stories: setting, trigger, events and ending, linked with connectors like soudain, au bout d'un moment and le lendemain. You'll also learn adverbs in -ment and how to react when someone tells you a story.
fr-u08-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Setting the scene, moving the story

You know the two past tenses and how to choose between them. Now let's tell a real story, with a beginning, a twist and an ending. A good anecdote in French follows a simple shape:

StepTenseUseful words
1. The settingimparfaitC'était l'été, il faisait chaud, j'étais à…
2. The triggerpassé composéun jour, ce jour-là, soudain, tout à coup
3. What happened nextbothalors, pendant que, au bout d'un moment
4. The endingpassé composéfinalement, le lendemain
ConnectorEnglish
un jourone day
ce jour-làthat day
soudain, tout à coupsuddenly
alorsso, then
pendant quewhile
au bout d'un momentafter a while
finalementin the end, eventually
le lendemainthe next day
C'était l'été et j'étais en vacances à Nice. Un jour, je me promenais sur la plage. Soudain, j'ai vu un chien dans l'eau. Alors, j'ai appelé le chien et, au bout d'un moment, il est sorti de l'eau. Finalement, j'ai trouvé son maître. Le lendemain, le chien m'attendait devant l'hôtel !It was summer and I was on vacation in Nice. One day, I was walking on the beach. Suddenly, I saw a dog in the water. So I called the dog and, after a while, it came out of the water. In the end, I found its owner. The next day, the dog was waiting for me in front of the hotel!

Finalement means \"in the end\" or \"eventually\": this is the word English speakers want when they say éventuellement, which means \"possibly\". And le lendemain is \"the next day\" in a story; demain only works from today.

", "

Adverbs in -ment

French -ment is the English \"-ly\": lentement = slowly. To build it, take the feminine form of the adjective and add -ment.

Adjective (m. / f.)AdverbEnglish
lent / lentelentementslowly
heureux / heureuseheureusementfortunately, luckily
malheureux / malheureusemalheureusementunfortunately
doux / doucedoucementgently, quietly
sérieux / sérieusesérieusementseriously
final / finalefinalementin the end

Three special cases

  • When the masculine ends in a vowel, add -ment to the masculine: vrai → vraiment, poli → poliment, absolu → absolument.
  • -ant becomes -amment and -ent becomes -emment, both pronounced \"-amment\": constant → constamment, évident → évidemment.
  • Irregular: gentil → gentiment, bon → bien, mauvais → mal.

Where to put it

After the verb in the present and the imparfait: Il conduit lentement. In the passé composé, short common adverbs often go between the helper and the participle: J'ai vraiment aimé ce film. Adverbs that comment on the whole sentence go first, followed by a comma: Heureusement, le train était à l'heure.

Évidemment, il est arrivé en retard !Of course, he arrived late!
Malheureusement, le musée était fermé.Unfortunately, the museum was closed.

Remember the false friend actuellement: it looks like \"actually\", but it's built on actuel (current) and means \"currently\". Not every -ment adverb matches its English look-alike.

", "

Reacting to a story

A story is a conversation: the listener reacts, and the reactions push the storyteller to continue. Here are the most common ones:

ReactionMeaning
Ah bon ?Really? Is that so?
Et alors ?And then what?
Sans blague !No kidding!
C'est pas vrai !No way! You're kidding!
Oh là là !Oh dear! Wow!
Quelle chance !How lucky!
Heureusement !Thank goodness!

C'est pas vrai ! is the spoken form, without ne. In writing, it's Ce n'est pas vrai ! Et alors ? can also sound like \"So what?\" if you say it flatly: say it with curiosity, rising at the end.

—Hier, j'ai perdu mon portefeuille dans le métro. —Ah bon ? Et alors ? —Une dame l'a trouvé et elle l'a apporté à la police. —Quelle chance !—Yesterday I lost my wallet on the métro. —Really? And then? —A lady found it and took it to the police. —How lucky!

A story that ends well

Notice how the tenses alternate in an anecdote: the scene in the imparfait, then a chain of events in the passé composé, with adverbs to give your opinion.

Ce jour-là, il pleuvait et le train avançait lentement. Soudain, il s'est arrêté au milieu de la campagne. Au bout d'un moment, un contrôleur est passé. Heureusement, il était vraiment sympa, et finalement, nous sommes arrivés à Marseille avec seulement une heure de retard.That day, it was raining and the train was moving slowly. Suddenly, it stopped in the middle of the countryside. After a while, a conductor came by. Luckily, he was really nice, and in the end we arrived in Marseille only an hour late.

To start an anecdote among friends, French people often say Il m'est arrivé un truc incroyable ! (Something incredible happened to me!). Learn it as a fixed phrase.

fr-u09-l1.title: Tickets, timetables, transport
fr-u09-l1.topic: buying a ticket, reading a timetable
fr-u09-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on travel at the train station: buying a one-way or round-trip ticket, reading a timetable with the 24-hour clock, and finding your way between the big Paris stations by métro. You'll also learn the numbers up to 1 000 for prices and distances, and use the passé composé to explain a missed train.
fr-u09-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

At the station: buying a ticket

France has a dense rail network: high-speed trains between the big cities, regional trains (le TER) for smaller towns. Whether you buy your ticket at the counter (le guichet), at a machine or on your phone, the words are the same.

FrenchEnglish
un billeta ticket
un aller simplea one-way ticket
un aller-retoura round-trip ticket
en première / en seconde (classe)in first / second class
une place côté fenêtrea window seat
une place côté couloiran aisle seat
la voiture 12, place 45car 12, seat 45
le train à grande vitessethe high-speed train
le TERthe regional train

Watch the false friend: on a train, la voiture is the carriage (\"car\" in American English, \"coach\" in British English). Your ticket says voiture 12: that's where you sit, not a car park!

Bonjour, je voudrais un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.Hello, I'd like a round-trip ticket to Lyon, please.
—Vous voulez une place côté fenêtre ou côté couloir ? —Côté fenêtre, s'il vous plaît.—Would you like a window seat or an aisle seat? —A window seat, please.
C'est combien, un aller simple pour Bordeaux en seconde ?How much is a one-way ticket to Bordeaux in second class?

Use pour with the destination: un billet pour Lyon, le train pour Marseille. And keep je voudrais, your polite formula, for asking: je veux sounds too blunt at a counter.

", "

Reading the timetable

FrenchEnglish
le départ / l'arrivée (f.)departure / arrival
le quaithe platform
la voiethe track (voie 7 on the board)
la correspondancethe connection, the change
à l'heureon time
en retardlate, delayed
annulé / annuléecancelled
le contrôleur / la contrôleusethe ticket inspector, the conductor

Timetables always use the 24-hour clock, written with an h: 14 h 52 is read quatorze heures cinquante-deux. To ask about times, learn this question as it is (questions with the verb before the subject are studied in the next lesson):

À quelle heure part le prochain train pour Lyon ?What time does the next train to Lyon leave?
Le train de 14 h 52 a vingt minutes de retard.The 2:52 p.m. train is twenty minutes late.
Il y a une correspondance à Lyon : vous changez de train.There's a connection in Lyon: you change trains.

Numbers up to 1 000

For prices and distances, you need hundreds. Cent takes an -s when it's multiplied and ends the number (deux cents), but not when another number follows (deux cent cinquante). Mille never takes an -s, and you never say \"un mille\".

NumberIn words
100cent
101cent un
200deux cents
250deux cent cinquante
480quatre cent quatre-vingts
999neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf
1 000mille
1 200mille deux cents

French writes a space between thousands and a comma for decimals: 1 000 km, 148,50 €. The opposite of English (1,000 km, €148.50).

", "

In Paris: the big stations and the métro

Paris has several big train stations, each serving one part of the country. Their names tell you where the trains go, roughly:

StationTrains to…
la gare de LyonLyon, Marseille, Nice, the Alps
la gare du NordLille, the north, Belgium, London
la gare de l'EstStrasbourg, the east
la gare MontparnasseBordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, the west
la gare Saint-LazareNormandy

Note the contractions: la gare de Lyon, but la gare du Nord (de + le). To get from one station to another, take the métro. Each line has a number and is named after its last stop: la ligne 1, direction Château de Vincennes.

Pour aller à la gare de Lyon, vous prenez la ligne 4 jusqu'à Châtelet, puis vous changez à Châtelet et vous prenez la ligne 1, direction Château de Vincennes.To get to the Gare de Lyon, you take line 4 to Châtelet, then you change at Châtelet and take line 1 toward Château de Vincennes.

When you miss your train

The passé composé is perfect for travel trouble. Rater (informal) or manquer means to miss:

J'ai raté mon train ! Il est parti à 9 h 07 et je suis arrivé à 9 h 10.I missed my train! It left at 9:07 and I got there at 9:10.
Notre train était annulé, alors nous avons dû prendre le suivant.Our train was cancelled, so we had to take the next one.

Lyon is about 460 kilometers from Paris: quatre cent soixante kilomètres. By high-speed train, it takes about two hours.

fr-u09-l2.title: At the hotel: formal questions
fr-u09-l2.topic: inversion questions; the hotel; formal register
fr-u09-l2.why: This lesson finally explains inversion, the formal way to ask questions (Avez-vous… ?, A-t-il… ?), and compares it with intonation and est-ce que. It puts it to work at the hotel, the natural place for a polite, formal register on a trip.
fr-u09-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Inversion: the formal question

You already know two ways to ask a yes/no question: rising intonation (Vous avez une chambre ?) and est-ce que (Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?). French has a third one, the most formal: inversion. You swap the subject pronoun and the verb, and join them with a hyphen: Avez-vous une chambre ?

RegisterQuestionWhere you hear it
everydayVous avez une chambre ?with friends, in most conversations
neutralEst-ce que vous avez une chambre ?everywhere, always correct
formalAvez-vous une chambre ?hotels, shops, emails, phone calls

The three questions mean exactly the same thing: only the tone changes. English does something similar with \"Have you…?\" and \"Can you…?\", but in French the inversion works with every verb, not just a few auxiliaries.

Parlez-vous anglais ?Do you speak English?
Pouvez-vous m'aider ?Can you help me?
Êtes-vous libre demain ?Are you free tomorrow?

With a question word

The question word comes first, then the inverted verb: Où habitez-vous ?, À quelle heure fermez-vous ?, Combien de nuits restez-vous ? You have been using inversion since the first unit without knowing it: Comment allez-vous ?, Comment vous appelez-vous ?, Quel âge as-tu ?

Avoid inversion with je: it sounds old-fashioned, except in a few fixed polite phrases like Puis-je vous aider ? (May I help you?). Otherwise say Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ? In conversation with friends, inversion sounds stiff: keep it for formal situations.

", "

The extra -t- and noun subjects

When the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun is il, elle or on, French slips in a -t- between two hyphens, just so the two vowels don't clash. It has no meaning: it's only there for the sound.

StatementInversion
Il a réservé.A-t-il réservé ?
Elle parle anglais.Parle-t-elle anglais ?
On arrive à quelle heure ?À quelle heure arrive-t-on ?
Il y a un parking.Y a-t-il un parking ?

When the verb already ends in -t or -d, no extra letter is needed, and you hear a t sound: Est-il là ?, Prend-elle le train ?, Sont-ils arrivés ? Learn Y a-t-il… ? (Is there…?) as a fixed phrase: it's the formal version of Il y a… ?

With a noun as subject

You can't invert a noun. Instead, keep the noun first, then add the matching pronoun after the verb: Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ? (literally \"The breakfast, is it included?\"). The pronoun must match the gender of the noun.

Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ?Is breakfast included?
La chambre a-t-elle une douche ?Does the room have a shower?
Vos amis sont-ils arrivés ?Have your friends arrived?

In the passé composé

Only the auxiliary is inverted, the participle stays after it: Avez-vous bien dormi ?, A-t-elle payé ?, Êtes-vous allés au musée ?

With où, quand or comment and a short sentence, you can simply put the noun after the verb: Où se trouve l'ascenseur ?, À quelle heure commence le petit-déjeuner ?

", "

At the hotel

At the front desk or on the phone, people use vous and a polite, slightly formal tone, which is exactly where inversion belongs. Here is what you need, from booking to checking out.

You sayIt means
Je voudrais réserver une chambre.I'd like to book a room.
Avez-vous une chambre libre pour ce soir ?Do you have a room available for tonight?
Une chambre simple / double, pour deux nuits.A single / double room, for two nights.
J'ai réservé au nom de Martin.I booked under the name Martin.
Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ?Is breakfast included?
Quel est le code du wifi ?What's the wifi password?
À quelle heure faut-il libérer la chambre ?What time is checkout?

If the hotel is full, you'll hear Désolé, nous sommes complets or see a sign: Complet (no vacancy).

Floors: a classic trap

In France, the floor at street level is le rez-de-chaussée. The floor above it is le premier étage, which Americans call the second floor. So if your room is au deuxième étage, you climb two flights of stairs, to the American third floor.

Votre chambre est au troisième étage. L'ascenseur est à gauche.Your room is on the fourth floor (US). The elevator is on the left.
La réception est au rez-de-chaussée.The front desk is on the first floor (US).

Au nom de is the magic phrase for any booking: hotel, restaurant, train. And remember: la clé (the key) is often a card today, but people still call it la clé.

fr-u09-l3.title: The imperative
fr-u09-l3.topic: affirmative and negative imperative; pronouns with the imperative
fr-u09-l3.why: After formal questions, here is the form for telling people what to do: the imperative with tu, nous and vous, its few irregular verbs, and where the pronouns go. You'll use it for directions, recipes and friendly advice.
fr-u09-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Giving orders: the imperative

The imperative is the form for instructions, advice and requests: \"Come!\", \"Turn left\", \"Let's go\". French has three forms, built from the present tense: tu, nous and vous, used without the subject pronoun, exactly like English drops \"you\".

parlerfinirattendreallerprendre
(tu)parlefinisattendsvaprends
(nous)parlonsfinissonsattendonsallonsprenons
(vous)parlezfinissezattendezallezprenez

The tu form is the one to watch: -er verbs lose their -s. Tu parles becomes Parle !, tu manges becomes Mange !, and aller follows the same rule: Va à la boulangerie ! The other verbs keep their -s: Finis !, Attends !, Prends !, Fais !, Viens !

The nous form means \"let's\": Mangeons ! (Let's eat!), Partons ! (Let's leave!). The vous form is for one person you say vous to, or for several people.

Four irregular verbs

êtreavoirsavoirvouloir
(tu)soisaiesache–
(nous)soyonsayonssachons–
(vous)soyezayezsachezveuillez
Sois gentil avec ta sœur !Be nice to your sister!
N'ayez pas peur.Don't be afraid.

Veuillez is very formal: you'll read it on signs and hear it in announcements. Veuillez patienter = Please wait. Just recognize it.

", "

Don't…! Negatives, reflexives and pronouns

For the negative, put ne… pas around the verb, as usual: Ne parle pas !, Ne partez pas !, N'oublie pas ton passeport !

Pronouns after the verb

In an affirmative command, object pronouns move after the verb, joined with a hyphen, and me and te become moi and toi:

PresentAffirmativeNegative
Tu le prends.Prends-le !Ne le prends pas !
Vous m'attendez.Attendez-moi !Ne m'attendez pas !
Tu la regardes.Regarde-la !Ne la regarde pas !
Tu me donnes le sel.Donne-moi le sel !Ne me donne pas le sel !

In the negative, everything goes back to normal: the pronoun returns before the verb and keeps its usual form (me, te).

Reflexive verbs

Same logic: te becomes toi after the verb, and nous and vous stay the same.

Lève-toi ! Ne te lève pas !Get up! Don't get up!
Dépêchez-vous, le train part !Hurry up, the train is leaving!
Couchons-nous, il est tard.Let's go to bed, it's late.

Learn Asseyez-vous (Sit down) and Assieds-toi as fixed phrases: the verb s'asseoir is irregular.

One more fixed form: Vas-y ! (Go on! Go for it!). Here va gets its -s back before the little word y, which you'll study in the next unit.

", "

Directions, recipes, advice

The imperative is everywhere in daily life. Strangers giving directions use vous; a recipe often uses vous too; friends and family use tu.

Directions

You learned to give directions in the present (Vous tournez à gauche). The imperative is just as common, and shorter:

Allez tout droit, puis tournez à droite. Traversez la place et prenez la deuxième rue à gauche.Go straight ahead, then turn right. Cross the square and take the second street on the left.

A recipe: crêpes

FrenchEnglish
Mettez la farine dans un bol.Put the flour in a bowl.
Ajoutez les œufs et mélangez.Add the eggs and stir.
Versez le lait doucement.Pour in the milk slowly.
Faites chauffer la poêle avec un peu de beurre.Heat the frying pan with a little butter.
Mangez les crêpes avec du sucre.Eat the crêpes with sugar.

Take faites chauffer (heat up) as a fixed expression.

Advice, and softening it

A bare imperative can sound bossy. Add s'il te plaît or s'il vous plaît, or use a question with pouvoir for a request: Tu peux fermer la fenêtre ? For advice between friends, the imperative is perfectly warm: Repose-toi !, Bois de l'eau !, Ne travaille pas trop !

Watch the spelling: with the tu form, no -s for -er verbs, even when English speakers \"hear\" one: Écoute !, Regarde !, Achète du pain ! But Fais attention !, Prends ton manteau ! keep it.

fr-u09-l4.title: When things go wrong
fr-u09-l4.topic: complaining and solving a problem politely; at the doctor's
fr-u09-l4.why: This last lesson on travel gives you the words for when things go wrong: something that doesn't work, a lost or stolen object, a visit to the doctor or the pharmacy. You'll complain politely with Pourriez-vous… ? and say what hurts with avoir mal à.
fr-u09-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Something's wrong: complaining politely

A broken shower, a noisy room, a lost key: when things go wrong on a trip, the French expect you to stay polite, even when you complain. Start with Excusez-moi or Bonjour (never skip it!), then describe the problem.

FrenchEnglish
Il y a un problème avec la chambre.There's a problem with the room.
La douche ne marche pas.The shower doesn't work.
Le chauffage ne fonctionne pas.The heating isn't working.
Il n'y a pas d'eau chaude.There's no hot water.
La chambre est sale / très bruyante.The room is dirty / very noisy.
Je voudrais me plaindre.I'd like to make a complaint.

For a machine or an object, \"to work\" is marcher (everyday) or fonctionner (a bit more formal). Never travailler, which is only for people: Mon téléphone ne marche pas, but Mon frère ne travaille pas le lundi.

Pourriez-vous… ? The polite request

To ask for a solution, use Pourriez-vous… ? + infinitive (Could you…?). Take it as a fixed polite formula for now: it's the conditional of pouvoir, which you'll study in unit 11.

Pourriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?Could you help me, please?
Pourriez-vous appeler un technicien ?Could you call a technician?
Pourriez-vous me donner une autre chambre ?Could you give me another room?

Pourriez-vous is softer than Pouvez-vous, which is softer than an imperative. In a hotel or a shop, a polite tone gets things fixed much faster.

", "

Lost and stolen

To tell what happened, you need the passé composé. With avoir: J'ai perdu mon passeport (I've lost my passport). With être: Je suis tombé / Je suis tombée (I fell).

J'ai perdu mes clés. J'ai cherché partout, mais je ne les trouve pas.I've lost my keys. I've looked everywhere, but I can't find them.

On m'a volé… : someone stole…

When you don't know who did it, French uses on (someone): On m'a volé mon portefeuille = Someone stole my wallet / My wallet was stolen. Learn it as a fixed phrase: m' means \"from me\" here.

FrenchEnglish
On m'a volé mon sac.My bag was stolen.
On m'a volé ma carte bancaire.My bank card was stolen.
J'ai perdu mon téléphone dans le métro.I lost my phone on the metro.
Où est le commissariat ?Where is the police station?

Watch out: voler has two meanings, \"to steal\" and \"to fly\". Les oiseaux volent = Birds fly. Context always makes it clear.

At the police station, you'll describe the object with what you know: C'est un sac noir, assez grand. Il y avait mon passeport dedans. (There was my passport in it.) The imparfait describes, the passé composé tells what happened: J'étais dans le bus quand on m'a volé mon portefeuille.

For a lost card, call your bank right away: in French this is faire opposition (to cancel / block a card). You'll hear it at the bank and at the police station.

", "

At the doctor's and the pharmacy

To say what hurts, French uses avoir mal à + the definite article: J'ai mal à la tête (literally \"I have pain at the head\"). English says \"my head hurts\" or \"I have a headache\", with a possessive; French uses le, la, les, never ma tête. Don't forget the contractions: à + le = au, à + les = aux.

FrenchEnglish
J'ai mal à la tête.I have a headache.
J'ai mal à la gorge.I have a sore throat.
J'ai mal au dos / au ventre.My back hurts / I have a stomachache.
J'ai mal aux dents / aux pieds.I have a toothache / My feet hurt.
J'ai de la fièvre.I have a fever.
Je tousse.I'm coughing.
Je suis enrhumé / enrhumée.I have a cold.

Seeing a doctor

In France you first see le médecin généraliste (the family doctor, GP). You make un rendez-vous (an appointment) and leave with une ordonnance (a prescription), which you take to la pharmacie. At night and on Sundays, look for la pharmacie de garde (the on-duty pharmacy).

The doctor's advice comes in the imperative: Prenez un comprimé trois fois par jour, Reposez-vous, Buvez beaucoup d'eau.

J'ai mal à la gorge et je tousse depuis trois jours.I have a sore throat and I've been coughing for three days.

False friend: une prescription exists in French, but the paper the doctor gives you is une ordonnance. And French pharmacists give real advice: for a small problem, ask them first.

fr-u10-l1.topic: indirect object pronouns; verbs with à
fr-u10-l1.why: This first lesson of the pronoun unit adds lui and leur, the pronouns for "to him, to her, to them", and the verbs that take à before a person. It also tackles the classic trap of verbs that are indirect in French but not in English, like téléphoner à.
fr-u10-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

To him, to her, to them: lui and leur

You already replace a direct object with le, la, les: Je vois Paul → Je le vois. But when the person comes after à (to someone), French uses a different set of pronouns, the indirect object pronouns.

direct (someone)indirect (to someone)
meme (m')me (m')
you (tu)te (t')te (t')
him / herle / la (l')lui
usnousnous
you (vous)vousvous
themlesleur

Only two forms are new: lui and leur. And here is the surprise for English speakers: lui means \"to him\" and \"to her\". Context tells you who.

Je téléphone à Paul. → Je lui téléphone.I'm calling Paul. → I'm calling him.
J'écris à Sophie. → Je lui écris.I'm writing to Sophie. → I'm writing to her.
Je parle à mes parents. → Je leur parle.I'm talking to my parents. → I'm talking to them.

Where they go

Exactly like le, la, les: before the conjugated verb, inside ne… pas, and before an infinitive.

Je ne lui téléphone pas. Je vais lui écrire.I'm not calling him. I'm going to write to him.
Je lui ai parlé hier. Je ne lui ai pas répondu.I talked to her yesterday. I didn't answer her.

Leur the pronoun never takes an -s: Je leur donne des bonbons. Don't mix it up with the possessive leurs (their): leurs enfants.

", "

Verbs with à + person

The question is always the same: does the verb take à before the person? If yes, the pronoun is lui / leur. Many of these verbs follow the pattern \"something to someone\": donner quelque chose à quelqu'un.

VerbExampleWith a pronoun
téléphoner àJe téléphone à ma mère.Je lui téléphone.
parler àTu parles à tes voisins ?Tu leur parles ?
dire àJe dis bonjour à Léa.Je lui dis bonjour.
demander àJe demande l'heure au chauffeur.Je lui demande l'heure.
donner àIl donne un livre à son fils.Il lui donne un livre.
envoyer àJ'envoie un message à Hugo.Je lui envoie un message.
prêter àJe prête mon vélo à Inès.Je lui prête mon vélo.
rendre àJe rends le livre à Paul.Je lui rends le livre.
répondre àElle répond à ses amis.Elle leur répond.
écrire àNous écrivons à Mamie.Nous lui écrivons.

Two verbs to learn

Offrir (to give as a present) is conjugated like an -er verb in the present: j'offre, tu offres, il offre, nous offrons, vous offrez, ils offrent; its participle is offert. Plaire à (to please) is the French way of saying \"to like\" something: the thing is the subject. Le cadeau lui plaît = He likes the present (literally \"The present pleases him\"). You know Ça me plaît: it's the same verb.

Je vais lui offrir un livre. J'espère qu'il va lui plaire !I'm going to give her a book. I hope she'll like it!

To borrow is emprunter: J'emprunte le vélo de Paul. To lend is prêter: Paul me prête son vélo. Same situation, seen from both sides.

", "

Direct or indirect? The traps

English doesn't help you here, because \"to\" often disappears: \"I'm calling her\", \"I'm answering him\", \"I'm asking them\". In French, téléphoner, répondre and demander all take à, so they need lui / leur:

Je lui téléphone ce soir.I'm calling him/her tonight. (never je le téléphone)
Il ne leur répond pas.He's not answering them.

And it works the other way round: some verbs have a preposition in English but none in French, so they take le, la, les:

Direct in FrenchEnglishPronoun
attendre quelqu'unto wait for someoneJe l'attends.
chercher quelqu'unto look for someoneJe la cherche.
écouter quelqu'unto listen to someoneJe les écoute.
regarder quelqu'unto look at someoneTu le regardes.
aider quelqu'unto help someoneJe l'aide.

With the imperative

As with moi, the pronoun goes after an affirmative command, with a hyphen: Téléphone-lui !, Réponds-leur !, Dis-lui bonjour ! In the negative, it goes back before the verb: Ne lui dis pas !

One exception to recognize: with penser à (to think about), a person is not replaced by lui but by à + stressed pronoun: Je pense à lui, Je pense à elle, Je pense à eux.

fr-u10-l2.title: Y and en
fr-u10-l2.topic: the pronouns y and en; pronouns in the passé composé and participle agreement
fr-u10-l2.why: This lesson introduces y and en, two very frequent pronouns with no English equivalent, for places, things and quantities. It also shows where pronouns go in the passé composé and when the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it.
fr-u10-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Y: there, about it

English has nothing quite like y and en, two tiny words that French uses all the time to avoid repeating a place or a thing. Let's start with y.

Y replaces a place

After à, en, chez, dans, sur…, y means \"there\". It goes before the verb, like the other pronouns.

Tu vas à Lyon ? — Oui, j'y vais demain.Are you going to Lyon? — Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.
Elle habite en Bretagne ? — Oui, elle y habite depuis dix ans.Does she live in Brittany? — Yes, she's lived there for ten years.
Tu vas chez le médecin ? — Non, je n'y vais pas.Are you going to the doctor's? — No, I'm not (going).

English often just drops \"there\" (\"Yes, I'm going\"), but French can't: Je vais alone is incomplete. Say J'y vais.

Y replaces à + a thing

With verbs built with à, like penser à or répondre à, y replaces a thing or an idea: \"about it\", \"to it\".

Tu penses à ton examen ? — Oui, j'y pense souvent.Are you thinking about your exam? — Yes, I often think about it.
à + thingà + person
Je réponds à la lettre. → J'y réponds.Je réponds à Paul. → Je lui réponds.

With an infinitive, y goes before it: Je vais y aller. And you'll hear one phrase every day: On y va ! (Let's go!).

Remember the fixed form Vas-y ! (Go on!): the -s comes back so you can pronounce the liaison, « va-z-y ».

", "

En: some, of it, of them

En replaces a noun introduced by de: a partitive (du, de la, des), a quantity, or a verb built with de.

Partitives: some, any

Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux bien. / Non merci, je n'en veux pas.Do you want some coffee? — Yes, I'd love some. / No thanks, I don't want any.

English says \"some\" or \"any\", or nothing at all (\"Yes, please\"). French needs en.

Quantities and numbers

With a number or a quantity, en replaces the noun, and the number or the quantity stays at the end:

QuestionAnswer with en
Tu as des enfants ?Oui, j'en ai deux.
Il y a des pommes ?Oui, il y en a beaucoup.
Vous voulez combien de tomates ?J'en voudrais un kilo.
Tu bois du lait ?Non, je n'en bois jamais.

Never J'ai deux alone: J'en ai deux (I have two of them). And il y a becomes il y en a (there is some, there are some).

Verbs with de

Tu parles de ton voyage ? — Oui, j'en parle à mes amis !Are you talking about your trip? — Yes, I talk about it with my friends!
Tu as besoin de la voiture ? — Non, je n'en ai pas besoin.Do you need the car? — No, I don't need it.

En also replaces a place after venir de: Tu viens de la boulangerie ? — Oui, j'en viens.

A very useful phrase: Je m'en occupe = I'll take care of it (from s'occuper de).

", "

Pronouns in the passé composé

In the passé composé, every pronoun goes before the auxiliary, never before the participle:

PronounAffirmativeNegative
le, la, lesJe l'ai vu.Je ne l'ai pas vu.
lui, leurJe lui ai parlé.Je ne lui ai pas parlé.
yJ'y suis allé.Je n'y suis pas allé.
enJ'en ai mangé.Je n'en ai pas mangé.

The participle agrees with a direct object placed before it

Until now, the participle with avoir never changed. New rule: when a direct object pronoun (le, la, les, me, te, nous, vous) comes before avoir, the participle agrees with it, like an adjective.

Les clés ? Je les ai trouvées.The keys? I found them. (les = les clés, feminine plural)
La lettre ? Je l'ai écrite hier.The letter? I wrote it yesterday.
Léa ? Je l'ai vue au marché.Léa? I saw her at the market.

Most of the time you can't hear it (trouvé, trouvées sound the same), but you can with participles ending in a consonant: écrit / écrite, pris / prise, mis / mise, fait / faite.

No agreement with en or with lui / leur, which are not direct objects: Des pommes ? J'en ai acheté. / Ma sœur ? Je lui ai téléphoné.

Before writing the participle, ask: is there le, la, les (or me, te…) before avoir? If yes, find what it stands for and agree.

fr-u10-l3.why: This lesson completes the pronoun unit with the order of double pronouns (je te le, je le lui, il y en a) and their place with every tense and with the imperative. It's a full review of direct, indirect and reflexive pronouns, y and en, through the preparation of a surprise party.
fr-u10-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Two pronouns in a row: the order

You now know all the object pronouns. Sometimes a sentence needs two of them: \"I'm giving it to you\". English puts them after the verb; French puts both before the verb, in a fixed order.

12345
me, te, se, nous, vousle, la, leslui, leuryen
Tu me prêtes ton livre ? — Oui, je te le prête.Will you lend me your book? — Yes, I'll lend it to you.
Je donne la clé à Paul. → Je la lui donne.I'm giving the key to Paul. → I'm giving it to him.
Il y a des gâteaux ? — Oui, il y en a.Are there any cakes? — Yes, there are some.
Tu as parlé du projet à Marie ? — Oui, je lui en ai parlé.Did you tell Marie about the project? — Yes, I told her about it.

Three rules of thumb

  • me, te, nous, vous come before le, la, les: Il nous les montre.
  • But le, la, les come before lui, leur: Je le leur envoie.
  • y and en always come last, and en is the very last: Je vous en donne.

In practice, you'll mostly meet a few combinations, so learn them as sounds: je te le, je le lui, je lui en, il y en a.

Lui and leur never go together with me, te, nous, vous before the verb. And le lui is correct, while « lui le » never is.

", "

Two pronouns with every tense

The order never changes. Only the position depends on the tense, exactly as with a single pronoun. In the table, les stands for les photos (feminine plural) and te for the person you're showing them to.

TenseWhere the pronouns goExample
presentbefore the verbJe te les montre.
passé composébefore the auxiliaryJe te les ai montrées.
near futurebefore the infinitiveJe vais te les montrer.
with pouvoir, vouloir…before the infinitiveJe peux te les montrer.

In the negative, ne comes before the whole block, and pas after the conjugated verb:

Je ne te le prête pas.I'm not lending it to you.
Je ne le lui ai pas dit.I didn't tell him (it).
Je ne vais pas le leur dire.I'm not going to tell them (it).

Agreement still applies

In the passé composé, the participle agrees with the direct object le, la, les placed before avoir, even with a second pronoun in between:

Les photos ? Je te les ai envoyées hier.The photos? I sent them to you yesterday.
La lettre ? Je la leur ai écrite.The letter? I wrote it to them.

Still no agreement with en: Des fleurs ? Je lui en ai offert.

Translating \"I told him\" or \"I told her\" about a fact: French often adds le: Je le lui ai dit (I told him so). Without it, the sentence sounds incomplete.

", "

Pronouns with the imperative

In an affirmative command, the pronouns follow the verb, joined by hyphens, and the order is simpler: direct before indirect, and me, te become moi, toi.

AffirmativeNegativeEnglish
Donne-le-moi !Ne me le donne pas !Give it to me! / Don't give it to me!
Envoie-la-leur !Ne la leur envoie pas !Send it to them! / Don't send it to them!
Rends-les-lui !Ne les lui rends pas !Give them back to him! / Don't give them back to him!
Dites-le-nous !Ne nous le dites pas !Tell us! / Don't tell us!

In the negative, everything goes back to the normal order and position: ne + pronouns + verb + pas.

With y and en

Before y and en, the tu form of -er verbs gets its -s back, for the liaison: Vas-y !, Manges-en ! (Eat some!). Just recognize forms like Parle-lui-en (Talk to him about it): they are rare in conversation.

The chain-replacement method

To build a sentence with two pronouns, replace one noun at a time:

J'offre les fleurs à Camille. → Je les offre à Camille. → Je les lui offre.I'm giving the flowers to Camille. → I'm giving them to Camille. → I'm giving them to her.

When you're not sure in conversation, one pronoun is fine: Je lui offre les fleurs is perfectly correct. Double pronouns make you sound fluent, but you can build up to them.

fr-u11-l1.title: The futur simple
fr-u11-l1.topic: formation and uses of the future; quand + future; si + present + future
fr-u11-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on plans with the futur simple: its single set of endings, its irregular stems, and how it differs from aller + infinitive. It also tackles the classic trap of quand + future, where English uses the present, and si + present + future.
fr-u11-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Will: the futur simple

English builds the future with a helper word: \"I will speak\". French builds it in a single word, by adding endings to the infinitive: je parlerai. The endings are the same for every verb, and they look like the present of avoir (ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont), minus the av- in nous and vous.

parlerfinirprendre
jeparleraifiniraiprendrai
tuparlerasfinirasprendras
il / elle / onparlerafiniraprendra
nousparleronsfinironsprendrons
vousparlerezfinirezprendrez
ils / ellesparlerontfinirontprendront

-re verbs drop their final e before the ending: prendre → je prendrai, attendre → j'attendrai. The future always has an r before the ending: that r is how you recognize it.

Verbs with a spelling change keep it in every form: acheter → j'achèterai, appeler → j'appellerai, se lever → je me lèverai.

L'année prochaine, je travaillerai à Lyon.Next year, I'll work in Lyon.
Nous partirons en juillet et nous rentrerons en août.We'll leave in July and come back in August.

Pronunciation: in everyday speech, the e of parlerai often disappears: « parl'rai », « j'achèt'rai ». And the -ai of je parlerai sounds like é.

", "

Irregular stems

The most frequent verbs have an irregular stem, but the endings never change. Learn the stems in groups:

InfinitiveFutureInfinitiveFuture
êtreje seraipouvoirje pourrai
avoirj'auraivoirje verrai
allerj'iraienvoyerj'enverrai
faireje feraivouloirje voudrai
savoirje sauraivenirje viendrai
devoirje devraifalloiril faudra
pleuvoiril pleuvra

Notice the double rr in pourrai, verrai, enverrai: you hear a longer r. And aller becomes a tiny ir-: j'irai, tu iras, nous irons.

Futur simple or aller + infinitive?

You already know the near future: Je vais partir. Both talk about the future, but the feeling is different:

  • aller + infinitive: something close, planned or already under way: Attention, tu vas tomber !, Ce soir, je vais dîner chez Léa.
  • futur simple: predictions, promises, longer-term plans, things less certain: Un jour, j'habiterai près de la mer., Je t'appellerai, promis !

The weather forecast

The forecast is a classic use of the future:

Demain, il fera beau dans le Sud, mais il pleuvra en Bretagne. Le soir, il y aura du vent.Tomorrow, it will be sunny in the South, but it will rain in Brittany. In the evening, it will be windy.

Il y a becomes il y aura (there will be), and il faut becomes il faudra (it will be necessary / we'll have to).

", "

Quand + future, si + present

This is the big trap for English speakers. In English, after \"when\" and \"as soon as\" you use the present for a future action: \"When I get to Paris, I'll call you\". French is logical: if the action is in the future, the verb is in the future.

Quand je serai à Paris, je t'appellerai.When I'm in Paris, I'll call you.
Dès que j'aurai les billets, je te les enverrai.As soon as I have the tickets, I'll send them to you.

Never Quand je suis à Paris, je t'appellerai: that mixes two time frames.

But si + present

After si (if), it's the other way round: si is followed by the present, and the result is in the future. Here, French works exactly like English.

si + presentfuture
S'il fait beau,on ira à la plage.
Si tu as le temps,tu viendras avec nous ?
Si vous prenez le train de huit heures,vous arriverez à midi.

Never put the future after si: « si il fera beau » is a mistake twice over. Si elides only before il and ils: s'il, s'ils, but si elle, si on.

Resolutions

L'année prochaine, je ferai du sport, j'arrêterai de fumer et je lirai un livre par mois.Next year, I'll exercise, I'll quit smoking and I'll read a book a month.

A memory trick: quand looks to the future, so it takes the future; si is a condition, so it takes the present.

fr-u11-l2.title: The conditional
fr-u11-l2.why: Built on the future stems you just learned, the conditional finally explains je voudrais and pourriez-vous. You'll use it to ask politely, to talk about your wishes and to give advice with tu devrais and à ta place.
fr-u11-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Would: the present conditional

Good news: if you know the futur simple, you already know half of the conditional. Take the future stem (parler-, ser-, pourr-…) and add the imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient). English uses \"would\"; French uses a single word.

aimerpouvoirdevoirêtre
jeaimeraispourraisdevraisserais
tuaimeraispourraisdevraisserais
il / elle / onaimeraitpourraitdevraitserait
nousaimerionspourrionsdevrionsserions
vousaimeriezpourriezdevriezseriez
ils / ellesaimeraientpourraientdevraientseraient

All the irregular stems of the future work here too: j'aurais, j'irais, je ferais, je viendrais, je voudrais, je saurais, je verrais, il faudrait. As in the imparfait, five of the six forms sound alike: aimerais, aimerait, aimeraient are all « aim'rè ».

You've been using it all along

Je voudrais (from unit 3) and Pourriez-vous… ? (from unit 9) are both conditionals of vouloir and pouvoir. Now you know why they sound so polite: they mean \"I would like\" and \"Could you…?\"

Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.I'd like a coffee, please.

Future or conditional? Je voudrai (future, \"I will want\") and je voudrais (conditional, \"I would like\") differ by one letter. Many French speakers pronounce them the same, so in writing, think: is it \"will\" or \"would\"? In a shop, it's always je voudrais, with an -s.

", "

Politeness and wishes

The conditional softens everything. Compare these three ways of asking for the same thing:

DirectPolite (conditional)
Je veux une table pour deux.Je voudrais une table pour deux.
Vous pouvez fermer la fenêtre ?Pourriez-vous fermer la fenêtre ?
Tu as cinq minutes ?Tu aurais cinq minutes ?
Ça vous dérange d'attendre ?Ça vous dérangerait d'attendre ?
Il faut réserver.Il faudrait réserver.

To ask a friend for a favor, the magic phrase is Tu pourrais me rendre un service ? (Could you do me a favor?). With vous: Pourriez-vous me rendre un service ?

Je veux sounds blunt, even rude, when you ask for something: in a shop or a restaurant, always use je voudrais or j'aimerais.

Wishes and dreams

To say what you would like, use j'aimerais or je voudrais + infinitive:

J'aimerais habiter à Nice.I'd like to live in Nice.
Nous aimerions visiter la Corse un jour.We'd like to visit Corsica one day.
Une maison à la campagne, ce serait mon rêve !A house in the countryside would be my dream!

Add bien to make a wish sound softer, a little dreamy: J'aimerais bien partir en vacances… (I'd really like to go on vacation…).

", "

Giving advice

To advise someone, French has three common patterns, all with the conditional:

PatternExampleEnglish
devoir + infinitiveTu devrais te reposer.You should rest.
À ta place, je…À ta place, je partirais.If I were you, I'd leave.
Il faudrait…Il faudrait parler à ton patron.You ought to talk to your boss.

Tu devrais is the conditional of devoir, so it's softer than Tu dois (you must). With vous: Vous devriez, À votre place.

Tu as l'air fatigué. Tu devrais prendre des vacances.You look tired. You should take a vacation.
À votre place, j'irais chez le médecin.If I were you, I'd go to the doctor.
Vous ne devriez pas travailler le dimanche.You shouldn't work on Sundays.

Watch the English \"would\"

Not every English \"would\" is a conditional. When it describes a habit in the past (\"When I was a child, I would play outside\"), French uses the imparfait: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais dehors, as you saw in unit 8.

Pronunciation: je ferai (future) ends in « é », je ferais (conditional) in « è », at least for careful speakers. Context almost always tells you which one you hear: À ta place, je ferais du sport can only be a conditional.

fr-u11-l3.title: Inviting, accepting, refusing
fr-u11-l3.why: This lesson puts the future and the conditional to work in real social life: inviting someone, accepting warmly, refusing tactfully with an excuse and suggesting another time. It ends the unit with the phrases you need to fix a time and a place.
fr-u11-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Making an invitation

You can invite someone with a simple question (Tu viens au cinéma ?), but French has a few friendly formulas that make an invitation sound natural. Notice that most of them work like \"Do you feel like…?\" or \"How about…?\" in English.

With tuWith vousEnglish
Ça te dit de venir ?Ça vous dirait de venir ?Do you feel like coming? / Would you like to come?
Tu as envie de sortir ?Vous avez envie de sortir ?Do you feel like going out?
On pourrait aller à la plage.Nous pourrions aller à la plage.We could go to the beach.
Si on allait au cinéma ?Si nous allions au cinéma ?How about going to the movies?
Tu es libre samedi ?Vous êtes libre samedi ?Are you free on Saturday?

Ça te dit de and avoir envie de are followed by an infinitive, with de (d' before a vowel): Ça te dit d'aller au restaurant ?

Si on allait… ? uses si + imparfait. Take it as a fixed formula for a suggestion: you'll study si + imparfait properly at B1. On pourrait… is the conditional you just learned: softer than On va…

Il fait beau ! Si on allait se promener au parc ?The weather's nice! How about going for a walk in the park?

Careful with Je t'invite: in a café or a restaurant, it means \"It's my treat\", so the person who says it pays. To just suggest going together, say On va boire un verre ?

", "

Saying yes, saying no

Accepting

FrenchEnglishTone
Avec plaisir !With pleasure!warm, always polite
Volontiers !Gladly! I'd love to!warm, a little formal
Bonne idée !Good idea!neutral
Ça marche !Sounds good! Deal!informal
Pourquoi pas ?Why not?a bit lukewarm

Refusing politely

In France, a plain non sounds abrupt. A polite refusal has three steps: thank the person or say you're sorry, give an excuse, and suggest another time.

Désolée, je ne peux pas, je suis prise samedi. Une autre fois, peut-être ?Sorry, I can't, I'm busy on Saturday. Another time, maybe?

Je suis pris (literally \"I'm taken\") is the usual way to say \"I'm busy, I already have plans\". It agrees: je suis prise for a woman, nous sommes pris. J'ai un empêchement means something has come up: it's handy because you don't have to explain.

Merci pour l'invitation, mais malheureusement j'ai un empêchement. C'est dommage !Thanks for the invitation, but unfortunately something has come up. What a shame!

Suggesting another time

Use the conditional of aller (to suit): Et dimanche, ça t'irait ? (Would Sunday work for you?) or, with vous, ça vous irait ? You can also use the future: On ira la semaine prochaine.

Désolé agrees too: a woman writes désolée. You hear no difference, but you see it in a text message.

", "

Fixing the details

Once everyone agrees, you need a time and a place. The key verb is se retrouver (to meet up):

FrenchEnglish
On se retrouve à quelle heure ?What time shall we meet?
On se retrouve où ?Where shall we meet?
Rendez-vous devant la gare à sept heures.Let's meet in front of the station at seven.
On se retrouve chez moi ?Shall we meet at my place?
Je passe te prendre à huit heures.I'll pick you up at eight.
Je serai là vers midi.I'll be there around noon.

Un rendez-vous is any arranged meeting: with friends, with a doctor, or a date. It's not just romantic, unlike English \"rendezvous\".

Saying goodbye until then

À + the day or the time: À samedi !, À demain !, À ce soir !, À tout à l'heure ! (See you later today!)

A birthday invitation

Samedi, je fais une fête pour mes trente ans. Tu viendras ? Tu peux venir avec ta copine, bien sûr !On Saturday, I'm having a party for my thirtieth birthday. Will you come? You can bring your girlfriend, of course!
Volontiers ! J'apporterai le dessert. Je serai là vers vingt heures.I'd love to! I'll bring dessert. I'll be there around 8 p.m.

Even when you accept, a small offer is polite in France: J'apporte quelque chose ? (Shall I bring something?). The usual answer: Non, rien, juste toi !

fr-u12-l1.title: Comparing
fr-u12-l1.topic: comparatives and superlatives; meilleur vs mieux; large numbers
fr-u12-l1.why: This lesson opens the last A2 unit with comparisons: plus, moins, aussi… que with adjectives, nouns and verbs, the tricky pair meilleur / mieux, and superlatives with de. It also covers large numbers, so you can compare cities, apartments and prices.
fr-u12-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

More, less, as… as

English has two ways to compare: \"bigger\" (with -er) and \"more expensive\" (with more). French has only one, and it's always regular: plus, moins or aussi before the adjective, and que before the second element.

ComparisonExampleEnglish
plus + adjective + queLe métro est plus rapide que le bus.The metro is faster than the bus.
moins + adjective + queLe bus est moins cher que le taxi.The bus is less expensive than a taxi.
aussi + adjective + queLe train est aussi rapide que l'avion.The train is as fast as the plane.

The adjective still agrees with the noun: Ma rue est plus calme que ta rue, Les loyers sont plus chers à Paris qu'à Lyon. Que elides before a vowel (qu'à Lyon), and after que you use the stressed pronouns: plus grand que moi, aussi sportive que toi, moins riches qu'eux.

With a noun: plus de, moins de, autant de

To compare quantities, use de + noun, with no article, as with beaucoup de:

Il y a plus de touristes à Nice qu'à Nantes.There are more tourists in Nice than in Nantes.
J'ai moins de temps que l'année dernière.I have less time than last year.
Lille a autant de charme que Lyon.Lille has as much charm as Lyon.

With a verb: plus, moins, autant

After a verb, no de: Je travaille plus que toi, Elle sort moins que son frère, Il dort autant que moi.

Equality has two words: aussi with an adjective or an adverb (aussi grand), autant with a verb or a noun (autant de livres, il mange autant). English uses \"as\" for both.

", "

Better and worse: meilleur, mieux, pire

English \"better\" hides two different words in French, and choosing the right one is a classic difficulty:

Basic wordBetterTypeExample
bon (good)meilleuradjective: agreesLe gâteau au chocolat est bon, mais la tarte est meilleure.
bien (well)mieuxadverb: never changesElle chante bien, mais tu chantes mieux.

The test: if you could say bon, use meilleur; if you could say bien, use mieux. Never « plus bon » or « plus bien ».

C'est un meilleur restaurant que l'autre.It's a better restaurant than the other one.
Ma sœur est meilleure que moi en maths.My sister is better than me at math.
Tu parles mieux français que l'année dernière.You speak French better than last year.
Je vais mieux aujourd'hui.I feel better today.

Notice meilleur goes before the noun, like bon: un meilleur prix, de meilleures notes.

Worse: pire

The comparative of mauvais is pire (or plus mauvais, also correct): La pluie, c'est pire que le froid !, Le film est pire que le livre.

With c'est, a general comment, French often uses mieux: C'est mieux comme ça (It's better like that). That's because c'est bien is the basic phrase.

", "

The most, the least, and big numbers

For the superlative, add the definite article: le / la / les plus, le / la / les moins. After it, \"in\" is de, never dans: la plus belle ville de France, le restaurant le moins cher du quartier.

Adjective before the nounAdjective after the noun
la plus belle ville de Francela ville la plus chère de France
le plus grand musée de Parisle quartier le plus calme de Lyon
le meilleur restaurant de la villeles rues les plus bruyantes du quartier

When the adjective comes after the noun, the article appears twice: la ville la plus chère. English has nothing like it, so learn the rhythm by heart. With a verb, it's le plus, le moins, le mieux, always with le: Parmi mes amis, Léa chante le mieux (Of all my friends, Léa sings best).

Big numbers

NumberFrenchRule
1 000milleno un: never « un mille »
3 000trois millemille never takes -s
2026deux mille vingt-sixyears too
1 000 000un milliona noun: un million d'habitants
2 000 000deux millionstakes -s: deux millions de personnes

French writes thousands with a space (10 000), not a comma: the comma is the decimal point (2,5 millions).

Million works like un kilo: it's a noun, so it needs de before the next noun: un million de touristes. Mille doesn't: mille euros.

fr-u12-l2.title: In the shops
fr-u12-l2.topic: buying clothes and objects; demonstratives; lequel; tout
fr-u12-l2.why: After comparing things, you now learn to point at them and choose: this one, that one, which one, all of them. It's the vocabulary of clothes shopping in France, from the fitting room to the sales, and the last new point before the big A2 review.
fr-u12-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

In a clothes shop

Shopping for clothes in France follows a little ritual. You walk in and say Bonjour (always: entering a shop without greeting the staff sounds rude), the assistant asks Je peux vous aider ?, and you answer Oui, je cherche un pull or Non merci, je regarde. Then come the sizes, the fitting room and the checkout.

FrenchEnglish
Je peux l'essayer ?Can I try it on?
Où est la cabine d'essayage ?Where is the fitting room?
Vous faites quelle taille ? — Je fais du 38.What size are you? — I'm a 38.
Vous faites quelle pointure ? — Je fais du 42.What's your shoe size? — I'm a 42.
C'est trop grand / trop petit / trop serré.It's too big / too small / too tight.
Vous l'avez en bleu ? en 40 ? en plus grand ?Do you have it in blue? in a 40? in a bigger size?
Ça vous va très bien !It really suits you!
Je le prends.I'll take it.

Two words for “size”: la taille for clothes, la pointure for shoes. And notice Je fais du 38: French uses faire, where English uses “to be”. French sizes are not American sizes, so check the label.

Aller = to suit

You know aller for movement and for Ça va ?. With an indirect pronoun, it means “to suit, to fit”: Cette veste te va bien (this jacket suits you), Ces chaussures vous vont bien. The thing you wear is the subject, the person is me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Careful: Ça vous va ? can also mean “Is that OK for you?”, for a time or a price.

Les soldes (the sales) are always plural and masculine: les soldes d'hiver, in January, and les soldes d'été, in summer. Keep your ticket de caisse (receipt): you will need it to échanger (exchange) an item or to be remboursé (refunded).

", "

This one, that one, which one?

English has “this” and “that”. French has one demonstrative adjective that agrees with the noun, like an article. It does not say “near” or “far” by itself.

before a consonantbefore a vowel or silent h
masculinece pullcet article, cet homme
femininecette robecette écharpe
pluralces chaussuresces‿articles (liaison)

Cet and cette sound exactly the same. Ce pull can mean “this sweater” or “that sweater”: the context decides. To insist, add -ci (here) or -là (there): ce pull-ci, cette robe-là.

Celui-ci, celle-là

To avoid repeating the noun, use the pronoun, which also agrees: celui (masc.), celle (fem.), ceux (masc. plural), celles (fem. plural), followed by -ci or -là.

Quel manteau préférez-vous ? Celui-ci ou celui-là ?Which coat do you prefer? This one or that one?
Ces bottes sont trop petites. Je peux essayer celles-là ?These boots are too small. Can I try those ones?

In everyday speech, -là is used much more than -ci, even for something close: Je prends celui-là is simply “I'll take that one”.

Lequel ? Laquelle ?

“Which one?” is lequel (masc.), laquelle (fem.), lesquels, lesquelles: it's quel glued to the article, and it agrees with the noun you have in mind.

— J'adore cette jupe ! — Laquelle ? La rouge ?— I love this skirt! — Which one? The red one?

You will also hear the possessive pronouns: le mien, la mienne, les miens, les miennes (mine), le tien, la tienne (yours), le sien, la sienne (his or hers), le nôtre, le vôtre, le leur. Like mon / ma, they agree with the thing owned: C'est ton sac ? — Non, ce n'est pas le mien. Just recognize them for now.

", "

Tout, tous, chaque

Tout agrees with the noun that follows, and it comes before the article: tout le magasin, not “le tout magasin”.

FrenchEnglish
masculine singulartout le magasinthe whole shop
feminine singulartoute la journéeall day, the whole day
masculine pluraltous les joursevery day
feminine pluraltoutes les taillesall the sizes

Watch the trap: English “every day” is tous les jours (plural!) and “all day” is toute la journée (singular). Tout alone means “everything”: Tout est en soldes (everything is on sale), C'est tout, merci.

Chaque (each, every) is invariable and always followed by a singular noun with no article: chaque jour, chaque client, chaque semaine. Chaque jour and tous les jours mean almost the same thing.

Tous before a noun has a silent s: tous les jours. On its own, as a pronoun, the s is pronounced: Ils sont tous là (“touss”).

Putting it together

Now combine everything you know: comparatives, object pronouns and demonstratives.

Celle-ci est plus jolie que celle-là, mais elle est plus chère.This one is prettier than that one, but it's more expensive.
Ces chaussures ? Je les ai essayées, mais elles sont trop petites.These shoes? I tried them on, but they're too small.
Je peux l'échanger ? — Oui, avec le ticket de caisse.Can I exchange it? — Yes, with the receipt.
Tous les manteaux sont à moins trente pour cent.All the coats are thirty percent off.

fr-u12-l3.title: A2 review: a whole trip
fr-u12-l3.why: This big review closes the A2 level with a complete trip: the station, the hotel, a problem, memories told in the past and plans for next time. It checks that you can combine the two pasts, the future, the conditional, the imperative, pronouns and comparisons before the B1 level begins.
fr-u12-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Telling the trip: the two pasts

This lesson brings together the whole A2 level around one story: a week in Provence, from the train ticket to the plans for next year. Start with the heart of any travel story, the choice between the passé composé and the imparfait.

passé composéimparfait
rolethe events, what happenedthe background, what it was like
EnglishI went, I have been, I did goI was going, I used to go, it was
examplesNous sommes partis samedi.
J'ai perdu mon portefeuille.		Il faisait beau.
L'hôtel était petit mais calme.

The test: if you can answer “and then what happened?”, it's the passé composé. If you are describing the scene (the weather, the place, how you felt, a habit), it's the imparfait.

Il pleuvait quand nous sommes arrivés à Avignon.It was raining when we arrived in Avignon.
Le matin, on allait au marché. Un jour, on a acheté des calissons.In the mornings, we would go to the market. One day, we bought some calissons.

Être or avoir?

Movement verbs (aller, partir, arriver, rester, rentrer…) and all pronominal verbs take être, and the participle agrees with the subject: Léa est partie, nous nous sommes baignés. With avoir, the participle agrees only with a direct object placed before it: Les valises ? Je les ai mises dans la voiture.

English speakers often say “j'ai allé” because English uses “have” everywhere. Say it aloud a few times: je suis allé, elle est allée, on est allés. And with on meaning “we”, the participle usually agrees in the plural.

", "

On the road: getting by

A trip is a series of small situations: a station, a hotel, a restaurant, sometimes a problem. Here are the tools you have learned for each one.

situationuseful French
at the stationUn aller-retour pour Marseille, s'il vous plaît. Le train part de quelle voie ? Il y a une correspondance à Lyon.
at the hotelAvez-vous une chambre pour deux nuits ? Le petit-déjeuner est-il compris ? J'ai réservé au nom de Martin.
at the restaurantJe vais prendre le plat du jour. Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît. L'addition, s'il vous plaît.
a problemJ'ai perdu mon passeport. La douche ne marche pas. J'ai mal à la tête.

To be polite, use the conditional: Pourriez-vous m'aider ?, Je voudrais une chambre calme. For directions or advice, the imperative: Prenez la deuxième rue à droite, Ne partez pas sans votre billet.

Pronouns save time

A travel story repeats the same places and things. Pronouns avoid that, and they go before the auxiliary in the past.

Marseille ? On y est allés mardi.Marseille? We went there on Tuesday.
Des calissons ? J'en ai acheté deux boîtes.Calissons? I bought two boxes of them.
Mon portefeuille ? Un vendeur me l'a rendu.My wallet? A stallholder gave it back to me.
Tes photos ? Montre-les-moi !Your photos? Show them to me!

y replaces a place (à Marseille), en replaces a quantity or de + noun (des calissons). After the affirmative imperative, pronouns follow the verb with hyphens: montre-les-moi.

", "

Next time: plans, wishes, comparisons

Back home, you compare, you dream and you plan. Three more tools of the A2 level.

The future

Use the futur simple for plans and promises: L'année prochaine, nous irons en Corse. Remember the two traps. After quand, French uses the future where English uses the present: Quand je serai à Aix, je t'appellerai (“when I am”). After si, it's the reverse: present, then future: S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage.

infinitivefuture stemexample
êtreser-je serai
allerir-nous irons
fairefer-il fera beau
venirviendr-je viendrai
pleuvoirpleuvr-il pleuvra

Wishes and advice

The conditional expresses a wish or gives advice gently: J'aimerais retourner en Provence. À ta place, je prendrais le train. Tu devrais réserver tôt.

Comparing

Le train est plus rapide que la voiture. Ce restaurant est meilleur que l'autre (never “plus bon”). Gordes est le plus beau village de la région: after a superlative, “in” is de.

Si tu y retournes, je viendrai avec toi !If you go back there, I'll come with you!
C'était le meilleur voyage de ma vie.It was the best trip of my life.

A good travel story in French alternates the tenses: Il faisait chaud (background), on a visité Gordes (event), c'était magnifique (comment), j'y retournerai (plan). If you can do that, you have the A2 level in hand.

fr-u13-l1.title: Introducing yourself at work
fr-u13-l1.topic: professional background and role; depuis, pendant, il y a
fr-u13-l1.why: The B1 level begins at work: you learn to present your job, your role and your career path the way French colleagues do. You also sort out the four French words for English “for” (depuis, pendant, il y a, pour), a classic stumbling block.
fr-u13-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

What do you do?

Welcome to the B1 level! You start with a situation you'll meet on your first day in a French company: introducing yourself to colleagues. The question is Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ? or, more casually, Tu fais quoi ? Here is how to answer.

FrenchEnglish
Je suis comptable.I'm an accountant.
Je travaille comme développeuse.I work as a developer.
Je suis chargée de la communication.I'm in charge of communications.
Je m'occupe des clients.I deal with the customers.
Je travaille chez Lemoine.I work at Lemoine (a company).
Je travaille dans une entreprise de transport.I work for a transport company.
Auparavant, je travaillais dans une banque.Before that, I worked in a bank.

Remember the rule from the very first unit: after je suis, a job takes no article. English says “I'm an accountant”, French says Je suis comptable. But with c'est, you need it: C'est une comptable très sérieuse.

Chez, dans, à

Chez + the name of a company: Je travaille chez Lemoine, like chez le médecin. Dans + a type of company or sector: dans une banque, dans le tourisme. À + a city or a public place: à Lyon, à la mairie, à l'hôpital.

Être chargé de and s'occuper de are followed by a noun, with the usual contractions: chargé du recrutement, je m'occupe des commandes. Chargé agrees like an adjective: a woman says je suis chargée de…

Auparavant (before, previously) is a slightly formal word, perfect at work. In conversation, you'll also hear avant: Avant, j'étais à Lille. The imparfait describes your previous situation.

", "

Four French words for “for”

English uses “for” for every duration. French has four different words, and choosing the wrong one changes the meaning. This is one of the most frequent mistakes of English speakers.

wordusetenseexample
depuisstill going on nowpresentJe travaille ici depuis trois ans.
ça fait… quesame, at the start of the sentencepresentÇa fait trois ans que je travaille ici.
pendanta finished periodpassé composéJ'ai travaillé à Lyon pendant cinq ans.
il y aagopassé composéJe suis arrivé il y a six mois.
poura planned durationwith partir, venir…Je pars à Londres pour deux semaines.

The big trap: “I have worked here for three years” is in the present in French, because you still work here: Je travaille ici depuis trois ans. If you say J'ai travaillé ici pendant trois ans, you no longer work there!

Depuis combien de temps êtes-vous dans l'entreprise ?How long have you been with the company?
Depuis 2021. Avant, j'ai fait un stage à Bordeaux pendant six mois.Since 2021. Before that, I did a six-month internship in Bordeaux.

Depuis also means “since” with a date or a moment: depuis janvier, depuis 2021, depuis lundi. So one French word covers “for” and “since”, as long as the action continues.

Ask yourself: is it still true now? Yes → depuis + present. Finished → pendant. A point in the past → il y a. A plan → pour.

The world of work in France

Some words of French working life have no exact English equivalent, and some look familiar but are traps.

Frenchmeaningnote
le CDIpermanent contractcontrat à durée indéterminée: the one everyone wants
le CDDfixed-term contractcontrat à durée déterminée: un CDD de six mois
le stageinternshipfalse friend! A stagiaire is an intern
le télétravailremote workJe suis en télétravail le vendredi.
les congéstime off, vacation daysles congés payés: five weeks a year
le postethe position, the jobun poste de comptable
le bureauthe office; the deskJe suis au bureau.
le / la responsablethe manager, the person in chargela responsable de l'équipe

L'entreprise (the company) is feminine; in casual speech, people say la boîte: Je change de boîte (I'm changing jobs). L'équipe (the team) is feminine too. And un collègue / une collègue works with you.

Je suis en CDI depuis un an et je fais du télétravail deux jours par semaine.I've had a permanent contract for a year and I work from home two days a week.
Ma responsable est en congé pour deux semaines.My manager is on vacation for two weeks.

At work, people often switch to tu quickly among colleagues, but not always with the boss or with clients. Listen first, or ask: On se tutoie ?
