fr-u13-l2.title: Writing an email
fr-u13-l2.why: Writing to a client or a colleague in French means knowing a set of fixed formulas, from Madame, Monsieur to Cordialement. This lesson gives you the greetings, the polite requests in the conditional, the follow-ups and the closings, so that your emails sound natural from the first line.
fr-u13-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Opening a professional email

A French professional email follows set formulas, more than in English. Use them and you will sound competent; forget them and even perfect grammar sounds odd. In France, people say un mail or un e-mail; un courriel is the official word, very common in Quebec.

The greeting

situationFrenchnote
you don't know the nameMadame, Monsieur,the safe choice for a first contact
you know the nameBonjour Madame Martin,the most common today
more formalMadame, / Monsieur,title alone, no name
warmer, after a few exchangesChère Madame, / Cher Monsieur,no surname after cher / chère
a colleagueBonjour Julien,first name, often with tu

Avoid copying English “Dear Ms. Martin”: Chère Madame Martin sounds clumsy to many French readers. Abbreviations are M. (Monsieur, not “Mr”) and Mme (Madame).

The first sentence

Say straight away why you are writing.

Je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de votre annonce.I am writing to you regarding your ad.
Suite à notre échange téléphonique de ce matin, je vous envoie le devis.Following our phone conversation this morning, I'm sending you the quote.
Je vous écris pour vous demander un rendez-vous.I'm writing to ask you for an appointment.

Je me permets de… literally means “I take the liberty of…”. In English that sounds stiff, but in French it is a very common, polite way to start: learn je me permets de vous écrire as a fixed expression. Use vous by default in a first email; among colleagues, tu depends on the company.

", "

The body: attaching, asking, following up

Most professional emails do one of three things: send a document, ask for something, or follow up when nobody answers.

to…FrenchEnglish
attachVous trouverez ci-joint mon CV.Please find attached my résumé.
attachJe vous envoie ci-joint la facture.I'm attaching the invoice.
askPourriez-vous me confirmer la date ?Could you confirm the date?
askJe souhaiterais savoir si le prix comprend la livraison.I would like to know whether the price includes delivery.
askSerait-il possible de décaler le rendez-vous ?Would it be possible to move the meeting?
follow upJe me permets de revenir vers vous concernant ma commande.I'm following up regarding my order.
follow upSauf erreur de ma part, nous n'avons pas reçu votre paiement.Unless I'm mistaken, we haven't received your payment.
apologizeJe vous prie de m'excuser pour ce retard.Please accept my apologies for the delay.

Requests use the conditional you learned in the A2 level: pourriez-vous, je souhaiterais, serait-il possible. A plain present (Pouvez-vous… ?) is fine too, but the conditional is softer. Never use the imperative with a client: “Send me the file” is too direct.

Ci-joint (attached) is fixed before the noun: ci-joint la facture, ci-joint les documents. Revenir vers quelqu'un is office jargon for “to get back to someone”: Je reviens vers vous demain.

Un devis is a quote (an estimate of price), une facture an invoice, une commande an order. And the subject line of an email is l'objet: Objet : demande de devis.

", "

Closing the email

The ending comes in two parts: a last polite sentence, then the sign-off.

FrenchEnglish
Je reste à votre disposition pour tout renseignement complémentaire.Please don't hesitate to contact me if you need any further information.
Dans l'attente de votre réponse,I look forward to your reply,
Je vous remercie par avance.Thank you in advance.
Cordialement, / Bien cordialement,Best regards, / Kind regards,
Bonne journée, / Belle journée,Have a nice day,

Cordialement is the all-purpose sign-off; it does not mean “cordially” in a warm sense, just “regards”. Among close colleagues you may see Bonne journée, À demain or even Bises, but never with a client.

The very formal letter

For an official letter (an administration, a resignation), you will read: Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées. or Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de mes sentiments distingués. Just recognize these: they are the French equivalent of “Yours faithfully”.

A complete email

Objet : demande de devis
Madame, Monsieur,
Suite à notre échange téléphonique, je me permets de vous écrire au sujet de votre offre. Pourriez-vous m'envoyer un devis pour vingt chaises ? Vous trouverez ci-joint le plan de la salle.
Je vous remercie par avance et reste à votre disposition.
Bien cordialement,
Camille RobertSubject: request for a quote. Dear Sir or Madam, Following our phone conversation, I am writing regarding your offer. Could you send me a quote for twenty chairs? Please find attached the floor plan of the room. Thank you in advance; please let me know if you need anything else. Kind regards, Camille Robert

In French, after the greeting and its comma, the next line starts with a capital letter: Madame, Monsieur, then Je me permets…

fr-u13-l3.topic: professional spoken exchanges; spelling out names and addresses
fr-u13-l3.why: Phone calls and video meetings are where a foreign language gets truly tested. This lesson gives you the fixed phrases of a professional call, the French alphabet for spelling names and email addresses, and the vocabulary of video calls, building on the pronouns you already know.
fr-u13-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

On the phone

Phone calls are hard in a foreign language: no gestures, no lips to read, and set phrases that go fast. The good news is that professional calls in French always use the same handful of formulas.

FrenchEnglish
Allô ?Hello? (only on the phone)
Agence Garonne, bonjour !Garonne Agency, good morning!
Je voudrais parler à Madame Fabre, s'il vous plaît.I'd like to speak to Ms. Fabre, please.
C'est de la part de qui ?Who's calling, please?
Ne quittez pas.Hold on, please. (don't hang up)
Je vous la passe. / Je vous le passe.I'll put you through to her / to him.
Elle est en réunion. / Il est en ligne.She's in a meeting. / He's on another call.
Voulez-vous laisser un message ?Would you like to leave a message?
Je lui transmets votre message.I'll pass on your message to him / her.
Je vous rappelle. / Elle peut me rappeler ?I'll call you back. / Can she call me back?

Notice the pronouns from unit 10: in Je vous la passe, vous is “to you” and la is Madame Fabre (“I pass her to you”). Indirect before direct, both before the verb. For a man: Je vous le passe.

Allô is only for the phone: never use it to greet someone in the street. A company answers with its name + bonjour, and you answer with Bonjour + who you are: Bonjour, Karim Benali, de la société Duval.

Ne quittez pas literally means “don't leave”: it's the fixed phrase for “please hold”. And rappeler doubles its l like appeler: je vous rappelle, but nous vous rappelons.

", "

Spelling it out

You will constantly be asked to spell your name: Vous pouvez épeler, s'il vous plaît ? The French alphabet uses the same letters as English, but several of them sound confusingly different.

lettersounds liketrap for English speakers
A“ah”not “ay”
E“euh”not “ee”
I“ee”not “eye”
G“zhay”sounds like an English J
J“zhee”sounds like an English G
H“ash”ache
R“air”, from the throaterre
Uthe French u (lips rounded)different from ou
W“doo-bluh-vay”double vé
Y“ee-grek”i grec

The usual pairs to watch: G / J, E / I, and A / R. When spelling, add the extras: e accent aigu (é), e accent grave (è), e accent circonflexe (ê), c cédille (ç), deux l (ll), tiret (hyphen), majuscule (capital).

Héloïse : H, E accent aigu, L, O, I tréma, S, E.Héloïse: H, E acute accent, L, O, I with a dieresis, S, E.

Email addresses and phone numbers

For an email address: arobase (@), point (.), tiret (-), tiret du bas (_), and tout attaché (all one word).

karim.benali@duval.fr : karim point benali arobase duval point frkarim.benali@duval.fr

French phone numbers have ten digits, read in pairs: 06 42 17 85 30 is zéro six, quarante-deux, dix-sept, quatre-vingt-cinq, trente. A number starting with 06 or 07 is a cell phone.

When people spell on the phone, they often add a first name to avoid confusion: B comme Bernard, N comme Nicolas. Use it for your own name if the line is bad.

", "

Video calls, messages and appointments

Meetings on video have their own little phrases, often in the tu form among colleagues.

FrenchEnglish
Vous m'entendez ? / Tu m'entends ?Can you hear me?
Je vous entends mal.I can't hear you well.
Ça a coupé.We got cut off. / It cut out.
Ton micro est coupé.Your mic is muted.
Tu partages ton écran ?Can you share your screen?
Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?Could you repeat that, please?
La connexion est mauvaise.The connection is bad.

Note entendre mal: French puts the adverb after the verb, where English says “I can't hear you well”. French also drops “can” with verbs of perception: Je vous entends = I can hear you.

Leaving a message

On a messagerie (voicemail), keep the order: who you are, why you're calling, how to call back.

Bonjour, c'est Karim Benali, de la société Duval. Je vous appelle au sujet du devis. Vous pouvez me rappeler au 06 42 17 85 30. Merci, bonne journée !Hello, this is Karim Benali from Duval. I'm calling about the quote. You can call me back at 06 42 17 85 30. Thanks, have a nice day!

Setting an appointment

Vous êtes disponible jeudi ? — Jeudi à 10 h, ça vous va ? — Parfait, c'est noté.Are you free on Thursday? — Thursday at 10, does that work for you? — Perfect, I've made a note of it.

On the phone, the 24-hour clock is normal for appointments: à quatorze heures trente (2:30 p.m.). Repeat the time to confirm: Donc jeudi, quatorze heures trente.

fr-u13-l4.title: In a meeting
fr-u13-l4.why: This lesson closes the work unit with the meeting: taking the floor, proposing, agreeing or disagreeing with tact, and concluding. You reuse the conditional and the connectors you know, and you learn the vocabulary of projects, including the false friend délai.
fr-u13-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Opening the meeting and taking the floor

French meetings (les réunions) can be lively: people interrupt, add comments, come back to an earlier point. To take part, you need a few formulas to start, to take the floor and to add an idea without sounding rude.

FrenchEnglish
Bon, on commence ?Right, shall we start?
Le premier point à l'ordre du jour, c'est le budget.The first item on the agenda is the budget.
On fait le point sur le projet.Let's review where we are on the project.
Si je peux me permettre…If I may…
Je peux dire un mot ?Can I say something?
Je voudrais ajouter que…I'd like to add that…
Pardon de vous interrompre, mais…Sorry to interrupt, but…
Pour revenir au budget…To come back to the budget…

L'ordre du jour is the agenda of a meeting (your personal planner is un agenda: careful!). Faire le point means to take stock, to review where things stand: On fait le point lundi ? is one of the most frequent sentences in a French office.

Si je peux me permettre, je voudrais ajouter que le client est très content.If I may, I'd like to add that the client is very happy.

Si je peux me permettre is the polite door-opener, a cousin of je me permets de vous écrire from the email lesson. In a meeting it softens anything that follows, even a disagreement.

", "

Proposing, agreeing, disagreeing

To make a proposal, French has several options, from the most direct to the softest.

FrenchEnglish
Je propose de reporter la réunion.I suggest postponing the meeting.
On pourrait demander l'avis du client.We could ask the client's opinion.
Il faudrait finir avant vendredi.We ought to finish before Friday.
Et si on faisait une pause ?How about taking a break?

After je propose de, use an infinitive: English “I suggest postponing” becomes je propose de reporter (not an -ing form). Et si on faisait… ? is the fixed formula you met for invitations: si + imparfait = “how about…?”. The conditional (on pourrait, il faudrait, nous devrions) makes everything more diplomatic.

Reacting

agreeingdisagreeing (politely)
Je suis tout à fait d'accord.Je ne suis pas d'accord.
Bonne idée !Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord.
Exactement.Je comprends, mais…
Je suis d'accord avec Léa.Je ne suis pas sûr / sûre.

Être d'accord means “to agree”: never say “je suis agréé” or “j'agrée”. Tout à fait (completely) strengthens it; pas tout à fait (not entirely) is the classic French way to disagree softly.

In speech, par contre (on the other hand, however) is everywhere in meetings: L'idée est bonne. Par contre, le délai est court.

", "

Concluding and following up

At the end of a meeting, someone sums up, opens the floor for questions and asks who will write the report.

FrenchEnglish
Pour résumer…To sum up…
En conclusion…In conclusion…
Avez-vous des questions ?Do you have any questions?
Qui fait le compte rendu ?Who's taking the minutes?
Je m'en occupe.I'll take care of it.
On se retrouve mardi pour faire le point.We'll meet again on Tuesday to review.

Words of the project

Le projet, la date limite (the deadline), le délai and le compte rendu (the minutes, the report). Watch the false friend: le délai is the time allowed to do something (un délai de deux semaines, le délai est court), not a delay. A delay, being late, is un retard.

Le délai est court : la date limite, c'est le 15 mars.The timeline is tight: the deadline is March 15.

On or nous?

In the meeting itself, people say on: On commence ? On fait le point. In the written minutes, you switch to nous: Nous gardons la date du 15 mars. The verb changes too: on garde but nous gardons.

The French love to end a meeting by scheduling the next one. If you volunteer for the minutes, say Je m'en occupe, then Je vous l'envoie cet après-midi: you'll sound perfectly at ease.

fr-u14-l1.title: Relative pronouns: qui, que, où, dont
fr-u14-l1.topic: relative pronouns; ce qui / ce que
fr-u14-l1.why: Relative pronouns are what turn short sentences into precise, natural ones: the colleague who, the book that, the day when. This lesson explains qui, que, où and dont by contrast with English, where that is often dropped and prepositions end up at the end of the sentence.
fr-u14-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Qui and que

Relative pronouns let you build longer, more precise sentences: “the colleague who works with me”, “the book that I'm reading”. English chooses between who, which and that depending on whether it's a person or a thing. French doesn't care about that: it chooses depending on the role of the pronoun in its clause.

pronounrolewhat followsexample
quisubjecta verble collègue qui travaille avec moi
que / qu'direct objecta subject + verble collègue que je vois tous les jours

The quick test: look at the word right after the gap. If it's a verb, it's qui: la femme qui parle. If it's a subject (je, tu, Paul, les enfants…), it's que: la femme que Paul connaît. And it works the same for people and things: le train qui part, le train que je prends.

J'ai une amie qui habite à Rennes.I have a friend who lives in Rennes.
C'est le livre que je lis en ce moment.It's the book (that) I'm reading at the moment.
Le film qu'on a vu hier était génial.The movie we saw yesterday was great.

The big trap for English speakers: English can drop “that”: “the book I'm reading”, “the man I met”. French never drops que: le livre que je lis, l'homme que j'ai rencontré. Without it, the sentence is simply wrong.

Que becomes qu' before a vowel (qu'il, qu'on, qu'elle). Qui never elides: l'ami qui arrive, never “qu'arrive”.

", "

Où and dont

Où: where… and when

Où introduces a place, as in English: la ville où j'habite (the town where I live). But it also introduces a moment, where English uses “when” or nothing at all:

Lyon, c'est la ville où je suis né.Lyon is the city where I was born.
Le jour où je suis arrivé à Paris, il pleuvait.The day (when) I arrived in Paris, it was raining.
C'était l'année où on a acheté la maison.It was the year we bought the house.

Never use quand after a noun of time: “le jour quand” is a typical English speaker's mistake. Say le jour où, le moment où, l'été où.

Dont: replacing de + noun

Dont replaces a complement introduced by de. Think of the verbs and expressions with de you know: parler de, avoir besoin de, s'occuper de, avoir envie de, être content de.

with dewith dont
Je parle de ce film.le film dont je parle (the film I'm talking about)
J'ai besoin de cet outil.l'outil dont j'ai besoin (the tool I need)
Je m'occupe de ce projet.le projet dont je m'occupe (the project I'm in charge of)

Dont also translates “whose”: la femme dont le fils est médecin (the woman whose son is a doctor). Careful, no possessive after it: not “dont son fils”.

English often ends the sentence with a preposition: “the film I'm talking about”, “the tool I need”. French can't do that: the de moves to the front and becomes dont.

", "

Ce qui, ce que, and agreement

When English says “what” in the middle of a sentence (not a question), French uses ce qui or ce que, with the same rule as qui and que: a verb follows → ce qui; a subject follows → ce que.

Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est l'histoire.What interests me is history.
Ce que je veux, c'est un café.What I want is a coffee.
Je ne comprends pas ce que tu dis.I don't understand what you're saying.
Dis-moi ce qui ne va pas.Tell me what's wrong.

The structure Ce que…, c'est… is very common in speech to highlight something: Ce que j'aime à Bordeaux, c'est la Garonne. Never use quoi here: “je ne sais pas quoi tu veux” is wrong; say je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.

Agreement after que

You know the rule from unit 10: with avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it. Que is exactly that: a direct object placed before the verb. So the participle agrees with the noun que stands for.

nounexample
la robe (fem. sing.)la robe que j'ai achetée
les photos (fem. pl.)les photos que tu as prises
les gâteaux (masc. pl.)les gâteaux qu'elle a faits

Most of the time you can't hear the agreement (achetée sounds like acheté), but with participles ending in a consonant you can: prise, mise, faite, écrite. La lettre qu'il a écrite: the t is pronounced.

fr-u14-l2.title: On and se: speaking in general
fr-u14-l2.topic: impersonal on; pronominal passive; ça se fait
fr-u14-l2.why: French rarely uses the passive to talk about what people generally do: it prefers on and pronominal verbs like ça se fait or ça ne se dit pas. This lesson teaches these structures through French customs and etiquette, from la bise to table manners.
fr-u14-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

On: people in general

You have used on since the start as an everyday “we”: On va au cinéma ? But on has a second, very common meaning: people in general. English expresses this idea with “you”, “they”, “people”, “one”… or with a passive.

Ici, on parle français.French is spoken here. / We speak French here.
En France, on dîne vers vingt heures.In France, people have dinner around 8 p.m.
On dit que ce restaurant est le meilleur de Lyon.They say this restaurant is the best in Lyon.
On ne sait jamais.You never know.

Whatever its meaning, on always takes the verb in the third person singular, like il or elle: on parle, on dit, on fait, on peut.

Three meanings of on

meaningexampleEnglish
weOn part demain.We're leaving tomorrow.
people in generalEn Bretagne, on mange des crêpes.In Brittany, people eat crêpes.
someoneOn a sonné.Someone rang the doorbell.

The third meaning replaces many English passives: On m'a volé mon vélo (my bike was stolen), On m'a dit que le musée était fermé (I was told the museum was closed). French prefers an active sentence with on to a passive.

When an English sentence starts with “You…” but means anybody (“You can't park here”), think on: On ne peut pas stationner ici. Using tu or vous there would sound as if you were talking about the listener personally.

", "

Se: “it's done”, “it's said”

French has another way to express a general rule or habit: a pronominal verb with a thing as the subject. English uses a passive (“it's eaten cold”), French uses se + verb.

FrenchEnglish
Ça se mange froid.It's eaten cold.
Ce vin se boit frais.This wine is drunk chilled.
Le français se parle dans trente pays.French is spoken in thirty countries.
Comment ça se dit en français ?How do you say that in French?
Ça s'écrit comment ?How is it spelled?
Ça ne se dit pas.You don't say that.

The verb agrees with its subject: le fromage se mange, but les huîtres se mangent crues (oysters are eaten raw). And the negation goes around se + verb: ça ne se dit pas.

Ça se fait / ça ne se fait pas

This is the key expression for talking about etiquette. Ça se fait means “it's the done thing, it's normal”; ça ne se fait pas means “it's not done, it's rude”.

Apporter des fleurs quand on est invité ? Oui, ça se fait.Bringing flowers when you're invited? Yes, that's what people do.
Mettre le pain sur l'assiette ? Non, ça ne se fait pas en France.Putting the bread on your plate? No, that's not done in France.

Don't confuse this se with the reflexive verbs you know (je me lève). Here, the thing doesn't do anything to itself: ça se mange doesn't mean “it eats itself”! It means people eat it.

", "

Customs, rules and signs

To state a rule, French also uses impersonal phrases with il, which means nobody in particular: Il faut + infinitive (you have to) and Il est interdit de + infinitive (it is forbidden to). Learn il est interdit de with its de as a fixed expression. On signs, you often just read Interdit de fumer or Interdiction de stationner.

Il est interdit de fumer dans les gares.Smoking is not allowed in train stations.
Dans un magasin, il faut toujours dire bonjour.In a shop, you always have to say hello.

A few French customs

customin French
greeting friendsOn se fait la bise: two kisses in Paris, three or four in some regions.
at a dinner partyOn apporte du vin, des fleurs ou un dessert. But not chrysanthemums: they are for funerals.
arrivingOn arrive avec un petit quart d'heure de retard: arriving early is awkward.
at the tableLe pain se pose sur la table, and on garde les mains sur la table.
the cheeseLe fromage se mange après le plat et avant le dessert.

La bise is the light kiss on the cheek between friends, family, and often colleagues. With strangers and in formal situations, on se serre la main (people shake hands). If you are not sure, wait for the other person to lean in.

All these sentences use on or se because they describe what people in general do. They are perfect for comparing cultures: Chez moi, ça ne se fait pas ! or Aux États-Unis, on dîne plus tôt.

fr-u14-l3.why: Should it be commencer à or commencer de, essayer à or essayer de? This lesson sorts out which verbs take à, de or nothing before an infinitive, and shows how English -ing forms become infinitives in French. It prepares the next step: the subjunctive, for when the second verb has a different subject.

{"lessons": ["

Verb + infinitive: no preposition

When a verb is followed by another verb, French puts the second one in the infinitive. Sometimes nothing comes in between, sometimes à, sometimes de. There is no logic you can deduce from English: learn each verb with its little word, the way you learn a noun with its article.

Group 1: nothing in between

You already know most of these verbs. English often has “to”, French has nothing.

verbexampleEnglish
aimer, adorer, détesterJ'aime cuisiner.I like to cook / cooking.
préférerJe préfère rester ici.I'd rather stay here.
vouloirJe veux partir.I want to leave.
pouvoirTu peux venir ?Can you come?
devoirJe dois travailler.I have to work.
savoirElle sait nager.She can swim.
espérerJ'espère vous voir bientôt.I hope to see you soon.
allerOn va dîner.We're going to have dinner.
il fautIl faut partir.We have to go.

Never add a preposition after these verbs: “j'aime de cuisiner” or “je veux de partir” are typical mistakes.

Watch venir. Je viens manger (no preposition) means “I'm coming to eat”. Je viens de manger means “I've just eaten” (unit 6). One little word changes the whole meaning!

", "

Group 2: verbs with à

A smaller group takes à before the infinitive. Many of them express an effort or a progression: starting, learning, managing, continuing.

verbexampleEnglish
commencer àIl commence à pleuvoir.It's starting to rain.
apprendre àJ'apprends à conduire.I'm learning to drive.
réussir àTu as réussi à dormir ?Did you manage to sleep?
aider quelqu'un àTu m'aides à porter la valise ?Will you help me carry the suitcase?
continuer àIls continuent à travailler.They keep on working.
penser àPense à réserver !Remember to book!
hésiter àJ'hésite à lui téléphoner.I'm hesitant to call him.

This à never contracts, since it's followed by a verb: j'apprends à écrire. And with aider, the person comes first as a direct object: J'aide ma sœur à faire ses devoirs, je l'aide à…

Penser à + infinitive is the everyday way to say “remember to” or “don't forget to”: Tu penses à acheter du pain ? (Will you remember to buy bread?).

Continuer also exists with de: ils continuent de travailler. Both are correct, with no difference in meaning. With commencer, use à.

", "

Group 3: verbs with de

The biggest group takes de (d' before a vowel). Many verbs about stopping, trying, deciding and feeling are here, as well as the expressions with avoir.

verbexampleEnglish
arrêter deJ'ai arrêté de fumer.I stopped smoking.
finir deOn a fini de manger.We've finished eating.
essayer deJ'essaie de comprendre.I'm trying to understand.
décider deNous avons décidé de partir.We decided to leave.
oublier deN'oublie pas d'appeler ta mère.Don't forget to call your mother.
accepter de / refuser deIl a refusé de répondre.He refused to answer.
avoir besoin de / envie de / peur deJ'ai envie de voyager.I feel like traveling.

The English -ing trap: after “stop”, “finish”, “enjoy”, English uses -ing. French has no -ing form: always the infinitive. “I stopped smoking” → J'ai arrêté de fumer, never “arrêté fumant”.

Asking or telling someone to do something

With demander and dire, the person takes à and the action takes de: demander à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose.

Je lui ai demandé de venir.I asked him / her to come.
Dis à Lucas de m'appeler ce soir.Tell Lucas to call me tonight.
Le médecin leur a dit de se reposer.The doctor told them to rest.

English “I asked him to come” has the same shape as “I want him to come”, but French separates them: Je lui ai demandé de venir works with an infinitive. For “I want him to come” you need a new tense, the subjunctive, in the next lesson.

fr-u15-l1.title: The present subjunctive
fr-u15-l1.topic: formation and triggers of the subjunctive
fr-u15-l1.why: The subjunctive is the new mood you need as soon as you want, require or wish something for someone else: Je veux que tu viennes. This lesson shows how to form it from the ils form of the present, the key irregulars, and its main triggers, by contrast with the English infinitive.
fr-u15-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

A new mood: the subjunctive

Until now, every verb you conjugated was in the indicative (present, past, future) or the conditional. The subjunctive is a different mood: it doesn't present a fact, it presents something wished, required or intended. English still has traces of it (“I insist that he be on time”), but French uses it every day, after il faut que, je veux que and a few other expressions.

The regular formation

Take the ils form of the present, remove -ent, and add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. The subjunctive is almost always introduced by que, so it's learned with it.

parler
(ils parlent)		finir
(ils finissent)		attendre
(ils attendent)
que je / j'parlefinisseattende
que tuparlesfinissesattendes
qu'il / elle / onparlefinisseattende
que nousparlionsfinissionsattendions
que vousparliezfinissiezattendiez
qu'ils / ellesparlentfinissentattendent

Good news for -er verbs: the je, tu, il, ils forms are identical to the present, and the nous, vous forms look like the imparfait (que nous parlions). For -ir and -re verbs, the difference is audible: il finit but qu'il finisse, il attend but qu'il attende (the d is pronounced).

Il faut que tu finisses tes devoirs.You have to finish your homework.
Je veux que vous attendiez ici.I want you to wait here.

Spelling-change verbs keep their change where the present has it: que j'achète, que nous achetions; que j'appelle, que nous appelions. The boot pattern from unit 3 still works.

", "

Two stems and true irregulars

Some verbs have two stems in the present (ils prennent / nous prenons). In the subjunctive, nous and vous take the nous stem; the others take the ils stem.

prendrevenirboire
que jeprennevienneboive
que tuprennesviennesboives
qu'il / elle / onprennevienneboive
que nousprenionsvenionsbuvions
que vouspreniezveniezbuviez
qu'ils / ellesprennentviennentboivent

The same goes for devoir (que je doive, que nous devions) and voir (que je voie, que nous voyions).

The irregulars to learn by heart

êtreavoirallerfaire
que je / j'soisaieaillefasse
que tusoisaiesaillesfasses
qu'il / elle / onsoitaitaillefasse
que noussoyonsayonsallionsfassions
que voussoyezayezalliezfassiez
qu'ils / ellessoientaientaillentfassent
pouvoirsavoirvouloir
que jepuissesacheveuille
que tupuissessachesveuilles
qu'il / elle / onpuissesacheveuille
que nouspuissionssachionsvoulions
que vouspuissiezsachiezvouliez
qu'ils / ellespuissentsachentveuillent

And for falloir, only one form: qu'il faille. Notice that que j'aie sounds exactly like j'ai: only the spelling shows the subjunctive. You already know sache, ayez and veuillez from the imperative: they come from the same forms.

Don't try to memorize everything at once. Être, avoir, aller, faire cover a huge share of everyday use: il faut que je sois…, il faut que j'aille…, il faut que tu fasses…

", "

When to use it

The subjunctive comes after que when the main verb expresses an obligation, a wish, a preference or a goal, and the two verbs have different subjects.

triggerexampleEnglish
il faut queIl faut que tu partes.You have to leave.
vouloir queJe veux que tu viennes.I want you to come.
aimer queJ'aimerais que vous soyez là.I'd like you to be there.
souhaiter queJe souhaite qu'il réussisse.I hope he succeeds.
préférer queElle préfère que nous prenions le train.She'd rather we took the train.
pour queJe parle lentement pour que tu comprennes.I'm speaking slowly so that you understand.

The big English trap: “I want you to come” uses an infinitive in English. French can't say “je veux toi venir”: when the subject changes, you need que + subjunctive: Je veux que tu viennes.

Same subject → infinitive

If the person who wants and the person who acts are the same, no que, no subjunctive: just the infinitive, as in the last lesson.

same subjectdifferent subjects
Je veux venir. (I want to come.)Je veux que tu viennes. (I want you to come.)
Je préfère partir. (I'd rather leave.)Je préfère que tu partes. (I'd rather you left.)
Je travaille pour réussir. (I work to succeed.)Je travaille pour que tu réussisses. (I work so that you succeed.)

Il faut works both ways too: Il faut partir (we have to go, in general) or Il faut que je parte (I have to go, specifically me).

Not every que triggers the subjunctive: Je sais que tu viens and Je pense que tu as raison state facts or opinions, so they stay in the indicative. The next lesson is all about that choice.

fr-u15-l2.title: Subjunctive or indicative?
fr-u15-l2.why: This lesson answers the question every learner asks after meeting the subjunctive: when exactly do you need it? You learn to choose between indicative and subjunctive after opinions, feelings, doubt and possibility, and to avoid the classic traps espérer que, quand and après que.
fr-u15-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Opinions: the indicative by default

In the last lesson, the subjunctive came after wishes and necessity: il faut que, je veux que. Now the everyday question: after que, how do you know which mood to choose? Good news first. When you simply say what you think or believe, French uses the ordinary indicative, the forms you have known for months, present, past or future.

Opinion or certainty+ indicative
je pense que (I think that)Je pense qu'il a raison.
je crois que (I believe that)Je crois que Léa est malade.
il me semble que (it seems to me that)Il me semble que la boulangerie est fermée.
je suis sûr / sûre que (I'm sure that)Je suis sûre qu'elle viendra.
il est probable que (it's likely that)Il est probable qu'il pleuvra demain.

The switch: negation and inversion

As soon as the opinion becomes negative, or a question with inversion, the fact is no longer presented as true. It becomes uncertain, and French switches to the subjunctive. English changes nothing: \"I think he's right\", \"I don't think he's right\".

Je pense qu'il a raison. → Je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.I think he's right. → I don't think he's right.
Je crois que c'est vrai. → Je ne crois pas que ce soit vrai.I believe it's true. → I don't believe it's true.
Penses-tu qu'elle puisse venir ?Do you think she can come?

In conversation, a question asked with simple intonation usually keeps the indicative: Tu penses qu'il va venir ? is perfectly natural. With inversion (Penses-tu que… ?, Croyez-vous que… ?) or with a negation, use the subjunctive.

", "

Feelings, doubt, possibility

The subjunctive is the mood of what you feel about a fact, of doubt, and of what is only possible. English uses an ordinary verb here (\"I'm glad you're here\"), so this is where English speakers slip. In French, the fact may be perfectly real: what counts is that the main verb expresses an emotion or a doubt.

TriggerExample
joy, sadnessje suis content / contente que, je suis triste queJe suis contente que tu sois là.
surprise, regretje suis surpris / surprise que, je regrette que, c'est dommage queC'est dommage que tu partes déjà.
fearj'ai peur queJ'ai peur qu'il fasse froid à Lille.
doubtje doute que, je ne suis pas sûr / sûre queJe doute qu'elle sache la réponse.
possibilityil est possible queIl est possible que nous soyons en retard.

Possible or probable?

The pair il est possible que / il est probable que shows the logic of the whole system. Something possible is uncertain: subjunctive. Something likely is almost a fact: indicative.

Il est possible qu'il pleuve. / Il est probable qu'il pleuvra.It might rain. / It will probably rain.

Careful with the false friend sans doute: it does not mean \"without a doubt\" but simply probably. Il viendra sans doute = he'll probably come. For real certainty, French says sans aucun doute.

After j'ai peur que, careful written French often adds a small ne that is not negative at all: J'ai peur qu'il ne pleuve means exactly the same as J'ai peur qu'il pleuve. Learn to recognize it; you don't need to use it.

", "

Three traps and one shortcut

Trap 1: espérer que + indicative

It looks like a wish, yet espérer que takes the indicative, very often the future. Its cousin souhaiter que takes the subjunctive. Learn the pair together.

espérer que + indicativesouhaiter que + subjunctive
J'espère que tu vas bien.Je souhaite que tu ailles mieux.
J'espère qu'il fera beau samedi.Je souhaite qu'il fasse beau samedi.

Trap 2: quand + future, never the subjunctive

Quand introduces a fact in time, not a doubt: Quand tu seras à Lyon, appelle-moi. English uses the present (\"when you are\"), French uses the future, and never the subjunctive.

Trap 3: après que + indicative

Avant que takes the subjunctive (the event has not happened yet), but in the norm après que takes the indicative (the event has happened): Après que les invités sont partis, on fait la vaisselle. You will often hear the subjunctive after après que; in an exercise, choose the indicative. Even simpler: après le départ des invités.

The shortcut: same subject → de + infinitive

As with vouloir, if both verbs have the same subject, drop que and use de + infinitive after feelings:

Je suis content de te voir. / Je suis content que tu sois là.I'm glad to see you. / I'm glad you're here.
J'ai peur de me tromper. / J'ai peur qu'il se trompe.I'm afraid of making a mistake. / I'm afraid he's making a mistake.

A quick test: is the main verb a simple opinion or a certainty, said positively? Indicative. Is it a negative opinion, an emotion, a doubt or a possibility? Subjunctive.

fr-u15-l3.title: Debating
fr-u15-l3.why: After the mechanics of the subjunctive, this lesson gives you the words of a real discussion: framing your opinion, agreeing, disagreeing politely and nuancing. It closes the unit on opinions with debates on very French topics: city or countryside, remote work and the long lunch break.
fr-u15-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Saying what you think

You now have the grammar of opinion: the indicative after je pense que, the subjunctive after je ne pense pas que. This lesson gives you the words that frame an opinion and link arguments, so you can hold your own in a real discussion: at a dinner, in a meeting, at the coffee machine.

FrenchEnglishNote
À mon avis, …In my opinion, …never \"dans mon opinion\"
Selon moi, … / D'après moi, …As I see it, …also selon toi ?, selon vous ?
Pour moi, …For me, …very common in speech
Personnellement, …Personally, …to set yourself apart
Je trouve que…I think, I find that…a personal impression, + indicative

Être d'accord, avoir raison

Two small words, two classic mistakes. \"I agree\" is built with être: je suis d'accord, never \"j'accorde\". \"You're right\" and \"you're wrong\" are built with avoir, like avoir faim or avoir froid: tu as raison, tu as tort.

— À mon avis, Lyon est plus agréable que Paris. — Je suis d'accord avec toi.— In my opinion, Lyon is nicer than Paris. — I agree with you.
Vous avez raison, c'est trop loin.You're right, it's too far.

À mon avis and selon moi already mean \"I think\": don't add je pense que after them. À mon avis, je pense que… sounds as clumsy as \"In my opinion, I think that…\". Say À mon avis, c'est trop cher, or simply Je pense que c'est trop cher.

", "

Agreeing, disagreeing, nuancing

A good discussion is rarely yes or no. Here is a scale, from full agreement to full disagreement:

FrenchEnglish
Je suis tout à fait d'accord.I completely agree.
Tu as raison. / Vous avez raison.You're right.
Tu as raison, mais…You're right, but…
Il est vrai que…, mais… / C'est vrai que…, mais…It's true that…, but…
Ça dépend.It depends.
Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord.I don't completely agree.
Je ne suis pas du tout d'accord.I don't agree at all.
Tu as tort.You're wrong.

Don't mix up pas tout à fait (not completely: polite nuance) and pas du tout (not at all: a clear no). Ça dépend takes de before a noun: ça dépend du travail, ça dépend des gens.

The subjunctive comes back

When you disagree or regret something, the triggers of the last two lessons appear naturally:

Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.I don't think it's a good idea.
Je ne suis pas sûr que tout le monde puisse travailler à la maison.I'm not sure everyone can work from home.
C'est dommage que les gens prennent moins le temps de déjeuner.It's a shame people take less time for lunch.

Il est vrai que and c'est vrai que take the indicative: you admit a fact before answering it. C'est vrai que la ville est chère, mais il y a tout.

", "

Linking arguments

To build an argument, you need words that show contrast. French has a richer set than \"but\" and \"however\", and each one has its own nuance:

FrenchEnglishUse
d'un côté… de l'autre…on the one hand… on the other…weighing two sides
pourtantyet, and yeta surprising contrast
cependanthowevermore formal: writing, meetings
en revancheon the other hand, by contrastcomparing two different things
par contreon the other handthe spoken version of en revanche
Il fait très beau. Pourtant, Hugo reste à la maison.It's a beautiful day. And yet Hugo is staying home.
La ville est bruyante. En revanche, tout est près.The city is noisy. On the other hand, everything is close by.
D'un côté, le télétravail évite les trajets ; de l'autre, on voit moins ses collègues.On the one hand, remote work saves commuting; on the other, you see your colleagues less.

A very French topic: the lunch break

In France, la pause déjeuner often lasts an hour, and many people still eat a real meal, sitting down, with colleagues. It's a perfect topic to practice: D'un côté, c'est long ; de l'autre, on mange mieux et on discute.

English often says \"on the other hand\" without \"on the one hand\". In French, use en revanche or par contre for that. On its own, de l'autre côté means \"on the other side\" (of the street, of the river).

fr-u16-l1.title: If I had…: hypotheses
fr-u16-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on imagining and regretting with hypotheses: si + imparfait + conditional, to talk about what you would do with more time or money. It builds on the futur simple and the conditional of unit 11 and drills the golden rule: never the conditional after si.
fr-u16-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Imagining: si + imparfait + conditional

In unit 11 you met two tools: si + present + future for real conditions (S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage), and the conditional for politeness and advice. Put them together and you can imagine: what would you do if you had more time, more money, another life?

ConditionTensesExample
real, possiblesi + present → futureSi j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
imagined, unlikely, unrealsi + imparfait → conditionalSi j'avais le temps, je viendrais.

The logic is the same as in English: \"If I have time, I'll come\" (it may happen) versus \"If I had time, I'd come\" (I probably don't). Even the tenses match: the English past after \"if\" becomes the French imparfait, and \"would\" becomes the conditional.

si + imparfaitconditional
jeSi j'avais le temps,je voyagerais.
tuSi tu avais le temps,tu voyagerais.
il / elle / onSi elle avait le temps,elle voyagerait.
nousSi nous avions le temps,nous voyagerions.
vousSi vous aviez le temps,vous voyageriez.
ils / ellesS'ils avaient le temps,ils voyageraient.

Si becomes s' only before il and ils: s'il, s'ils. Never before elle or on: si elle avait, si on partait.

", "

Never the conditional after si

This is the golden rule. In casual English you sometimes hear \"if I would have money…\", and learners translate it as \"si j'aurais\". In French, the conditional never goes in the si clause: si takes the imparfait, and the conditional goes in the other half of the sentence.

Si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais une maison à Nice.If I had money, I'd buy a house in Nice.

If I were…

English \"if I were\" is simply si j'étais: Si j'étais riche, je ne travaillerais plus. For advice, \"if I were you\" is usually à ta place or à votre place, followed by the conditional: À ta place, je refuserais.

Either order

The si clause can come first or second, with the same tenses: Je voyagerais plus si j'avais le temps. Use a comma only when si comes first.

Hear the r

The imparfait and the conditional share their endings. The only difference is the r of the future stem, so pronounce it clearly:

imparfaitconditional
je parlaisje parlerais
tu finissaistu finirais
il faisaitil ferait
nous pouvionsnous pourrions
ils étaientils seraient

Irregular verbs use their future stem in the conditional: ferais, serais, aurais, irais, pourrais, viendrais, voudrais, devrais, saurais, verrais.

", "

Dreams, wishes, suggestions

Si seulement… ! (if only…!)

On its own, si seulement + imparfait expresses a wish or a regret about the present: Si seulement j'avais plus de vacances ! Si seulement il faisait beau !

Et si… ? (how about…? what if…?)

Et si + imparfait makes a friendly suggestion, with no conditional at all. You know Si on allait au cinéma ? from unit 11: it's the same structure.

Et si on partait ce week-end ?How about going away this weekend?
Et si on invitait Thomas ?What if we invited Thomas?

Au cas où (in case)

To recognize: unlike si, au cas où is followed by the conditional: Prends un parapluie au cas où il pleuvrait. In conversation it often stands alone at the end: Prends un parapluie, au cas où.

Talking about your dreams

Useful phrases: gagner beaucoup d'argent, faire le tour du monde, prendre une année sabbatique, changer de métier, s'installer à la campagne, arrêter de travailler.

Si je prenais une année sabbatique, je m'installerais à la campagne et j'apprendrais à faire du pain.If I took a year off, I'd move to the countryside and learn to make bread.

To ask about someone's dreams: Qu'est-ce que tu ferais si… ? or, in casual speech, Tu ferais quoi si… ? The answer often keeps only the conditional: Moi ? Je partirais !

fr-u16-l2.title: The plus-que-parfait
fr-u16-l2.why: This lesson adds the plus-que-parfait, the French past perfect, to the passé composé and the imparfait. With these three past tenses you can tell a story precisely, including what had happened before, as in a failed evening or a trip full of surprises.
fr-u16-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

One step further back

The plus-que-parfait is the French equivalent of the English past perfect: \"I had finished\", \"she had left\". It works almost exactly like English, and you already know all its pieces: take the passé composé and put the auxiliary avoir or être in the imparfait.

finir (avoir)partir (être)se lever (être)
jej'avais finij'étais parti(e)je m'étais levé(e)
tutu avais finitu étais parti(e)tu t'étais levé(e)
il / elle / onil avait finiil était parti / elle était partieil s'était levé / elle s'était levée
nousnous avions fininous étions parti(e)snous nous étions levé(e)s
vousvous aviez finivous étiez parti(e)(s)vous vous étiez levé(e)(s)
ils / ellesils avaient finiils étaient partis / elles étaient partiesils s'étaient levés / elles s'étaient levées

Same rules as the passé composé

  • Same auxiliary: movement verbs like aller, venir, arriver, partir, rester, tomber and all pronominal verbs take être.
  • Agreement with the subject after être: Elle était déjà partie.
  • Agreement with a direct object placed before avoir: Les billets ? Je les avais oubliés.
  • Negation around the auxiliary, and déjà or jamais after it: Je n'avais pas compris. Il avait déjà mangé.

With on meaning \"we\", everyday French makes the participle agree with the real people: On était partis tôt.

", "

The past before the past

Use the plus-que-parfait for an action that happened before another moment in the past. Choosing it or not can change the whole story:

Quand je suis arrivé, le film avait déjà commencé.When I arrived, the movie had already started. (it started before I arrived)
Quand je suis arrivé, le film a commencé.When I arrived, the movie started. (right at that moment)

Where English is relaxed, French is strict

English often uses the simple past when the order of events is obvious: \"I saw that I forgot my keys\". French is stricter: if one action came before another in the past, the earlier one goes in the plus-que-parfait.

J'ai vu que j'avais oublié mes clés.I saw that I had forgotten my keys.
Elle était fatiguée parce qu'elle avait mal dormi.She was tired because she had slept badly.
Je n'avais jamais vu la mer avant ce voyage.I had never seen the sea before that trip.

Background information

It also gives what you had heard or what had happened before the story starts: On m'avait dit que ce restaurant était excellent. Il avait plu toute la nuit et les rues étaient mouillées.

Little words often signal the plus-que-parfait: déjà (already), jamais (never), pas encore (not yet), la veille (the day before), avant (before).

", "

A story with three past tenses

A good French story uses three past tenses, each with its own job:

TenseRoleExample
imparfaitthe setting: description, situation, what was going onIl faisait doux, j'étais content.
passé composéthe events that move the story forwardNous sommes arrivés au restaurant.
plus-que-parfaitwhat had happened beforeIls avaient annulé ma réservation.
C'était samedi soir et il faisait doux. J'avais réservé une table à Bordeaux pour l'anniversaire de Chloé. Quand nous sommes arrivés, le restaurant était fermé : le patron était parti en vacances la veille !It was Saturday evening and the weather was mild. I had booked a table in Bordeaux for Chloé's birthday. When we arrived, the restaurant was closed: the owner had left on vacation the day before!

Look at the rhythm: two descriptions (c'était, il faisait), one earlier action (j'avais réservé), the main event (nous sommes arrivés), a description (était fermé), and a flashback that explains it all (était parti).

Si seulement j'avais su !

After si seulement, the plus-que-parfait expresses a regret about the past: Si seulement j'avais su ! (If only I had known!), Si seulement on était partis plus tôt ! You'll see the full structure of past regrets in the next lesson.

Think of the plus-que-parfait as a flashback in a movie: the narrator steps back in time for a moment, then the passé composé brings you back to the main story.

fr-u16-l3.title: The past conditional
fr-u16-l3.topic: aurais / serais + participle; regrets; si + plus-que-parfait
fr-u16-l3.why: This lesson completes the unit on imagining and regretting with the past conditional: j'aurais dû, tu aurais pu, si j'avais su, je serais venu. It also shows the present conditional as a future seen from the past, which prepares reported speech in unit 18.
fr-u16-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

I would have…

The past conditional is the French \"would have\": \"I would have liked\", \"she would have come\". You form it with the auxiliary avoir or être in the present conditional + the past participle. Auxiliaries and agreements follow the same rules as the passé composé and the plus-que-parfait.

aimer (avoir)venir (être)
jej'aurais aiméje serais venu(e)
tutu aurais aimétu serais venu(e)
il / elle / onil aurait aiméil serait venu / elle serait venue
nousnous aurions aiménous serions venu(e)s
vousvous auriez aimévous seriez venu(e)(s)
ils / ellesils auraient aiméils seraient venus / elles seraient venues

Should have, could have

Here English and French are built differently. English puts \"have\" after the modal: \"should have called\". French puts the modal itself in the past conditional and keeps a plain infinitive: j'aurais dû appeler.

EnglishFrench
I should have called.J'aurais dû appeler.
You could have told me.Tu aurais pu me le dire.
I would have liked to come.J'aurais aimé venir. / J'aurais voulu venir.

Never \"je devrais avoir appelé\": the past goes on devoir, not on the infinitive. And dû keeps its circumflex, which tells it apart from du.

", "

Regrets, reproaches, past hypotheses

The past conditional is the tense of what didn't happen. Use it for your own regrets and for gentle (or less gentle) reproaches:

J'aurais dû partir plus tôt. Je n'aurais pas dû dire ça.I should have left earlier. I shouldn't have said that.
Tu aurais pu me prévenir ! Vous auriez dû réserver.You could have warned me! You should have booked.

Si + plus-que-parfait → past conditional

Now you have the complete set of si sentences. The third one is about the past: it's too late, the condition was not met.

ConditionTensesExample
realsi + present → futureSi je pars tôt, j'arriverai à l'heure.
imaginedsi + imparfait → conditionalSi je partais tôt, j'arriverais à l'heure.
past, unrealsi + plus-que-parfait → past conditionalSi j'étais parti tôt, je serais arrivé à l'heure.

The golden rule still holds: never the conditional after si. \"If I would have known\" is si j'avais su.

Si j'avais su, je serais venue.If I had known, I would have come.
Si tu m'avais demandé, je t'aurais aidé.If you had asked me, I would have helped you.

Mixing times

To recognize: a past condition can have a present result. Si j'avais accepté ce poste, j'habiterais à Lyon maintenant. (If I had taken that job, I'd be living in Lyon now.)

To answer someone's regret kindly: Tant pis ! (oh well), Ce n'est pas grave, Tu ne pouvais pas savoir (you couldn't have known).

", "

The future seen from the past

In English, \"would\" also works as a future seen from the past: \"He said he would come.\" French does exactly the same with the present conditional:

Il dit qu'il viendra. → Il a dit qu'il viendrait.He says he'll come. → He said he would come.
Je pensais que tu serais là.I thought you would be there.
Elle savait que ce serait difficile.She knew it would be difficult.
Ils m'avaient promis qu'ils m'appelleraient.They had promised me they would call me.

Don't confuse the two \"woulds\":

FrenchEnglishMeaning
Il a dit qu'il viendrait.He said he would come.present conditional: a future seen from the past
Il serait venu, mais il était malade.He would have come, but he was sick.past conditional: it didn't happen

You'll study all the rules of reported speech in unit 18. For now, remember the pattern \"said / thought / knew that… would\" → a dit / pensait / savait que + present conditional.

Words for decisions: prendre une décision, faire un choix, hésiter, accepter or refuser une offre, changer d'avis (to change your mind), déménager (to move house).

fr-u17-l1.title: Talking about a film or a book
fr-u17-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on culture and leisure: you learn to summarize a movie, a series or a book in the narrative present and to give your opinion with precise adjectives. It reuses the past tenses, relatives and connectors of earlier units in one of the most common conversations in France.

{"lessons": ["

What's it about?

Telling a friend about a film, a series or a book is one of the most natural conversations there is. It needs a few key phrases, and one tense you already know: the present. As in English, a summary is told in the present, even if the story is set in the past. This is called the narrative present.

FrenchEnglish
Ça parle de…It's about…
C'est l'histoire de…It's the story of…
L'histoire se passe à Paris / en Bretagne / dans les années 1960.The story takes place in Paris / in Brittany / in the 1960s.
Le personnage principal, c'est…The main character is…
C'est un film de… / un roman de…It's a film by… / a novel by…
C'est l'histoire d'une jeune femme qui quitte Lille et part vivre à Nice. Là-bas, elle rencontre un vieux pêcheur et tout change.It's the story of a young woman who leaves Lille and goes to live in Nice. There, she meets an old fisherman and everything changes.

Genres

une comédie, un drame, un film policier (in speech, un polar), un film d'animation, un documentaire, une série, un roman, une BD (bande dessinée, comics, hugely popular in France and Belgium).

False friends: un roman is a novel, not a romance (that's une histoire d'amour). Une nouvelle is a short story, not a novel. And the person who directs a film is le réalisateur or la réalisatrice; un directeur runs a company or a school.

", "

What did you think?

The most natural way to give your impression is j'ai trouvé ça + adjective. Ça has no gender, so the adjective stays masculine singular: J'ai trouvé ça génial. If you use an object pronoun instead, the participle and the adjective agree with the film, the series or the book:

Le film ? Je l'ai trouvé émouvant. / La série ? Je l'ai trouvée drôle.The movie? I found it moving. / The series? I found it funny.
AdjectiveEnglish
passionnant / passionnantegripping, fascinating
émouvant / émouvantemoving, touching
bouleversant / bouleversantedeeply moving, overwhelming
drôlefunny
ennuyeux / ennuyeuseboring
décevant / décevantedisappointing
lent / lenteslow

Careful with two traps. Décevant means disappointing, never \"deceiving\". And to say a film is exciting, choose passionnant: excitant can sound sexual or simply odd.

Recommending (or not)

Je le recommande / Je te le conseille (I recommend it), Ça vaut le coup (it's worth it), À voir absolument ! (a must-see), La fin est surprenante (the ending is surprising). And when you didn't get into it: Je n'ai pas accroché (informal).

Don't give away the ending! Say Je ne te raconte pas la fin (I won't tell you the ending).

", "

Going to the movies in France

The French love cinema: there are movie theaters even in small towns, and Paris offers one of the widest choices of films in the world. A few words to get by:

FrenchEnglish
la séance de 20 hthe 8 p.m. showing
en VO (version originale) sous-titréein the original language, with subtitles
en VF (version française)dubbed into French
la bande-annoncethe trailer
l'acteur / l'actricethe actor / the actress
l'auteur / l'autricethe author, the writer

French cinema is famous for its comedies, its family dramas and its films d'auteur, where the director's personal style comes first. Each year, the Cannes festival and the César awards are big events.

Putting it all together

J'ai vu un film italien en VO. Ça parle d'un vieux musicien qui retourne dans son village. J'ai trouvé ça très beau, mais un peu lent. Je te le recommande quand même !I saw an Italian movie in the original version. It's about an old musician who goes back to his village. I found it very beautiful, but a bit slow. I recommend it anyway!

You'll also hear l'auteure, a feminine form that started in Quebec. Both autrice and auteure are used in France today.

fr-u17-l2.title: Reading a simple article
fr-u17-l2.why: This lesson takes you into the French press with a short article written for you on bikes in Strasbourg. You learn how an article is built, how to decode verbless headlines, and the key words for figures, trends and sources, including the conditional journalists use for unconfirmed news.
fr-u17-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

How a French article works

Reading the press is a great way to build your French, and short local news articles are the perfect place to start. They all follow the same structure:

PartEnglishWhat it does
le titrethe headlineshort, often without a verb
le chapeauthe leadtwo or three lines in bold that sum up the news
le corps de l'articlethe bodydetails, figures, quotes
la légendethe captionthe text under the photo

Headlines without verbs

French headlines love nouns made from verbs, with no article at the start. English headlines prefer verbs (\"Prices rise\"); French says Hausse des prix, literally \"rise of prices\".

VerbNounHeadline
augmenterla hausse, l'augmentationHausse des prix du café
baisserla baisseBaisse du nombre de touristes
ouvrirl'ouvertureOuverture d'une nouvelle piscine
fermerla fermetureFermeture du musée pendant l'été
créerla créationCréation d'un festival à Nantes

To understand a headline, turn the noun back into a verb: Fermeture du musée pendant l'été → Le musée ferme pendant l'été.

", "

The article: bikes in Strasbourg

Here is a short article written for this lesson. Read it once for the general idea, then a second time with the glossary below.

Strasbourg : toujours plus de cyclistes

Selon un sondage publié cette semaine par la mairie, près d'un habitant sur cinq va au travail à vélo. Un chiffre en hausse de 10 % en deux ans.

Strasbourg est depuis longtemps la ville française du vélo. Avec plus de 600 kilomètres de pistes cyclables, elle attire chaque année de nouveaux cyclistes.

Les raisons de ce succès ? D'abord, le prix : le vélo ne coûte presque rien. Ensuite, la santé. « Je fais du sport sans y penser », explique Camille, 34 ans, infirmière.

En revanche, la hausse du nombre de cyclistes pose aussi des problèmes : les parkings à vélos sont souvent pleins près de la gare. La mairie promet 2 000 nouvelles places d'ici l'année prochaine.

Et en hiver ? La baisse est réelle, mais faible : selon le sondage, 70 % des cyclistes continuent à pédaler quand il fait froid.

FrenchEnglish
un sondagea poll, a survey
la mairiethe town hall, the city government
près d'un habitant sur cinqnearly one resident in five
en hausse de 10 %up 10%
une piste cyclablea bike lane
poser des problèmesto cause problems
d'ici l'année prochaineby next year
pédalerto pedal, to ride

French writes a space before the percent sign and uses a space, not a comma, for thousands: 10 %, 2 000 places.

", "

Figures, trends and sources

News articles are full of numbers and trends. Here are the words to understand them:

FrenchEnglish
augmenter / être en hausseto go up, to rise
baisser / être en baisseto go down, to fall
doublerto double
la moitié, un tiers, un quarthalf, a third, a quarter
environ, près de, plus deabout, nearly, more than
selon, d'aprèsaccording to

Nombre, numéro, chiffre

English has one word, \"number\"; French has three. Le nombre is a quantity (le nombre d'habitants), le numéro is a number in a series (le numéro de téléphone, la chambre numéro 12), and le chiffre is a digit or a statistic (un chiffre en hausse).

The \"news\" conditional

Journalists use the conditional for information that is not confirmed. English says \"reportedly\" or \"is said to\":

Le festival aurait attiré 50 000 visiteurs.The festival reportedly attracted 50,000 visitors.
Selon la mairie, les travaux dureraient six mois.According to the town hall, the work would last six months.

Headlines often use the present for something that has just happened: Strasbourg inaugure sa nouvelle piste cyclable = Strasbourg has opened its new bike lane.

fr-u17-l3.title: Idiomatic expressions
fr-u17-l3.why: This lesson closes the unit on culture and leisure with a dozen idioms you'll hear every day in France, from avoir le cafard to poser un lapin. You learn their literal image, their real meaning and their English equivalent, and how to use them in the right register.
fr-u17-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Moods and energy

Idioms are the spice of everyday French. You'll hear them all the time among friends and colleagues, and using one at the right moment makes you sound instantly more natural. The trick: never translate them word for word. Learn each one with its literal meaning (it helps you remember) and its real meaning.

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
avoir le cafardto have the cockroachto feel down, to have the blues
avoir un coup de barreto get a blow from the barto suddenly feel exhausted, to hit a wall
avoir la flemmeto have the lazinessto not be bothered, to feel too lazy
faire la grasse matinéeto do the fat morningto sleep in
avoir la tête dans les nuagesto have your head in the cloudsthe same as in English: to be daydreaming

These are normal verb phrases: conjugate avoir and faire in any tense. Avoir la flemme takes de + infinitive, like avoir envie de.

J'ai la flemme de faire la vaisselle.I can't be bothered to do the dishes.
Dimanche, on a fait la grasse matinée jusqu'à midi.On Sunday, we slept in until noon.
Après le déjeuner, j'ai toujours un coup de barre.After lunch, I always hit a wall.

These expressions are informal: perfect with friends, family and most colleagues, but avoid them in a formal email. To a client, say je suis très fatigué, not j'ai un coup de barre.

", "

People and situations

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
poser un lapin à quelqu'unto put down a rabbit for someoneto stand someone up
donner un coup de main à quelqu'unto give someone a blow of the handto give someone a hand
mettre les pieds dans le platto put your feet in the dishto put your foot in it
appeler un chat un chatto call a cat a catto call a spade a spade

Watch the pronouns: poser un lapin and donner un coup de main are built with à quelqu'un, so they take indirect pronouns, me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur:

Julien m'a posé un lapin. Il lui a posé un lapin.Julien stood me up. He stood her up.
Tu peux me donner un coup de main samedi ?Can you give me a hand on Saturday?
Je ne savais pas qu'ils étaient séparés : j'ai mis les pieds dans le plat !I didn't know they had split up: I put my foot in it!
Avec Camille, pas de détour : elle appelle un chat un chat.With Camille, no beating around the bush: she calls a spade a spade.

Notice how close some are to English (a hand, a foot), and how others use a completely different image (a rabbit!). The close ones are easy wins; the different ones are worth a little extra practice.

Mettre les pieds dans le plat is about a social blunder: saying the wrong thing at the wrong moment. For a simple mistake, just say je me suis trompé(e).

", "

Price and difficulty

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
coûter les yeux de la têteto cost the eyes of the headto cost an arm and a leg
c'est du gâteauit's cakeit's a piece of cake
ce n'est pas la mer à boireit's not the sea to drinkit's not that hard, it's no big deal
Les appartements à Paris coûtent les yeux de la tête.Apartments in Paris cost an arm and a leg.
— Tu as réussi l'examen ? — Oui, c'était du gâteau !— Did you pass the exam? — Yes, it was a piece of cake!
Ne t'inquiète pas, ce n'est pas la mer à boire.Don't worry, it's not that hard.

Using idioms well

  • Use them in the right situation: one well-placed idiom is better than five in a row.
  • Keep the words exactly as they are: les yeux de la tête, never \"les yeux de ma tête\".
  • Don't translate English idioms into French: \"it's raining cats and dogs\" means nothing in French, where it rains ropes, il pleut des cordes.

In speech, ce n'est pas la mer à boire often becomes c'est pas la mer à boire, but in writing keep the full negation.

A good way to remember them: picture the literal image. A rabbit waiting alone at a café, someone drinking the whole sea, a price tag asking for your eyes!

fr-u18-l1.title: He says that…: reported speech
fr-u18-l1.topic: reported speech in the present and the past
fr-u18-l1.why: This lesson teaches reported speech: passing on statements, questions and orders, first after il dit que, then after il a dit que with the tense shift. It brings together the imparfait, the plus-que-parfait and the conditional, and prepares the big B1 review.
fr-u18-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

He says that…

Reported speech (le discours indirect) is how you pass on what someone said: \"She says she's tired\", \"He asked me where I lived\". French works much like English, with a few strict rules. When the reporting verb is in the present (il dit que), the tense of the original sentence doesn't change; only the pronouns and possessives adapt, exactly as in English.

Léa : « Je suis fatiguée. » → Léa dit qu'elle est fatiguée.Léa: \"I'm tired.\" → Léa says she's tired.

Statements: que, always

Useful verbs: dire que, répondre que, expliquer que, raconter que, annoncer que, ajouter que. English often drops \"that\" (\"he says he's tired\"); French never drops que, and repeats it before each new clause: Il dit qu'il est fatigué et qu'il rentre.

Questions

Direct questionReported question
yes / no: Tu viens ? / Est-ce que tu viens ?Il me demande si je viens. (si + il = s'il)
question word: Où habites-tu ?Il me demande où j'habite.
Qu'est-ce que tu veux ?Il me demande ce que je veux.
Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?Il demande ce qui se passe.

In a reported question, use ordinary statement word order: no est-ce que, no inversion, and no question mark.

Orders and requests: de + infinitive

As you saw with verbs + de: Viens ! → Il me dit de venir. Pouvez-vous attendre ? → Elle nous demande d'attendre.

Ce que is the object (ce que je veux = what I want), ce qui is the subject (ce qui se passe = what's happening). It's the same pair you met with relative pronouns.

", "

He said that…: the tense shift

When the reporting verb is in the past (il a dit que, elle m'a demandé si), the tenses move one step back into the past, just as in careful English (\"I'm tired\" → he said he was tired). Here you need the plus-que-parfait and the conditional you just learned.

Direct speechAfter il a dit que…Example
presentimparfait« Je travaille à Lyon. » → Il a dit qu'il travaillait à Lyon.
passé composéplus-que-parfait« J'ai fini. » → Il a dit qu'il avait fini.
futurepresent conditional« Je viendrai. » → Il a dit qu'il viendrait.
imparfaitno change« J'étais malade. » → Il a dit qu'il était malade.
aller + infinitiveallait + infinitive« Je vais partir. » → Il a dit qu'il allait partir.

The same shift applies to reported questions: « Où habites-tu ? » → Il m'a demandé où j'habitais. « Qu'est-ce que tu feras ? » → Elle m'a demandé ce que je ferais.

Orders don't change at all, since the infinitive has no tense: « Rappelle-moi ! » → Il m'a dit de le rappeler.

In conversation, when something is still true, French sometimes keeps the present: Il m'a dit qu'il habite à Lyon. In writing and in the exercises, apply the shift.

", "

Shifting time and place

When you report words said on another day, \"today\" and \"tomorrow\" no longer fit. French then changes the time words, which English does too, though less systematically:

Direct speechReported (in the past)English
aujourd'huice jour-làthat day
demainle lendemainthe next day
hierla veillethe day before
ce matince matin-làthat morning
la semaine prochainela semaine suivantethe following week
la semaine dernièrela semaine précédentethe week before
icilàthere
Léa : « Je suis arrivée hier et je repars demain. »Léa: \"I arrived yesterday and I'm leaving again tomorrow.\"
Léa m'a dit qu'elle était arrivée la veille et qu'elle repartait le lendemain.Léa told me she had arrived the day before and was leaving again the next day.

Check the whole chain: pronoun (je → elle), tense (suis arrivée → était arrivée, repars → repartait), time words (hier → la veille, demain → le lendemain), and que repeated.

If you report the words on the same day, keep the normal time words: Ce matin, Paul m'a dit qu'il viendrait demain. The shift is only needed when \"tomorrow\" is no longer tomorrow.

fr-u18-l2.title: B1 review: a real conversation
fr-u18-l2.why: This big review closes the B1 level: opinions with the subjunctive, the three past tenses, hypotheses and regrets, relatives, verbs + à / de and reported speech, all in one real conversation. It ends with a family Sunday lunch in Montpellier and a long role play among friends.
fr-u18-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Opinions, feelings, wishes

This is the big review of the B1 level. No new grammar: just the tools you need to hold a real conversation, about work, plans, memories, and to report what others said. First, the choice of mood after que:

IndicativeSubjunctive
je pense que, je crois que, je trouve queje ne pense pas que, je ne crois pas que, penses-tu que… ?
je suis sûr(e) que, il est probable queje doute que, il est possible que
espérer que (the trap!)il faut que, vouloir que, souhaiter que, pour que
quand + future, après queêtre content(e) que, avoir peur que, c'est dommage que
Je pense que c'est une bonne idée, mais j'ai peur que ce soit trop cher.I think it's a good idea, but I'm afraid it's too expensive.

Same subject for both verbs? Use an infinitive instead: Je veux partir / Je veux que tu partes; Je suis content de venir / Je suis content que tu viennes.

Verbs + à / de

A quick reminder of the most frequent ones: commencer à, réussir à, apprendre à, hésiter à; décider de, essayer de, arrêter de, oublier de, avoir envie de. English \"-ing\" becomes an infinitive: J'ai arrêté de fumer.

Debating

À mon avis, selon moi, je suis (tout à fait) d'accord, tu as raison, mais…, ça dépend, pourtant, en revanche, d'un côté… de l'autre…

Remember the two classic mistakes: \"I agree\" is je suis d'accord (with être), \"you're right\" is tu as raison (with avoir).

", "

Telling and imagining

Three past tenses

TenseRoleExample
imparfaitsetting, description, habitsQuand j'étais petit, on passait l'été à Montpellier.
passé composéevents, the story moving onUn jour, mon grand-père a acheté un bateau.
plus-que-parfaitwhat had happened beforeIl n'était jamais monté sur un bateau !

Don't forget the auxiliary être with movement verbs and pronominal verbs, and agreement: elle est partie, nous nous étions levés.

The three si sentences

ConditionTensesExample
realsi + present → futureSi j'ai des vacances, je partirai au Canada.
imaginedsi + imparfait → conditionalSi j'avais des vacances, je partirais au Canada.
past, unrealsi + plus-que-parfait → past conditionalSi j'avais eu des vacances, je serais parti au Canada.

And the golden rule: never the conditional after si.

Regrets and advice

J'aurais dû (I should have), j'aurais pu (I could have), j'aurais aimé (I would have liked), tu aurais pu me prévenir !; advice in the present conditional: Tu devrais…, À ta place, je…

J'aurais aimé voyager plus jeune. À ta place, je partirais maintenant.I would have liked to travel when I was younger. If I were you, I'd go now.

Listen for the r: je partais (imparfait) / je partirais (conditional). It changes everything!

", "

Linking, reporting, keeping it going

Relative pronouns

PronounUseExample
quisubjectun ami qui habite à Montréal
queobject, never droppedle livre que tu m'as prêté
oùplace and timela ville où je suis née, le jour où…
dontreplaces de + nounle restaurant dont je t'ai parlé
ce qui / ce quewhatCe que je veux, c'est voyager.

Reported speech

After il a dit que: present → imparfait, passé composé → plus-que-parfait, future → conditional; questions with si, ce que, ce qui; orders with de + infinitive; demain → le lendemain, hier → la veille.

Julien m'a dit qu'il avait quitté son travail et qu'il partirait au Canada.Julien told me he had quit his job and would go to Canada.

Keeping a conversation going

A real conversation is not a series of questions and answers. React and ask for more: Ah bon ?, C'est vrai ?, Et alors ?, Sans blague !, Raconte !, Et toi ?, Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ? And when you're stuck, gain time: Comment dire…, Tu vois ce que je veux dire ?

At a French family lunch, the conversation can last for hours, from the starter to the coffee. It's the best possible training: everyone gives their opinion, tells stories, and talks about the future.

he-u01-l1.title: Shalom! Reading direction
he-u01-l1.topic: reading right to left; ש ל מ ם; the vowels a and o
he-u01-l1.why: Your very first Hebrew lesson: we set up the reading direction, how vowels (niqqud) work, and five letters, along with the essential greetings.
he-u01-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

We read from right to left

Hebrew is written and read from right to left. There are no capital or lowercase letters, and the alphabet, the alef-bet, has only consonants: 22 letters.

The vowels are small marks, dots and dashes, placed under or above the letters: the niqqud. Children's books and textbooks use it; newspapers and street signs almost never do. To start with, you'll always have the vowels.

שָׁלוֹםshalom: hello, goodbye, peace

The right reflex: always start with the letter furthest to the right.

", "

Your first five letters

LetterNameSound
שׁshinsh (dot at the top right)
לlamedl
מmemm
םfinal memm, at the end of a word
הhelight h, silent at the end of a word
וֹvav + doto

Five letters have a special form at the end of a word. The first one: מ becomes ם, as in שָׁלוֹם and שָׁם (there).

The trap: ה at the end of a word is not pronounced. מָה is read simply \"ma\".

", "

The vowels a and o

MarkSoundExample
מָ / מַ (a dash or a small T under the letter)a (as in father)מָה ma
לוֹ (dot on the vav)o (as in more)לוֹ lo

The vowel is read after the letter that carries it: מָ = ma. Then you put the syllables together:

שָׁ + לוֹ + םsha + lo + m = shalom

To ask how someone is: מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? to a man, מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ? to a woman. Hebrew always distinguishes between a masculine \"you\" and a feminine \"you\". The answer is טוֹב, תּוֹדָה: fine, thanks.

Two dots, one above the other, under a letter: that's the shva. At the start of a word, it's read as a very short e (like the a in \"about\", said very quickly); in the middle or at the end of a word, it isn't read at all.

he-u01-l4.topic: ד ר; the vowels e (tsere, segol) and u (shuruk, kubutz)
he-u01-l4.why: Two letters (ד and ר) and the last two vowels, e and u: you can now read all the basic vowels. You also discover the three uses of ו and job words in the masculine and the feminine.

Two new letters: ד and ר

LetterNameSound
דdaletd
רreshr, from the back of the throat, like the French r (not the English r)

Look closely at the shape: ד has a sharp corner at the top right, ר is completely rounded. With them, you can finally read תּוֹדָה and מְאוֹד without help.

דּוֹדdod: uncle
הַרhar: mountain

The dot in דּ (the dagesh) changes nothing: דּ and ד are always read d. Only a few letters change their sound with the dot, like בּ (b) and ב (v).

", "

The vowel e: two marks

MarkSoundExample
נֵ (two dots side by side: tsere)eנֵר ner, candle
דֶ (three dots in a triangle: segol)eדֶּלֶת delet, door

In modern Hebrew, both marks are read the same way: an e as in \"bed\", never \"ee\". There is never a silent e: every e is pronounced, דֶּלֶת = de-let.

יֶלֶד / יַלְדָּהyeled / yalda: a boy / a girl (a child)

", "

The sound \"u\" (like the oo in food) is written in two ways: a vav with a dot in the middle, וּ (shuruk), as in רוּת (Rut, Ruth), or three slanted dots under the letter (kubutz), as in בֻּבָּה (buba, doll).

The final forms ם and ן are only used at the end of a word: שָׁלוֹם, לָבָן.

The holam (o) goes on a vav, וֹ, or on its own, at the top left of the letter: לֹא is read lo.

he-u02-l1.title: K, kh, and g: כּ כ ך ק ג
he-u02-l1.topic: כּ (k) and כ ך (kh); ק (k); ג (g)
he-u02-l1.why: Start of the second unit: the sounds k, kh and g, with the letter כ that changes its sound depending on the dot, and the final ך. You can finally read מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ, and you discover that the adjective comes after the noun.
he-u02-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

K, kh and g: five new forms

LetterNameSound
כּkafk (with the dot)
כkhafkh (without the dot)
ךfinal khafkh, at the end of a word
קkufk
גgimelg, always hard as in \"go\"

The kh sound doesn't exist in English: it's a raspy breath from the back of the throat, like the ch in Scottish \"loch\" or German \"Bach\". It's a bit like the throaty Hebrew r, only with more friction.

מֶלֶךְmelekh: king

ג is always read g, never j as in \"gem\": גְּלִידָה is read glida (ice cream), not \"jlida\".

", "

Two k's, two kh's

Like בּ / ב, the letter kaf changes its sound depending on the dot: כּ = k, כ = kh. And ק also makes k: כֶּלֶב (kelev, dog) and קָר (kar, cold) start with the same sound. Only the spelling tells them apart, like \"c\" and \"k\" in English (cat, kit): learn each word with its letter.

The final ך is always read kh. Sometimes it carries a kamats: לְךָ is read lekha (to you, to a man); לָךְ is read lakh (to you, to a woman). You can finally read מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? and מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ?.

תּוֹדָה לְךָ! / תּוֹדָה לָךְ!Thank you! (lit. thanks to you; to a man / to a woman) [toda lekha! / toda lakh!]

A famous exception: in כָּל הַכָּבוֹד (well done!), כָּל is read kol, not \"kal\". You'll hear it often in the app!

", "

Big, cold, here

The adjective goes AFTER the noun, and it agrees: כֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל (a big dog), כַּלְבָּה גְּדוֹלָה (a big female dog). Still no verb \"to be\": הַכֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל, the dog is big.

כָּאן קָר.It's cold here. [kan kar]
מָה קוֹרֶה?What's new? [ma kore?]
גַּם אֲנִי בַּגַּן.Me too, I'm at the park. [gam ani ba-gan]

After הַ (the), the next letter usually takes a dot (not א or ר: הָאִישׁ): so הַכֶּלֶב is read ha-kelev, with a k. גַּן is the garden, the park… and also kindergarten!

he-u02-l2.title: Z, s, and the silent letter ע
he-u02-l2.why: Three more letters: ז, ס and ע, the second silent letter after א. You learn to point things out and ask with זֶה / זֹאת and מָה זֶה, while discovering that every Hebrew noun has a gender, which you learn along with the word.

Some Israelis pronounce ע from deep in the throat; most don't do anything with it. For you: it's silent.
