he-u10-l1.why: The first new binyan of the unit: the hitpa'el, the verb pattern for actions "turned back on yourself" (getting dressed, washing, getting married). After the pi'el in unit 9, you describe your morning routine in the present and the past.
he-u10-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

The hitpa'el: the verb turned back on yourself

In English, you \"get dressed,\" \"wash up,\" \"get married,\" or you add a word like myself: \"I dress myself.\" Hebrew needs none of that: it's the shape of the verb, the hitpa'el binyan, that tells you the action comes back to the person doing it.

אֲנִי מִתְלַבֵּשׁ.I'm getting dressed. [ani mitlabesh]

In the present, the hitpa'el is easy to spot: it starts with מִתְ־ (mit), followed by the three letters of the root, with a then e: מִתְ + לבשׁ → מִתְלַבֵּשׁ. You already know one verb from this binyan: מִתְכַּוֵּן (mitkaven, to intend).

FormHebrewPronunciation
m. sg.מִתְלַבֵּשׁmitlabesh
f. sg.מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁתmitlabeshet
m. pl.מִתְלַבְּשִׁיםmitlabshim
f. pl.מִתְלַבְּשׁוֹתmitlabshot

The trap for English speakers: looking for a word for \"myself, yourself, herself.\" No need! הִיא מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת simply means \"she's getting dressed.\"

", "

In the past and the infinitive

In the past, מִתְ־ becomes הִתְ־ (hit), and you add the same person endings as for כָּתַבְתִּי:

PronounPastPronunciation
אֲנִיהִתְלַבַּשְׁתִּיhitlabashti
אַתָּההִתְלַבַּשְׁתָּhitlabashta
אַתְּהִתְלַבַּשְׁתְּhitlabasht
הוּאהִתְלַבֵּשׁhitlabesh
הִיאהִתְלַבְּשָׁהhitlabsha
אֲנַחְנוּהִתְלַבַּשְׁנוּhitlabashnu
אַתֶּםהִתְלַבַּשְׁתֶּםhitlabashtem
הֵם / הֵןהִתְלַבְּשׁוּhitlabshu

The infinitive starts with לְהִתְ־: לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ (lehitlabesh), לְהִתְקַלֵּחַ (lehitkaleakh). It follows the verbs you already know:

אֲנִי צָרִיךְ לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ.I have to get dressed. [ani tsarikh lehitlabesh]

The letter ח doesn't like e: when it ends the root, the feminine takes a. הוּא מִתְקַלֵּחַ (mitkaleakh), but הִיא מִתְקַלַּחַת (mitkalakhat).

", "

My morning routine

Two verbs take a preposition, just like in English: מִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ־ (to be interested in) and מִתְחַתֵּן עִם (to marry, to get married to). Note that Hebrew says \"marry with\" someone.

he-u10-l2.title: Starting, inviting: the hif'il
he-u10-l2.why: The second binyan of the unit: the hif'il (to start, to invite, to understand), very common in everyday life. You use it to book, order and make yourself understood at a restaurant and on the phone.

{"lessons": ["

The hif'il: doing, making something happen

One more binyan. The hif'il often expresses an action you set off or make happen: מַתְחִיל, to start; מַזְמִין, to invite, to order. In the present, it starts with מַ־ and has a long i (ִי) before the last letter: מַ + תחל → מַתְחִיל.

FormHebrewPronunciation
m. sg.מַתְחִילmatkhil
f. sg.מַתְחִילָהmatkhila
m. pl.מַתְחִילִיםmatkhilim
f. pl.מַתְחִילוֹתmatkhilot

A difference from the hitpa'el: the feminine ends in a (מַתְחִילָה), not in et (מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת).

Compare with the previous lesson: מִתְלַבֵּשׁ, to get dressed (yourself); מַלְבִּישׁ, to dress someone (a child, for example).

A few short verbs start with מֵ־: מֵבִין (mevin, he understands), מְבִינָה (mevina, she understands).

", "

In the past and the infinitive

In the past, מַ־ becomes הִ־: הִתְחִיל (he started). With I, you and we, the i turns into a:

PronounPastPronunciation
אֲנִיהִתְחַלְתִּיhitkhalti
אַתָּההִתְחַלְתָּhitkhalta
אַתְּהִתְחַלְתְּhitkhalt
הוּאהִתְחִילhitkhil
הִיאהִתְחִילָהhitkhila
אֲנַחְנוּהִתְחַלְנוּhitkhalnu
אַתֶּםהִתְחַלְתֶּםhitkhaltem
הֵם / הֵןהִתְחִילוּhitkhilu

The infinitive starts with לְהַ־: לְהַתְחִיל (lehatkhil), לְהַזְמִין (lehazmin), לְהַרְגִּישׁ (lehargish); and for the short verbs, לְהָבִין (lehavin, to understand).

הַסֶּרֶט מַתְחִיל בְּתֵשַׁע.The movie starts at nine. [ha-seret matkhil be-tesha]
אֶתְמוֹל הִתְחַלְתִּי לִלְמֹד עִבְרִית.Yesterday, I started learning Hebrew. [etmol hitkhalti lilmod ivrit]
", "

At the restaurant, on the phone

מַזְמִין is an all-purpose verb: you invite friends, order a dish, book a table. English needs three verbs; Hebrew uses just one.

אֲנִי רוֹצָה לְהַזְמִין שֻׁלְחָן לִשְׁנַיִם.I'd like to book a table for two. [ani rotsa lehazmin shulkhan li-shnayim]
מָה אַתָּה מַמְלִיץ? — אֲנִי מַמְלִיץ עַל הַדָּג.What do you recommend? — I recommend the fish. [ma ata mamlits? — ani mamlits al ha-dag]
סְלִיחָה, אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין. אֶפְשָׁר לְאַט?Sorry, I don't understand. Could you speak more slowly? [slikha, ani lo mevin. efshar le-at?]

With מַרְגִּישׁ, \"well/good\" stays טוֹב, even in the feminine: הִיא מַרְגִּישָׁה טוֹב (she feels good). Here, טוֹב works as an adverb: it doesn't agree.

A little word to watch for: before a definite direct object (a noun with הַ־, a first name), Hebrew adds אֶת, which isn't translated: הוּא מַזְמִין אֶת נֹעָה (he invites Noa), אֲנִי מַזְמִין אֶת הַדָּג (I'm ordering the fish). No article, no אֶת: הוּא מַזְמִין פִּיצָה. Not after a preposition either: מַמְלִיץ עַל הַדָּג.

he-u10-l3.topic: Israeli holidays; the months; giving holiday wishes
he-u10-l3.why: A practical culture lesson: the five holidays you'll come across in Israel, the months, the seasons and the greetings to know. It reuses the hitpa'el and the hif'il (to dress up, to light) in real-life situations.

{"lessons": ["

Months and seasons

In everyday life, Israelis use the same months as you, with almost the same names:

MonthHebrewPronunciation
Januaryיָנוּאָרyanuar
Februaryפֶבְּרוּאָרfebruar
Marchמֶרְץmerts
Aprilאַפְּרִילapril
Mayמַאיmai
Juneיוּנִיyuni
Julyיוּלִיyuli
Augustאוֹגוּסְטogust
Septemberסֶפְּטֶמְבֶּרseptember
Octoberאוֹקְטוֹבֶּרoktober
Novemberנוֹבֶמְבֶּרnovember
Decemberדֶּצֶמְבֶּרdetsember

\"In January\": בְּיָנוּאָר (be-yanuar). \"Which month?\": אֵיזֶה חֹדֶשׁ? (eize khodesh?).

The seasons: אָבִיב (aviv, spring, as in Tel Aviv, \"the hill of spring\"), קַיִץ (kayits, summer), סְתָו (stav, fall), חֹרֶף (khoref, winter).

The holidays, on the other hand, follow the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar: their date changes every year on the usual calendar, but each holiday stays in the same season. The Hebrew year begins in the fall, in September or October.

", "

The major holidays

HolidayWhenWhat people do
רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (rosh ha-shana)fallthe New Year: a family meal, people eat an apple dipped in honey, תַּפּוּחַ בִּדְבַשׁ (tapuakh bi-dvash), for a sweet year
חֲנֻכָּה (khanuka)winter, eight dayspeople light candles, נֵרוֹת (nerot), and eat doughnuts, סֻפְגָּנִיּוֹת (sufganiyot)
פּוּרִים (purim)end of winterkids and adults dress up in costumes; parties and parades in the streets
פֶּסַח (pesakh)spring, one weeka big family meal, people eat מַצָּה (matsa, flatbread); school vacation, many Israelis travel
יוֹם הָעַצְמָאוּת (yom ha-atsma'ut)springnational holiday: picnics and barbecues, מַנְגָּל (mangal), in the parks

\"On Passover,\" \"on Purim\": בְּפֶסַח, בְּפוּרִים; but before the חֲ of חֲנֻכָּה, בְּ is pronounced ba: בַּחֲנֻכָּה (ba-khanuka). \"During the holiday\": בַּחַג.

Two new verbs follow the binyanim of this unit: מִתְחַפֵּשׂ (hitpa'el, to dress up in a costume) and מַדְלִיק (hif'il, to light).

בְּפוּרִים הִיא מִתְחַפֶּשֶׂת לְמַלְכָּה.On Purim, she dresses up as a queen. [be-purim hi mitkhapeset le-malka]
בַּחֲנֻכָּה אֲנַחְנוּ מַדְלִיקִים נֵרוֹת.On Hanukkah, we light candles. [ba-khanuka anakhnu madlikim nerot]
", "

Wishing someone a happy holiday

GreetingPronunciationWhen
חַג שָׂמֵחַ!khag sameakhfor every holiday: \"happy holiday\"
שָׁנָה טוֹבָה!shana tovaon Rosh Hashanah: \"happy new year\"
שָׁנָה טוֹבָה וּמְתוּקָה!shana tova u-metuka\"a good and sweet year\"
חֲנֻכָּה שָׂמֵחַ! / פּוּרִים שָׂמֵחַ!khanuka sameakh / purim sameakhthe name of the holiday, then שָׂמֵחַ, always in the masculine, because you're thinking of חַג

To reply: גַּם לְךָ! (gam lekha, to a man) or גַּם לָךְ! (gam lakh, to a woman), \"you too.\" To several people: גַּם לָכֶם! (gam lakhem).

Practical tip: on the eve of a holiday, עֶרֶב חַג (erev khag), stores close early and the roads are packed. On the day itself of the major holidays (Rosh Hashanah, Passover), many shops and public transportation stop, just like on Shabbat. Do your shopping ahead of time!

he-u10-l4.title: Comparing
he-u10-l4.why: Comparing is essential for giving your opinion: with יוֹתֵר, פָּחוֹת, מִ־ and הֲכִי, you can say more, less, than and the most. You'll practice on a great Israeli classic: Tel Aviv versus Jerusalem.

{"lessons": ["

More… than, less… than

To compare, Hebrew puts יוֹתֵר (yoter, more) or פָּחוֹת (pakhot, less) in front of the adjective, and \"than\" is מִ־, attached to the next word, just like in מִפָּרִיז (from Paris). So Hebrew literally says \"hotter from Paris.\" There is no \"-er\" ending: \"hotter\" is simply \"more hot.\"

תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חַמָּה מִפָּרִיז.Tel Aviv is hotter than Paris. [tel aviv yoter khama mi-pariz]
הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס פָּחוֹת יָקָר מֵהַמּוֹנִית.The bus is less expensive than the taxi. [ha-otobus pakhot yakar me-ha-monit]

The adjective agrees with the first noun, as usual. Cities are feminine: תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חַמָּה.

When?ExamplePronunciation
before most letters: the letter gets a dotמִתֵּל אָבִיבmi-tel aviv
before א ה ח ע רמֵחֵיפָהme-kheifa
before the article הַ־מֵהַבַּיִתme-ha-bayit

Don't mix up \"than\" and \"that\": שֶׁ־ means \"that,\" as in \"I think that…\" In a comparison, \"than\" is always מִ־: יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל מִ־.

", "

The most: הֲכִי

For the superlative, just one word: הֲכִי (hakhi) in front of the adjective. The noun keeps its article, the adjective doesn't:

זֹאת הַמִּסְעָדָה הֲכִי טוֹבָה בָּעִיר.This is the best restaurant in town. [zot ha-mis'ada hakhi tova ba-ir]

No special words like \"better\" or \"best\": you simply say הֲכִי טוֹב (\"the most good,\" best) and יוֹתֵר טוֹב (\"more good,\" better). הֲכִי also works with a verb: מָה אַתָּה הֲכִי אוֹהֵב? (what do you like most?).

Equality: כְּמוֹ (like, as… as). Excess: מִדַּי (too), after the adjective.

חֵיפָה יָפָה כְּמוֹ תֵּל אָבִיב.Haifa is as beautiful as Tel Aviv. [kheifa yafa kmo tel aviv]
הַדִּירָה יְקָרָה מִדַּי.The apartment is too expensive. [ha-dira yekara midai]

In speech, people say יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל; in writing, you'll also see the reverse order, גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר. Both mean \"bigger.\" And \"much more\": הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר (harbe yoter).

", "

Tel Aviv or Jerusalem?

Israelis love comparing their two big cities. Here's what you often hear:

תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר חֲדָשָׁה וְיוֹתֵר רוֹעֶשֶׁת.Tel Aviv is newer and noisier. [tel aviv yoter khadasha ve-yoter ro'eshet]
יְרוּשָׁלַיִם יוֹתֵר עַתִּיקָה וְיוֹתֵר שְׁקֵטָה.Jerusalem is older and quieter. [yerushalayim yoter atika ve-yoter shketa]
בַּחֹרֶף יְרוּשָׁלַיִם הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר קָרָה מִתֵּל אָבִיב.In winter, Jerusalem is much colder than Tel Aviv. [ba-khoref yerushalayim harbe yoter kara mi-tel aviv]
הַדִּירוֹת בְּתֵל אָבִיב הֲכִי יְקָרוֹת בָּאָרֶץ.Apartments in Tel Aviv are the most expensive in the country. [ha-dirot be-tel aviv hakhi yekarot ba-arets]

בָּאָרֶץ (ba-arets), \"in the country\": that's how Israelis talk about Israel in everyday life. And watch out: עִיר (city) is feminine, even though its plural is עָרִים.

he-u11-l1.title: Giving your opinion
he-u11-l1.why: The first lesson of level B1: you learn to give your opinion, say whether you agree and weigh the pros and cons. You reuse the comparative and the hif'il from unit 10 in small everyday debates (vacations, city or countryside, working from home).
he-u11-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

In my opinion…

To give your opinion, three phrases come up all the time:

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
לְדַעְתִּיleda'atiin my opinion (word for word: \"according to my opinion\")
אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁ… / אֲנִי חוֹשֶׁבֶת שֶׁ…ani khoshev she… / ani khoshevet she…I think that… (man / woman)
נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁ…nir'e li she…it seems to me that…

\"That\" is שֶׁ (she). In English you can often leave \"that\" out (\"I think it's good\"), but in Hebrew it's required. Like בְּ or וְ, it attaches to the next word, which often gets a dot (dagesh):

אֲנִי חוֹשֶׁבֶת שֶׁזֶּה רַעְיוֹן טוֹב.I think that it's a good idea. [ani khoshevet she-ze ra'ayon tov]
נִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁהַכְּפָר יוֹתֵר שָׁקֵט.It seems to me that the village is quieter. [nir'e li she-ha-kfar yoter shaket]

חוֹשֵׁב agrees like any present-tense verb: a man says חוֹשֵׁב, a woman חוֹשֶׁבֶת. On the other hand, לְדַעְתִּי and נִרְאֶה לִי never change: very handy when you're talking fast!

", "

Agreeing, disagreeing

מַסְכִּים is a hif'il verb, like מַתְחִיל or מַרְגִּישׁ (unit 10). Just like English \"I agree,\" Hebrew uses a simple present-tense verb, with no \"to be.\" Like any present-tense verb, it agrees in gender and number:

HebrewPronunciationWho's speaking
אֲנִי מַסְכִּיםani maskima man
אֲנִי מַסְכִּימָהani maskimaa woman
אֲנַחְנוּ מַסְכִּימִיםanakhnu maskimima group (mixed or all men)
אֲנַחְנוּ מַסְכִּימוֹתanakhnu maskimota group of women

\"With you\": אִתְּךָ (itkha) to a man, אִתָּךְ (itakh) to a woman.

אֲנִי לֹא מַסְכִּימָה אִתְּךָ.I don't agree with you. (a woman to a man) [ani lo maskima itkha]

{"lessons": ["

One word for \"who,\" \"which\" and \"that\"

You've seen שֶׁ in אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁ…. The same little word works as a relative pronoun. Where English chooses between \"who,\" \"which\" and \"that\" (or even leaves it out: \"the book I read\"), Hebrew always says שֶׁ, attached to the next word, never left out, and it doesn't change in the feminine or the plural.

הָאִישׁ שֶׁגָּר פֹּהthe man who lives here [ha-ish she-gar po]
הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁקָּרָאתִיthe book (that) I read [ha-sefer she-karati]
בֵּית הַקָּפֶה שֶׁפָּתוּחַ כָּל הַלַּיְלָהthe café that is open all night [beit ha-kafe she-patu'akh kol ha-layla]

Notice the last example: no verb \"to be\" in the present, even after שֶׁ. \"That is open\" = \"that open.\"

To recognize: with a preposition, Hebrew adds a little pronoun at the end. הַדִּירָה שֶׁגַּרְנוּ בָּהּ [ha-dira she-garnu bah], \"the apartment where we lived,\" word for word \"the apartment that we lived in-it\" (דִּירָה is feminine). No need to produce it right away.

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
כְּשֶׁ…kshe…when (in a statement, never in a question)

כְּשֶׁהָיִיתִי יֶלֶד, גַּרְתִּי בְּחֵיפָה.When I was a child, I lived in Haifa. [kshe-hayiti yeled, garti be-Kheyfa]

The \"when\" trap: in English, the same word works for the question and the statement. In Hebrew, the question is מָתַי?; in a statement, it's כְּשֶׁ. Never use מָתַי in the middle of a sentence that isn't a question!

Because, because of, if

Just like in English, you distinguish \"because\" + a clause (כִּי, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁ) from \"because of\" + a noun (בִּגְלַל).

לֹא נָסַעְנוּ לַיָּם בִּגְלַל הַגֶּשֶׁם.We didn't go to the beach because of the rain. [lo nasanu la-yam biglal ha-geshem]
לֹא נָסַעְנוּ לַיָּם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁיָּרַד גֶּשֶׁם.We didn't go to the beach because it rained. [lo nasanu la-yam mipnei she-yarad geshem]

אִם (if) is simple to use, with the present, just like in English:

אִם יֵשׁ לְךָ זְמַן, תָּבוֹא לְבַקֵּר!If you have time, come visit us! (to a man) [im yesh lekha zman, tavo levaker!]

אִם is also used for the \"if\" (or \"whether\") of an indirect question: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדַעַת אִם הוּא בַּבַּיִת (I don't know if he's home). And for imaginary \"ifs\" (if I were rich…), see you in the next lesson.

he-u11-l3.title: If I had…: the conditional
he-u11-l3.why: The third B1 lesson: the conditional (הָיִיתִי + present) and the two kinds of "if": the possible condition (אִם + future) and the imaginary one (לוּ + past). You reuse הָיִיתִי (unit 8) and the future (unit 9) to imagine and dream out loud.

{"lessons": ["

I would travel: הָיִיתִי + present

The Hebrew conditional is built from two pieces you already know: the past of \"to be\" (הָיִיתִי, הָיִיתָ…, unit 8) followed by the verb in the present. The first word changes with the person; the second agrees in gender and number, as always in the present. Think of it as Hebrew's \"would.\"

PersonHebrewPronunciation
I (man / woman)הָיִיתִי נוֹסֵעַ / הָיִיתִי נוֹסַעַתhayiti nose'a / hayiti nosa'at
you (man)הָיִיתָ נוֹסֵעַhayita nose'a
you (woman)הָיִית נוֹסַעַתhayit nosa'at
he / sheהוּא הָיָה נוֹסֵעַ / הִיא הָיְתָה נוֹסַעַתhu haya nose'a / hi hayta nosa'at
weהָיִינוּ נוֹסְעִיםhayinu nos'im
they (m. / f.)הֵם הָיוּ נוֹסְעִים / הֵן הָיוּ נוֹסְעוֹתhem hayu nos'im / hen hayu nos'ot

You already know the polite phrase הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה (I would like): that's exactly this conditional!

Watch out: הָיִיתִי נוֹסֵעַ can also mean \"I used to go,\" just like English \"would\" in \"when I was a kid, I would go to the beach.\" Context decides; with an \"if,\" it's the conditional.

", "

Two kinds of \"if\"

If it's possible and it's about the future: אִם + future. English uses the present after \"if\" (\"if I have time\"); Hebrew happily uses the future, since it hasn't happened yet.

אִם יִהְיֶה לִי זְמַן, אֶלְמַד לְבַשֵּׁל.If I have time, I'll learn to cook. [im yihye li zman, elmad levashel]

יִהְיֶה (yihye) is the future of \"to be, there is.\" Like הָיָה לִי, it agrees with the thing you have: יִהְיֶה (m.), תִּהְיֶה (f.), יִהְיוּ (pl.). So: אִם תִּהְיֶה לִי חֻפְשָׁה (if I have a vacation).

If it's imaginary (it isn't true, you're dreaming): לוּ + past, then the conditional.

לוּ הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי קוֹנֶה בַּיִת בַּכְּפָר.If I had money, I would buy a house in the countryside. (a man speaking) [lu haya li kesef, hayiti kone bayit ba-kfar]

לוּ is a bit formal. In speech, Israelis very often say אִם for imaginary situations too: אִם הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי… It's the past followed by the conditional that shows you're dreaming.

", "

Dreaming out loud

To get the conversation going: מָה הָיִיתָ עוֹשֶׂה לוּ…? (to a man) / מָה הָיִית עוֹשָׂה לוּ…? (to a woman), \"what would you do if…?\".

מָה הָיִית עוֹשָׂה לוּ הָיְתָה לָךְ שָׁנָה שְׁלֵמָה בְּלִי עֲבוֹדָה?What would you do if you had a whole year without work? (to a woman) [ma hayit osa lu hayta lakh shana shlema bli avoda?]
הָיִיתִי מְטַיֶּלֶת בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם.I would travel all over the world. (a woman speaking) [hayiti metayelet be-khol ha-olam]

Two words for reacting: כְּדַאי (it's worth it) and חֲבָל (too bad). \"Too bad that…\" is חֲבָל שֶׁ…:

חֲבָל שֶׁאֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית!Too bad I don't have a car! [khaval she-ein li mekhonit!]

After \"too bad that,\" the sentence stays completely normal, just like in English. Good news: Hebrew has no special subjunctive forms to learn!

he-u11-l4.title: The passive
he-u11-l4.why: The fourth B1 lesson: you learn to recognize the passive, which is everywhere in newspaper headlines, signs and menus. Each active binyan you've seen (pa'al, pi'el, hif'il) has a passive twin: nif'al, pu'al and huf'al.

{"lessons": ["

A passive in a single word

In English, the passive needs extra words: \"was written,\" \"was canceled.\" In Hebrew, one word is enough: you simply switch binyan (the verb pattern you saw in unit 9). The active binyanim pa'al, pi'el and hif'il each have a passive twin (the hitpa'el doesn't):

ActivePassivePronunciationPassive meaning
כָּתַב (pa'al)נִכְתַּב (nif'al)nikhtavwas written
סִפֵּר (pi'el)סֻפַּר (pu'al)suparwas told
הִזְמִין (hif'il)הֻזְמַן (huf'al)huzmanwas invited, was ordered
הַסִּפּוּר הַזֶּה סֻפַּר לִי עַל יְדֵי סַבְתָּא.This story was told to me by my grandmother. [ha-sipur ha-ze supar li al yedei savta]

\"By\" is עַל יְדֵי (al yedei). But in speech, Israelis often prefer the active with a \"they\" that has no subject, just like English \"they\" in \"they opened a new restaurant\": פָּתְחוּ מִסְעָדָה חֲדָשָׁה. You'll come across the passive mostly in writing: newspapers, signs, menus.

In this lesson, the goal is to recognize these forms when you read them, not to produce all of them.

", "

The nif'al: נִ at the start

In the past, you can recognize the nif'al by the נִ at the beginning. It takes the same endings as the past tense you know:

MasculineFemininePlural
נִפְתַּח niftakhנִפְתְּחָה niftekhaנִפְתְּחוּ niftekhu
נִסְגַּר nisgarנִסְגְּרָה nisgeraנִסְגְּרוּ nisgeru
נִכְתַּב nikhtavנִכְתְּבָה nikhtevaנִכְתְּבוּ nikhtevu
סִפְרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה נִפְתְּחָה בְּחֵיפָה.A new library opened in Haifa. [sifriya khadasha niftekha be-Kheyfa]

The nif'al often matches an English verb used without an object: \"the door opens,\" \"the store closes,\" or \"is found / is located\" (נִמְצָא, was found or is located). In the present, you'll read it on store doors:

הַחֲנוּת נִפְתַּחַת בְּתֵשַׁע וְנִסְגֶּרֶת בְּשֶׁבַע.The store opens at nine and closes at seven. [ha-khanut niftakhat be-tesha ve-nisgeret be-sheva]

The trap: a נִ at the beginning can also be the \"we\" of the future. נִכְתֹּב (we will write) and נִכְתַּב (was written) differ by just one vowel, o or a. In a newspaper without vowels, the meaning of the sentence decides.

", "

Pu'al and huf'al: the \"u\" sound

The pu'al (passive of the pi'el) and the huf'al (passive of the hif'il) have something in common that's easy to spot: the u sound (as in \"rule\") under the first letter (the kubutz, three diagonal dots).

ActivePassivePronunciationMeaning
בִּטֵּלבֻּטַּלbutalwas canceled
שִׁפֵּץשֻׁפַּץshupatswas renovated
הִזְמִיןהֻזְמַןhuzmanwas invited, ordered
הִגִּישׁהֻגַּשׁhugashwas served
הַקּוֹנְצֶרְט בַּפַּארְק בֻּטַּל בִּגְלַל הַגֶּשֶׁם.The concert in the park was canceled because of the rain. [ha-kontsert ba-park butal biglal ha-geshem]
כָּל הַתּוֹשָׁבִים הֻזְמְנוּ לַחֲגִיגָה בַּכִּכָּר.All the residents were invited to the celebration in the square. [kol ha-toshavim huzmenu la-khagiga ba-kikar]

In the present, these passives start with מְ or מֻ and are often used as adjectives: מְשֻׁפָּץ (renovated), מֻזְמָן (invited). At a hotel, you'll read:

אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר מֻגֶּשֶׁת עַד הַשָּׁעָה עֶשֶׂר.Breakfast is served until ten. [arukhat ha-boker mugeshet ad ha-sha'a eser]

In newspapers, without niqqud, this \"u\" sound is written with a ו (full spelling). So a ו right after the first letter of a verb is a good clue that it's a pu'al or a huf'al.

he-u11-l5.why: Review of unit 11: you bring together everything you need for a real discussion in Hebrew: giving your opinion, backing it up with שֶׁ clauses, imagining with the conditional and understanding a news story in the passive. It's the last step before the everyday Hebrew of unit 12.

Talking like an Israeli

Spoken Hebrew is very relaxed: there's no formal \"you,\" you speak to everyone the same way, and a lot of informal expressions are also heard at the office or in a store. But in official writing (a letter to city hall, an email to a government office), people avoid them.

Several come from Arabic (יַאלְלָה, אַחְלָה, סַבָּבָּה, כֵּיף), others from Yiddish (תַּכְלֶס).

ExpressionMeaningRegister
בְּסֵדֶרokay, all right [be-seder]everyday, with everyone
אֵין בְּעָיָהno problem [ein be'aya]everyday
בְּכֵּיףmy pleasure [be-kef]everyday, warm
סַבָּבָּהokay, cool [sababa]informal
אַחְלָהgreat [akhla]informal
יַאלְלָהcome on!, let's go! [yalla]informal

The trap: בְּסֵדֶר and סַבָּבָּה both mean \"OK,\" but סַבָּבָּה is for friends or coworkers. With a stranger, at the bank or at the doctor's, בְּסֵדֶר is safer.

", "

Saying yes, saying it's awesome

אַחְלָה goes before the noun and doesn't agree, unlike adjectives: אַחְלָה יוֹם, אַחְלָה מְסִבָּה. מַגְנִיב, on the other hand, is a real adjective, placed after the noun and agreeing with it: סֶרֶט מַגְנִיב, מְסִבָּה מַגְנִיבָה.

Watch out: חֲבָל on its own means \"too bad.\" But חֲבָל עַל הַזְּמַן, literally \"a pity about the time,\" means \"awesome, amazing\" in slang. And in words borrowed from other languages, the dot (dagesh) keeps the b or k sound: סַבָּבָּה [sababa], בְּכֵּיף [be-kef].

ExpressionMeaning

he-u12-l2.why: A real reading without vowels: a simplified news brief about the opening of the swimming season, with a five-reflex method (function words, prefixes, roots, patterns, ktiv male). It puts into practice the passive and the binyanim you've seen at level B1.

{"lessons": ["

Reading the news: five reflexes

Newspapers, news websites and signs have no vowels. Don't panic: with context and a few reflexes, you can rebuild every word. Here's the method, from the simplest to the finest.

  • Function words can be recognized at a glance: של, עם, כל, רק, גם, עד.
  • Prefixes: separate ו ה ב ל מ ש and כש at the start of the word. מהציבור = מ + ה + ציבור, \"from the public.\"
  • The root: look for the three basic consonants. רחצה (swimming) and מתרחץ (he washes) share the root ר־ח־צ; נפתחה contains פ־ת־ח, like פָּתוּחַ (open).
  • The pattern: the shape of the word tells you its function. נפתחה starts with נ: nif'al passive, like נכתב. מומלץ, with מו־: huf'al passive, \"(it is) recommended.\" מציל has the shape of מזמין and מתחיל: hif'il present, \"the one who saves.\"
  • Ktiv male (full spelling): ו = o or u, י = i or e; doubled, וו and יי mark the consonants v and y: עירייה [iriya].

Don't try to understand everything on the first read: read the headline first, spot the words you know, then go back to the hard words with these five reflexes.

", "

The news brief: without vowels

Read it on your own first, without rushing. The headline is in bold.

עונת הרחצה נפתחה בחופי תל אביב

ביום ראשון נפתחה עונת הרחצה בחופי תל אביב. כבר בבוקר הגיעו אלפי אנשים לים. העירייה מבקשת מהציבור לשחות רק כשיש מציל בחוף. המצילים עובדים כל יום משבע בבוקר עד שבע בערב. בשבוע הבא צפוי חום כבד. כדאי לשתות הרבה מים. מומלץ להגיע עם כובע וקרם הגנה.

The key words, with their vowels:

Without vowelsWith vowelsMeaning
עונת הרחצהעוֹנַת הָרַחְצָהthe swimming season
נפתחהנִפְתְּחָהopened (passive)
בחופיבְּחוֹפֵיon the beaches of
אלפיאַלְפֵיthousands of

מצילמַצִּילlifeguard

he-u12-l3.topic: סִפְרִי, בֵּיתֵנוּ, אִשְׁתּוֹ: the formal possessive
he-u12-l3.why: The formal possessive, attached to the noun (sifri, beitenu, ishto), which you'll meet in writing and in set phrases like "in my opinion" or "my husband." It builds on the smikhut and prepares you to read more polished texts.

{"lessons": ["

Two ways to say \"my\"

You know הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי: it's the everyday way, in speech as well as in writing. Hebrew has a second, more formal way: attaching the possessive to the end of the noun, a bit as if English said \"book-my.\"

הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי = סִפְרִיmy book [ha-sefer sheli = sifri]
Whose?bookhouse
myסִפְרִי sifriבֵּיתִי beiti
your (m.)סִפְרְךָ sifrekhaבֵּיתְךָ beitkha
your (f.)סִפְרֵךְ sifrekhבֵּיתֵךְ beitekh
hisסִפְרוֹ sifroבֵּיתוֹ beito
herסִפְרָהּ sifraבֵּיתָהּ beita
ourסִפְרֵנוּ sifrenuבֵּיתֵנוּ beitenu
your (pl. m.)סִפְרְכֶם sifrekhemבֵּיתְכֶם beitkhem
theirסִפְרָם siframבֵּיתָם beitam

The endings look like those of לִי, לוֹ, לָהּ, לָנוּ: i = my, o = his, a with a dot in the הּ = her, enu = our, am = their. Like English, Hebrew tells \"his\" and \"her\" apart.

The noun often changes a little, as in smikhut: סֵפֶר becomes סִפְר־, בַּיִת becomes בֵּית־, as in בֵּית סֵפֶר.

", "

Feminine nouns: ה becomes ת

As in smikhut (שָׂפָה → שְׂפַת), the final ה of a feminine noun becomes ת before the suffix:

Nounmyhisour
מִשְׁפָּחָה familyמִשְׁפַּחְתִּי mishpakhtiמִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ mishpakhtoמִשְׁפַּחְתֵּנוּ mishpakhtenu
דִּירָה apartmentדִּירָתִי diratiדִּירָתוֹ diratoדִּירָתֵנוּ diratenu
עֲבוֹדָה work, jobעֲבוֹדָתִי avodatiעֲבוֹדָתוֹ avodatoעֲבוֹדָתֵנוּ avodatenu

Family words are a bit irregular, but very common: אִשְׁתִּי (my wife), בַּעֲלִי (my husband), אָחִי (my brother), אֲחוֹתִי (my sister), בְּנִי (my son), בִּתִּי (my daughter).

אִשְׁתּוֹ עוֹבֶדֶת בְּבֵית חוֹלִים, וּבְנָם לוֹמֵד בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.His wife works in a hospital, and their son is studying at the university. [ishto ovedet be-veit kholim, u-vnam lomed ba-universita.]

The trap: אִשָּׁה becomes אִשְׁתּ־, not \"ishat-\": אִשְׁתִּי [ishti], אִשְׁתּוֹ [ishto].

", "

In real life

In speech, Israelis mostly say הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי. The suffixes are kept for polished writing (letters, articles, speeches) and for set phrases everyone uses:

  • שְׁמִי…: my name is… (a bit formal; in speech, קוֹרְאִים לִי…)
  • בַּעֲלִי, אִשְׁתִּי: very common in speech too
  • לְדַעְתִּי (in my opinion), לְצַעֲרִי (unfortunately, lit. \"to my regret\")
  • אָחִי: my brother… and, in slang, \"bro\"

Two rules: no article on a noun with a suffix (you say סִפְרִי, without הַ), but the adjective that follows takes the article: סִפְרִי הֶחָדָשׁ (my new book), בֵּיתֵנוּ הַגָּדוֹל (our big house).

In the plural, a י appears before the suffix: חֲבֵרַי (my friends), יְלָדֵינוּ (our children). For now, just learn to recognize them.

Yesterday, today, tomorrow

You've reached the end of the program: well done! This review goes back over the main tools of level B1. First, the three tenses: the past is conjugated with endings, the future with prefixes, and the present has only four forms, depending on gender and number.

The Italian meal

An Italian menu always follows the same order. Knowing it already means understanding half of what the waiter says.

On the menuWhat it is
l'antipastothe starter: cold cuts, vegetables, bruschette
il primopasta, risotto or soup
il secondomeat or fish
il contornothe side dish, ordered separately
il dolcedessert

The trap: il secondo arrives alone on the plate. If you want vegetables or potatoes, you have to order un contorno.

On the bill at most restaurants, il coperto is a fixed amount per person for the place setting and the bread. It is not a tip.

", "

Useful phrases

WhenWhat you say
ArrivingAvete un tavolo per due?
OrderingVorrei… / Per me… / Prendo…
HesitatingChe cosa mi consiglia?
AskingMi porta il menù, per favore?
WarningSono allergico a…
PayingIl conto, per favore.

To order, vorrei (I would like) is the polite phrase. Per me (for me) and prendo (I'll have, literally \"I take\") are just as natural. With the waiter, you use the formal Lei: \"Mi porta dell'acqua?\"

Some bread, some water, some potatoes

For an unspecified quantity, Italian uses di + the article, where English says \"some\" or nothing at all. These are the articulated prepositions you already know.

Vorrei del pane, della frutta e delle patate.I'd like some bread, some fruit and some potatoes.

Before a vowel: dell' (dell'acqua). In the masculine plural: dei (dei funghi).

{"lessons": ["

The imperfect subjunctive

To imagine what isn't real, Italian needs one more tense. Good news: it's very regular.

parlareaveredormire
ioparlassiavessidormissi
tuparlassiavessidormissi
lui/leiparlasseavessedormisse
noiparlassimoavessimodormissimo
voiparlasteavestedormiste
loroparlasseroavesserodormissero

The irregular ones to know: essere (fossi, fossi, fosse, fossimo, foste, fossero), fare (facessi), dire (dicessi), stare (stessi), dare (dessi).

", "

Se + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

This is the sentence for dreams and advice: an unreal condition, then its consequence.

Se avessi tempo, viaggerei di più.If I had time, I would travel more.
Se fossi in te, prenderei il treno.If I were you, I would take the train.

The trap for English speakers: in English, \"if\" is followed by the simple past (if I had), so you're tempted to use an Italian past tense. Not here: no \"se avevo\" — Italian needs the subjunctive, se avessi. And never a conditional right after se: no \"se avrei\", just as English doesn't say \"if I would have time\".

Don't mix them up

A real or likely condition keeps the indicative: \"Se ho tempo, vengo\" (if I have time, I'll come).

The same tense follows magari to express a wish: \"Magari fosse vero!\" (if only it were true!).

it-u01-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Essere and avere: the two pillars

Just like \"to be\" and \"to have\" in English, these two verbs are irregular and show up everywhere. Learn them by heart, out loud.

essere (to be)avere (to have)
iosonoho
tuseihai
lui, leièha
noisiamoabbiamo
voisieteavete
lorosonohanno

The subject is often left out: the verb ending is enough. Most of the time you just say Sono francese; \"Io sono francese\" is for emphasis or contrast (io… e tu?).

Sono francese e ho trent'anni.I'm French and I'm thirty (literally: I have thirty years).

Unlike English, age is expressed with avere (Ho trent'anni, \"I have thirty years\"), and so is hunger: avere fame (to be hungry, literally \"to have hunger\"). A profession takes no article: Sono medico, \"I'm a doctor\" — no word for \"a\". A yes/no question is made with intonation alone, with no word-order change: Sei di Parigi?

The trap: the h is never pronounced; it's only there to tell words apart in writing. ho (I have) / o (or), ha (he has) / a (to, at), hanno (they have) / anno (year). In the same way, è with an accent means \"he/she/it is\", while e without an accent means \"and\": Luca è italiano e Anna è spagnola.

", "

Masculine, feminine, plural

In Italian, almost every noun ends in a vowel, and that vowel often shows the gender. For the plural, you change the last vowel: you don't add an -s.

SingularPluralExample
-o (masculine)-iil fratello → i fratelli
-a (feminine)-ela sorella → le sorelle
-e (masculine or feminine)-ilo studente → gli studenti, la chiave → le chiavi

Nationalities follow the same rule: italiano, italiana, italiani, italiane; francese, francesi (same form for masculine and feminine). Unlike English, they're written with a lowercase letter.

Two traps: l'amico → gli amici (\"ch\" sound as in \"church\"), but l'amica → le amiche (the h keeps the hard \"k\" sound). And gli occhiali is always plural, like \"glasses\" in English.

", "

Articles

English gets by with \"the\" and \"a\". Italian has many more, because the article changes with gender and number, and also with the first letter of the word that follows.

Before…Definite singularDefinite pluralIndefinite
masculine, consonantil libroi libriun libro
masculine, s + consonant or zlo zaino, lo studentegli zaini, gli studentiuno zaino
masculine, vowell'amicogli amiciun amico
feminine, consonantla borsale borseuna borsa
feminine, vowell'amicale amicheun'amica
Ho uno zaino e una borsa.I have a backpack and a handbag.

Remember lo / gli / uno before s + consonant and before z: lo zaino, lo studente, lo stadio. And the apostrophe: un amico (masculine, never an apostrophe), but un'amica (feminine).

{"lessons": ["

Parlare: one verb, six endings

Most verbs in -are are conjugated like parlare: you remove -are and add the ending. It's the biggest verb family in Italian.

PersonparlarelavorareIn English
ioparlolavoroI speak, I work
tuparlilavoriyou speak, you work
lui / leiparlalavorahe / she speaks
noiparliamolavoriamowe speak
voiparlatelavorateyou (all) speak
loroparlanolavoranothey speak

In English, \"I speak, you speak, they speak\" all sound the same: you need the pronoun to know who's speaking. In Italian, every ending can be heard. So the subject disappears, just as with sono and ho.

Lavoro in un ufficio. Abiti a Parigi?I work in an office. Do you live in Paris?

Stress trap: with loro, the stress doesn't fall on the ending. You say parlano, lavorano, tornano, arrivano. And abitare keeps the stress right at the start: abito, abiti, abita, abitano (but abitiamo, abitate).

", "

Spelling, negation and questions

cercare, pagare: add an h

The hard sound of the infinitive (\"k\" in cercare, hard \"g\" in pagare) stays hard everywhere. So before an i, you write ch and gh.

Personcercarepagare
iocercopago
tucerchipaghi
lui / leicercapaga
noicerchiamopaghiamo
voicercatepagate
lorocercanopagano

mangiare, studiare: just one i

The i of the stem and the one of the ending merge into one: tu mangi, noi mangiamo, tu studi, noi studiamo. Never \"mangii\".

Non, all on its own

Non goes right before the verb and that's all: no helper like \"don't\" or \"doesn't\". No is only used to answer.

No, non lavoro il sabato.No, I don't work on Saturdays.

To ask a question, keep the sentence exactly as it is and raise your voice at the end: no word-order change, no \"do\".

Parli inglese? / Parli inglese.Do you speak English? / You speak English.

With the article, il sabato means \"on Saturdays, every Saturday\", and la sera \"in the evening, usually\". And keep the accent on è (he/she is): without it, e means \"and\". Marco è di Roma e lavora a Milano.

{"lessons": ["

A question is a sentence that goes up

English builds questions with a helper and a word-order change: \"You speak English\" becomes \"Do you speak English?\". Italian does none of that: you keep the sentence exactly as it is and raise your voice at the end. No inversion, no \"do\".

StatementQuestion
Parli inglese.Parli inglese?
Sei francese.Sei francese?
Marco lavora il sabato.Marco lavora il sabato?
Non abiti qui.Non abiti qui?

The rule: a yes/no question keeps the word order of the statement; only the intonation changes.

The trap: looking for an equivalent of \"do\" or \"are you\". There isn't one. Sei francese? is enough, in writing and in speech.

To answer: sì or no, then the sentence, with non before the verb for the negative.

Parli spagnolo? — No, non parlo spagnolo.Do you speak Spanish? — No, I don't speak Spanish.

Watch the accent: è (it is) is not e (and).

L'autobus è in orario?Is the bus on time?
", "

Question words

ItalianEnglishExample
chiwhoChi è? — È Anna.
che cosa (or cosa)whatChe cosa studi?
dovewhereDove abiti?
di dovewhere from (origin)Di dove sei? — Sono di Lione.
quandowhenQuando lavori?
comehowCome ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Luca.
perchéwhy, becausePerché studi l'italiano? — Perché amo l'Italia.

The rule: the question word goes first and the verb follows immediately; if the subject is a noun, it comes after the verb.

Dove lavora Marco?Where does Marco work? (not \"Dove Marco lavora?\" — and no word for \"does\")

A single word, perché, is used both to ask (why) and to answer (because). It takes an acute accent: é.

Two little contractions with è: dove + è = dov'è, come + è = com'è. But qual è is written without an apostrophe.

", "

How much and which: they agree

Unlike English \"how many\" and \"which\", quanto and quale agree with the noun that follows.

SingularPlural
Masculinequanto tempo?quanti anni? quanti fratelli?
Femininequanta acqua?quante lingue? quante sorelle?

One word covers both \"how much\" and \"how many\": it's the ending that changes. How many languages? = Quante lingue? On its own before a verb, quanto stays masculine: Quanto costa? (How much does it cost?)

Quale has one form for masculine and feminine singular, and one for the plural: quali. English often says \"what\" where Italian uses quale.

Quali lingue parli?Which languages do you speak?
Qual è l'indirizzo di Luca?What is Luca's address?

Four ready-made questions

QuestionAnswer
Come ti chiami?Mi chiamo…
Di dove sei?Sono di…
Che lavoro fai?Sono architetto. / Lavoro in banca.
Quanti anni hai?Ho trent'anni.

In Che lavoro fai?, fai means \"you do\": learn the question as a whole; the verb fare will come later.

{"lessons": ["

Verbs in -ere

You already know the verbs in -are: parlo, parli, parla… Verbs in -ere work the same way: remove -ere and add the ending. Good news: for io, tu and noi, the endings are the same as for -are.

parlareprendere
ioparloprendo
tuparliprendi
lui / leiparlaprende
noiparliamoprendiamo
voiparlateprendete
loroparlanoprendono

Where English just adds an -s for he/she (I take, she takes), Italian has an ending for every person — but the pattern stays regular: prendo, prendiamo, prendono. Same for reading, writing, living: leggo, scrivo, vivo.

La sera Marco legge e Anna scrive.In the evening, Marco reads and Anna writes.

Pronunciation

Before o, a, u, the g is hard (as in \"go\"); before e and i, it is soft (as in \"gem\"). So leggo sounds like \"LEG-go\", but leggi and legge sound like \"LED-jee\", \"LED-jeh\". In scrivo, you clearly hear all three consonants: \"skree-vo\".

With loro, the stress stays at the start of the verb: prendono is said \"PREN-do-no\", like parlano. Never \"pren-DO-no\".

Verbs in -ire: two families

Verbs in -ire have almost the same endings as -ere; only voi changes: -ite. But some of them add -isc- between the stem and the ending.

dormirecapire
iodormocapisco
tudormicapisci
lui / leidormecapisce
noidormiamocapiamo
voidormitecapite
lorodormonocapiscono
  • Like dormire: partire, sentire, aprire, offrire.
  • Like capire: finire, preferire, pulire.

The trap: -isc- appears with io, tu, lui / lei and loro, but disappears with noi and voi (finiamo, finite). In the table, it draws a \"boot\" shape: the top three rows and the last one.

Nothing in the infinitive tells you whether a verb takes -isc-: learn each verb with its io form (capire, capisco). For pronunciation, sc sounds like \"sk\" before o (capisco, capiscono) and like \"sh\" before i and e (capisci, capisce).

", "

The three groups at a glance

-are-ere-ire
io-o-o-o / -isco
tu-i-i-i / -isci
lui / lei-a-e-e / -isce
noi-iamo-iamo-iamo
voi-ate-ete-ite
loro-ano-ono-ono / -iscono

The rule in one sentence: io, tu and noi have the same endings in all three groups (adding -isc- for capire, finire…), and voi keeps the vowel of the infinitive (parlate, prendete, dormite).

A few meanings to remember

  • vivere and abitare: Vivo a Parigi = Abito a Parigi (I live in Paris).
  • sentire means to hear, but also to feel or to smell: Sento la musica (I hear the music).
  • chiedere = to ask, rispondere = to answer, credere = to believe.

At the café, among friends: Offro io! It's on me!

{"lessons": ["

The unit's verbs at a glance

Everything you've seen fits in this table: two irregular verbs and one model for each regular group.

essereavereparlareprenderedormirecapire
iosonohoparloprendodormocapisco
tuseihaiparliprendidormicapisci
lui / leièhaparlaprendedormecapisce
noisiamoabbiamoparliamoprendiamodormiamocapiamo
voisieteaveteparlateprendetedormitecapite
lorosonohannoparlanoprendonodormonocapiscono

Good news: in every group, io ends in -o, tu in -i and noi in -iamo.

Since the verb already tells you who's speaking, Italian drops the subject: Sono francese (I'm French), Abito a Parigi (I live in Paris). Careful: sono is used for both io and loro — the context decides.

The unit's traps

  • è with an accent = \"is\"; e without an accent = \"and\". Laura è di Napoli e abita a Roma.
  • ha, hanno are written with an h, which is not pronounced: Marco ha trent'anni.
  • cerchi, paghi: add an h to keep the hard sound of c and g.
  • capisco, capisci, capisce, capiscono take -isc-, but capiamo and capite don't.
", "

Questions for getting to know someone

In Italian, a question is built just like a statement: no inversion and no \"do\" — the intonation goes up. \"Do you speak Italian?\" = Parli italiano?

QuestionAnswerIn English
Come ti chiami?Mi chiamo Claire.What's your name?
Di dove sei?Sono di Lione.Where are you from?
Dove abiti?Abito a Milano.Where do you live?
Che lavoro fai?Sono infermiera.What do you do for a living?
Quanti anni hai?Ho trent'anni.How old are you?
Perché studi l'italiano?Perché ho un'amica a Roma.Why are you studying Italian?
  • Di dove sei? asks about origin: you answer with di (Sono di Lione). For the city where you live, it's a: Abito a Milano.
  • For jobs, no article, unlike English \"a\": Sono infermiera (I'm a nurse), Sono cuoco (I'm a cook).
  • Perché means both \"why\" and \"because\".
  • Quanti agrees with the noun: quanti fratelli, quante sorelle.

At a party among friends, Italians switch to the informal tu right away. Go for it with a smile: Ciao! Piacere!

{"lessons": ["

Mi alzo: reflexive verbs

Italian adds a small pronoun where English usually doesn't. \"I get up\" is mi alzo (literally \"I raise myself\"): a little pronoun before the verb, then the verb conjugated the way you already know (alzare → alzo, vestire → vesto).

alzarsi (to get up)vestirsi (to get dressed)
iomi alzomi vesto
tuti alziti vesti
lui, leisi alzasi veste
noici alziamoci vestiamo
voivi alzatevi vestite
lorosi alzanosi vestono

What to watch out for:

  • the pronoun is mi, ti, si, and it goes before the conjugated verb; the subject is usually left out: mi alzo is enough;
  • we → ci, you (plural) → vi;
  • si is used for he, she and also for they: si alza, si alzano;
  • in the infinitive, the pronoun is attached to the end, replacing the final -e: alzare → alzarsi = to get up, svegliarsi = to wake up.

You already know one: Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Anna. That's the verb chiamarsi (literally \"to call oneself\").

Non mi sveglio presto.I don't wake up early.

Non goes before the pronoun: non mi alzo = I don't get up. And Italian says mi lavo i denti (I brush my teeth, literally \"I wash myself the teeth\"): the article, not a possessive like \"my\".

", "

Che ore sono? Telling time

To ask the time: Che ore sono? (you'll also hear Che ora è?). To answer, Italian says \"they are the eight\": sono le otto. The word ore (hours) is understood: you don't say it.

123456
unoduetrequattrocinquesei
789101112
setteottonovedieciundicidodici
It's…In Italian
8:00Sono le otto.
8:10Sono le otto e dieci.
8:15Sono le otto e un quarto.
8:30Sono le otto e mezza (you'll also hear e mezzo).
8:45Sono le nove meno un quarto.
1:00È l'una.
12:00 noonÈ mezzogiorno.
12:00 midnightÈ mezzanotte.

The trap: one o'clock, noon and midnight are singular (è l'una, è mezzogiorno). All the other hours are plural (sono le due, sono le sette).

At what time?

A che ora…? = at what time? In the answer, a merges with the article of the hour: alle sette, all'una. But noon and midnight have no article: a mezzogiorno, a mezzanotte.

A che ora ti alzi? — Mi alzo alle sette e un quarto.What time do you get up? — I get up at a quarter past seven.

For the parts of the day: la mattina (the morning), il pomeriggio (the afternoon), la sera (the evening), la notte (the night). To be precise about a time: le otto di sera, eight in the evening (8 p.m.).

{"lessons": ["

The adjective agrees

In English, an adjective never changes. In Italian, it agrees in gender and number with the noun. There are two families.

masc. sing.fem. sing.masc. pl.fem. pl.
in -otranquillotranquillatranquillitranquille
in -egrandegrandegrandigrandi

The -o family: four forms, like the nouns libro / libri and casa / case.

The -e family: only two forms, -e in the singular and -i in the plural, for masculine and feminine alike. The adjective doesn't change for the feminine.

un quartiere tranquillo, una strada tranquillaa quiet neighborhood, a quiet street
i vicini gentili, le stanze grandithe kind neighbors, the big rooms

The trap: never an -s in the plural: le stanze grandi, not \"grandes\". And the noun and the adjective don't always have the same ending: il quartiere tranquillo, la stanza grande.

A masculine noun and a feminine noun together: the adjective goes in the masculine plural.

La cucina e il bagno sono nuovi.The kitchen and the bathroom are new. (In Italian, bagno is masculine.)
", "

Before or after the noun?

In Italian, the adjective usually goes after the noun — the opposite of English.

un appartamento luminoso, una strada rumorosaa bright apartment, a noisy street

Always after: colors (un balcone verde) and nationalities (un vicino francese). Long adjectives also almost always go after.

A few short, very common adjectives can also go before, as in English: buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio. Both orders are correct: una casa piccola or una piccola casa. Bello changes form before a noun: for now, use it after essere (la casa è bella).

Buono before the noun

After the noun, buono is regular. Before a masculine singular noun, it loses its -o, exactly the way uno becomes un.

After the nounBefore the noun
un vino buonoun buon vino
un ristorante buonoun buon ristorante
una pizza buonauna buona pizza

If you're not sure, put the adjective after the noun: it's almost always correct.

", "

Molto: \"very\" or \"a lot of\"?

English uses different words here (very, a lot, many, much). Molto covers them all, but it behaves in two different ways.

UseMeaningAgreementExample
molto + adjectiveveryinvariableLe stanze sono molto grandi.
verb + moltoa lotinvariablePaolo lavora molto.
molto + nouna lot of, many, muchagrees with the nounmolto traffico, molta luce, molti negozi, molte finestre

Before a noun, no \"of\": molti negozi = a lot of stores. Don't say \"molto di negozi\".

La casa è molto bella e ha molte finestre.The house is very beautiful and it has a lot of windows.

The trick: if you'd translate it as \"very\" or as \"a lot\" on its own, molto doesn't change. If you'd translate it as \"a lot of\", \"many\" or \"much\", it agrees with the noun that follows.

{"lessons": ["

Numbers from 0 to 1000

In English, 13 to 19 all end in \"-teen\". Italian works differently: 11 to 16 form one family (ending in -dici), then 17, 18 and 19 start with \"ten\" (dici-): diciassette, diciotto, diciannove.

NumberItalianNumberItalian
0zero11undici
1uno12dodici
2due13tredici
3tre14quattordici
4quattro15quindici
5cinque16sedici
6sei17diciassette
7sette18diciotto
8otto19diciannove
9nove20venti
10dieci

The tens

30 trenta · 40 quaranta · 50 cinquanta · 60 sessanta · 70 settanta · 80 ottanta · 90 novanta

Watch out for the look-alikes: sei (6) and sette (7), sessanta (60) and settanta (70). Say them out loud until they sound clearly different to you.

Building numbers: one word, never \"e\"

You stick the ten and the unit together, with no hyphen: venti + due = ventidue. Never say \"venti e uno\": 21 is ventuno. Two rules:

  • Before uno and otto, the ten loses its final vowel: ventuno, ventotto, trentotto, ottantuno.
  • Tre at the end of a number takes an accent: ventitré, trentatré.

Cento and mille

Unlike English \"one hundred\" and \"one thousand\", you don't put \"one\" in front: cento (100), mille (1000). Hundreds are written as one block: duecento, trecento, centoventi (120), trecentocinquanta (350). Cento doesn't change, but mille becomes mila in the plural: duemila, tremila.

La bicicletta costa trecentocinquanta euro.The bike costs three hundred fifty euros.
", "

Days, months and dates

ItalianEnglish
lunedìMonday
martedìTuesday
mercoledìWednesday
giovedìThursday
venerdìFriday
sabatoSaturday
domenicaSunday

Unlike English, the days are written with a lowercase letter. They are masculine, except one: la domenica. The days ending in -dì have an accent on the last syllable.

Lunedì or il lunedì?

ItalianMeaning
Lunedì lavoro a casa.That Monday, just once.
Il lunedì lavoro a casa.On Mondays, every Monday.
La domenica pranzo con i nonni.On Sundays, every Sunday.

English makes the same distinction with \"on Monday\" / \"on Mondays\". The only trap: with domenica, the article is feminine.

Months and dates

gennaio, febbraio, marzo, aprile, maggio, giugno, luglio, agosto, settembre, ottobre, novembre, dicembre: lowercase too, unlike English.

A date is built with il + number + month, day first: il tre giugno (June 3), il venti luglio (July 20). No \"of\" and no \"-th\". Two special cases:

  • The 1st uses the ordinal, like \"the first\": il primo maggio.
  • Before a vowel, il becomes l': l'otto marzo, l'undici settembre.
Che giorno è oggi? Oggi è il diciassette ottobre duemilaventisei.What's the date today? Today is October 17, 2026.
", "

Age and prices

Age: with avere, not \"to be\"

Quanti anni hai? Ho trentadue anni.How old are you? I'm thirty-two. (Literally: how many years do you have? I have thirty-two years.)

Quanti agrees with anni (masculine plural). For someone else: Quanti anni ha Marco?

Prices: the verb agrees with what costs

One thingSeveral things
Quanto costa il libro?Quanto costano le scarpe?
Costa dodici euro.Costano novantotto euro.

Euro doesn't change in the plural: un euro, dieci euro (never \"euros\"). For cents, you simply say tre euro e cinquanta (€3.50).

For the total: Quant'è? (How much is it?) As soon as it's more than one euro, the answer is plural: Sono quaranta euro.

The trap: saying \"quanto costa le scarpe\". Look at the noun: singular, costa; plural, costano.

{"lessons": ["

Always, often, sometimes

To say how often you do something, Italian has a handful of simple words and phrases.

ItalianEnglish
semprealways
spessooften
di solitousually
qualche voltasometimes
raramenterarely
non... mainever
ogni giorno / tutti i giornieach day / every day
una volta alla settimanaonce a week
due volte al mesetwice a month

Rule: short adverbs (sempre, spesso, mai) go right after the conjugated verb — not before it as in English (\"I often read\").

Leggo spesso il giornale.I often read the newspaper.
Mi alzo sempre alle sette.I always get up at seven.

With a reflexive verb, nothing can slip in between mi and the verb: the adverb comes after (mi alzo sempre).

Longer expressions (di solito, qualche volta, ogni giorno, una volta alla settimana) go at the beginning or the end of the sentence.

Di solito mi sveglio alle sette.I usually wake up at seven.

Two traps. Qualche and ogni are always followed by the singular: qualche volta, ogni giorno. And \"a week\" in \"twice a week\" is alla settimana: due volte alla settimana.

", "

Non... mai, non... più: the double negative

In Italian, the negative has two pieces: non before the verb, and mai (ever) or più (anymore) after it. This double negative isn't sloppy, as it would be in English: it's the correct, required form.

EnglishItalian
I never work on Sundays.Non lavoro mai la domenica.
I don't smoke anymore.Non fumo più.
I never rest.Non mi riposo mai.

Rule: with mai and più, non is required before the verb, and before the pronoun of a reflexive verb.

Non mi alzo mai alle sei.I never get up at six.

The trap for English speakers: \"never\" is a single word, so you're tempted to say \"lavoro mai\". In Italian, that's a mistake. Always say non lavoro mai.

", "

Ancora and già: still, yet, already

\"Always\" and \"still\" are two very different ideas, and Italian uses two different words for them. Don't mix them up.

MeaningEnglishItalian
every timeI always get up at seven.Mi alzo sempre alle sette.
still, right nowDo you still live in Paris?Abiti ancora a Parigi?

Rule: \"still\" is ancora; sempre means \"always, every time\".

Già means \"already\", and non... ancora means \"not yet\". Like sempre and spesso, they go after the verb.

Sono già le otto!It's already eight o'clock!
Luca dorme ancora.Luca is still sleeping.
Non sono ancora pronto.I'm not ready yet.

To answer \"not yet\", two words are enough: Sei pronto? — Non ancora.

The word order is close to English, with two differences: the negation non and the pronoun (mi, ti, si) go before the verb; sempre, spesso and mai go right after it.

Before an adjective, molto doesn't change (\"very\"). Before a noun, it agrees (\"a lot of\").

Three verbs of movement

Andare (to go), venire (to come) and uscire (to go out) are irregular, but each one follows a simple logic.

Andare mixes two stems, a bit like English \"go / went\": vado, vai, va, vanno on one side, and andiamo, andate, built on the infinitive, on the other.

Venire changes its stem: vieni, viene, but veniamo, venite. On top of that, a g appears with io and loro: vengo, vengono.

The uscire trap: when the stress falls on the beginning of the word, the u becomes e: esco, esci, esce, escono. Only noi and voi keep the u: usciamo, uscite. \"Uscono\" doesn't exist.

Stasera andiamo in pizzeria. Vieni anche tu?Tonight we're going to the pizzeria. Are you coming too?

{"lessons": ["

Four short irregular verbs

These four verbs are short, very common and irregular. Look first at voi: fate and dite are shorter than you'd expect from the infinitive (no \"facete\", no \"dicete\"), and there are a few other surprises.

faredirestaredare
iofacciodicostodo
tufaidicistaidai
lui / leifadicestadà
noifacciamodiciamostiamodiamo
voifateditestatedate
lorofannodiconostannodanno

The rule in one sentence: dire keeps the stem dic- everywhere except voi (dite), fare takes facc- only with io and noi (faccio, facciamo), and stare and dare are conjugated like very short -are verbs (with a double n in loro: stanno, danno).

Pronunciation: dico and dicono are said with a [k] sound; dici, dice, diciamo with a [ch] sound as in \"church\", because c before i or e is pronounced \"ch\". Faccio sounds like \"FAHT-cho\".

The trap: dà (he/she gives) takes an accent, so you don't confuse it with the preposition da you already know: \"Vado da Marco\" (I'm going to Marco's place), but \"Marco dà un libro a Sara\" (Marco gives Sara a book). Do, fa, sta have no accent.

", "

Everyday expressions

With fare (to do, to make), Italian often uses \"do\" where English says \"have\", \"take\" or \"go\".

ItalianEnglish
fare colazioneto have breakfast (no article)
fare la docciato take a shower
fare la spesato go grocery shopping
fare una passeggiatato take a walk
fare sportto play sports, to exercise (no article)
fare un regalo a…to give a gift to…

The weather: Italian has no word for \"it\" in front of the verb. You just say fa (literally \"makes\").

Che tempo fa? Oggi fa molto freddo.What's the weather like? Today it's very cold.

Stare: how you are, and staying

Stare is used to say how you're doing and to say that you're staying somewhere: Come stai? Sto bene. / Stasera sto a casa. To describe someone, keep essere: sono stanco (I'm tired), not \"sto stanco\".

Oggi Sara non sta bene e sta a casa.Today Sara isn't feeling well, and she's staying home.

Dire and dare: a + the person

The person always comes with a (to): dico a Marco (I tell Marco), do il numero di telefono a Giulia (I give Giulia the phone number). English can drop \"to\"; Italian never drops it. Also remember dire di sì, dire di no (to say yes, to say no) and dare una mano (to give a hand).

A ready-made phrase to learn as is: Come si dice « fork » in italiano? (How do you say \"fork\" in Italian?)

{"lessons": ["

Voglio, posso, devo

Like their English counterparts (want, can, must), these three verbs are irregular and are followed by an infinitive. You'll use them all the time: to say what you want, what you can and what you have to do.

volere (to want)potere (can, to be able)dovere (must, to have to)
iovogliopossodevo
tuvuoipuoidevi
lui, leivuolepuòdeve
noivogliamopossiamodobbiamo
voivoletepotetedovete
lorovoglionopossonodevono

The trick for voi: start from the infinitive, drop -re and add -te. vole-re → volete, pote-re → potete, dove-re → dovete. So for dovere it's dovete, with an o: “devete” and “debbete” don't exist.

The traps to watch for

  • I want = voglio, never “vuo”: Voglio andare a casa.
  • You (plural) must = dovete (with o), but you must (one friend) = devi and he must = deve (with e).
  • We must = dobbiamo, with a double b.
  • He can = può, with an accent on the o.
", "

+ infinitive, and asking politely

The second verb stays in the infinitive and follows directly, with no preposition. Careful: English says “I want to go”, but Italian has no “to” here, and you never add a or di. Only the first verb is conjugated.

Devo lavorare. Non posso venire.I have to work. I can't come.

The negation non goes before the conjugated verb, like “not” but placed in front: Non voglio uscire.

To ask for something

You want to…You say
ask for permissionPosso entrare? Posso provare? Posso andare in bagno?
ask a friend for a favorPuoi aiutare Marco?
ask a favor formally (to a stranger)Può ripetere, per favore?
invite someoneVuoi venire con noi?
say politely what you'd likeVorrei prenotare un tavolo.

To address one person formally, Italian uses the 3rd person singular (Lei): Può ripetere? means “Could you repeat that?” said to a stranger. To several people, you say potete.

Voglio un caffè is correct, but it sounds a bit blunt at the bar, just like “I want a coffee” in English. To be polite, use vorrei (I would like): Vorrei un caffè, per favore.

Sapere and conoscere in the present

Sapere (to know a fact, to know how) is irregular. Good news: it's conjugated almost like avere, which you already know. Conoscere (to know a person or place, to be familiar with) is a regular -ere verb.

sapereavereconoscere

tusaihaiconosci
lui / leisahaconosce
noisappiamoabbiamoconosciamo
voisapeteaveteconoscete
lorosannohannoconoscono

“Seppo” doesn't exist: I know is so. Also remember: sa has no accent (unlike dà), sappiamo has a double p, sanno a double n.

For conoscere, watch the pronunciation, just like leggo / leggi: before o, sc sounds like “sk” (conosco, conoscono); before i and e, it sounds like the “sh” in “ship” (conosci, conosce, conosciamo, conoscete).

", "

Sapere or conoscere?

English has just one verb, “to know”, where Italian has two. The rule of thumb: if you know a fact or know how to do something, it's sapere; if you know a person or a place (you're acquainted or familiar with it), it's conoscere.

sapereconoscere
a piece of information: so che…, so dove…, so a che ora…a person: conosco Marco
a skill + infinitive: so nuotare, sai ballare?a place: conosci Napoli?
Non lo so. (I don't know)something you're familiar with: conosco un buon ristorante
Conosco Giulia, ma non so dove abita.I know Giulia, but I don't know where she lives.
Sai suonare la chitarra?Can you play the guitar? (Do you know how to play the guitar?)

Sapere + infinitive, like volere, potere, dovere

No preposition before the infinitive (no “how to”): so cucinare, voglio sapere, dovete sapere. And don't mix up knowing how (you've learned it) and being able to (you have the opportunity). English uses “can” for both, Italian doesn't:

So guidare, ma oggi non posso.I know how to drive, but I can't today.

Non lo so = I don't know: learn it as a set phrase; the little lo means “it”, literally “I don't know it”. To address a stranger formally, use the 3rd person, as with può: Scusi, sa dov'è la farmacia?

Rimanere, salire, tenere: the -g- of vengo

You already know vengo, vieni, viene… vengono. Three very common verbs follow the same pattern.

venire (seen before)rimanere (to stay)salire (to go up)tenere (to keep)
iovengorimangosalgotengo
tuvienirimanisalitieni
lui, leivienerimanesaletiene
noiveniamorimaniamosaliamoteniamo
voiveniterimanetesalitetenete
lorovengonorimangonosalgonotengono

The rule: the -g- shows up with io and loro, and only there. The other persons are regular. Tenere is conjugated exactly like venire: tieni, tiene, with -ie-.

Stasera rimango a casa, ma i ragazzi salgono in terrazza.I'm staying home tonight, but the guys are going up to the rooftop terrace.
Tengo il posto per Anna.I'm saving the seat for Anna.

Don't let the spelling fool you: salire has nothing to do with sailing. It means to go up, and also to get on or into a vehicle. Salgo in macchina: I get in the car. Salgo le scale: I go up the stairs.

", "

Scegliere and bere

Scegliere (to choose) follows the same idea, with a little acrobatic twist: with io and loro, gl becomes lg.

scegliere (to choose)bere (to drink)
ioscelgobevo
tusceglibevi
lui, leiscegliebeve
noiscegliamobeviamo
voisceglietebevete
loroscelgonobevono

Pronunciation: scelgo sounds like “SHEL-go”, scegli like “SHEL-yee”.

Bere is simpler than it looks. The infinitive is short, but every form uses the stem bev- (from the old infinitive “bevere”) plus the regular -ere endings, like prendo, prendi. The rule: conjugate bev- like a regular verb. Forms like “bero” or “beriamo” don't exist.

Che cosa bevi? Io scelgo un analcolico.What are you drinking? I'm going for a non-alcoholic drink.

Just like English (“I drink water”), Italian usually puts nothing before the noun: bevo acqua. Non bevo vino. Bevono acqua frizzante.

{"lessons": ["

This unit's irregular verbs

No new rule today: we're bringing back all the irregular verbs from this unit. Two tricks are enough to find most of the forms.

Trick 1: the loro form is built on the io form

Take the io form and replace the final -o with -ono: you get the loro form.

ioloroverb
escoesconouscire
vengovengonovenire
vogliovoglionovolere
possopossonopotere
devodevonodovere
bevobevonobere
rimangorimangonorimanere
scelgoscelgonoscegliere

The exceptions are very short verbs: vado → vanno, faccio → fanno, sto → stanno, do → danno, so → sanno.

The trap: uscire starts with e- for io, tu, lui and loro: esco, esci, esce, escono. Only noi and voi keep the u: usciamo, uscite. “Uscono” doesn't exist.

Trick 2: the voi form is almost always regular

Drop the -re of the infinitive and add -te: that's the voi form.

infinitivevoi
doveredovete
poterepotete
volerevolete
saperesapete
farefate
uscireuscite

Only one exception in this unit: bere → bevete.

“Devete” and “debbete” don't exist: dovere → dovete. The o of the infinitive only stays with voi; elsewhere you have dev- (devo, devi, deve, devono) and noi is dobbiamo. And for sapere, the first person is so, never “seppo”.

", "

Making plans to go out

With these verbs, you already have everything you need to suggest, accept, decline and set up a meeting.

To…In ItalianIn English
suggestVuoi venire? / Perché non andiamo in centro?Do you want to come? / Why don't we go downtown?
acceptSì, d'accordo! / Buona idea!Yes, OK! / Good idea!
declineNon posso, devo lavorare.I can't, I have to work.
hesitateNon lo so.I don't know.
set the timeA che ora? Facciamo alle nove?What time? Shall we say nine?
set the placeDove ci vediamo? In piazza.Where shall we meet? In the square.

After volere, potere and dovere, the infinitive follows directly, with no “to” in between, unlike English “I want to go”: voglio andare, posso venire, devo lavorare. In the first person, it's always voglio, never “vuo”.

Ci vediamo (let's meet, see you) is a very common set phrase: ci vediamo alle nove, ci vediamo in piazza.

Where? a, in, da

Vado a casa, a teatro, in centro, in piazza, in pizzeria.I'm going home, to the theater, downtown, to the square, to the pizzeria.
Stasera andiamo da Giulia.Tonight we're going to Giulia's.

To go to someone's place (or to see a professional), it's always da, never “a”, even where English says “to the”: vado da Marco, vado dal dentista (not “al dentista”).
